en: Preface to the Newly Carved Annotated *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karma-vinaya) To begin with, the essence and nature of the equal Dharma-realm are eternally pervasive; it emerges without direction and enters without location.

What comes forth has no beginning, and what departs has no end. It is one with the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), neither existent nor empty. That which is not empty is itself true emptiness. There is no...
When evil does not cease therein, it is not that there is a "wondrous existence" (miao-you) apart from it;

when no good is not performed, this very cessation and activity is called the śīla of the fundamental nature (benxing). This is the unconditioned precept (wuwei jie). How could it be easy to speak of its possessing all myriad virtues?
From the supreme sages above down to the most dull-witted below, who among them does not possess these myriad virtues? Nevertheless...
The Buddhas realized this and opened the blissful land of nirvāṇa, while sentient beings were deluded by and attached to it, thereby creating the realm of the suffering of birth and death.
Thereupon, our Great Muni, out of compassion for their dogmatic attachments, caused them to attain liberation;

he likewise established the two precepts of abandoning evil and cultivating good. These acts of restraint and performance are called the *prātimokṣa* of formal undertaking, which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The precepts encompass all myriad practices; how could they ever be fully exhausted?

If one were to examine them closely, there is fundamentally no distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor is there any duality between the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and the formal upholding of the precepts.

Yet, why is it that the Vinaya distinguishes between the Great and Small Vehicles, and the precepts are categorized as Exoteric and Esoteric? It is said that this is because the mind differs in its coarseness or subtlety, and wisdom differs in its shallowness or depth.

Therefore, regarding what has been heard—the Great and Small Vehicles, the Exoteric and Esoteric Vinayas, their compilations, their translations from India and their transmission to China, the masters who summarized and clarified them, and the distinctions between prohibitions and permissions—the Buddhist community has deeply investigated the profound mysteries and meticulously examined the characteristics of upholding and violating the precepts.
That the study of the precepts is considered urgent is evident from their application of mind; for although it is said that the ten thousand practices are fully encompassed therein.
The two types of precepts—those of restraint and those of performance—may be called the governing principles of the immeasurable vehicles.
That which clarifies the precept of restraint is the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Jieben); that which elucidates the precept of performance is the *Karmavācanā* (Jiemobu).

Reaching the Tang dynasty, the Great Master Zhizhao of Nanshan bore the seal of the precepts revealed by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and maintained the virtuous vessel of the teachings supported by the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, widely propagating the Vinaya teachings.
Taking it upon himself as his own responsibility, he personally compiled two commentaries on the *Karmavācanā* and the *Śīlasūtra*.

Prior to this, for the sake of those studying the precepts, he composed the *Xingshichao*, which synthesizes the two types of observance (*dvi-saṃvara*), encompasses the three modes of conduct (*tri-karma*), and establishes the definitive tenets of his own school based on the great achievement of the three sections.
Later, during the Song dynasty, the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master Lingzhi succeeded to his lineage, researching and investigating its depths with such devotion that he produced detailed records.
To have this great compendium explained for the sake of later students is surely more than merely filling a basket with gold;
it is like water and fire to human beings—essential tools that cannot be dispensed with for even a single day. It is the same with the three versions of the Vinaya:
those who uphold the precepts must not be parted from them for even a moment. Regarding the transmission of the Vinaya in our own dynasty, let us investigate its original foundations.

Then, at the request of the Great Master Hōzō of Tientai Shengbao Monastery—the Dharma-grandson of the Dragon-Rising [Kaiyuan] era—and the Great Vinaya Master Jianzhen, who arrived for a visit, Emperor Shōmu was greatly pleased and ordered the construction of a ritual platform before the Vairocana Hall.
Thereupon, the Emperor, the Retired Emperor, the Crown Prince, and others successively received the Bodhisattva precepts; subsequently, the Precept Platform was moved to the Great [Hall].

To the west of the Hall, the Precept Platform Courtyard (Jie Tan Yuan) was constructed; those holding various offices for the transmission of the precepts were all appointed by authentic masters and bestowed with the title of Great Master (Daheshang).

From that time, the practice of receiving the Dharma through the *karmavācanā* ritual was established, so that monastics from throughout the world flocked to this capital like the hundred rivers pouring into the great ocean.
The Great Master presided over the administration of the Precept Platform.
The monk Roku-sōza Kuga retired to Zōdai-ji Temple.
Thereafter, Seppō Daishi [Kōbō Daishi] revived the Dharma at Senyū-ji, and Seidai-kōshō Bosatsu [Kūkai] took up the precepts, which flourished throughout the land.
Later, Ritsu-shi Makishō Meinin arose; the Makishō Vinaya tradition branched into two schools: the Shinryū school was located south of Senyū-ji, and—

The Blue Dragon (Qinglong) was originally at Heyang; now its branches have been unified, and these three monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma*) for the study and exposition of the Vinaya truly do not disgrace their predecessors.

Within the Shenfeng Gate resides the Venerable Dharma Master Chanlong, who is single-minded and tireless in his practice. Like a polished pearl or the full moon, he is renowned in the world for his clear observance of the precepts, and those seeking refuge flock to him by the day.
Recently, one came and said to me: "That which is studied in the School of the Patriarchs (*zongmen*) is threefold..."

Each fascicle of this work contains three types of topical outlines (kōbun): the general, the specific, and the sequential. For those who have only recently begun their studies, there is often the affliction of having to cross-reference these.
Previously, someone compiled these outlines from the *Shōsōji* and inserted them beneath the main text, arranging the topical divisions above it;
this was truly sufficient to remedy that affliction. Although I am not gifted, I have devoted myself to this task and have likewise produced a commentary on one fascicle.
As I was about to fulfill my commitment to carve the woodblocks for its wide distribution far and near, I hoped that you, Master, would assist me with a preface.
I replied to him, saying: "By nature, I am utterly devoid of literary talent; how could I dare accept such a request? Although he pressed me repeatedly, I humbly reflected upon myself:

having recently taken up residence at the Precept Platform, my original vow lies in the promotion of the Vinaya. How could I avoid the clumsiness of my words? It is simply that I do not wish to further propagate this [work].
I have skillfully composed this preface at the beginning of the scroll to briefly praise his meritorious achievements.
Written on the day of the Buddha’s Joy (Buddha-ānanda), during the month of Phālguna in the year of the *Chongguang* cycle and the *Duiyuanxian* branch, in the sixteenth year of the Kenpō era.
Written respectfully by the Elder Bhikṣu Huiguang, Abbot of the Great Monastery’s Precept Platform in the East of the City, for this woodblock edition of the *Commentary on the Karmavācanā*.
I have heard that the Piṭaka of Vinaya is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma; only when the Piṭaka of Vinaya abides does the Buddha-dharma truly endure.

Abiding in this, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) takes as its primary purpose the production of good and the cessation of evil, while the *prātimokṣa* (liberation) takes as its foundation the severing of delusions and the realization of principle.
Thus, among the means for producing good, none is greater than receiving the vows; among the means for ceasing evil, none is more exalted than the repentance of grave offenses.
How magnificent is the virtue of the *karmavācanā*! It is surely through the practice of it—whether by those in the past, future, or present—that [these goals are achieved].
The stage of realized awakening may be called a ship for crossing the ocean or a staircase for ascending a tower.
Indeed, since the Sun of the Buddha set in the West and the Vinaya gradually spread to the East, the time has come for the opportune moment to be fulfilled;

thus, our Patriarch, having manifested as an emanation of the Tathāgata, appeared in this land of China (Chixian), composed commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Śīla-karma-vastu*, and authored the *Jiaojie qing* [Treatise on the Lightness of Instruction].

The gravity of his ritual protocols reflects upon previous generations; thus, the Dharma-cloud is once again spread across Zhendan (China), and the jade-hair radiance shines anew in the Eastern Realm.
Therefore, a monk from India who had attained the third fruit of the path praised him, saying:

"Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, among those who have arisen to promote the Vinaya while the Semblance Dharma remains in the world, you alone are the one. Indeed, throughout the realm under heaven, there must not be a lack of such a person.

This master [Yuanzhao] held that throughout the realm, this book must not be absent. Hereafter, for those who engage in the matters of conduct, movement, and action, how could they not exert themselves?
My senior disciple, Vinaya Master Daci, personally received these secret instructions from him and has solemnly transmitted and upheld them.
I have now composed this sub-commentary (*chao*) based on what the Patriarch [Yuanzhao] once revealed.

The *Kī* (Commentary) was intended to point toward the moon beyond the finger; although its name is renowned in the world, its language is plain while its meaning is profound, making it difficult to comprehend.
Consequently, great Vinaya masters such as Tansheng and Daorong vied with one another to compose commentaries, resulting in as many as sixty different works.

Yet these all rely on diffuse citations and redundant phrasing, occasionally even conflating "yu" and "lu" (mistaking one character for another), and none have ever succeeded in explaining the essential core of the doctrine.
When selecting those words that reach the ultimate and exhaust the principle, I have taken "Huizheng" as the foremost; yet once the "Dazhi" appeared, I discarded it and did not adopt it.
This was because I deeply lamented that the practice of the Way remained hidden and grieved that those lost on their path had missed the true direction.

I did not wish to vainly construct flowery rhetoric to needlessly fill silk volumes, but rather desired to proclaim the correct principles of what is maintained and what is transgressed, and to skillfully lay out the tracks of the Eightfold Path.

Shi De resolved the most critical points and cleared away all obstructions; with a single sweep of his jade whisk, he first refuted the *Huizheng* [commentary], and the rest submitted before his reputation like soldiers facing the wind.
He was truly the preeminent leader among the various commentators. However, regarding the two commentaries on the *Śīla* and *Karma*, few have recorded them;
only Master Yun, though he compiled a record for them, provided convoluted proofs and forced citations, recklessly displaying the contents of his own breast.
His intentions were contrary to his actions, for he was a man of hidden intent. He possessed only the records of the present; his words were few, yet their purport was profound.

Not a single phrase or solitary character ever lacked a source. His purpose was solely to glorify his own compositions, and the benefit derived from these writings is truly great, sufficient to serve as a mirror for future generations.
This is precisely how Master Zhi rendered service to the two principles of "stopping" and "creating," thereby manifesting the *Vibhāṣā*.
As for Master Niyu, his merit is not easily described; what he esteemed was only the *Sūtra*, and what he treasured was only the *Record*.
There has never been one who could penetrate the profundities of cessation and activity while abandoning these two. How is it that those who read them fail to observe this?
I privately believe that as for the three versions existing in separate volumes, they were difficult to examine at will because one had to search right and left to find them. Therefore...
Now, filled with solemn resolve, I have sought to compile these commentaries and records so that students may obtain them as needed.
This is my humble intention to revive the correct principles of the True Dharma, providing a small measure of benefit for those—whether monks or nuns—who are dedicated to the study of the Vinaya.
I have thus engraved them upon woodblocks to disseminate them throughout the world, and herein I record their origins.

The *saṃgha* takes the multitude as its name, and the multitude takes harmony as its meaning. It is truly because emotions arise that nature becomes obscured, and because conduct diverges that affairs fall into discord;
thus, people follow the current without knowing how to investigate the root. This is why they return to the lineage of a single teacher and equalize their deportment with that of the Three Sages.
As for their virtue, their precepts, views, and benefits are made uniform; as for their application, it extends to body, speech, and mind.

Once disputes and conflicts have ceased and my own delusions are thus leveled, it will be possible for the innate nature (*xing*) to manifest, for emotions (*qing*) to revert to their source, and for the flow [of existence] to return to its origin.
Now, when Yin and Yang nourish all things, they do not succeed without this; when rites and music govern the people, they do not establish the four classes of society without this.
What is called "the timing of Heaven and the advantages of the land are not as good as human harmony" is the Way of the former kings.

To employ this as a source of beauty is truly sublime; how much more so when it manifests the Buddha’s transformation, establishes the principles of the Sangha, provides the conditions for extinguishing evil and generating good, and opens the path for transcending the mundane and attaining sainthood. Only this supreme Dharma possesses such great merit.

Since the radiance of the jade-hair [Buddha] faded in Western India and the essence of the palm-leaf scriptures flowed eastward to China, the subtle words have nearly vanished while heterodox compilations have flourished in abundance.
Relying upon my holy teacher, who took pity on these common folk and, knowing the time was ripe, compiled the essential points into eight chapters to form this text;

he sought out the hidden and probed the profound, composing this commentary to elucidate the four conditions. Having been humbly graced by his slight virtue, I have received this transmission of the sound. Exhausting my thoughts to investigate its subtle mechanisms, how could it be merely like the three-fold breaking of the bamboo slips?
As I record what I have heard as it comes to me, I dare to follow the four methods of seeking according to the seal of Master Mo, hoping that—

To bestow ample benefits upon future generations is surely to reflect glory back upon preceding eras. May the ocean of the Sangha return to the single flavor, and may the ancestral lamp shine its light throughout infinite kalpas.
Even as the kalpa-stone may be worn away, how can my aspirations ever be exhausted? Exhort those who study hereafter to persevere without indolence in the propagation of this teaching.

Preface to the *Sifenlü Shanchu Suji Jiemeng* (Abridged and Supplemented *Karmavācanā* According to Capacity) of the Dharmaguptaka School, composed by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Chongyi Temple in the Capital of Tang.

Originally, when the Great Hero governed the universe, how could he have intended to rescue and deliver only a single person? When the Great Teaching met its destined era, it was universally directed toward manifesting [the truth] for all.

The single principle is simply this: because sentient beings are attached to desire, and the root of desire is what is called the "self-centered mind," one can reveal the method for calming the mind according to their inclinations.
Thus, the mind is the root from which desire arises; to extinguish desire, one must necessarily calm the mind. Calming the mind fundamentally depends upon clear wisdom (*prajñā*).

The arising of wisdom relies upon the development of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the efficacy of developing concentration is not propagated without the power of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Therefore, one must especially revere the precepts; as a sutra says: "The precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed bodhi; one should single-mindedly maintain pure precepts.
Regarding the mind that maintains the precepts, there are essentially two paths: *zhichi* (maintaining by cessation), for which the root precepts are the primary standard;

and *zuochi* (maintaining by action), for which the *karmavācanā* rites constitute the major categories. Those who follow later and those who practice before have both taken this Dharma as their sublime essence. Thus it is said.
The Vinaya states: "If one does not recite the precepts and the *karmavācanā*, one shall not be separated from one's reliance [on a teacher] for as long as life lasts.

When the moon of self-insight set in the west and the water of the Dharma flowed eastward, the times encompassed both the Semblance and True Dharma eras, and the people were characterized by varying degrees of purity and impurity. Initially, there was the distinction between the two schools and the five schools;

in the middle period, there arose the divisions of the eighteen schools and the five hundred schools; and in the final age, various factions rose up against one another, each vying to lead the way, with some people following them.

The Dharma of dependent origination is without decline; thus, the Way is initiated through faith, yet its propagation depends upon man. When people are on the verge of perishing, how can the Dharma remain clear and correct?
Consequently, the sacred teachings of the *karmavācanā* have endured from antiquity to the present, gradually increasing in complexity until they merely fill the scrolls.

Yet when one examines their actual records, most are merely summaries of prior oral traditions; when scrutinizing their fundamental lineages, they lack any original basis, being instead fabricated according to the individual teacher’s own mind.
The Dharma is not something that can be practiced through mere superficial study; yet those who recite it are exceedingly numerous in their contempt for the holy words.

Their every movement is ensnared by the net of formalism, as they all strive for views of novelty and conformity, vying with one another in the delusion of grasping at right and wrong. They do not contemplate returning to the source, but instead further increase their ignorance and entanglement, causing the True Dharma to gradually sink into the earth along with the times.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "If one performs a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) in a manner that does not accord with the method of the *jñapti* (motion)," [it is invalid].
To perform a *karmavācanā* by means of a mere motion (*jñapti*) rather than the formal *karmavācanā* procedure will cause the True Dharma to perish rapidly;
one should therefore follow the wording precisely without adding or subtracting anything that would contravene the Dharma and the Vinaya. One should train in this way with compassionate instruction.

If such [errors] were to occur, it would be difficult to rectify them. Previously, while at the various passes and the capital region, I compiled the *Xing-shi-chao*, in which the various categories and miscellaneous characteristics were fully set forth.

However, because the demands of administrative duties and the constant pursuit of understanding are difficult to master, I have briefly cited the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) as a single category and provided a distinct title for its appraisal.

As for the detailed discernment of income and expenditure, or the rise and fall, right and wrong, these are clarified in that commentary (*chao*). This work merely applies the Dharma to specific matters;

those who cite evidence for its application in practice will find it within this volume. Nevertheless, since the Vinaya Piṭaka is incomplete and its meanings require supplementation, [I have provided this].

This work synthesizes the various sections and extracts the essential texts; it is intended so that where both [traditions] lack a particular point, the principle may be understood and the precedents established.

Each chapter is clearly arranged for practical convenience, differing from the ancient records. Although the *Karmavācanā* (Ritual Procedures) are numerous, they are essentially divided into eight types, beginning with the "mental recitation" (*manasikāra*) and ending with the "fourfold proclamation" (*jñapti-caturtha*).
Each possesses its own efficacy in accomplishing the rite; therefore, the Vinaya generally designates them by a single title. I shall now proceed to discuss them.
At this time, I have gathered and compiled those points that are essential and significant into ten chapters; their meaning is intended to apply to all seven classes of practitioners.
May this be transmitted today to the various masters of learning, serving as a constant guide for their own practice.

Regarding the practice of the Dharma-path, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ratnāvatī: "One does not abandon old friends, recognizes kindness and repays it,
has compassion for all beings, practices patience, gives what is difficult to give, protects the precepts with a compassionate heart,
contemplates the meaning of the good, upholds the True Dharma, well-protects sentient beings, purifies body, speech, and mind, and makes one's conduct pure, even unto diligence."
Cultivating the six *pāramitās*, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the eightfold noble path—this is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma-practice (*dharmacaryā*).
The *Mahā-śīla-varga* (Great Chapter on Precepts) states: "During the first and last watches of the night, one should exert oneself in wakefulness;
whether walking or sitting during the day, one should always maintain a single-minded focus to remove all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). This is what the Sūtra refers to as the Dharma.
The aim of practice lies in cultivating the Vinaya precepts while constantly maintaining a single-minded focus on mindfulness. If one does not embody this principle, one loses the essential core;
though one may benefit others, it will be without merit, resulting ultimately in a mere superficial discourse. Therefore, it is said: "If one does not examine this," and so forth.
One should further know that this present commentary is specifically intended for those who engage in cultivation, lecturing, and discussion; do not forget this intent.

Because this work corrects the excesses and omissions of those [other versions], it is titled *Shānbǔ* (刪補, Revised and Supplemented). Because it addresses their hidden deficiencies, it is so called.
The term *karmavācanā* (Skt. is translated into Chinese as "karma" (*ye*). Whatever it may apply to, there is nothing that it does not successfully accomplish and save.

Thus, summarizing what is commonly observed: the movement [of the teaching] is itself time; within the first millennium of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was divided into five schools.

Therefore, it is said that in the initial stage, the title of the Vinaya consists of "severed chapters" (*duànzhāng*). This means that the transmitted text is divided into four parts before the work as a whole is completed;

each point at which the discourse concludes is established as a single section, hence the term "severed chapter. The character "severed" (*duàn*) is pronounced with an upper tone (*shàngshēng*) when referring to the practice of the path.
The term "explanatory" (*xuán*) refers to the specific terminology used here that distinguishes it from other collections; thus, it is called the "Explanatory Basis.
In the original title, the phrase "in contrast to those" refers to the ancient versions. The meaning of their being more extensive or concise has been seen in the preceding text.

Regarding the "hidden practices," these refer to those not currently in practice at the time, such as the two *mahā*, three *mahā*, the minor admonitions, the methods for governance, and the heavy rules for repentance; these were all fully set forth in the ancient versions, whereas the current version retains them only partially.
Because it concerns what is currently required for practice, it is said to be "according to capacity" (*yathā-vainayika*). "Capacity" (*jī*) refers here to the trigger of a crossbow;

this metaphor signifies its essential nature. *Karma* is translated as "action" (*ye*). The details are fully distinguished below in the text. Being applied to accomplish matters and provide salvation is precisely the meaning of "action.

The principle is profound and subtle; this pivotal essence of our school is briefly indicated here to awaken those who are still ignorant.

Now, if one understands that all phenomena abide eternally, one realizes that the true and the false share a common source. Because skillful means are applied according to what is appropriate, it is taught that the false arises from the true.
The ultimate truth is fundamentally quiescent, pure, and serene; yet, failing to maintain its own nature, it is stirred by conditions. This stirring is precisely the mark of karma.

When movement continues without ceasing, it becomes intensely manifest as the coarse and apparent arising of transformation within the world of sentient beings and their lands, encompassing all phenomena of cause and effect for both the ordinary and the sagely.
This is the differentiation of karma through the correlation of principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*). Furthermore, from within a single mind, various karmas branch out:
the six classes of ordinary beings are defiled, while the four types of noble ones are pure; these arise because sentient beings are deluded regarding the fundamental principle.
To follow delusion and give rise to delusive karma, thereby transmigrating through the six realms, constitutes defilement (*saṃkleśa*).

To be able to awaken, turn back from delusion to return to the True, cultivate the path of liberation, and arise beyond the two realms of existence—this is termed "untainted karma" (*anāsrava-karma*) for those of the Two Vehicles, and "karma of great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā-karma*) for Bodhisattvas and Buddhas.
When viewed in contrast to the six ordinary classes of beings, these are collectively termed "pure. This is an analysis based on the distinction between the defiled and the pure.

This clarifies the nature of karma. Furthermore, the afflictions of the three realms—namely, the views, the thoughts, and ignorance—are all produced by karma and possess no separate substantial entity.
As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra states: "Karma produces afflictions; afflictions produce karma. All retributive suffering within the three realms and the six paths of existence is a repayment for past karma.
Since karma produces retribution and the substance of that retribution is itself karma, one knows that karma accumulates to form [the world].
Delusion, karma, and the transformation into retribution constitute the three paths of cyclic existence; there is nothing therein that is not karma. This explains karma by way of the three paths.
Furthermore, karma arises from the mind, and the mind is produced in accordance with objects. Since objects are infinite, karma is likewise manifold.
Although the conditions for its production are numerous, the actual agents are only three: body, speech, and mind. Of these, the mental constitutes the essence of karma; the mind itself is karma.

As soon as one thinks, the mind acts; thus, all characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome karma are created by the mind. This explains karma in terms of the relationship between the mind and its objects.
Furthermore, the ten unwholesome actions arising from the three poisons constitute the karma for the three miserable realms;

flattery, deceit, and ferocity constitute the karma for the *asuras*; returning to the precepts and practicing giving constitute the karma for humans and devas; and the eightfold [path] free from outflows constitutes the karma for the noble ones.
The karma of the two vehicles is precisely the karma of the bodhisattvas—the myriad practices of the six pāramitās;

the unconditioned great compassion and inconceivable function are the karma of the Buddhas. As the *Praise of the Buddha* in the *Awakening of Faith* says: "The supreme karma is all-pervasive knowledge," and so forth.

While the six classes of ordinary beings are deluded regarding karma and the three sages cultivate karma, it is only the Buddha who realizes karma. Thus, one knows that karma universally encompasses all.
Regarding the ten realms, some say three are evil and three are good; others say four are evil and humans and devas are good;

still others say the six ordinary beings are evil and the four noble ones are good. These are explanations of karma in terms of cause and effect. Furthermore, among the five aggregates, one aggregate is form (*rūpa*) and four aggregates are mind-consciousness;
of these, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*saṃskāra*) are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), flowing into the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*).
The mind itself constitutes good and evil; based on this mental activity, it is further divided into the three natures. Good and evil are as described above. As for indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) karma:
that which is performed by one who is insane, mentally deranged, asleep, or acting through error or delusion is all indeterminate karma.

While the two types of karma—good and evil—generate and elicit retribution, indeterminate karma cannot generate such retribution. Some say it does not generate a collective retribution, yet it still generates [individual] results.

Retribution for distinct actions is as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, such as the karma created in dreams—namely, the five types of offenses (*pañca-gilā*) incurred in a dream—and other similar cases;

these clarify karma according to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the teachings within the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, that which is expounded consists solely of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*);
one should know that these three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) are the foundation of practice. Practice arises from the teachings.

This means that karma is what defines the formation of practice, and this constitutes the teaching; thus, all the Buddha-dharma of the three periods and ten directions is nothing other than the definition of karma.

This explains karma by way of the teachings and practices. Furthermore, the ten wholesome paths, the five stabilizing meditations, the four great vows, the six perfections, and all contemplative practices are the karma of the transformative teachings (*vaipulya*).
All prohibitions and permissions, as well as the gravity of offenses, as defined in the Vinaya, are the karma of the disciplinary teachings (*vinaya*).

The *Zang* (Treasury) compendium establishes the Vinaya teachings as the basis for transformation according to the principle of reality (*li*). Within this principle, there are both conformity and contrariety; regarding the Vinaya teachings themselves, there is observance and violation.

This distinguishes karmic action (*karman*) by way of transformation and regulation. Furthermore, summarizing the three distinct schools within the entirety of the Buddha’s transformation, the first clarifies the essence of the undertaken and subsequent manifest and unmanifest [karma], as detailed in the "Chapter on the Threefold Distinction of the Essence of Precept-Karma. The second concerns the practice of following [the precepts].

Regarding the basis for the accomplishment of upholding or violating precepts, all schools—whether concerning movement, form, or the provisional teachings—regard the gravity of the conditions as their standard;

in the Perfect Teaching, even a fleeting thought is sufficient. Whether upholding or violating, both are measured according to these three [categories]. This explains karma in terms of the Great and Small Vehicles.

Furthermore, regarding killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and other non-virtues of body and speech, which are the roots of birth and death, one should protect the fundamental through skillful means and right mindfulness.

That which is received is called "cessation-virtue" (*śīla-karman*); the diligent application of the three karmas to give rise to virtue and to protect the community and its distinctions is called "action-virtue.
Contrary to cessation is action-evil; conversely, acting contrary to action is cessation-evil.

Thus, both cessation and action are categorized as transgressions. This explains karma by way of cessation and action. Now, the meaning of this *karmaṇa* (formal ritual) is translated as "karma"; while the name is general, its essence is specific.
Furthermore, by examining and clarifying each point through ten gates, one will achieve success in every situation when wielding authority;
thus, the primary teachings and transmissions will be thoroughly understood without any obstruction.

*Commentary on the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemó* (Exegesis on the *Sifenlü* with Supplements according to Circumstances), Fascicle One (beginning from the "Collection of the Dharma" and concluding with the "Section on the Formation of Conditions").
The titles preceding the headings in this text are the titles of the sub-commentary (*śāstra*); some manuscripts lack them due to scribal omission.
These titles must necessarily be present in the *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts) and the *Shìchão* (Excerpts on the Meaning).

The characters noted beneath the titles indicate the beginning and end of each fascicle, intended to allow the reader to first know the scope of the textual content from start to finish; they must not be removed at will.
Desiring to compose this text as an exegesis, one first opens up an understanding through thematic gateways (*arthamukha*) to deeply seek the purport of the teaching.

The underlying intent consists of resolving practical tasks (*kṛtya*), and according to these tasks, the establishment [of the doctrine] does not exceed four positions: first, the sacred Dharma, which is the teaching that performs the discernment;

second, the objective tasks, which are the matters for which the teaching is intended; third, the wielder and controller, who is the person who propagates the Dharma; and fourth, the establishment [of the doctrine].

Because it establishes the locus of the Dharma, the Vinaya manifests the full realization of the Dharma; now, in consideration of the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, it cannot be established without these four [factors].

In the first section of the introductory chapter, the initial passage sets forth the intended meaning: "creating" (*zào*) refers to the act of composing, while "opening" (*pī*) refers to the act of analyzing and deciding—that is, the definitive resolution of matters.

"Affairs" (*wù*) refers to the specific events to which the Dharma applies. Following this, the four categories are sequentially presented: namely, the Dharma, the matter (*shì*), the person (*rén*), and the location (*chù*), as well as the *karma* (formal ritual).
The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-mātṛkā* states that neither the general nor the specific rules can be established without these four; from beginning to end, the entire work does not depart from this intent.
First, the essential point is set forth here: if one looks toward the establishment of dharmas through various conditions, the sacred Dharma is its primary orthodoxy;

if one relies on the performance of rituals through the administration of the law, then the practical application of conditions is its fundamental purpose. Therefore, the following passage cites the scriptural authority.

Regarding the *vinaya* that clarifies the Dharma, this refers to the explanation within the section on the settlement of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*) concerning the requirement for various formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) to be accompanied by "presence" (*sammukha-vinaya*).
It states there are five kinds of presence. What is "presence of the Dharma" (*dharma-sammukhatā*)? That which settles a dispute through the Dharma upheld [is the answer];

here, "Dharma" refers to the formal procedure (*karman*). What is "presence of the discipline" (*vinaya-sammukhatā*)? That which settles a dispute through the discipline upheld [is the answer]; this refers to resolving a dispute in accordance with the teachings (*śāsana*). What is...?
"Those who are present and engage in dialogue regarding the dispute" refers to the evaluation of the matter under contention.

"How is it that those who should be present in the Saṃgha come, and those who should give their consent (chanda) give their consent? This means that those who might criticize do not criticize; this is the harmony of the three karmas. "How is it that the boundary (sīmā) is present?

This refers to the proclamation of the *karmavācanā* and the establishment of limits; this is the formal act (*dharmakarma*) of the boundary. Because these factors resolve the dispute, they employ the *vinaya*.

Because the *bhikṣuṇīs* now apply [these rules] to all dharmas, only four remain; the third refers to the object to which they apply, while the fifth is restricted to formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) based on the communal dharma (*saṃghadharma*).
Now, in clarifying the establishment [of these categories], it must encompass both realms; thus, that text states:
"This present dharma applies to all *karmans*. From this, we know that the five types of "present" [dharmas] therein correspond to the four positions mentioned here.
Furthermore, one should first investigate each of the four specific categories according to their meaning, and subsequently determine the boundaries of their mutual inclusion within the *Abhidharma*.

In the formal explanation of the chapters, there are two major divisions. Regarding "investigating according to the four specific categories," this refers to the detailed analysis of each of the four conditions (*pratyaya*) presented below as separate chapters.
"Mutual inclusion according to the *Abhidharma*" refers to the general discussion of these four [conditions] that follows.
This is because the subsequent text cites the following: "The mutual inclusion and exclusion of the aforementioned four conditions.

First, the exposition of the sacred Dharma—namely, the *karmavācanā* (ecclesiastical rite)—is presented briefly through four sections: first, the fundamental intent for the arising of the teaching; second, the manifestation of names and the determination of the essence;
third, the discernment of duties and the accomplishment of conditions; and fourth, the extensive clarification of non-characteristics.

Regarding the initial intent for the arising of the teachings: since the Three Jewels descended into the world, they have all cultivated the capacities of sentient beings who possess both the wholesome and the deficient.
Whatever teachings were established were none other than for the purpose of preserving the existent and extinguishing the deluded.
In the first section of the initial analysis of the intent for the arising of the teachings, the first two phrases clarify the intent for transcending the world, fully enumerating it.
Because the Three Jewels do not abandon one another and because they have manifested their response from the very beginning, it is said that [the Buddha] descended into the world.

Those who loathe the world and withdraw from secular life are called "deficient in opportunity" unless they are sincere and reverent. The latter two lines clarify the intent behind establishing the teachings;
all that has been stated encompasses the entire dispensation, and this applies equally to the Tripiṭaka in its eradication of delusions and its transcendence of the world.
Thus, while the two positions within the Buddha-dharma extend to both the monastic and the lay, it is only this Jewel of the Sangha that uniquely occupies the state of renunciation;
its manifest merit ranks above as neighboring the Supreme Sage, and its revealed virtue descends below to succor all living beings.
In the first section of the separate exposition, the first two lines provide a general summary: "Buddha-dharma" (*buddhadharma*) is used because it encompasses both the Buddha and the Dharma;

"aspiring to the Buddha and receiving the Dharma" is mentioned because one is not restricted to a single path. The subsequent lines provide a specific clarification regarding the Jewel of the Sangha: the first two lines indicate the stage, for those who enter the ocean of the Sangha must necessarily be renunciants;
the final two lines praise their virtues, as they approach the supreme sages and possess the causal seeds of the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, as in the Vinaya accounts where King Bimbisāra offered a garden to the Buddha and Mother Viśākhā offered robes to the Buddha, the Buddha in both cases exhorted them to give to the Saṃgha;
from this we know that their merit and power were equal to those of the Buddha, let alone those of the Lesser Sages (hīnayāna-āryas).

Furthermore, because they provide relief to all sentient beings, they are fields of merit for the six realms of existence. Regarding the term "all sentient beings" (qunyou): their primary retribution consists of the four modes of birth, while their secondary retribution consists of—
The three realms are opened up into nine, comprising twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
These distinctions arise solely from the vastness of the ocean of the Sangha and the diverse ranks of practice and position;

they may be distinguished by the internal and external paths, or by the routes of the mundane and the sagely, or by applying the term "Jewel" to both monastics and laypeople, or by examining the observance or violation of ritual precepts.
Next, the first two lines of the section provide a general indication: the upper line clarifies their great number, while the lower line reveals the distinctions among their practices.

Alternatively, the lower part lists four pairs in detail: 1. The pair of outer and inner: the five *sthāpanā-citta* (stabilizing minds) with their general and specific characteristics of mindfulness are called "outer ordinary monks" (*bāhyapṛthagjana-bhikṣu*);

the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and the first stage of the world are called "inner ordinary monks" (*ādhyātmikapṛthagjana-bhikṣu*). 2. The pair of ordinary and noble: [this refers to] the general category above.

The two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), together with those on the preparatory stages (*tanubhūmi*), are collectively termed "ordinary monks" (*prthagjana-bhikṣu*). From the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) up to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they are collectively termed "noble monks" (*ārya-bhikṣu*).
Their paths diverge as they set out, yet their underlying principle is the same, though the expressions differ.

Regarding the three distinctions between the monastic and the lay, that which is called the "jewel of principle" refers to the untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) from the first fruit upward; this is also termed the "Sangha of the Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-saṃgha*).

One merely takes the realization of the fruit as the criterion, regardless of outward appearance or attire; for according to the Vinaya, even laypeople who have seen the Truth enter the ocean of the Saṃgha. Thus, the distinction between the "black" (monastics) and the "white" (laypeople) applies universally.

Regarding the four pairs and eight classes, the first pair refers exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the third refers exclusively to noble ones (*ārya*); the other two apply to both. As for the four pairs, they are distinguished by the maintenance or violation of the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*)—that is, the observance or breach of the rules concerning the various categories of offenses (*āpatti-skandha*).
This constitutes the eight positions discussed above. The first is restricted to ordinary beings, and the third is restricted to noble ones. The other two apply to both.
Furthermore, the fourth [category] encompasses both ordinary beings and sages alike.
In the coordination of worldly affairs, the essential requirement is that one's sentiments and views accord with one another;

through harmony, the highest good may be attained, and through shared forbearance, even the lowest evils may be extinguished. Since this cannot be achieved without relying on vocal instruction, the Tathāgata embodied this principle.
Because it propagates the principle, the methods for governing the Saṃgha differ according to the specific circumstances of residence, yet they universally ensure that all follow the same path;
whenever the proper conditions are met, nothing fails to be accomplished.

Among the three [sections], the first phrase clarifies the essential origin of the matter, while the following reveals the necessity of harmonizing mental views—this being one of the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*).

The superior good is immediately received as full ordination (*upasampadā*), while the inferior evil is immediately repented; these two are briefly cited to encompass all other rites for generating goodness and extinguishing evil, whereby all *karmavācanā* (formal acts) are successfully established.
This is not to say that the teaching is merely provisional, but rather that harmony and patience must reside within the mind;

since they are not manifested without words, verbal instruction is required to communicate with the sentiments of the assembly. The preceding section described the conditions and opportunities, while this section correctly clarifies the regulations.
The first two phrases of the Dharma clarify the discernment of capacities; the subsequent section clarifies the method for establishing the rules and governing the Saṃgha, which is the *karmavācanā*.

Following this, the "manifestation of the conditions for success" indicates that the regulations are established according to the specific boundaries (*sīmā*) so that all may comply together without deviation.
Alternatively, the phrase "conditions such as persons and dharmas" admits of both interpretations.

Within the second section, there are again four subdivisions: first, the explanation of the title; second, the determination of its essential nature and characteristics; third, the reason for its extensive classification;
and fourth, the similarities and differences among the various schools.
First, regarding the explanation of the title:

Regarding the term *karma*: in the Central Indic original, its phonetic transcription is *jiewo* (羯磨), which is translated here as "action" (*karma*). "Action" refers to the accomplishment of prior tasks;

it necessarily entails the merit of successful fulfillment. Thus, in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, it is likewise translated as "action. When contemporary translators transmit the sounds of the scriptures, they invariably translate *karma* as "action."

The second section, titled "Explanation of Terms," begins with the first sub-section: "Explanation of the Term *Karma*. This means that what is explained below regarding the fulfillment of the purpose constitutes the *karmavācanā* (the formal act) which applies to the preceding preparatory duties (*pūrvakṛtya*).
It refers to the verbal expressions and physical postures that do not deviate from the prescribed ritual forms, and the mental state free from divergent thoughts.
Because the three types of action (*trikarma*) thus combine to produce various distinct practices, and because these result in a definitive resolution, this very method is termed *dharma*.

This is called "karma" (*karman*). "Karma" has the meaning of performing an action through construction; for instance, because the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome paths can act as causes that evoke results, they are both termed "karma.
This is a designation based on the nature of the agentive body itself. If one discusses the nature of the non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*) that is produced, it will be explained extensively later;
therefore, the citation from the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on Elucidation) provided below is exactly as cited later in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.
The present translation of the *Sūtra* refers specifically to the Patriarchs of the Tang dynasty who participated in the translation assemblies; thus, it captures the true meaning.

From antiquity to the present, there have been those who translated *karmavācanā* as "discerning matters" (*biànshì*); while this is not without its merit, they translated it based on its functional capacity.

However, the actual functions are numerous, yet essentially there are only two types. The first refers to the performance of wholesome deeds (*kuśala-karma*), such as [receiving] food, clothing, and so forth.

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) for the purification of persons (*pudgala-viśuddhi*) involves both the binding and the releasing [of prohibitions], and it arises through the practice of wholesome deeds.

Later, regarding the cessation of unwholesome matters—such as the confession of offenses, disciplinary measures, the settling of disputes, and the offering of admonitions—the name applies to both the wholesome and the unwholesome; the principle lies in the removal of faults.

All of these proceed by means of the *karmavācanā*, which is so named because its primary function is to clear away [impurities]. Furthermore, there is nothing that surpasses the reception of the precepts (*śīla-samādāna*) as the ultimate means of generating the wholesome, for this is achieved through the performance of the ritual act.

Furthermore, considering that both the motion and the formal act jointly establish the efficacy of the rite, it should properly be named a "motion-and-one-act" (*jñapti-ekakarma*).
It is said: "The *jñapti-dvitīya* (the motion followed by one announcement).

Within the *jñapti-dvitīya*, because the initial presentation of the matter refers back to what preceded it, it is difficult to respond; since responding to what follows is relatively easier, it is described as "slightly" (*shāo*).

Since "slightly" (*shāo*) is glossed as "few" (*shǎo*), the subsequent clarification of the procedure is further divided into two parts: first, the analytical demonstration, and second, the determination of the name below.

If the circumstances are grave and the proceedings are difficult to initiate—as in the case of receiving a formal confession (*poṣadha*) or the rituals for treating and expelling those subject to heavy penalties—one must first present a motion (*jñapti*) and then perform three *karmavācanās*.

Only when these measures are fulfilled can the rite be successfully accomplished; thus it is called "one motion and four *karmas*" (*jñapti-caturtha*), as the one motion and three *karmavācanās* together constitute the four.
Regarding the four types of *jñapti* (motions), citing the specific matter to reveal the dharma and determining the name are all identical to those mentioned above.

However, these three stages—when considered according to the text—are restricted; yet when judged by their meaning, they generally establish the procedure. Specifically, the *jñapti* relies on the conditions of the formal announcement (*prātimokṣa*), while the *karmavācanā* (formal act) reveals the function of the completed efficacy;
this is what constitutes the restriction. The single method of the simple *jñapti* (single motion) distinguishes the initial and final conditions of the preceding [matter].
The statement that *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) is not non-informative (*avijñapti*) refers to its general application.

Within the analysis of the general and the specific, the first part provides a general indication, while the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation. First, it clarifies the restriction of the formal procedure to a single motion; next, it clarifies the universal scope of its meaning.

Even when distinguishing the conditions for a single motion (*jñapti*), it is not limited solely to the vocal expression; how could the *karmavācanā* fail to accomplish its purpose through its expressive intent alone?

Both [the *jñapti* and the *karmavācanā*] possess dual meanings and are not restricted to either the beginning or the end; the "initial *karmavācanā*" refers precisely to the *jñaptidvitīya* and the *jñapticaturtha*.

Nevertheless, the text is divided into preceding and succeeding parts because, among the expressions of one's intent, nothing is not termed a *jñapti*, whereas the accomplishment of the function and the completion of the task depend solely upon the *karmavācanā*.
Thus, those who compiled and translated [the canon] took the underlying meaning and divided it into preceding and succeeding sections.

Regarding the arrangement of the three phases—beginning, middle, and end—the single-announcement (*ekajñapti*) comes first; although both [the *jñapti-caturtha* and the *jñapti-dvitīya*] apply in general, there is no lack of specific predominance.
According to the treatises, when the Buddha was in the world, he established the Dharma according to circumstances, so there was originally no fixed sequence of before and after.

Therefore, it is inferred that when the compilers and others performed the compilation, Upāli’s Dharma was the primary standard. It was only upon the subsequent translation and transmission by Faxian, Baoyue, and Zhu Fonian that this became clear; thus, in the Vinaya catalogues, it stands as an independent text.

The reason for placing the *jñapti* (motion) first is that regarding the two types of *karmavācanā*, the sequence of the *jñapti* and the subsequent formal acts was established by the Buddha himself from the beginning, not devised later.

If one consults the *Vinaya-mūla*, it is generally termed *karmavācanā*, as extensively listed above; however, here we rely on the specific matters at hand, according to their magnitude and difficulty.
Because they differ, the characteristics of the various categories of *dharma* (teachings) and *niśraya* (reliances) are explained in detail.

Regarding the section on "separation" (*vibhāga*), the Vinaya states that there are three types of *karmavācanā*: the single motion (*jñapti-karman*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), and the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

These are established according to their names, each having its own basis without any hierarchical distinction, as extensively listed above. This refers to the essential characteristics within the detailed exposition.
The superiority and inferiority of the three types of legal procedures explained in the preceding text are not based on the original Vinaya text; therefore, it says, "Now, according to...

Question: Regarding the mental procedure (*cittavijñapti*) and the formal procedure for the assembly (*sāṃghika-karman*), each is divided into three grades according to the matter at hand; I do not yet understand upon what basis the procedure for a pair (*dvayavijñapti*) alone is established as having only two grades.
Regarding the question of "separation and combination" within the *Liaojian*: previously, the eight categories were arranged according to the sequence of the Vinaya;

now, from among those [categories], the *zhonglan* (intermediate offenses) are extracted to form a separate category. Following this precedent, they are further divided into three, resulting in nine categories in total.

In the initial question, it is noted that while the mental and vocal offenses are treated identically for the *zhòngduìshǒu* (confession before a group), the *duìshǒu* (confession before an individual) alone differs.

Answer: Regarding the discourse on matters as a treatise, they are distinct categories of measurement; yet, if we summarize and regulate them, they generally comprise three levels. When categorized by matter, there are nine grades, and the same applies to the dharmas. How is this clarified?
For instance, within the *cetanā-dharma* (mental-recitation dharma), the lower matters it governs are already restricted to three levels, which themselves divide into three grades:
namely, the lowest-of-the-low, the middle-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low. This same principle applies to those [dharmas] governed among the *saṃgha-karma* (communal legal acts).
Regarding the superior matters, there are three grades based on the status of the officiating authority: namely, superior-inferior, superior-middling, and superior-superior.

Among the procedures performed before a counterpart (*pratimukha*), there should likewise be three grades, as explained in the context of the ritual for holding robes or the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-vyākarana*). Regarding middling matters, such as the confession and relinquishment of an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), this constitutes the middling-middling grade.
If one confesses many *sthūlātyaya* offenses before a counterpart, it may constitute the middling-superior grade; thus, they are also categorized according to their specific characteristics.

This constitutes the ninth category. Because the *stūlātyaya* (grave offense) is not expiated through confession before the Sangha, it is subsumed under the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring individual confession).
Now, according to the Vinaya, because one is permitted to repent before a small group while listening to and questioning those on the periphery, this is opened as a single distinct category.
In the answer, the first part provides a general explanation of the three stages of the "Dharma according to the object" (*vastu-anuvartana-dharma*), namely the three grades of objects.
Since each of these three grades of objects can be further divided into three, one grade is set apart from the *pratyekasammuti* (confession before another person), resulting in nine grades.

Because the Dharma categorized by object also consists of nine, it is said that they are "the same. Next, the second part specifically lists the grades of the positions; this also has three sections, the first of which clarifies...

Regarding mental reflection (*cittānuvartana*): reflecting on a single individual is the lowest of the low; reflecting on a group is the lowest of the middle; reflecting on a multitude is the lowest of the high.

Second, regarding the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) for the community (*saṃgha*): a single motion (*jñapti*) is the highest of the low; a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*) is the highest of the middle; a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*) is the highest of the high.

Third, regarding the face-to-face procedures (*pratyekamukha*), they are listed in the text as appropriate. Regarding the three grades of *sthūlātyaya*, the heavy ones are subsumed under the community procedures, while the light ones are [treated] individually.
The "returning to the middle and lower" now establishes the "middle and upper," which is strictly limited to the *pāyattika* (saṃghāvaśeṣa) offenses;

however, according to the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), it simply corresponds to the position at the head of the assembly in the *pratyekapratideśanīya* (confession before an individual). Thus, the various questions and answers arise from this.
The preceding section reconciles the "upper and lower" to resolve the intent of the previous combination; the current section clarifies the intent of the present separation.

Question: Regarding the distinction between the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) and the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), why are they divided into two separate categories rather than being treated as distinct groups?

Furthermore, in the section on "Difficult Questions," it is stated that even for minor offenses requiring confession (*deśanā*) or grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*), the rule against performing them before a small group (*pratyeka-saṃgha*) applies; since the prohibition against performing them separately from others is the same, there would logically be no reason for the procedure of forfeiture (*niḥsarga*) to differ.

Answer: According to the principle that one should not perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) before a separate group, one should first repent for the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). Regarding the three [categories], they should be returned to the middle grade;

however, because the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) applies even when facing a single person, it is called "middle-middle" for repenting the *sthūlātyaya*. It must be asked about the limits, as the principle returns to the middle-upper grade.

This is because the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that what is heavy is within the boundary (*sīmā*) and what is light is outside the boundary, and because the lower section of the *Caturvarga-vinaya* refers to a small assembly. Furthermore...

At that time, the addition of the *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena) is likewise inclusive, being identical to what was previously stated regarding the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation ceremony). Because the number of persons present varies, there are different levels [of practice].

In the response, the initial refutation sets aside the previous objection; while the confession (*pratideśanā*) is restricted to separate gatherings, the *pravāraṇā* is universally inclusive of both internal and external matters.
If one were to take [the view] that it refers to a separate assembly, it would be necessary to argue that the *zizhi* (invitation for confession) does not accord with the present intent;

therefore, that position is temporarily set aside. However, below this, the present thesis is extended to clarify the distinction between the universal and the specific regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture). First, in contrast to the *naiḥsargika*, it is shown that while the lower [category] applies universally to a single person, the middle *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) is restricted to three or two people.
This is based on the sequential classification of the grades [of offenses], and the principle is thus evident. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the first stage arises at the beginning of the section.
**The Heavy Confession of the Assembly within the Boundary (High Grade)** 1. **Initial Section:** Light offenses arising; Second Section: Heavy offenses arising.

These should be confessed before an assembly of four bhikṣus outside the boundary (*sīmā*). [Note: The "four bhikṣus" refers to the combination of both the officiant and the recipient; they must be outside the boundary because of the rule regarding the limits. This is inferred from the concern that if someone were inside the boundary, it might be considered a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*);

by extension, it is understood that if no one is present, it is also permissible within the boundary. 2. **Saṃghāvaśeṣa:** Light offenses arising. These should be confessed before a single bhikṣu (Low Grade). According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this immediately extinguishes the dispute.

Regarding the *Khandhaka*, it is stated below that "the small group" refers to two or three people. Furthermore, the subsequent section explains the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) in relation to others to clarify similarities and differences:
the preceding part clarifies the similarity based on a separate group, while the following part reveals the difference by referring to specific individuals.

As for the inclusion of the "boundary" (*sīmā*), even if there are people within the boundary, one may not perform the rite separately; however, the communal *pravāraṇā* dharma must necessarily involve both the Saṃgha and the individual.

Regarding the method for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of concealment (*steyasaṃvāsa*), it is established even if not confessed in an assembly; here, we provisionally rely on the rule that one must necessarily question a person at the boundary.

While the subsequent section appears to speak of the number of people present in a general sense, the procedure for confession is not fixed below [in the text], as it applies even to a single individual.
Thus, it is clear that the status of the person confessing the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is determined by this [rule], and therefore it is considered superior.

Question: Regarding the explanations of *pravāraṇā* (the invitation ceremony) and *niḥsargika* (formal relinquishment), it is established that these must be performed by assembling within a single boundary (*sīmā*).

However, for those who are present and available, the rule is relaxed to allow for a face-to-face procedure (*pratyekamukha*) with two or three people. How can this be considered a "middle" [category]? Even if there is no assembly, the rite should still be validly accomplished;
compared to the previous method, this principle should logically not be classified as "superior."

Regarding the first of the three difficult points: since the formal procedures (*saṃghakarma*) for the assembly should logically take precedence over those for a group of individuals (*pudgalakarma*), yet these individual procedures cannot be established as distinct from the assembly’s;

regarding the second difficult point: since the meaning of repenting a *sthūlātyaya* offense should logically occupy the middle position, because although this is a distinct procedure, it can still be established even when distinct, it may nevertheless contravene the regulations without preventing the establishment of the formal act.

Answer: If one were to judge based on the comprehensive collection of actual *tathāgatas*, it would be difficult; however, judging now by the magnitude of the matter and the frequency of the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), we determine them as being of medium or superior grade.

As it is said regarding the *pāṭimokkha* (confession) and other dharmas, even mental recollection (*manasikāra*) is permitted for the abandonment of offenses involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*); yet, through mere confrontation [with the Sangha], one becomes pure.

This is not the case for the *thullaccaya* (grave offense): confession must necessarily involve a group of people, as the offenses arise from the first two categories [of the *pātimokkha*], and the confession is divided into three spheres of objects.
If one departs from [the literal] and follows the meaning, it may be considered middling or superior.
Answer: First, the initial section provisionally grants the preceding objection; now, the following section refutes it and returns to the correct principle. This further has two parts:

first, it demonstrates that the matters established are vast and the circumstances numerous—this refers to what is stated below regarding "offenses arising in the first two chapters"—and thus the performance of the ritual procedures is rare; this refers to what is stated below.

Regarding the section on confession (*pratideśanā*), it is divided into three because the objects differ, as will be explained below through comparison. The *pravāraṇā* (invitation) allows for solitary recollection;

the forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) applies to both individual and communal confession, which clearly shows that the matter is light and repentance is easy. Conversely, according to the two principles mentioned above, if one must confess a *sthūlātyaya* offense before a group, this is already not permitted with a single person, let alone by solitary recollection.
As for the term "following the meaning" (*yì*), it does not exist in the literal text; it is established by weighing the underlying principle.
The three objects of focus correspond to the three aforementioned stages.

Question: As for the various distinctions among the three groups of nine according to the specific matters described above, what are the characteristics of the "one hundred and one *karmas*" (formal acts) transmitted from antiquity?
Next, regarding the section on the number of questions, first is the initial step that follows upon the preceding grades and positions;

second is the citation of ancient authorities to raise a doubt concerning the *Baiyi jiemu* (One Hundred and One Karmas), which is seen today within the Tripitaka as a collection compiled by former sages, hence it is called "ancient tradition."

Answer: As transmitted in ancient tradition, "one hundred" is a collective designation for the number; since each matter involves a single *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), it is called "one hundred and one.

It is not that there is no sense of distinct matters; if one examines them closely, there are instances where a single matter requires three or four [ritual acts], such as the reception of the precepts, the relinquishing of a bowl, the *kaṭhina* robe, or the distribution of the property of the deceased. Furthermore, it is also permissible to speak in terms of the majority of cases.
The Bureau states that there is not a single dharma that does not follow the performance of action to achieve its result;

all such cases are termed *karmavācanā* (ritual action). In the primary response, first relying on ancient explanations, it is said that "one hundred" refers to the matters (*vastu*) to be addressed, while "one" refers to the dharma that can address them.
Since these matters are limitless, "one hundred" is cited as a comprehensive total; since this dharma universally applies to all, "one" is cited to unify them—this is certainly not without reason.

Regarding the principle that there is a logical basis for these matters, if one examines cases such as [the ordination], it serves to preclude later doubts; for fear that one might think a single matter employs only a single ritual act, [the text] cites the case of receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) and others to explain this.

In the fourfold procedure for receiving the precepts, there is: (1) the formal motion (*jñapti*) to appoint a preceptor (*ācārya*); (2) the formal motion to summon the candidate into the assembly; (3) the formal motion to interrogate the candidate before the assembly;

and (4) the formal motion for the actual conferral of the precepts. Regarding the threefold procedure for relinquishing the alms bowl (*pātra*), there is: (1) the formal motion; (2) the announcement (*anujñā*); and (3) the formal motion for the final decision. Thus, there are four [procedures] for receiving the precepts and three for relinquishing the bowl.

1. The Single Motion for Accepting the Confession (if the distribution of bowls is not performed, this is used instead of the two methods for accepting the confession and returning the bowls). 2. The Single Motion for Distributing the Bowls. 3.

The Two-fold Motion for Guarding the Bowls (the *Jieshu* [Commentary on the Precepts], following the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, adds a two-fold motion for appointing a person to distribute the bowls). The Three Methods for the *Guṇavastu* (Virtuous Robe): 1. Appointing the Five Virtuous Ones. 2. Entrusting the Robe, both by means of a single motion and a two-fold motion.
The Three Methods for the Property of the Deceased: 1. Rewarding the Attendant. 2. Appointing the Five Virtuous Ones.

Regarding the threefold classification of virtues and the application of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement), although the methods of application are numerous, they converge into a single principle when viewed in terms of their actual purpose;

thus, there is no contradiction in using the designation "one hundred and one. This is why it is said, "according to the majority," and so forth. The subsequent explanation of the *karman* (formal ecclesiastical acts) may be understood accordingly.

If one relies on the *Gāthā-śāstra*, there are exactly one hundred and one [rules], as it enumerates twenty-four for the *jñapti* (motion), forty-seven for the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation),

and thirty for the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion with three proclamations). However, according to the ancient recitation of other schools, which abridged their own fundamental texts based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
the total number of such procedures, when comprehensively collected, amounts to one hundred and thirty-four dharmas.
In the first section of the *Xianshu* (Exposition of Numbers), the initial passage cites a treatise to demonstrate the number of categories within the Vinaya-piṭaka;

specifically, the *Baiyi jiemu* (One Hundred and One Karmavācanās) explicitly identifies the Sarvāstivāda school, making it clear that it originates from the tradition of the *Shisong lü* (Ten Recitations Vinaya).

Since the numerical categories in that Vinaya are identical [to those here], the subsequent section refutes ancient misconceptions regarding the school and cites the great numbers of its own specific lineage (*mubu*) to demonstrate them. Because this comprehensively summarizes the entire body of the Vinaya, it is termed "comprehensive" (*tong*).

I have compiled one hundred and thirty-four [rules]; furthermore, as many of the communal (*saṃgha*) and individual (*pudgala*) rules are found extensively in other schools (*tāny-anya-samaya*), they are not included here.
Some who have carefully examined the original Vinaya texts have added ten more rules, which include those concerning the differing rules for monks and nuns (*bhikṣu-bhikṣuṇī-vaiṣamya-dharma*).
Those who held the same [catalog] calculated the number as two hundred and sixty-one rules;

if one were to categorize each according to the precepts, there would be two sections of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, totaling one hundred and twenty rules, while the remainder were further reorganized.
Next, regarding the classification of the three schools' enumerations: first, adding ten methods results in one hundred and forty-four;

second, the Master [Daoxuan] calculated two versions, both of which are now lost and it is unclear what methods they comprised; subsequently, the latter Master alone divided them into thirty categories:

(1) the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, (2) the confession of offenses, and (3) the returning of robes—these three items, combined with the two divisions of monks and nuns, allow the total number to be known. Furthermore, there are many other schools that list their own enumerations.
