As for the procedures regarding medicine and formal announcements, these two are combined.

However, because the various dharmas are collectively assigned to the respective matters, it is said that they "pervade the three" while not obstructing the "one"; each dharma corresponds to one matter alone.
Since the medicinal dharma and the person’s ailment are combined, and the white announcement pertains to the preceding matters, these two are joined together.

Regarding persons, one must face only a single individual and not two; this principle applies to all cases involving pairs. If two or three individuals are involved, it is termed a "small assembly" (*parṣad*), and one must inquire about their boundaries and harmony;
furthermore, because such a group would overlap with other categories of assemblies, it is not permitted [to perform the rite before them].

Even when performing repentance for thirty offenses, it is limited to a single person who makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to seek harmony; this is done to serve as a witness for the preceding repentance, as the offense is common to all.
This is because there are three types of confession (*tri-vidha-deśanā*).

Regarding the initial presentation of the fundamental position for the *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession before another person): if one excludes the small assemblies and the rules applicable to other groups, this refers to the *sabhā-vastu* (rules for the assembly).

As for the *prātimokṣa-deśanā* (confession before an individual), even if it is presented below, the confession prior to the forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) is the confession of the preceptor’s offense; this applies to all three types of confession mentioned above.
The meaning of the text has already been clarified.

If so, why does the text add the confession and announcement (*kṣānti-śrāvaṇa*)? The answer is: because the relinquishing occurs within the Saṃgha, it clarifies that the matter of the downfall and repentance is not solely a matter of the *dāna* (offering/act);

one must inquire about the offense with the harmony of the assembly. Since the offense is not removed by the Saṃgha alone, it is the same as the [rules] numbered ninety. Therefore, the text says this.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe, one must not perform the ritual separately from the assembly; this does not refer to the confession of the offense itself.

The remainder is as stated in the subsequent announcement. Since the preceding section in the "Resolution of Doubts" provides only a brief indication without clarifying the intent of the announcement, it is questioned again.

In the response, the first part indicates the confession and announcement of the offense, while the following clarifies the formal repentance. Below, scriptural evidence is cited to demonstrate that this [procedure] pertains specifically to robes.
As for the "pointing" (indicating), it is as explained below in the section on the *śuddhaka-śveta* (single-announcement) procedure.
Regarding the location where one faces [the assembly], this applies universally across all realms (*dhātu*) without the fault of having a separate group;
however, while this applies to all locations, one must specifically exclude those cases involving the *chanda* (consent) ritual and the *svayambhū* (natural) procedure.

Regarding the fivefold dharma for the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) within the *pañcavargika-dharma*, there are five methods concerning the text: the abandonment of the offense, the confession, and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation/invitation ceremony).

Regarding the actual matters, there are two types: the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture), where two are combined and explained, and the *aprāṇika-pravāraṇā* (the invitation ceremony regarding non-sentient objects).
Among the *pratideśanīya* (confession) offenses, because they involve both the forfeiture of the object and the act itself, these two are combined.

Regarding the person before whom the confession is made, it begins with one person and may extend to three or four; the single motion (*jñapti*) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is established from one up to four, forming a *saṃgha*, as detailed in the text.

This differs from the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticize), which is still termed "three-fold speech" (*trivācika*), as it lacks the five qualities [of a formal assembly] and cannot [proceed otherwise].

Because of the transgression, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; this extends through the four categories of offenses that require the forfeiture of property to both the Sangha and an individual. Once the property has been forfeited and the robe returned, one must perform the formal ritual within the Sangha to repent for the original offense.

One must first inquire of the three [offenders] individually regarding the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. If they are in harmony as previously described, even if the practice has long been neglected, it applies generally to groups of three or fewer.
Regarding the five conditions, their application is determined by addition or subtraction according to the specific circumstances.

Among humans, first the status of the human position is shown; next, the distinction between the general and the specific is clarified. First, it is explained that for the four persons, the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) rite is exclusively a practice for individuals;
however, regarding the one type of offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), it still involves both the *saṃgha* and the individual.

When there are four persons, they return to their original status as members of the *saṃgha*. Furthermore, within the offenses involving forfeiture, the forfeiture of property and the restitution of property require that the presiding monk (*pratideśanā-ācārya*) be included in the count.

Regarding the confession of receiving [an offering] while repenting for bodily transgressions: because one does not perform the *avadāna-dharma* (pure dharma) outside the Saṃgha, one only asks about the boundaries as previously set forth;
this is the aforementioned citation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* that refutes ancient views. Second, next, the explanation of two or three people facing one another:

whereas the aforementioned four people are restricted solely to two methods, these are called "universal practice" (*sāmānya-caryā*). There are five conditions (*pratyaya*), and "condition" here refers to the *dharma*. However, regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), one must ask.
Because the phrases "at the boundary," "existence and non-existence," "speaking at will," and so forth have been added or modified, it is said that this is "in terms of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Question: There are four people who receive or relinquish [the precepts], making five including oneself; one is the object of the action (*karma*), while the others are those who perform the holding.

Since the *jñapti* (formal motion) is performed by a single person, they do not themselves fall under the category of the *saṃgha*. If the number in the preceding context is already four, is this not indeed the *saṃgha*? Answer: The one who relinquishes the offense is the object of the action.
If the [robe] has not yet been relinquished or returned, one is ultimately not included among the Saṃgha.

In the question-and-answer section, fearing that the person in question might be counted toward the required number for the Saṃgha, the question is raised to resolve this; the answer is clear from the text.
Regarding the *dharmas* of the boundary, seven are common; the minor *vedanā* is not opened because the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) performed on a single seat is never used again.

In the two boundaries, the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) is recited together; once the offense has been raised, it is abandoned. That which is prepared according to the occasion constitutes the method for the two groups of four or five monks.

Within the categories of boundaries (*sīmā*), eight types are mentioned; however, because one small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) is excluded, there are effectively seven. This is because when the [boundary] is established, it simultaneously relinquishes [the previous state].

Regarding the confession of a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, the small boundary for the *poṣadha* (confession) rite performs four monastic legal acts (*saṃghakarma*), while the small boundary for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) rite performs five monastic legal acts.

If one considers the primary object [of these rites], they pertain to the legal acts for groups of three or four persons; however, here we speak in terms of both the primary object and the agent of the action.

Regarding the meaning of the "confession before six minor groups": for light offenses such as *pāyantika*, confession is performed before a single person; for heavy offenses, it is performed within the assembly of the larger community (*sīmā*);
for middling offenses, one must wait for conditions, requiring a small group.

Among the six types of small assemblies (*kṣudrasaṃgha*), those who are subject to confession (*pratideśanā*) and those whose offenses are *sthūlātyaya* are combined here as requiring only a face-to-face procedure; thus, in terms of their meaning, three types of confession are listed collectively.
The text is derived from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

As for the matter, it concerns emotional transgressions; the persons involved are restricted to two or three because questions must be asked. If fewer than this are present, the rite is not accomplished and is not termed a "small assembly."
The *dhātu* (elements) may also correspond to the aforementioned five;
among those enumerated, the person who knows the matter can understand that the *dhātu* refers to the aforementioned five, which, as before, are common to the seven.
In the text of the single-announcement (*jñapti*) for the seven classes of practitioners (*saptasaṃgha*), thirty-nine dharmas are listed.
The matter applies to three types of objects, as in other cases: verbal contact and provocation; the two categories of form and dharma are likewise identical in being sentient matters.

The proclamation of *prātimokṣa*, the various increased fetters, and the compilation of the *śukla* (white) [deeds] are insentient matters. The settling of disputes through reconciliation, the robe of virtue (*guṇavastuka-cīvara*), and the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) constitute a combination of two.
This brief outline is thus; it cannot be demonstrated in full detail.

Regarding the matters of the *śuddha-śveta* (single-announcement) procedures, since there are two additions each for the *poṣadha* (recitation of precepts) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults), they are called "the various additions.

Taking four or five people as the standard for addressing others, those with three or fewer lack sufficient virtue to manifest [the formalities] and thus merely receive the designation of "face-to-face" (*pratyekamukha*).
This can be understood from the two divisions of the *pravāraṇā* procedure; ten or twenty people, however, exceed the proper limit.
Among humans, four types of persons are common to all, while five types exclude four dharmas.

When it is said that the *zì* (invitation) is twofold—namely, the communal and the individual—it is because the ten and twenty [karmas] each rely on the *báisì* (one motion and three proclamations); thus, the *dānbái* (single proclamation) is not applicable.

Regarding the *dhātu* (elements), there are only four types of formal acts (*karmas*) that are naturally and simultaneously non-participatory. As for the mutual pervasion and obstruction among the seven *dharmadhātus*, these will be extensively cited when the time comes.

For instance, regarding the three grades of minor boundaries (*sīmā*), if one asks why the three "whites" (*śukla*) exist only within the act of receiving [the precepts], and since they are restricted to a single moment and do not extend to others, the principle applies equally to the other two minor boundaries; it is not that there is no raising of charges (*codanā*).

Regarding the formal motion (*jñapti*) for the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the path for common use (*samanta-kṛtya*), and the precept platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*): these are restricted to the procedures for carrying the alms bowl, the virtuous robe (*guṇa-cīvara*), and the formalities of the ritual form (*vidhi*).

A formal motion cannot be performed without the presence of necessary difficult circumstances; however, when performing the two formal motions for the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), they may also be conducted upon the platform.
Within the section on the *dharmas* (界), the first part provides a general indication of the two *dharmas*; the subsequent section specifically distinguishes the procedures for the lower [offenses].

One should carefully examine the various *śuddhika* (formal announcements) cited therein; here, a brief distinction of the general outline is sufficient to see the path. First, the two minor offenses (*dva-kṣudra*) are restricted to three *śuddhika* and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation).

For each of the two minor [offenses], there is only one *śuddhika*. Since the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture) and the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses) can be confessed according to their respective categories, they are collectively subject to confession.
The announcement for the subsequent selection of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) applies to all general procedures;

the announcement for the specific selection of the ritual platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*), the walking of the alms bowl, and so forth, must be performed upon the great boundary platform itself, while all other matters may be carried out generally, as detailed below in the section on the formal establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).
The eighth section, "Clarifying the White," outlines fifty-seven dharmas according to the text.

These are categorized by their application to objects, their commonality across the three types of persons, their specific functions, and their status as mental fetters or non-mental; furthermore, the rules for robes and dwellings are combined into two.

In matters requiring a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), the various *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), the construction of dwellings, the repair of dwellings, and the guarding [of property]—these involve the keeper of the storehouse and the virtuous robe-holder;
the remainder should be sought elsewhere.
Regarding persons, there are only four types who do not apply to groups of five, ten, or twenty: [the aforementioned roles].

Among humans, all *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one proclamation) procedures must be conducted by four monks; they do not apply to the other three assemblies (*parṣad*). This may be understood from what precedes. Question:
It was stated above that a *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) requires a sangha of five monks; how is it now that this is contradicted? Answer: It was simply not clarified there.

When four monks appoint a person [to act as proxy], the quorum for the formal boundary (*sīmā*) is insufficient; this is because the conditions have not yet been fulfilled, and the formal procedure (*jñapti*) is subsequently performed in harmony with the assembly.

Regarding the performance of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) for five people or fewer, this should be understood by analogy with the other cases.

In recent times, there has been a widespread abuse of the practice, whereby whatever is done is indiscriminately categorized as being included within the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); therefore, I clarify this again, fearing that practitioners might still be confused when following these procedures.

As for the previous statement that it does not apply to five people, this does not mean that a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* cannot be performed for a hundred or a thousand; rather, it was a restriction specifically against five people acting alone for a separate matter.
The *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one proclamation) is entrusted only to four persons; others are not established by rule.

In the question-and-answer section, the initial question is easy to understand, yet fearing confusion, the answer is divided into four parts: first, the answer generally covers the preceding object, as it is insufficient for the purpose intended;
second, the remainder points to the precedent; third, the passage beginning with "頃" (a moment/occasion) refutes over-extension; fourth, the passage beginning with "前" (the former) precludes doubt.
If that is so, when returning or handing over robes, you both speak of them being passed along in succession; is it not then necessary to have five? The answer is:
it is still only four people, because those who are formally listed do not count as part of the *saṃgha*—as has already been clarified above. Why then do you still harbor doubts?
Regarding the subsequent objection: the original rule prohibits returning property after a day has passed; however, if there is a specific reason, one may open and hand over the items on the spot.
Furthermore, when distributing the estate of the deceased, it is first entrusted to those possessing five virtues to divide and give to the Saṃgha.
Based on these two methods, the person who receives the property is not the one acting independently; rather, it should be understood that the answer refers to the aforementioned five persons.
The wise see that among the various dharmas, within the face-to-face (pratyakṣa) procedure, with respect to the boundary (sīmā), it also applies to all boundaries.
The seven types of *jñapti-dvitīya* [karmas] apply to the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*), because since the initial establishment [of the boundary], re-establishment is not permitted;

otherwise, the ritual boundary (*dharma-sīmā*) would be obstructed. All others pertain to the ritual boundary (*dharma-sīmā*). Among the three small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*), they belong to their respective corresponding boundaries.

The specific restriction regarding the matter of individuals receiving the *zì* (unrestricted) [privileges] is not without its distinctions; other matters are routine tasks and do not necessarily require a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*).

Thus, the text states that once the ritual is performed, the *śīlākṣetra* (field of precepts) is immediately dissolved. Whether it is general or specific can be understood through inquiry, as in the cases of the *cīvaradhāraṇa* (retaining robes), the *rātrisaṃvṛti* (receiving days), the *pātra* (alms bowl), and the *vihāra* (monastery)—where the *jñaptidvitīyakarman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) does not apply to other instances; similar categories may be inferred accordingly.

Within the section on boundaries (*sīmā*), the first part provides a general overview of seven types; the second part provides a detailed explanation of each. First, it clarifies the seven types of natural (*prakṛti*) boundaries: the three small, the three large, and the boundary of the precept platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*).
The rules for the hall for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha-śālā*) are also included under the category of the natural. Next, it clarifies the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*):

the small boundary for the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) and confession (*jñapti*) applies universally, while the principle of returning robes is logically applicable; as for the boundary of the precept platform, it is restricted to the interior, so it is briefly mentioned here. Finally, the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) is discussed.

Regarding the *deyi* (robe of merit) and other methods of resolution, none are applicable; however, upon careful examination of the textual annotations, the permissibility and prohibitions are clearly evident:
the three small boundaries do not apply, while for the remaining methods of resolution, all others are generally applicable.
The text of the nine *jñapti-caturtha-karman* enumerates thirty-eight methods.

When applied to specific matters, these—such as admonition, confession, certification, formal accusation, and disciplinary treatment—are all conferred upon individuals; their fundamental principle is nothing other than the generation of good and the eradication of evil.
It is clear that the other two [categories] lack such significance.

Among the matters of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), all forms of "receiving" (*pratigraha*) give rise to wholesome qualities; "admonishing" (*codanā*), "correcting" (*śamanā*), and so forth, all eliminate unwholesome qualities.

These are restricted solely to matters of mental disposition and do not apply to the other two [types of formal acts]. Speaking in terms of persons, these three types of persons are not applicable; they apply only to a *saṃgha* of four persons. Five persons are not applicable; it applies only to a single *jñapti-karman*.

Since ten people and twenty people both require one motion followed by four proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), we know that for other dharmas, the initial stage is subsumed within the *saṃgha*.

Among humans, five people require only one motion; this does not apply universally to the *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and one proclamation) or *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations), but is stated merely with reference to a single category.

Regarding the discussion of the *dhātu* (elements/boundaries), it does not apply to the spontaneous formation of a boundary. Within the three types of small boundaries (*kṣudrakasīmā*), only the conferral of the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) is performed by the formal motion and resolution with four parts (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

As for the explanation of the small boundary for the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), that too does not apply; for there is no case where one is immediately subjected to disciplinary action (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) due to a groundless accusation, as such matters arise from subsequent events and do not pertain to the present act itself.

Within the *dharmadhātu*, the formal acts (*karmas*) of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the Precept Platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*), and the Universal Passage (*sarva-gati*) are all included; however, the text specifically excludes the three minor procedures of governance (*vinaya*).
This is because "governance" refers to the act of expelling—that is, the removal of offenses—and it arises as the cause for the proclamation of the *pravāraṇā*.
It is not a current performance, as it is still in the process of being carried out. This differs from the act of receiving the precepts, which constitutes a formal performance.

Above, the general characteristics of the remaining three conditions for the *karmavācanā* have already been revealed; now, regarding these four conditions, each shall be clarified according to its specific application to demonstrate their respective universal and particular scopes.

Within the second section, which clarifies each [condition] individually, the first subsection notes that while the preceding text followed the dharmas through the various conditions to show their pervasion and obstruction, the four conditions themselves had not yet been seen.
Because each possesses its own specific meaning, they are called "coarse characteristics.
Regarding the first category, the *cittavijñapti-karman* (mental-act ritual), there are fourteen dharmas; however, only three are performed solely through mental intention (*cittavijñapti*).

If one attempts to perform them as a *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (face-to-face procedure), they are not accomplished; other cases may be inferred accordingly. Seven of these dharmas are common to the *pratyakṣa-vinaya*, while four are restricted to the *cittavijñapti*.
The Dharma applies to the Saṃgha as a whole, while the specific names and meanings are to be understood according to the text.
In the first section on the Dharma, the initial clarification of mental recollection (*manasikāra*) lists the number of formal procedures (*dharmasaṃkhyā*), both of which appear in the textual notes.

When applied to mental recollection or face-to-face confession (*pratyakṣavijñapti*), these do not constitute [valid] procedures; how much less so for entering a small group or a quorum of four monks? Since all such cases are non-Dharmic, it is so stated.

Other examples may be inferred accordingly; however, regarding the thirty-three *pratimokṣa* procedures, seven types apply to both mental recollection (*manasikāra*) and face-to-face confession (*sammukha*), while five types apply to both the Saṃgha and the individual. The remainder must necessarily be confessed face-to-face with another person.
The *pārājika* offenses are restricted to a small group; a rough classification is thus as follows. As for those that apply to both the Saṃgha and the individual, they are not [restricted].
This means that what was originally common to the Saṃgha is extended to individuals, as it was originally a rule for the Saṃgha that is now opened up for private persons.

Regarding the mention of "mental intimation" (cittānujñā), this was originally a rite performed in the presence of another (pratyekamukha), but because there is no one present to witness it within the boundary (sīmā), it is extended to include mental intimation.

Regarding the first part of the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) procedures, there are seven categories: those common to the *saṃgha*, those applicable to the mind, and those belonging to oneself, which pertain to the first position;

the five types of *pratimukha* procedures for the *saṃgha* and for individual monks are included here. All others necessarily require a person as a counterpart; these are the various cases of "only face-to-face.

Next, the two types of "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) procedures will be explained: "common to the *saṃgha"* refers to the performance of major formal acts (*karmas*) within the assembly; "common to the mind" refers to the opening of the procedure for minor matters within the assembly.
Regarding the statement "the Dharma is also mutually applicable" mentioned previously, this refers precisely to that meaning.

Among the one hundred and thirty-four *karmavācanā* (formal acts) of the various dharmas, a single dharma applies to a single matter such that they do not mutually apply to one another—for example, the formal act of appointing someone to pose questions does not apply to the formal act of summoning by announcement.
However, when multiple dharmas accomplish a single matter, there is mutual applicability.

The general principle is as in the case of receiving the precepts: through one *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations) or one *jñapti-ekavācika* (one motion and one proclamation), the *avijñapti* (unmanifest karma) is accomplished throughout the four directions.

Generally speaking, for the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) and the maintenance of a community (*saṃgha*), it is necessary that there be a formal motion (*jñapti*). Among these, the seven methods for establishing boundaries cannot be added repeatedly;

they are restricted to natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*) and do not apply to constructed boundaries (*kṛtrima-sīmā*). The other types—the *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and two proclamations), the *jñapti-ekavācika*, and the *jñapti-caturtha*—are the reverse of this [in their application].
[The author] knows. Among the various dharmas, first the total number is indicated; next, the pervasion and obstruction are revealed. First, the three dharmas are discussed in general;

now, to clarify the specific matters, two paths must be distinguished. First, regarding the general, they are distinguished individually; for example, the four dharmas of receiving the precepts each apply to their respective cases.

Second, subsuming the particulars into the general: just as the four conditions for receiving [ordination] collectively constitute a single act of receiving, this text relies on this principle to distinguish between what is universally applicable and what is restricted.

Based on the original [rules], each applies to its specific case; however, according to the meaning of "universally applicable," when considering the collective conditions, such as the desire to practice the precepts, or the earth, or natural occurrences, one must first establish the boundary (*sīmā*).
Whether it be an *upādhyāya* ordaining a person or requesting permission to maintain a community of disciples (*śrāmaṇera*), all may be encompassed [by these principles].

Returning to receive the precepts serves to manifest the principle that many dharmas constitute a single unity. The *pravāraṇā*, the forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), the punishment of the bowl, and the loss of robes all share this same principle.

When examining the texts, one should raise these points oneself. Regarding the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), the seven types of boundaries are not established redundantly;

this is because it serves as a restriction for the remainder, whereas all other matters pertain to the general ground of the Dharma. Therefore, it is said that this is the opposite of the aforementioned cases.
Regarding the classification of matters, there are three; however, as they have already been explained in accordance with the preceding rules, they are not reiterated here.

Next, to clarify the matters themselves, these consist of the two categories of sentient and insentient beings, which together make three. For specific examples, refer to the aforementioned conditions within the section on "Following the Rules."

Regarding individuals, when one person harbors a thought in their mind and speaks it with their own mouth, this constitutes the proper domain [of a formal act]. Even if it extends to the two aforementioned [categories], these are incidental and not primary.

If there are people within the boundary, how could one act alone? As for the "multiple *pratideśanīya*" (confession before others), the preceding evidence shows that the objective condition must necessarily involve a general appeal to the assembly;
only when the facts are reported and the signs of understanding are received can the act be accomplished. Although this involves the methods of the assembly, it is nonetheless an opening provision.

Four persons constitute a Saṃgha; their superior utility is not uniform. In terms of the actual matter, there are three categories, but they ultimately revert to the first position. Any deficiency therein is a transgression, and the more deficient, the more severe the fault.

Regarding the three types of persons, first, as for the single person: although they may be proficient in the three dharmas, one must distinguish between the primary and secondary roles within the assembly. Next...

It is clear that the "many" are the same as the two aforementioned categories, while the "four" below are distinct. Regarding the third point, the assembly is one in essence but threefold in function;
since function still relies upon essence, it returns to the initial position.

Discussing this in terms of the *dhātu*, [the individual] is naturally weak and incapable of managing monastic affairs; if the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) for binding the community were not established, there would be no basis for the existence of the Sangha-dharma.

It is permitted only for the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to be performed within the seven boundaries, as these do not interpenetrate; however, the texts do not allow for them to be layered or joined together.
Although the three large and three small [boundaries] share many names but a single meaning, because the *sīmā* (monastic boundary) is self-contained, it must be encircled.
Even if they appear to be layered, there is empty space between the two.

Fourth, within the section on realms (*dhātu*), first the natural realm (*prakṛti-dhātu*) is explained; once the demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) is opened, it then applies to both ritual procedures (*kriyā*) and formal acts (*vidhi*).

Next, the dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*) is explained. First, there is a general indication, followed by specific distinctions. First, the large and small, as well as the opening and closing, are distinguished;

next, the two differences between the site and the boundary are distinguished. Because these are established separately within the realm, it is said that "the space between the two parts is naturally separated."
The preceding summary of the conditions for the accomplishment of *karmavācanā* through brief analysis is concluded.

Twenty-seven: Although one may recite the precepts and the Vinaya, if what one perceives is heterodox and biased, this too must be removed and discarded.

The twenty-eighth method, the "Covering with Grass" (*tṛṇapraticchādana*), is as follows: When two factions engage in mutual dispute, each exposing the other's faults, and even after investigating the root of the matter, their afflictive emotions do not subside, it is necessary to remain compliant and refrain from speaking of right or wrong.

Furthermore, since there has been no grave transgression and it would otherwise violate the regulations for interacting with the laity, both assemblies should each take upon themselves the burden of the offense.
Like being covered by grass, they should feel mutual shame before the ground and each confess this white offense (*avadāta-āpatti*).

"Disputes are both dissolved": some seek the scriptural text of the Vinaya; the procedure for granting formal permission (*jñapti*) to nuns is largely the same as that for monks, and thus it is not set forth here.
Twenty-eight: these are mutual defects, meaning that all [actions] involve transgression. "The afflictions cannot be stilled" means they are impossible to cease.
"Zhi" (stopping) refers to a state of being supple, harmonious, and compliant; it corresponds to the musical pitch of "Cao Fu Di" (Grass Covering the Ground).

The rule is that, with the sole exception of those who have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) or are barred from entering the homes of laypeople (*pravāsanīya*), all other [offenses] may be extinguished; hence it is said: "Originally there were no grave transgressions," referring to conduct inconsistent with the laity.

When performing this rite, the two assemblies face each other; one assembly prostrates on the ground while the presiding elder (*sthavira*) makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to the other assembly.
Likewise, when an offense is extinguished along with the dispute itself, there is no need for further confession. This is illustrated by the metaphor of "covering mud with grass.

To provide a contrast, the procedure for receiving the *jñapti* (formal motion) from a *bhikṣuṇī* is presented; since the *Vinaya* follows the extinction of the dispute with the rules concerning *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is listed here.
However, we do not adopt that [specific rule] at present.

Twenty-ninth: Regarding those dispatched to the royal city to assemble for the Dharma—since one who intends to propagate the Dharma must await necessary resources and companions, it is required that they first announce their arrival at a specific location.
The six dharmas from the twenty-ninth downward all concern the events of the First Council. Regarding their initial departure together, they first announced their destination.

As the Vinaya states: "All the bhikṣus said, 'Only in Rājagṛha are dwellings, food, drink, and bedding so abundant that we ought to go there together for the council. Kāśyapa then made the formal announcement."

Regarding the "Proclamation of the Dharma" (*dharmapravāraṇā*): when the monastic community first assembles for the fundamental purpose [of the council], it must be conducted with harmony. If one does not proclaim it, there is no means by which the intention can be made manifest.
As for the "Proclamation of the Dharma," it is fully termed the *Kāśyapīya-dharmavinaya-pravāraṇā*, which refers to the formal convocation (*saṃgīti*) of the Great Assembly.
Once the assembly has gathered, one must declare the original intent.
Regarding the thirty-one questions posed by Upāli: the Vinaya is the life-force of the Dharma, upheld equally by the noble ones;

it must first be expounded so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. However, because one must strike at and elevate the core tenets rather than merely recounting them superficially, it is necessary to inquire with harmony to represent the assembly.
It is because they share the same mind that it is so called.
"Vinaya" refers to the Dharma-life, meaning the life-force of the Buddha-dharma; "striking and arousing" refers to its manifestation. "Root" (zong) means the fundamental basis.
Regarding Upāli’s response to the thirty-two questions: since there was already a prior inquiry, he could not remain silent; his answering preceded the rest of the Sangha.
The subsequent explanation clarifies that this is not a private matter.

Regarding the thirty-three questions, Ānanda’s petition is as follows: since the fundamental lifeblood of the Buddha-dharma has already been transmitted and the scriptures that elucidate the spirit have been fully explained, it is now necessary to expound upon Ānanda, the master of transformative teaching; therefore, he is questioned so that he may recount it.

The sūtras and śāstras constitute the transformative teachings that elucidate the study of concentration and wisdom for clarifying the mind; thus, they can open up intellectual understanding and bring joy to the spirit.
While the text mentions only "sūtra," its meaning should encompass the śāstras as well. Some say that Kāśyapa compiled the Śāstra Piṭaka.

34. As for the answer, it is also because the teaching is not transmitted in vain that there is a basis for its propagation; responding in accordance with this, the manifestation of the Dharma is shown to be without error. 35.
Regarding the "Seven Hundred" [verses], the "Dharma-śataka" refers to the period one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during which time Vatsa...

Because monks were arbitrarily practicing ten kinds of evil dharmas that obscured worldly affairs and needed to be eradicated, the monk Gaṇa, undaunted by toil and hardship, searched throughout the country and assembled seven hundred men to sever these practices. Since this was initially a discussion of the meaning of the Dharma, it was necessary to announce the cause for harmony;
thus, the number was used as a pretext to establish the name [of the order].
Thirty-five minor points and five dharmas; the circumstances of the Council of Seven Hundred.
In the city of Vaiśālī, the Vatsiputrīyas arbitrarily practiced ten kinds of unrighteous acts, all claiming they were taught by the Buddha to convert the people of that time.
When the bhikṣu Yaśa Kākaṇḍaka heard of this, he went to refute them, saying, "These are not the Dharma. They then united and performed a formal act (*karma*) to suspend him.
That [monk] who had been suspended then traveled to various countries to seek companions;
he obtained Revata and seven hundred other arhats, who gathered together to adjudicate the matter and reconvened the Dharma-piṭaka. The ten matters are fully cited in the lower volume of the *Zizhi*.

36. Regarding the "Method of Assigning Persons to Discuss the Dharma": This refers to the practice where, before the assembly, one evaluates the wise and the foolish, distinguishing between the worthy and the mediocre, and screens those who discuss the Dharma to thoroughly discern the heterodox from the orthodox;
hence this name. 37. Regarding the "Method of Right Discussion":
Once the discussion has been concluded in private and the three measures of evaluation have removed all doubt, one desires to bring an end to subsequent conditions and must [proceed accordingly].
One must first harmonize one's intention before the assembly.

There are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which accords with the manifest principle; second, inference (*anumāna*), which relies on examples from other cases;
and third, authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), which is the testimony of the holy word.
Regarding the thirty-eighth question, "The Elder Spoke": This refers to Ajita, who had one hundred and sixty years of seniority;
because he was rich in both years and virtue, and was one whom the assembly looked up to with reverence, he was questioned first—not out of partiality, nor out of inability to bear it.
Regarding the question "to the Elder," the Vinaya states that in the city of Vaiśālī there was an elder named Sarvakāmin, who was the foremost elder of Jambudvīpa.
Because he had witnessed the events of the Buddha’s lifetime, Upāli questioned him to obtain his testimony;
therefore, he first addressed and informed the Elder.

The thirty-ninth Elder replied: "One whose virtue abides in dignity and whose speech is worthy of trust and acceptance may transmit what was discussed in private to the assembly and proclaim it there.
This is because the meaning of the discussion transmitted from the private place does not differ from the previous discourse."

Regarding the subsequent procedure for distributing voting tallies (*śalākā*) before the assembly to establish the correct [number], it is necessary to first announce it; the text is abbreviated here and does not provide a full account, as the general outline is as described above.

As for the "abbreviated explanation" (*saṃkṣipta-vyākhyāna*) following this, because there are principles present where the text is absent, the exposition is incomplete; what has been presented thus far merely cites the major points.
Because it is abbreviated, it says: "The general outline is as above.
Next, regarding the two texts on the *bai-ming* (white-inscription) [stūpas], fifty-seven items are listed.

First, concerning the method for constructing a small dwelling: if one engages in many affairs and labors, it will disturb and confuse both [the donor and the recipient] of the two destinies; furthermore, if it does not conform to the prescribed measurements, it will obstruct the Path.
The rules for soliciting [wood] and requesting formal authorization (*jñapti*) regarding the measurement and limits were few in number and largely absent from the texts.

Regarding the second of the two types of *śuklā* (white) offenses: the first two correspond to the second of the thirteen [offenses], concerning the method of requesting authorization for two small rooms.

Since there was no established regulation for the measurement, it is called "small. Because one requests from others the felling of sacred trees (*devavṛkṣa*), it causes affliction to the two realms of existence; thus, it is classified as "low."
These two sentences reveal the reason why the latter section does not appear [in this context].

Regarding the two matters concerning the *mahallaka* (large dwelling): since there is already a designated master who exercises exclusive authority and autonomy, and because of the two conditions of obstruction and difficulty, one cannot avoid them through mere thought;
therefore, the regulation requires reliance upon the Saṃgha to obtain its direction, and the matter is the same as before—thus it does not appear in the text.

Because there is no regulation regarding the size for those with owners, it is called a "large room"; however, since construction is not permitted in either obstructed or difficult locations, one must determine the boundaries and measurements—this refers to the assignment [of space].

Third, regarding the distribution of bedding: as a monastic administrator (*karmadāna*), one must act with universal impartiality; if one does not communicate with harmony, one may fall into partiality.
Because I am biased, I shall first inform you of the details before proceeding with the distribution.

Regarding the three matters, as for the distribution of communal property to individual rooms, it is necessary to appoint someone possessing the five virtues; therefore, I announce this to formally designate him.

Regarding the fourth method, the proclamation of a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*): if a member of the Sangha commits a transgression that ought not to be made public, such as Devadatta’s accumulation of faults which were linked to the royal lineage, and if this is not reported early on, it will indiscriminately defile the Buddha and the Sangha;
furthermore, once the fault becomes manifest, it is necessary to first clearly demonstrate the separation from him. Therefore, [this method] is established.
Among the four [cases], Devadatta split the Saṃgha and established the practice of five heterodox dharmas; at that time, he further incited King Ajātaśatru to commit treason.
Because this involved the royal lineage and the matter of instructing a layperson (śrāvaka) exceeded the ordinary course of affairs, the Buddha dispatched Śāriputra to go and inform him.
The fifth, the procedure for returning robes after twenty-seven days, is explained extensively in the subsequent text.

Regarding the sixth, the procedure for being separated from one’s robes: when one has contracted a serious illness and intends to travel elsewhere, the weight and bulk of one's clothing become an impediment;
therefore, one may request from the Saṃgha permission to be separated from one robe.

Sixth, regarding the precept on being separated from one’s robes: among the two upper robes permitted except by formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*), it is not allowed to be separated from even one of them; as for the lower robe, there is no such restriction.
Seventh, regarding the reduction of bedding to six years: because making numerous dharma-robes causes confusion and hinders constant practice, a time limit is established to govern them.

Regarding the permission to manage [affairs], although it is generally restricted by conditions and obstacles, this provision is opened for them; yet, fearing that private interests might be overstepped, one must exercise careful judgment.
Thus it is said:
"In the seven cases, outside of the fixed period, one may freely manage affairs; however, if within the period there are circumstances that necessitate it, one must formally request the Dharma."

Regarding the eight methods for protecting the alms bowl: when begging for many bowls, one should set aside the extra ones; if they are taken away, one should exchange them and return them to the owner. Fearing that the owner might become angry or resentful, one employs these ritual methods as a form of punishment.
Thus, using the old bowl while holding the new one, one maintains constant supervision over them from beginning to end.

The *Madhyamāgama-vinaya* states: "If one receives a fine item, it should be confiscated and kept [as a penalty to be entered into the kitchen]; the lowest-quality inferior item should be taken and given to them [to exchange it].

If the original holder continues to use the new item while the one who returned it always keeps the old one, fearing that the latter might be damaged, they shall be penalized and ordered to guard it."
Regarding the appointment of nine persons to instruct the nuns: since they must possess the ten virtues and propagate the teachings to transform the world, they must first be formally appointed;
however, because their majestic demeanor has not yet been fully manifested, the public appoints them on behalf of the community so that the influence of the Way may easily spread.

Among these nine, the Buddha established the rule that a teacher of nuns must possess ten qualities: first, observance of the precepts; second, extensive learning; third, recitation of the two sections of the Vinaya;
fourth, the ability to resolve doubts without hesitation; fifth, skill in preaching the Dharma; sixth, being of noble lineage and having left the household life;

seventh, having a handsome and upright appearance; eighth, being capable of instructing nuns; ninth, not having committed a grave offense (*pārājika*); and tenth, having completed twenty years since full ordination (*varṣa*).

The tenth and eleventh points concern the rules for the "Householder of Liberated Bonds" (*kula-putra-vimukta-bandhana*). When a layperson who has seen the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*) maintains right faith while living at home, they do not think to beg for alms, which causes their resources to be depleted.
Seeing this, the foolish and ignorant say that giving results in calamity; thus, to quell external criticism, a regulation was established to sever [the flow of offerings].

Later, when the situation becomes grave again, it is appropriate to honor a merit-gathering assembly (*puṇya-sabhā*), and one must once more resolve the matter according to the Dharma so that distribution may resume as before; hence these [rules] exist.

Second: The tenth and eleventh [offenses] concern the third *pratideśanīya* precept. It originated from a family in Rājagṛha where both husband and wife attained the vision of the Truth (*dṛṣṭisatya*).
Having no stinginess toward material things, they gave much in alms until they became impoverished. Consequently, people of the world criticized them, saying it was because of their giving...
As a result, the establishment of the rules for the Saṃgha prohibited [monks] from going to beg for alms; later, when wealth increased, these were reopened because there are two categories of rules.
Regarding the twelve rules on "keeping a retinue" (saṅgraha):
the first twelve apply to both assemblies, while the remaining two are restricted specifically to the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha.
13. Nuns dispatch a person to request the Dharma; 14. Nuns dispatch a person to go for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony with the monks, which differs from that of the great assembly of monks;

15. Regarding those who dwell together with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), even though their various views and ego-inversion have not yet been eliminated, they may suddenly resolve their minds [to seek the Path].

If those who seek refuge in the Great Dharma are granted full ordination immediately without undergoing trial and refinement, their natures—being as yet untamed—may instead become a source of difficulty.
Therefore, they should first dwell together as śrāmaṇeras for four months to be molded through practice; only when they have gained faith should the [ordination] be opened to them.
Regarding the sixteenth and seventeenth [rules] concerning the untying of boundaries for receiving the precepts within a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*):

since the Saṃgha has adopted the six points of harmony and ought not to be divided, and because it was feared that refusing to grant the ordination would hinder the lives of sentient beings, the Great Sage, through his skillful means, provisionally established this method. Once the matter is accomplished and the rite is finalized, both parties find it acceptable;
they disperse from their seats immediately, leaving no further complications. It is settled that the boundary is untied as soon as one sits down; there is no doubt in this determination.
Therefore, two dharmas are established.

[Regarding] "sixteen or seven": this arises because the minds of people in the fundamental realm differ; thus, they come to raise objections, and the Buddha opens this teaching so that sentient beings may attain universal understanding.

"Sentient beings" (*sattva*) is a general term for those who possess life, while "recipient" (*pratigrāhaka*) specifically designates the one who receives [the precepts]. The preceding section describes the opening and concluding [of the teaching], while the following clarifies the regulations.
Since the binding and the releasing are established, one can verify that this boundary does not extend to subsequent conditions; there is no doubt about this.

Regarding the explanation of the eighteenth and nineteenth [rules] concerning the *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-binding) of the *uposatha-śālā* (preaching hall): when many people build it separately, it must be determined at the time [of the assembly];
therefore, the rule is established to show that there will be no doubt regarding the later gathering. Once the preaching has been conducted, it must be released, and then bound again.
Among the eighteen [karmas], the boundary has not yet been established; therefore, a separate *śīlāgāra* (precept hall) is designated for the general assembly to gather together.

Since there are many locations and it is difficult to expect the multitude to arrive from all of them, one must formally mark and establish the site so that they know the fixed location. According to the *Vinaya-karman*, the formal motion (*jñapti*) is stated as follows: "Venerable Sangha, listen!
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let us designate a certain place to serve as the *Poṣadha-hall*. This is the formal motion.

Thus (the *karmavācanā* is to be understood accordingly). This merely indicates the location; it does not proclaim the boundaries (*sīmā*) themselves, as this is fundamentally not a rite for establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*).

Nevertheless, it is called "establishing" because it refers to the formal determination of the site according to one's intent. (This is specifically set forth here because ancient records erroneously cited the subsequent method for establishing boundaries as the ritual for the Precept Hall.

"Once the proclamation has been made" means that since the [boundary] has already been established at this spot, there is a "dissolution" (*pratisaṃharaṇa*) when it is subsequently moved to another location.
Twenty and twenty-one: binding and releasing the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Twenty-two:
binding the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept enclosure). Twenty-three and twenty-four:
binding and releasing the *acīvara-apatti-sīmā* (the boundary where one is not liable for the offense of being without robes).

Regarding the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth points, the explanation of the *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-binding) for the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts): the practice and the teaching are mutually dependent; the essential point lies in the person and the Dharma.

If one constantly harbors this intent during the fortnightly [observance], it becomes visible. Now, when the time for the recitation arrives, if the minds do not converge, and if the binding and releasing of the boundary are not performed according to the teachings so as to meet the needs of the practitioners, then the lower path will be quickly obstructed.
If the binding is lax and the recitation is hurried, once the matter is concluded, the boundary is immediately dissolved, and the defining characteristics are lost.
In the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth rules, on the day of the *poṣadha* for a single assembly, while traveling through the wilderness, the group was not in harmony.
Following their teacher and virtuous friends, they diverged from the main path and gathered at separate locations to establish small boundaries (*sīmā*) and recite the precepts.
Because their actions followed their words, it is said that they were "mutually dependent. However, the establishment of such conduct and speech must necessarily rely upon a pure Saṃgha.
Because the holy Dharma is to be widely propagated, it is said that the essentials lie in both person and dharma; this clarifies the purpose of the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
As for the "lower path," this refers to forest hermitages (*araṇya*); if one is in a city or town, such an allowance is not granted, as there is a fear that others might come to rebuke them.
Therefore, the boundary must be quickly established. Once established, with no outsiders present, the recitation may proceed at a relaxed pace.

Regarding the twenty-seventh point, "the two are the same": when the two *vihāras* (monasteries) mutually lack [certain requisites], it is necessary to harmonize them through mutual exchange; thus, both the Dharma and the material provisions (*dharma-āmiṣa*) shall serve to assist one another's affairs.
Regarding the twenty-seventh and below, the three Vinayas list four kinds of *mahā-sīmā* (great boundaries); the first is as previously enumerated, while this refers to the remainder.
Regarding the third point, the reason why only one [of the two] is not a *dharmadhātu* (a common boundary) is that the general meaning only enumerates three types.

As for the mutual absence of the two types of residence (*āvāsa*), the Vinaya clarifies that there are two kinds of residences: first, a single location where the *poṣadha* is recited but no offerings (*lābha*) are received; second, a location where offerings are received but the *poṣadha* is not recited.
The Buddha permitted these to be separately dissolved and jointly re-bound; this is called the "common boundary of both Dharma and food" (*dharmabhaktasamānasīmā*).

The twenty-eight single dharmas being identical also refers to the matter of each dwelling within the combined boundary (*sīmā*). One [group] has both the Dharma and the food in abundance, while the other has food but lacks the Dharma;
because the Sangha dwells by means of the Dharma, the separate liberation (*prātimokṣa*) and the collective binding of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) together bring about their mutual sustenance.
28. When two places each receive offerings of sustenance but perform a single *poṣadha*, this is called "identity of Dharma with separation of food" (*dharmasamatā-bhaktapṛthaktva-sīmā*).
29. Regarding "single food with identity": if both are abundant in provisions, it is one; if one lacks food and there is no mutual assistance, it is entirely [the latter].
Because it deviates from the essence of the monastic community, it must be harmonized and sent forth; this is not one of the three dharmas regarding the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).
There should be a text for its dissolution, and the *Vinaya* sets forth its conditions, which all become manifest when the time arrives.
Twenty-nine: in both cases, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*—one where there is a gain of offerings and one where there is no gain of offerings—is called "sharing of food" (*samabhojana*).

The Dharma, the distinct realm (*dhātu*), the characteristics, the causes, and the names are called "realms" (*dhātu*); in substance, however, they are not so designated. Regarding the lower [text], it says:
"If later the Dharma and the food are both abundant, the Vinaya rules require them to be resolved into two separate entities. Thus, one knows that these three must all be resolved.
The Vinaya below points to the extensive explanation; within the subsequent section on the formal demarcation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), the origins and circumstances are fully clarified.

Those aged thirty or thirty-one who suffer from insanity or delusion, as well as those whose minds are deranged, whose spirits are broken, or who do not maintain their natural state, may commit transgressions through coming and going that greatly violate the rules of propriety.

Because these acts are non-offenses according to internal criteria yet invite suspicion from an external perspective, they are removed by means of the Dharma; thus, even while in such a state, they do not constitute an obstacle.
Later, when the illness has been cured, they may request the formal act of release (*mokṣa*).
Thirty-third: The case of the bhikṣu Nandika, who suffered from insanity and committed many offenses against the community; therefore, this rule was established.

As for those who are not actually offenders within [the community], it is because they lack the intent; as for those who provoke suspicion externally, it is because people do not fully understand them.

Although such a person remains within the boundary, they do not hinder the affairs of the Saṃgha. There are three grades of insanity: the lowest grade appears constantly, while the highest grade does not.

Since it is uncertain whether those who have come will remain for the middle period of the retreat, one must grant the *dharmayukti* (the method of healing through the Dharma), whereby the illness will be cured.
[Section 32: The Method for Receiving the Day; [Section 33: The Method for Granting the *Pravāraṇā* to One Who Has Recovered.
Regarding the third, fourth, and fifth points concerning the formal resolution of the *pravāraṇā* and the binding and releasing of small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*):

at the end of the summer retreat, when traveling together reaches its appointed time, if there is disagreement regarding the required ritual procedures and obstacles arise due to external conditions, it is permissible to temporarily establish a boundary according to the circumstances so that the path for mutual communication remains open. Once this has been done, it may likewise be released;
thus, it is not intended to be permanent or fixed.

35. As stated above regarding the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, if one considers that the *pravāraṇā* has not yet been performed at the end of the summer retreat, how could one [claim] that teachers and friends were traveling together on the road? Reflect upon this. 36.

Regarding the distribution of monastic property: once the Saṃgha has received a gift, one must not privately appropriate it for oneself; first inform them according to the Dharma, and afterwards [distribute it].
According to the rules for distribution:
thirty-six items are gifts obtained by the Saṃgha, which are objects present before the community from the ten directions;
the thirty-seventh is the rule for rewarding those who tend to the sick.
Thirty-eighth: The Method for Distributing the Clothing and Utensils of a Deceased Person. Thirty-ninth:

Regarding the Securing of the Storehouse. As for the property of the Saṃgha, it must be treated with gravity and may not be handled recklessly; therefore, one must entrust the matter to a reliable person and consult them to reach a harmonious and patient agreement.
39. This refers to the separate establishment of a storehouse within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), which still requires a person to guard it;
therefore, there is a subsequent rule regarding the measurement of goods by merchants.

40. Regarding the appointment of a person to guard the storehouse: since the goods belong collectively to all, if they are not kept under mutual supervision and collected, loss will result. Therefore [this rule was established].
41–2: Appointing those to untie and purify the *śuddhasthāna* (pure ground). 43:
Appointing persons to guard the *kaṭhina* (merit-cloth); since it is called "difficult to live by," it is also termed "firm" (*dṛḍha*), being [the basis] for merit.
It is not because [the robe] is small or lacks merit, but because one must maintain harmony and remain within the boundary; thus it is so called.

Regarding the forty-third name, "Difficult to Live" (*durlabha*): the *Chao* states that for a poor person, making a living is difficult, yet by being able to relinquish even a small amount of wealth to enter into this robe, the merit obtained is extremely great.
Furthermore, it is translated as "Firm and Substantial," meaning it is capable of bringing about many robes, and the robes do not fall into ruin.

Regarding "ruined," it may also be called "solid" or "sheltering"; having distinguished these differences, one must entrust [the robe] according to the established rules, for there are subsequent dharmas [to be observed].

As for the forty-fourth point, "entrusting the robe based on merit": since the matter has already been deliberated upon in harmony, it is necessary to entrust it for him to hold and offer with proper decorum;
it must not be entrusted in vain.

Forty-fifth: Regarding the dispatch of a person to perform repentance on behalf of a layperson who has slandered or reviled the Dharma improperly, or toward a lay follower who harbors faith—since even in the mundane world such acts are considered shameful, how much more so for one wearing the monastic robes?

If one were to let the offender go there personally, there would be no way to resolve the conflict; therefore, a person endowed with eight virtues shall be appointed according to the prescribed ritual to go in their stead.
45. Regarding this, because the bhikṣu Śubhadatta had reviled the householder Citta, the Buddha ordered him to go to him to offer an apology.

Since someone was needed to convey his message, he dispatched [the other] to go with him; this is the rule among the seven methods of discipline for prohibiting one from entering the homes of laypeople.
As for the eight qualities: first, being learned; second, being skilled in preaching the Dharma; third, having preached it oneself...

He understands the four [truths], can interpret the intentions of others, receives the words of others, possesses the power of retention, is free from lapses, and understands the discourse on good and evil as well as the distinctions of the Vinaya;
because Ānanda is endowed with these virtues, he is qualified.
Forty-sixth: Regarding the appointment of persons to distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*). When many people are involved in a dispute, various emotional attachments and views arise;

if one does not understand the underlying circumstances and acts indiscriminately or unrighteously, the three types of measurement and five types of examination will fail. Unless there is universal forbearance, the dispute will certainly be difficult to resolve;
therefore, when appointing those endowed with virtue for this task, one should ensure that the dispute is extinguished.
46. Regarding the resolution of disputes by means of the majority vote (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*): one must employ voting sticks (*śalākā*) and apply three methods of evaluation.

The Vinaya states there are three ways of casting the sticks: (1) openly (*prakāśa*), (2) in concealment (*pracchanna*; casting the sticks while covering them with an object), and (3) whispering (*upajjhāyika*; encouraging the voter by whispering in their ear as they cast).
If a senior elder (*sthavira*) or a wise person abides in accordance with the Dharma, the vote should be conducted openly; if they abide in what is contrary to the Dharma, [it should be otherwise].
Regarding the two lower types of legal procedures (*dharmakarma*) performed on the ground: if those who act contrary to the Dharma are numerous, one should generally proceed with caution.

There are five kinds of investigations for what is manifest (*āviṣkaraṇa*): first, the monks reflect that although those acting contrary to the Dharma are numerous within the assembly, their preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and teachers (*ācārya*) are all acting according to the Dharma;
thus, they should proceed with what is manifest. Second, those monks reflect within the assembly... [text continues].
1. Many are unrighteous persons, yet the elders who are wise—those who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātikā—should speak according to the Dharma and act with transparency;
yet the other bhikṣus do not recognize this, and instead mostly speak what is contrary to the Dharma. 2.
Likewise, the preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya) act according to the Dharma and with transparency; yet the other bhikṣus do not recognize this, and it remains as described above.
When wise persons who uphold the Dharma and Vinaya should practice openly, those bhikṣus recognize that this legal dispute involves many who speak according to the Dharma;
thus, while they practice openly, others conceal it through whispered words. In each case, there are the first four phrases, but no fifth phrase.

As for the forty-seven nuns who sent representatives to the assembly of monks to receive ordination: since these individuals possessed such exceptional appearance that they could sway the entire kingdom, and many were skilled in strategic planning, they only hoped to depart from the convent.

When they arrived before the monks to receive the precepts, they encountered difficulties along the way; therefore, the Master established a formal method by which he dispatched messengers to convey his intentions.
The monks bestowed their remote empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and when the messengers returned to inform them, they immediately attained the precepts.
Forty-seven: This concerns the occasion of a nun receiving the precepts by means of a messenger.
Because this nun was so exceptionally beautiful that she could overturn the kingdom of Aḍakāvatī, it is said she "captivated the hearts of the city. The rest is as described below.
Regarding the forty-eight or forty-nine rules concerning nuns who fail to perform the ritual of salutation toward the Sangha:

since the senior monks possess great dignity and formal decorum, it is a grave offense for a nun to treat them with such casual disrespect as to cause disorder within the community and undermine the respect due to those below her. Therefore, a regulation was established to be applied at a distance so that she might reform herself.
If, after having transgressed, she feels shame and regret, she may restore the practice as before by performing the rite of release.
"Forty-eight or forty-nine" refers to those who recklessly fall into error themselves, meaning they fail to recognize their noble station and willingly follow the base and inferior.
"Disorderly conduct among nuns" refers to those who do not maintain dignified decorum and act willfully in evil ways.
Regarding the appointment of fifty bhikṣus to repair dwellings: it is a principle that the monasteries belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions must be repaired when they are dilapidated;
since they have not been maintained and thus fail to remain in a state of continuity, these monks are appointed to manage the repairs, thereby increasing their merit.

Fifty-four: The Buddhas of the ten directions eternally abide throughout the three periods of time in continuous succession; if their dwellings are not repaired or maintained, they will not reach the future.
"Those who possess abundant merit" refers to those who benefit others through their merit.

Fifty-one and fifty-two: Because one maintains the quarters, one provides for both the clergy and the laity; when the dwellings of the Dharma and the Sangha have become old, they must be repaired and renovated, which requires manpower.

Previously, it was merely a modest undertaking that could suffice for enshrinement; now, as it is extremely dilapidated, much manual labor is required, and the matter must be handled with conciliation while granting a temporary suspension based on the circumstances of the timing—thus there are two reasons.

The fifty-first and fifty-second [rules] concerning "thinness" (tānuka) are brief; "to place" (kṣip-) is explained as "to set down. The preceding narrative explains the method of bestowal. Furthermore, below it clarifies the measurement.
Although there is no textual authority in the Vinaya for this specific method, it should be understood that the meaning is complete.

Fifty-three: Regarding the *pātrāvakṣepaṇa* (turning over the bowl) rite—when a lay devotee who has gained faith engages in frivolous debate, their respect and veneration are impaired, which results in self-injury.
Since the faults of failing to exercise restraint have not yet been clarified, this rite is established as a prohibition;
it does not permit coming and going, nor does it allow for the acceptance or use [of requisites]. It is named after the act of overturning a bowl (*pātra-avakṣepaṇa*).
53. The three dharmas of the lower section: This concerns the case where the great Licchavis of Vaiśālī, following the instructions of Mṛgāra, insulted the Arhat Trapusa;
the Buddha then enacted the *pātra-nyubja* (inverted-bowl) rite so that they would no longer have dealings with him.
The Buddha said there are ten kinds of dharmas for which the *pātra-nyubja* rite should be applied: [the first] is to revile and slander a bhikṣu. First, regarding the bhikṣu...
1. Causing harm and diminution; 2. Acting without benefit; 3. Using skillful means to deprive one of a dwelling place; 4. Inciting strife among bhikṣus; 5.
Speaking ill of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha in the presence of bhikṣus; 6–8. Slandering a bhikṣu with groundless charges of impure conduct;
9. Violating a bhikṣuṇī; 10. Among these ten, because most are due to verbal transgressions, they are termed "light."
The term "turning over the bowl" (pātra-nyāma), as in the case of engaging in frivolous debate and so forth, is derived from its metaphorical meaning.
Regarding the fifty-four types of messengers who announce the turning over of the bowl to the household: since the Saṃgha performs this rite itself, the householders might not be aware of it;
if they are not fully informed, there would be no basis for them to repent and reform. Therefore, [the messengers] must be dispatched.
Among the methods for revoking [the bowl], the Vinaya prescribes that Ānanda be dispatched as a messenger to speak with Liśa.

Regarding the fifty-fifth point on the revocation of the *pātra-pratigraha* (the bowl being turned upside down): once he has been informed, he becomes ashamed and uneasy, thinking, "They will surely kill me;
how could they be so lacking in trust? Therefore, one must wait until he offers an apology before the revocation is granted. No person who lacks faith shall be admitted to this rite.

In the Vinaya commentary on the method of resolution, it says: When the householder heard Ānanda’s announcement, he said, "If this is so, it is as good as killing me," whereupon he immediately fainted and fell to the ground;
only after a long time did he regain consciousness. Thus, one knows that only those with profound faith are fit for this dharma.

Regarding the fifty-six rules for the staff and the pouch: because the elderly, the sick, the frail, and the infirm use them to support themselves and maintain their precarious stability, they are permitted by reason of providing such relief.
To possess many and thereby foster arrogance is certain to obstruct harmony; otherwise, one who does not seek the proper method will grasp [the staff] without purpose.
56. Regarding the staff and the net-bag: it is not permitted for those who are young and strong; however, for the elderly and the infirm, the rule is opened [to allow their use]. 57.

Regarding the various methods for assigning people, the distribution of robes, the distribution of food, and other such methods of resolution: although these are clearly indicated in the Vinaya, the texts are mostly incomplete.
Based on the underlying principles, there is further material to be found; therefore, they are here preserved in an abbreviated form.
Among the fifty-seven [rules], those that merely refer generally to others not explicitly mentioned are intended to clarify the meaning of the Vinaya;

specifically, within the section on dwellings, it simply states that when dividing rice gruel or light meals, one who possesses the five qualities should be appointed to divide them—namely, one who is free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, and who knows what may be divided and what may not.
It is unreasonable to appoint someone arbitrarily; there must necessarily be a formal assembly (*saṃgha*).

Furthermore, regarding the dharmas mentioned previously, many of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) lack their corresponding methods of liberation (*vimukti*). Since liberation exists in dependence upon fetters, how could there be liberation without them?
Thus, we know that the text is merely abbreviated and need not be doubted.
Subsequently, it clearly sets forth the thirty-eight dharmas of the four noble truths.

Regarding the initial admonition against those who would split the Saṃgha by establishing five heterodox dharmas to replace the four authentic reliances, thereby defiling the world and leading the ignorant into confusion and disorder:
if one does not admonish them to clarify right from wrong, the matter will remain obscure and the Dharma will likewise fade into concealment.

Regarding the first four of the four "White" [announcements], they correspond to the four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. Regarding the latter four, which concern the precept against admonishing [Devadatta] when he persists in his refusal:

the five heterodox practices [proposed by Devadatta] were: (1) begging for food, (2) wearing robes made of refuse rags, (3) sitting in the open air, (4) not consuming butter or salt, and (5) not eating fish or meat.
Since these were all intended to be observed as long as one lived, they were heterodox practices; "to substitute" them means to abolish them.
The four correct reliances are briefly indicated below in the section on the "Matters of Receiving Precepts.

Second, regarding those who assist in causing a schism in the Saṃgha: one should admonish the leader of the schism; as for the associates, since their assistance differs from that of the leader, they are not subject to the same method of admonition.

Because the purpose is to provide instruction and persuasion so that the Saṃgha may cease [the conflict], this rule was established to cut off external support; therefore, the leader and the associates are divided into two categories.

Within these two [categories], there are three: namely, those who have heard and attained [the Dharma], and so forth; the four types of companion bhikṣus assist Devadatta by exhorting the Saṃgha not to admonish him, thereby bringing it to rest.
This refers to providing support and protection. The following section provides a double conclusion.

Those who slander others after being expelled following a threefold admonition must be banished because they defile the common people and cause confusion between right and wrong; thus, they are cast out to clear away the net of darkness.

However, since these six individuals committed the same offense yet their conduct in coming and going was contradictory, and two of them did not repent, it was necessary to act according to the Dharma.
Because they relied on this to slander [the Sangha] in return, they were admonished so that they might understand that the Sangha does not involve itself in private partiality.
Among the three cases, Aśvaka and others were living in the village of Kollāga; their defiled conduct brought reproach upon the family.
The Buddha commanded Śāriputra to go and expel them. Two of them came to repent, while two fled. Those who did not repent encountered expulsion and subsequently raised slanderous accusations.

Regarding the four admonitions for those of evil character: since individuals of middle or superior capacity can be instructed in higher teachings by virtuous friends, yet they may refuse to comply and act contrary to them, the Sangha is enjoined to offer formal admonition;
to violate this constitutes an offense.
Regarding the four [categories], it is because Chanda was of evil character and rejected the Sangha’s admonition that this dharma was added for him.
The two phrases beginning with "among people" are cited from the *Lunyu* (Analects), which states: "Those of middle capacity cannot be spoken to using the language of those of superior capacity."
