Now, in the initial phrase of this section, [the author] provisionally grants [the opponent's view]; in the subsequent phrase, he refutes it by dismantling their division of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they fail to distinguish between the agent and the object;

thus it is said, "it is universally confused. Below, under the heading "The Sublime," he demonstrates the correct principle: that which is recorded in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) is precisely the presentation of the specific dharma to be performed; since each dharma is distinct, they do not intermingle.

By briefly citing the procedures for receiving [ordination] and performing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), the remainder may be understood by analogy. From "It exists of its own accord" below... [is the next section].
Furthermore, regarding the fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi) concerning persons, robes, and illness, and the rule for being separated from one’s robe (nissaggiya-pācittiya):

these two are combined. Thus, when it says "one who holds a complete tally," this constitutes a full permutation. The *Mūla-vinaya*, in the section on the settlement of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), states: "When distributing tallies, there should be those who say:
'One who speaks thus shall hold a complete tally; one who speaks thus shall hold a broken tally. (The *Vinaya* does not provide the full text, but merely indicates the circumstances. As such...
That which is speech is the dharma, while that which is the person is the matter; is this not so?
Furthermore, when one extends the days for the *prātimokṣa* (self-restraint) to cultivate the Path, the "days" are the matter and the "self-restraint" is the dharma.
To further investigate this by way of other dharmas, I have briefly provided a diagrammatic illustration to distinguish between the agent and the object.

Regarding "separation and combination": for instance, in the methods for repenting offenses, those belonging to different categories are not treated together, whereas multiple offenses within the same category may be either separated or combined as appropriate;
other matters are to be understood by applying this principle through careful consideration.

Next, regarding the explanation of separation and combination: for the time being, this is based on the principle that expiating offenses is separated from other categories, whereas harmonizing with the same category involves both separation and combination.

Furthermore, cases such as receiving the precepts where many people receive them together on the same day, or combining multiple conditions, are all to be explained according to these same principles.
The phrase "relying on prior measurement" means that one should be exhorted to know [the situation] early, rather than making judgments of praise or blame only when faced with the matter.
Among the three points, being exhorted to know early refers to weighing the conditions; "praise or blame" refers to what is appropriate or inappropriate.
The second is the locus upon which the Dharma arises.

First, one relies on the scriptural authority, and subsequently seeks it through its meaning. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the explanation establishes that the place where the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) arises must necessarily be within the "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) and "natural ground.
Why is this so? For the monastic legal framework (*saṃgha-dharmavinaya*) arises...

Regarding the method for returning [the *karmavācanā*] to the stage of the Dharma: if one has previously failed to apply the ritual in accordance with the prescribed rules, then according to the evidence of the principles, when the matter has already arrived and one intends to perform the *pravāraṇā*, one should first establish the boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Although there is no textual evidence for this based on the original method, it serves as a standard of practice.
The first section of the commentary on the "Origin of the Two Dharmas" is divided into two parts: first, the marking of the textual divisions;

second, the sequential citation and explanation. Regarding the first, the textual division: because the noble dharmas have not yet been added, it is said that "the ground is weak" while "monastic affairs are powerful," and thus [the former] cannot prevail.
This is the meaning explained below. Regarding the second, the sequential citation and explanation: this passage cites the *Pravāraṇā* (invitation) discourse.

The small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) can be verified through the communal legal procedures; it is not permitted for the fundamental method to arise spontaneously. The "fundamental method" refers to the rules of the original Vinaya collection:

when there is no explicit text within one's own school but there is an underlying principle, one must resolve the matter using that principle. If one follows the five types of formal acts (*pañcakarmāṇi*), the requirement for a boundary is also a clear basis;
however, because this is not the primary intent [of the present discussion], it is said that there is none.

The statement that there are two types of locations (*sthāna*) reveals the distinction between the universal and the restricted; it does not mean that the monastic laws (*saṃghadharma*) exist only on the ground of formal boundaries (*dharmabhūmi*).

This single dharma of establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*) is not a dharma of the formal ritual sphere (*karmabhūmi*). For this reason, as a provisional basis for the initial establishment, this [location] was opened to serve as the locus of the school's doctrine.

If it were not so established naturally, subsequent communal dharmas would have no basis for their application. Thus, this *karma* (ritual act) is specifically distinguished from others, just as in the case of receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*).

Hearing the Dharma is not an obstacle, and so forth; all other matters may be understood by analogy as residing within the *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the passage or blockage of the two realms—of persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—by others, it is as described above.

The next section has two parts: first, a general indication, and second, a detailed explanation of what follows. The former clarifies the seven methods for establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) among the various dharmas.
Regarding the *dharmābhijñā* (non-obstruction of the Dharma), as described in the text, the initial matter of receiving the hearing of the Dharma is largely similar to other dharmas.

Because it does not involve natural non-obstruction (*svabhāvāpratibandha*) and is established through formal boundaries (*sīmābandha*), the subsequent cases can be understood by analogy. Later, in clarifying the distinct dharmas, the single dharma of receiving the consent (*chanda*) does not involve natural non-obstruction;
all others are obtained in both ways. This is the general meaning as seen together.

Regarding the third method for assembling the Saṃgha: for now, following the Western Indic manuscript, which lacks formal topical divisions, I shall explain it by citing the various textual passages as they appear.
Among the three ways of assembling the Saṃgha, the initial heading "following the Western Indic" indicates that in that land, when composing treatises to explain the Sūtras and Vinaya, they merely...
From the extensive opening sections down to the explanations of the text, there are no formal topical divisions; this present work follows that model, which represents a variation in composition.
This is why the seat is first spread and the gong is struck afterward: because the assembly gathers immediately upon hearing the sound, while the seats remain unspread as they wait.
To be filled with despondency and distress is not the way to fulfill one's duties; it is essential that the seating order be established beforehand.

In the first section of the commentary on the *Niedi* (the formal announcement), "despondency and distress" describes a state of mental agitation and vexation. Since the assembly is already displeased, this is certainly not in accord with the intent of providing guidance through the Dharma.
Regarding the *gandi*: according to the Sanskrit phonology, *gandi* means "stone chime" (*qing*) in Chinese, though it is also called a "bell.
It is actually made of two materials, bronze or stone; thus the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that it is used according to whatever sounds forth.

The intent is to summon the Sangha by the sound of its ringing. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Beating the drum to warn the soldiers, and sounding the *gandi* to assemble the multitude—this is the Dharma of the world."

In the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, when summoning the Saṃgha, there are seven signs that do not depart from sound and form; yet if they still do not come despite the proclamation, one may further investigate them—the intent of which can be seen therein.

Next, regarding the section on the *ghanṭā* (bell), it is called by its literal name; however, according to the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Phonetics), one must then transform the pronunciation. As for "today's people,"... [text ends]... one person.
In general, the character *chui* (槌) has been changed to *zhi* (稚), and it is commonly called "dì" (地). Without having consulted the Sūtras or Vinaya, people have arbitrarily altered the text;
this is explained in detail below in the *Shuochao* (疏鈔) and *Jiji* (記記). Sometimes it is written simply as *chui*; this is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term.

It applies to both bells (*zhong*) and chimes (*qing*), which are made of metal or stone. "Metal" refers to copper and iron. According to the *Wufen lü* (五分律), they may sound at will and need not necessarily be of metal or stone, as listed in the commentary.
In *nirvāṇa*, how could there be such things as striking the gong to assemble the saṃgha, beating the solemn drum, blowing the conch to warn the soldiers, or knowing the time?
These are called "Dharma" and "worldly speech," but they are merely matters of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). In the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, there are seven signs:

measuring the shadow, splitting bamboo, producing smoke, blowing the conch, beating the drum, striking the *gandī* gong, and striking the ground, when one calls out, "Venerable sirs, let us perform the *poṣadha*."

Regarding the timing and other criteria, according to the text there are eight [rules]: numbers one, eight, and three pertain to form (*rūpa*); the remainder all belong to sound (*śabda*). These collectively constitute the "proclamation" (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
As the Vinaya text states, when an old resident or a *kappiya-kāraka* of lower status is ordered to strike, this is a regulation for summoning the Saṃgha;
it is not something to be performed by one who is not fully ordained. Certainly, two persons must be present before assistance is permitted.
Among the three, the lower rank refers to the *śrāmaṇera*, while the full path refers to the *bhikṣu*. First, this is what has been assembled;
second, the ritual procedures are not redundant because there is no one to hear the assistance—this is the opening of the conditions.

Regarding the "three strikes" (*sāntōn*): this does not refer to three single downward strokes. It refers to the sequence from the subtle-thick (*wei-chou*) to the thin (*xi-zhu*), after which the sound has ceased;
one then adds three more strikes, hence the name.

Regarding the four [types of striking], the general method for ringing the bell is as follows: first, perform ten "empty" strokes, which constitute the subtle-thick; from the eleventh stroke onward...
As the intervals gradually become wider, this refers to "rarefied striking. Upon reaching the thirty-seventh stroke, strike three slow blows to signify the gathering of the Three Vehicles;
for regular morning and evening *zhāi* lectures, one should follow this method. The detailed procedure for the long striking during morning and evening services is as explained in the *Chao*.
The *Āgama* Sūtras state that those who hear the sound and cease their suffering do so because karmic actions are either determinate or indeterminate; thus, suffering may either cease or not cease.

If an action performed is determinate, it cannot be avoided even by a noble one (*ārya*). If an action is indeterminate, it will be experienced when conditions (*pratyaya*) are present, but it ceases when conditions are absent.
In this case, the "sinner" encounters goodness as the cause, while the "beater" establishes a vow as the condition; therefore, the sound is transmitted.
The cessation of suffering naturally evokes a response.

Among these five points, the *Zhujing* (Commentary on the Scriptures) cites the *Dharmatara-avadāna* (付法藏傳), which relates how King Kanishka fell into the form of a fish and suffered; upon hearing the sound of a bell, his pain ceased.
He sent word that the bells should be struck loudly, for such was the profound spiritual resonance. Thus, the *Āgama* is cited to clarify the reason for this intensity.
When the mind proceeds from beginning to end without interruption, it constitutes determinate karma (*niyata-karma*); if there is even slight regret in the interim, it is indeterminate.

Because the characteristics of the fruit of determinate karma have already been established, the Noble Ones cannot avoid them; because the force of the cause of indeterminate karma is still weak, it can be subverted by external conditions.

If this were so, one might ask: "Should not the karma of King Kṛkin be indeterminate? The answer is: since it is a projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), it is determinate, and therefore he fell into [hell] forever.

Because the ripening karma (*vipāka-karma*) regarding fish is not fixed, it may be suspended when encountering the right conditions. As for the offender who previously possessed wholesome causes, it was only by chance that they encountered a well-intentioned striker;
thus, they now make a vow, and through this vow, there is a hidden resonance with the Dharma. If one encounters such a circumstance, one should apply oneself with skillful care.
If one follows this text, the case of a bhikṣu striking himself contradicts the previous [case]. The Vinaya response is based on the matter of convening the Saṃgha.
One must descend to the level of the assembly to transmit [the teachings] for the sake of saving sentient beings; therefore, this is modeled after the Great Monks (bhikṣus).
Regarding the number of pestles clarified in the *Vinaya-vidhi-sūtra*, they are largely not practiced today, and thus the Dharma has fallen to the ground.

However, when facing actual matters, one should deliberate and measure the urgency of the timing; externally, this will inspire faith and extinguish suffering, while internally, it ensures there is no empty sound in the proclamation. If it is done in this way, it is acceptable.

Furthermore, regarding the number of pestles (*mudgara*) within the six types of scriptures, they are fully detailed in the *Chaoji* (Notes on the Excerpts). Now, below this, we shall refute worldly practices;

however, what follows below merely indicates the regulations for those who would measure [the space], so that one may act according to the circumstances—whether the monastery is large or small, the number of monks is few or many, or the timing of the conditions is relaxed or urgent.

It is not necessary to rely strictly on the scriptures; if one achieves merit externally and realizes its function internally, such that both internal and external aspects are supported, the endeavor will not be in vain.

As for why the treatises do not permit mutual substitution [of roles], it is because the monastic law establishes fixed standards; to arbitrarily alter them would disrupt the social order, and since the dharma itself would thus be contravened, it is forbidden.

Because such usage is contrary to principle, one must always remain settled in the practice. If one wishes to change it, one must first assemble the resident monks with the original instrument and inform them of the intention before making the alteration.

Should one wish to change it again later, one must summon them as before. By proceeding in this manner through successive changes, although the practice has been modified, it remains fundamentally consistent with the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*) from beginning to end.
If, however, two bells ring alternately at a single residence, causing the preceding and succeeding sounds to intermingle, it is improper.

"Disorder" is not termed "constant"; it follows four matters, which constitute stealing from the *Saṃghika* [monastic community]. Because the *saṃgha* and the individual are one, there is no disorder; there is no dharma of division or distinction.

Among the seven [sections], the first clarifies the intent of the regulation; the second clarifies the categories; the third necessarily shows the method of exchange; and the fourth reveals the transgressions.
Regarding this characteristic: there are people in the present age who claim that those who "know" the bell speak pure language, while those who strike the bell speak impure language.
Fundamentally, this "knowing" is pure in itself; it does not exist for the sake of causing others to act, which is why it is called "knowing. The bell, however, is not like this.

Since this practice is universally applicable to both oneself and others, and there is no specific characteristic of its seed-lineage, why should one avoid it? The statement in our own school regarding "striking" refers to a matter that is extremely common;

humans, animals, and even insentient objects all have their respective precepts, so it may also be changed to "knowing for the sake of purity. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of striking the *gandī* and *kettledrum*;

the *Āgamas* speak of beating the *gandī*; the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* speaks of striking three times; and in the sutras, the clashing of bells and drums is likewise used for the purpose of making known [the time].

The term "pure" (jing) implies that it serves a distinct purpose; thus, when the translation committees rendered this according to a single corresponding term in this land, they invariably translated it as "an object touched and a sound produced.
Therefore, one should know that although the word "bell" (zhong) is not a grave offense, it is a great taboo for those who understand the Dharma.

Third, the refutation of excessive applications within the section on "Refuting Excessive Applications": First, citing the excessive application, it is said that when instructing others, one must say "know the bell" and not "strike the bell.

Second, the formal refutation has four parts: first, showing that the pure basis of knowledge is established as a single rule for bhikṣus, whereby they themselves may not perform such acts as digging or damaging coins and treasures;
second, [showing] that there are living seeds and characteristics, which is restricted [to specific cases].

Regarding "destroying" and "producing," these two precepts are the opposite of this meaning; there is no need for them here. Next, the following passage cites other precepts by way of example and objection:

"Regarding humans and animals"—striking a *bhikṣu* constitutes a *thullaccaya*, while striking an animal constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding "inanimate objects"—striking old clothes, etc., is a *dukkaṭa*.

The three [preceding] citations demonstrate that while the actions of beating, striking, hitting, and clashing are identical, the terminology differs; they should be translated according to their specific usage.
For this reason, the four subsequent admonitions concern matters that, while not constituting a major violation of the Dharma, pertain deeply to ignorance;
since all who belong to the stream of the Sangha must observe these, they require avoidance.
Fourth, regarding the delimitation of the boundary for the assembly of monks: the purpose of establishing a boundary is to encompass the Sangha according to its specific limits.
These various forms of discord are all expedients for the purpose of relinquishing the self.

For ordinary beings bound by fetters, the inversion of the self (*ātma-viparyāsa*) burns fiercely; therefore, discord increases while harmony gradually subsides.
Because the principle is realized through phenomena, the absence of a self in dharmas is the Buddha’s skillful means; thus it is called a "strategic plan" (*upāya-kauśalya*).
In the text, two realms are first presented and subsequently explained individually.

In the response, the restriction on persons is established to prevent reproach; since gathering from outside would be of no avail if such a restriction were required, and since there is no difficulty regarding the large boundary itself, it is said that they are not the same.

Within the sphere of the three realms of existence (*traidhātuka*), the principle that matters are naturally gathered within their respective domains is easy to understand; however, this [text] specifically restricts itself to demonstrating the distinct characteristics of collective gathering.

however, if a *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) is performed, both those inside and outside are included. This is done to maintain the discipline of the Saṃgha, ensuring that both those within and without equally honor it; this is not permitted otherwise.
To evade [the formal assembly] and even seek out numerous recitations upon seeing signs of a boundary (sīmā) outside [the monastery] is precisely what is meant by this.

In the commentary on the response, the first phrase provides a general indication, while the subsequent sections provide a detailed explanation regarding the two conditions of communal and individual [assemblies], as well as the two modes of gathering—general and restricted.
Furthermore, the *Bhikṣu-vinaya-śīla-grantha* (Sectarian Vinaya on the Recitation of Precepts) states: "At that time... [The text continues: "...there was a time when... [and so forth].

Seeing them, they did not seek their presence and proceeded to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"The ritual is valid, but there is an offense regarding the recitation of the *poṣadha*. (First point: If, having seen them, one seeks them out, but having sought them out, does not call them, yet proceeds to perform the ritual and recite the *poṣadha*, there is an offense."

(Second sentence: If, having seen [the guest monks], one seeks them out, and having sought them out, one calls them, the *karmavācanā* for the *poṣadha* is accomplished without fault. (Third sentence: The same applies to hearing or suspecting [their presence].

or because the status of residents and guests may change, leading to false reports regarding established restrictions; therefore, one must assemble everyone first and inquire thoroughly into the circumstances to avoid any ambiguity.
If those who fall into such confusion inevitably base their actions on what is not the Dharma, they will surely defile subsequent conditions;

if the precepts are received in vain, the sacred Dharma is lost, and both self and others fall into deep ruin—this is something deeply worthy of reflection. These words are easy to say now, but difficult to alter when the time comes.

Next, regarding the ancient interpretations: this [section] concerns the private conditions (*pratyaya*) and the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmā*). It is not necessarily the case that there must be a collective assembly;

provided there is no doubt or confusion, it is unnecessary. First, the reason for requiring a collective assembly is stated. The phrase "if one does not distinguish the characteristics" refers to the first part;
the subsequent phrase, "the fundamental conclusion deviates from the Dharma," clarifies the error of not inquiring about the boundary, which results in failing to emerge [from the offense].
These two [cases] necessarily possess this condition. Having explained them, the re-binding is not the same as in the present age;

regardless of whether one was previously bound or not, there is uniformly an obstacle to doubt. Please examine this text, for it is sufficient to know that the transmission has been erroneous and confused. As for the subsequent condition, it applies generally to all communal dharmas (*saṃghakarma*);
yet, because the act of receiving the dharma (*upasaṃpadā*) is especially grave, it is mentioned separately. This statement regarding "ease" refers to the presiding [officer].
Because the formal act of binding [the boundary] is not difficult, it is hard to alter at the last moment; furthermore, because receiving [the precepts] again is not easy. Question:
As stated previously regarding the fourfold assembly for the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā), is there also an assembly within the Precept Platform (śīla-maṇḍala)? Answer:

Within the platform, two assemblies are also held for the purpose of declaring the *pravāraṇā*. This is as permitted by way of exceptional circumstances, as explained further in the *Sīmā-bandha* (Binding the Boundary) section.

Next, regarding the question on the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept boundary), following the precedent of the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), there are four types of assemblies (*saṃnipāta*). The answer states that there are two assemblies;
this refers to the two assemblies of the "universal" and the "restricted," or it may be that the character "two" (*liǎng*) is an error for "four" (*sì*).

Regarding the fourfold classification of natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*), there is no specific textual passage in our own school (*mūla-nikāya*) for this particular section; however, the four names found throughout the various Vinayas are listed here, and their respective explanations may be understood from those sources.

Within the first category of natural boundaries, the precept on stealing (*adattādāna*) in our own school contains three types of small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*): the village boundary (*grāma-sīmā*), the monastery boundary (*ārāma-sīmā*), and the *araṇya* (wilderness) boundary.
If one says that the path of practice is merely non-apparent and therefore called "non-existent," this is stated within the texts of the various schools themselves.

universal (sāmānya) and particular (viśeṣa)— the commentary on the designation explains that "universal" means that which cannot be differentiated, while "particular" means that which can be differentiated.

Regarding that which is "initially undifferentiable": this may refer to cases where the coming and going of the *saṃgha* makes it difficult to know [the boundaries], or to cases where the location is so scattered that its limits cannot be discerned.

Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the boundaries of cities, towns, or villages are dispersed and chaotic such that they cannot be known, one shall take five cubits as a bow (*dhanus*), plant one tree every seven bows, and establish the measure by taking seven trees as the interval between them."

Although there are differences in the ritual procedures, each member of the assembly does not commit an offense individually; however, when measured by their respective spatial boundaries, there are six intervals totaling sixty-three paces.
It is impossible to divide the first section into two parts: first, the enumeration of the characteristics, which consists of two types—the person and the location—which cannot be separated.
Whether [the factors] are simultaneous or mutually concurrent, they are all subsumed under this; since both can be divided, they belong to the latter category.

Therefore, the passage cited below refers exclusively to the meaning of the "location" (*sthāna*), yet it must necessarily include the "person" (*pudgala*). This is because when a Brahmin asked about the method for planting trees, the Buddha said:
"Measure with a bow of five cubits; plant one tree every seven bows, which will cause the roots and trunk to be firm and stable."
When the saplings had grown to the point where they no longer obstructed one another, Upāli addressed the Buddha: "I have already heard the measurements for planting trees.

Now I ask again: if there is a location such as a city, town, or village where the boundaries cannot be discerned, and one wishes to perform a *karmavācanā*, how far apart should the monks be so that the assembly remains distinct and each member can see the others, thereby ensuring the rite is accomplished without the fault of *pṛthagbhāva* (separateness)?"

In the aforementioned passage from the *Saṃyuktāgama*, the preceding section consists of the questions, while the following section comprises the Buddha’s answers: five cubits (*hasta*) equal nine feet;
seven bow-lengths (*dhanus*) equal sixty-three feet; and one tree [interval] equals ten and a half paces (*pada*).
The former claim that it is "seventy-three paces and a half" is an erroneous calculation of seven intervals.

In the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, it states that "seven trees have six intervals," just as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, where the boundary of a robe is eight trees with intervals between them.
How can it be that while the masters calculate the robe boundary as having only seven intervals, the monastic boundary consists of seven trees rather than six intervals?
In the initial calculation of the limits for the steps, the first section contains an error of ten and a half steps per period; hence it is called "mistaken.
Below, according to that commentary, one should reconcile this with the decision on the *araṇya* robe boundary within this same school to realize that [the former] was indeed in error.

others say that planting trees in a circle is like the halo of the moon, and thus there are seven bays. Furthermore, they change "Saṃghāṭī" to "eight trees.
Such self-indulgent and forced interpretations are excessive; where is there a tree that can be measured by the dimensions of a tree?
The Vinaya relies on worldly conventions to provisionally manifest [the truth].
In the first section of the following division, he first cites their tenets and then lists three types. The first two are shifting calculations; the last one is a deceptive claim.
Regarding the halo around the moon, it is called a "halo" (*pariveṣa*). Below this, there is a general refutation: the first two lines rebuke their emotional attachments, while the next two lines...
The two lines showing that the current measurement does not necessarily require being under a tree clarify the reason for relying on trees as the basis for the original Vinaya rules;
"borrowing" (假) here means "to take on loan" (借).
As it is so with the seven intermediate trees where the two assemblies perform monastic affairs at both ends facing one another, so too is it with the four directions across the length and breadth.
The *Lüji* (Collection of Precedents) states that because the two bodies [of the Buddha] are known to be distinct, a tree is used as the limit.
If one takes the appropriate portion, it is all halved; thus, the boundary of one's own share is only thirty-one paces and a half.

However, since the substance of the boundary is difficult to discern, the characteristics of the divisions are made broad, as clearly shown in the *Shu* (Commentary). Once this case is understood, the other instances of natural boundaries—whether large or small—are exceptional cases.
Both the general and specific cases are calculated as half [a *bu*].

Among the three [measures], there are two initial determinations of square and round; if there were no distinct boundaries for the substance, then the square would necessarily be circular and the pointed or slanted would be indeterminate.

Half belongs to the deep protection (*gupti*) and cannot be immediately pointed out; for the details, see the "Section on Assembling the Sangha" (*saṃgha-saṃnipāta*) in the *Vinayavibhāṣā*.

Below this, the principle applies generally across the six characteristics (*ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa*); with the exception of divisible clusters (*vibhajya-rāśi*), all others are halved. For example, in the case of a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) five *li* away, each person has two and a half *li*.
This is the general rule for the deep protection when taken together; the specific division into two parts is the restricted rule. Question: Now...
If one assembles the Sangha, the answer may depend on whether the case is general or specific. If there are no people present, it is sufficient to rely on the specific;

If this is so, even if someone should come who lies outside my own domain, logically there should be no fault. Answer: Although the person is outside the boundary, they have already encroached upon my own sphere.

That Vinaya further states that regarding the "village boundary" (*grāma-sīman*), even if the distance between points is not great, the area reached by footprints is also termed a "boundary.
