Regarding the two characters "ruò'ěr" (若爾) within the "Difficulties," they refer back to the preceding section and are categorized as part of the initial division of the response.

This first portion merely provides an evaluation of the Eightfold Path; the subsequent section, beginning with "chànggào xíng" (唱告行), arranges them in sequence. If one follows the vertical headings, this belongs to the third [section];
if one relies on the characteristics of the recitation, it must belong to the eighth. Therefore, this single condition is not fixed in its position, occurring either earlier or later.

Second, regarding the constant gathering of requisites: when the *zizhi* (invitation for criticism) is announced, items such as counting sticks (*śalākā*), flowers, and warm water are placed in the fourth row;
the text is rearranged so that the fourth becomes the fifth. The rest are to be sought according to one's own judgment, generally following the hierarchy of seniority.

Regarding the second section on "Constant Concentration," the initial presentation of the stages follows the *Jìshǒu shèngjiào yòngchāo* (Monastic Manual for the Use of Implements), as one begins by advancing the tally-sticks and water only after the monks have assembled in the hall;

thus, it belongs to the fourth stage. However, because the current practice often involves preparations in advance, it deviates from the proper sequence. The remaining cases below follow this same principle: all dharmas are subject to circumstances, and their order—whether preceding or following—is not fixed.

Regarding matters that violate or disturb private affairs, one must report the specific location regardless of whether the parties involved are laypeople or monastics, monks or nuns; they must then be either disciplined or regulated.

There must never be a request for leniency based on general expectations. Whether the petitioner or the respondent is acting against the grain of propriety, one need only ensure that the legal procedures are known and that a person of wisdom reports the matter, having verified the facts through careful investigation, so that the legal action may be applied accordingly.
In the first section of the "Private Circumstances Contrary to Sentiment" (私緣違情), the monks and nuns are treated as distinct categories within the path;

furthermore, śrāmaṇeras are included, such as in the cases of abandoning a nun who has violated her precepts or the formal admonition of a śrāmaṇera—both of which are matters contrary to sentiment. When an intelligent person reports these matters, it also falls under the fourth category.
If that is so, why is the legal procedure (*saṃghakarma*) of the Saṃgha called a "private matter"? Answer: Because the Saṃgha acts as the primary condition, it brings benefit to all;

it either subdues [the offender] or quells heterodox doubts. Once the formal act has been performed, one requests the Saṃgha for its dissolution. Since this is not a command issued by the Saṃgha, in principle it is categorized as a private matter.
In the subsequent section of the response, although the capacity to administer [the rite] is performed by the Saṃgha, it is initially described as private;

the "subduing" refers to disciplinary punishment, while the "stopping of heterodoxy" refers to various admonitions. Since the subsequent passage indicates the purpose for which it is performed, the request for release from it reveals its private nature.
Second, regarding matters that accord with one's own inclinations and require formal begging (*jñapti*): these may sometimes exist or not, as the textual descriptions are numerous;

however, for matters that pertain exclusively to oneself and do not involve the *saṃgha*, one must certainly employ the formal act of begging, such as when receiving the ritual of confession and absolution (*pāpadeśanā-vimocana*). Second, regarding being appointed by the *saṃgha* to perform duties: one may either announce it through a formal motion (*jñapti*) or deliberate for oneself;
it is not strictly necessary to employ the formal act of begging, though one may simply do so.

Regarding the first section of the "Conforming to Sentiments" (shunqing), the initial part consists of two sub-sections: first, citing and explaining [the text]; second, enumerating the characteristics, which refers to whether one is requesting or not.

"Self-measurement by the proclaimer" (bai ziliang) means that the preceptor (*śikṣācārya*) or the presiding master of confession (*karmavācanā-ācārya*) acts as the proclaimer; "proclaimer" (*bai*) refers to the one who requests, meaning that prior to the *karmavācanā*, one must first inform the assembly, which is equivalent to making a formal request.
If that is so, one might ask: "When appointing an official for the sake of the Saṃgha, how can it be considered a private matter? The answer is that the preceding conditions are not fixed;

if one were to solicit [the appointment] arbitrarily, the matter would likely be discordant. Since the specific person is listed within the formal text of the Saṃgha, and their name has been formally recorded, how can this be called private?
Therefore, it is said that in the formal declaration (*jñapti*), the name of the Saṃgha itself is recorded; all other matters may be inferred accordingly. Is this not a great mirror of discernment?

In the initial section of the response, it is first explained that there was no formal request to appoint a person to select those of virtue; because the sentiments of the assembly were not yet clear, it is said that "the location is not fixed.
Next, the private matters are revealed, and below, the *śikṣamāṇā-kaṭhina-utsarga* (the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe) is cited as a point of comparison.

Since the Sangha’s private distribution is judged according to this precedent, it is stated that "all other communal dharmas" are to be determined in the same way. Thus, the phrase "and the rest" is used.
Regarding the ninth inquiry into the sequence of events:
the reason it must be asked is that since the great assembly has gathered in detail, there is a basis for the discourse;

because the sentiments of harmonious admonition require that the meaning be proclaimed and made manifest, the conditions are presented and the intent of the original collection is set forth according to the text.
In the first section of the ninth commentary, the introductory text raises a question regarding the intent of the "collection" (saṃgraha) in contrast to the preceding phrase;

this corresponds to the subsequent sentence. Regarding the fact that the matter contains both general and specific aspects: for example, in the four dharmas of receiving the precepts, one must specifically ask repeatedly; however, if discussed generally, they may simply be subsumed under one category.

This is because the words do not simultaneously describe multiple matters, and since events do not arise in a redundant manner, they necessarily depend on what precedes and follows. Even if there are general and specific aspects, they merely cease [to apply].
This single statement must not be interpreted differently.

In the first section of the following division, the explanation of the "matter" (vastu) encompasses both the general and the specific; since the specific is easily understood, only the general is clarified.

This is not because they are being described simultaneously—as in the case of receiving the four dharmas, where they cannot be cited in full—nor because the matter does not arise repeatedly. Rather, it is because practice requires a sequential order.
Because it can be performed all at once; thus, the subsequent explanation consists of a single question regarding all *karmas*, whether general or specific, and there is no difference in the wording.
Tenth, as for the answer concerning the dharmas to be accomplished:
When a question is posed before him, there is no room for prolonged silence; therefore, he immediately answers it as a specific *karmavācanā*.
In the tenth response-text, the character "some" (*mǒu*) serves as a general placeholder for all administrative duties.

Within these texts, matters follow a sequence of priority; below, the procedure for the *poṣadha* is cited, as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "When the Saṃgha recites the *poṣadha*, there is further..."
When a matter arises, one must first perform this action and only then recite the *Poṣadha*.

As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when it was time to recite the *Pravāraṇā*, if there were those who raised objections or censures, one had to first apply the formal legal procedure (*dharma*) and only then recite the *Pravāraṇā*. By means of these two regulations, the Saṃgha remains unshakable.

If one were to recite the *Pravāraṇā* first and only then deal with those who raise objections, since they would be acting against individuals, harmony would likely not be maintained; therefore, this [procedure] is established here.
In the first section of the preceding analysis, the two cited passages must be understood as referring to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, which can be divided into a prior and subsequent sequence;

otherwise, there is no basis for such a division. Alternatively, it may be explained according to the principles of the person who performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*), the robe, the food, and the boundary (*sīmā*), as these are the reasons why the latter two [passages] emerge.

Regarding the distinction between the general and the specific in the conditions for the Dharma (*dharmapratyaya*), there are several types. First, when a single matter is answered with multiple responses, this is "specific," as in the three *śukravācanas* and one *karmavācana* for receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*).
Second, when multiple matters are answered with a single response, this is "general," as in the forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Third, when multiple matters are answered with separate responses, this is "specific," as in the individual confession for each offense when one has committed multiple *pāyattikas*. Fourth, when a single matter is answered with a single response, this is "general."

This is like the first case of receiving the precepts: although many people are involved, there are four aspects regarding the dharma. At dawn, a single response suffices for the entire duration until nightfall, and the ritual is accomplished.
Alternatively, one may respond collectively to a series of matters, as when one intends to perform multiple rites at a single sitting;

one should immediately respond by saying, "The *kaṭhina* robe-ritual" and "the food-ritual. Although the response is given once, it is logically permissible to perform the subsequent actions individually.
There is no hindrance to other ritual procedures; one response may serve as a standard for understanding all that has been practiced by this school thus far.

Next, regarding the section on receiving the confession (*poṣadha*), the initial passage first provides a general heading, followed by five specific items listed below: the first and fourth concern the general and specific aspects of receiving the precepts;

the second and third concern the general and specific aspects of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); and [the remaining items concern] the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), the virtuous robe (*guṇavastuka-cīvara*), and the property of the deceased.

However, when dealing with many dharmas, there are generally both general and specific categories. The fifth [category], which involves cumulative matters, is the specific; the first response serves as the general.

The preceding four constitute two single-membered propositions, while this [fifth] constitutes the proposition of "both" and the proposition of "neither. It is impossible to establish a separate [category] for itself.

The remaining items below refer to various single dharmas that possess only specificity and lack generality, such as the examples of precepts, receiving days, and training, which are indicated throughout the upper and lower sections.
Regarding the meaning of the different states produced by present actions in subsequent lives:

some say that since the Dharma is applied precisely to the specific characteristics and causes at hand, how could there be any universal application? Once one has received the fourfold degrees of ordination, the questions and answers before and after follow the inquiry;

as the matters and meanings are harmonized according to the question, how could there be a morning inquiry followed by an evening response, or a practice that persists regardless of its immediate utility?
Since there is an interval of separation, how could they be in direct contact? Therefore, the former interpretation is incorrect.
In the first section of the "Refutation of Divergent Views," this master establishes his own thesis to set aside the previous general response.

Now, [I] explain that since there is no scriptural injunction for either case, it is not permissible to establish a divergent view merely to provide a pretext for the matter; what harm is there in providing a general response based on the facts?
To respond immediately without hesitation or delay is also a form of definitive resolution.

In the subsequent section, the initial refutation of biased attachments—whereby this is established and that is discarded—is entirely a matter of interpretive judgment; since there is no explicit scriptural authority, one must not dogmatically adhere to it.

This is done in order to clarify that both [positions] are universally applicable. Furthermore, although the reception of the precepts is generally permitted at any time, day or night, it must nonetheless be observed according to specific requirements.

Regarding the statement "remaining seated without rising," there must necessarily be distinctions between entering and exiting, as sitting and standing are not the same; both require separate harmonization and cannot be used interchangeably.

As for the principle that the two boundaries—binding and releasing—cannot be answered simultaneously, it is because the two realms differ in their underlying ground (bhūmi), and thus there are two distinct acts: binding and releasing.

Regarding the formal acts for binding and releasing the boundaries (*sīmā-bandha-sīmā-mokṣa*), if the boundaries are different, one naturally abandons [the previous] and performs the act according to the two respective realms; thus, there is only one answer for each.

Next, regarding the matters of binding and releasing within a single assembly, although the ritual procedure is the same, because the entrusted boundaries differ, there is logically no universal answer.
The admonitions and exhortations in the following text can be understood; they are repeated according to the specific matters at hand, fearing that [the practice] might not be accomplished.
The three admonitions and exhortations are clear.
