Regarding the matters of the four intermediate periods, they are all subsumed under the categories of conditions (*pratyaya*), realms (*dhātu*), and specific affairs (*vastu*); their regulation depends solely upon these three. Within both the "black" and "white" fortnights, there are three days each.

When there are conditions that permit abbreviation, it refers to the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). If other conditions are lax, the abbreviation is slight; if they are urgent, the abbreviation is extensive.

Now, to abbreviate arbitrarily when there are no conditions, or to do so even when conditions exist without following their degree of laxity or urgency—this is why it is said they are "all" [subject to this].
This is a deviation.
There are four other dharmas that intersect with the three mentioned above; because they cannot be manifested all at once, a net is spread to encompass them completely.

Next, to demonstrate the simultaneous possession of both [the two and the three], there are three phrases that fully possess one phrase, which is then applied through the combination of the three single aspects. Proceeding through these:
These constitute seven points in total.
Having explained the dissolution of the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), I shall now offer a general evaluation of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) required within the Vinaya.

Specifically, regarding the nineteen types of cases where one is deemed to have received [the precepts] unconsciously: thirteen involve sentient beings, while the remaining six involve non-sentient objects.

In the general summary of Vinaya-mātṛkā, regarding those who lack the mental intention [to commit an offense], the Sangha’s legal procedure (*saṃghakarma*) is applied to them, as they previously lacked the mind of acceptance.

As for the "thirteen" [cases]: the seven disciplinary measures constitute seven offenses; the place of punishment constitutes the eighth; insanity is the ninth; the householder's family (*śikṣādattaka*) is the tenth;

the bowl-covering (*pātra-nikubjana*) is the eleventh; not paying homage is the twelfth; and the expulsion of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is the thirteenth. Regarding the division of these two meanings, one interpretation holds that they serve a practical purpose.

Since their essential nature (*ātman*) is that of the Saṃgha, there can be no limit to the duration of the two types of disciplinary measures; logically, they must be released, as in the cases of those from families of good repute (*kula-śikṣā-kula*) or novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*).
First, regarding the thirteen types of persons who are subject to these measures, they are categorized into two groups:

the first is the individual enumeration of their characteristics, which comprises seven disciplinary measures—namely, the four *karmas* and the three *udghāta*. Second, the subsequent section provides a general classification based on their meaning: the first category subsumes ten dharmas.
In terms of meaning, this subsumes the three dharmas and includes the *pātra-nyāsa* (the setting aside of the bowl).

Regarding the actual entities, there are six great boundaries (*mahā-sīmā*): the boundary of the precept-platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*), the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), the non-loss-of-clothing area (*acchinna-cīvara-bhūmi*), the pure ground (*viśuddha-bhūmi*), and the hall for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha-śālā*)—these constitute the six.
Although the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit) has a time limit, because its application is broad and prone to abuse, it must be relinquished.

Regarding the six items that are not sentient beings (*asattva*): the six listed above are explained [as requiring formal relinquishment], while the following demonstrates that the *guṇavastra* (robe of merit) is identical to non-sentient objects;

since it is based on a fixed time limit and is automatically lost when that limit is reached, there was originally no need for formal relinquishment, and thus it is treated under the category of "improper use" (*prasaṅga*). (The former claim that this is intended for the community to know and for those with a conscious mind to take note of is incorrect.)

Furthermore, regarding the thirteen grounds for censure (*terrasa aññā*), those who have undergone them without conscious intent do not require formal release from the censure, as they are not counted [among the intentional offenses].

As for the latter two types of persons among those subject to the thirteen grounds for censure, as well as those who have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), their censure is to be maintained until death and does not require formal release.

Regarding the reception of precepts while possessing a distracted mind, it must be understood that although one may lose them due to the pressure of circumstances, they are permitted as an opening for subsequent reception; this is the general outline.

As for "receiving precepts with a distracted mind must be understood," it means that even if one loses the precepts upon encountering such circumstances, one may receive them again later; thus, it is said that this "opens the way for subsequent [reception]."
In this text, the principles must be systematically organized. Regarding the various conditions, they are like following the branches to find the leaves;

although the leaves differ, each has its point of attachment. The analogy of objects being strung together applies equally here. If one wishes to know that these are not [independent] characteristics, one need only seek their root.

The subsequent section explaining success and failure serves as both a warning and an exhortation. As for citing the Buddha’s era, the Vinaya states that when performing a single *karmavācanā*, all [monks] act together.
Regarding the five [categories] rather than seven, they are collectively debated as to whether they are established or not.

In the initial explanation of the "Exhortation to Formulate" (*kṣepa*), the various conditions are systematically organized: the one hundred and thirty-four dharmas are like leaves or objects, while the seven non-[factors] (*avastu*) are like branches or strings that govern them.
Since the general must necessarily encompass the particular, one is led to seek the root, and thus each subsequent section is explained below.
The *Jièquàn běnlǜ* (Exhortations and Admonitions Based on the Vinaya), fascicle 43, states: At that time, in a certain residence, the Saṃgha was performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a bhikṣu;
it was not a *biezòng* (separate assembly) procedure. At that moment, many monks disputed among themselves: some said it was an illegal separate assembly (*adharma-bhezong*);

some said it was an illegal harmonious assembly (*adharma-hehé*); some said it was a legal separate assembly (*dharmabhezong*); and some said it was a quasi-legal separate assembly (*dharmasadṛśabhezong*). Or they said...

Regarding the "harmonious combination of similar dharmas" (this refers to the five improper acts which, because they involve re-evaluation across five locations, are termed "acts performed at five locations"):

one may say that the *karma* is accomplished, or one may say it is not accomplished (these together constitute seven types of persons). The *Jie tan jing* states: "In the Buddha’s time, even those who upheld the Dharma still practiced these five improper acts;
how could this be due to ignorance from a lack of study? It is because the mind was deluded and forgetful at the critical moment."
Regarding the initial section on "Facing One Another" (*pratideśanīya*), the enumeration of the categories and their characteristics can be understood from the text.
Within the section on "Facing One Another," the presentation of the categories serves as the heading, while the enumeration is the commentary.

As for those cases where there are differences in the conditions (*pratyaya*), they are subsumed under the principle of non-inclusion; thus, there is nothing that does not apply to persons, and this is sufficient.
Regarding the purity [of the gift], while it is based on the act of giving the Dharma (*dharmadāna*), its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ from those of the conditions (*pratyaya*).

Since the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*) applies universally across the Abhidharma, one must provide an analogy and resolve the distinctions by explaining them according to their specific characteristics; therefore, a detailed mastery of these points is required.
Regarding the initial general presentation, the specific distinction between what is common and what differs in relation to the conditions (*ālambana*) is as follows:

the twenty-eight factors are the specific, while the seven are not common. Do not [confuse] this subsequent comparison of the common and the specific with the initial general summary. According to the meaning, the first part provides a general explanation;
"the Abhidharma" therein refers generally to all twenty-eight factors. Following the second section, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are explained according to their differences.

First, it clarifies that the person is not identical to the precepts they receive. Since there are already grave conditions [for transgression], the three faculties are not false; thus, this is not a matter of numerical identity, as there is no common evidence for it.

Regarding the section on "the person does not commit a grave offense," the initial text merely explains the grave offense, with the commentary stating: "The prohibitions and difficulties refer to the original reception [of the precepts]."
Regarding the case where one obtains a person who does not acknowledge their name and so forth, although this constitutes an obstruction to the precepts, it is asked:
"If one has committed a grave offense oneself, is it appropriate to recite the confession? Answer: Since the precepts arise from distinct sources, they do not contradict one another.

If one does not undergo the purification (viśuddhi), one incurs an offense according to the specific characteristics of the act, such as the sequence of training and repentance. However, if one clearly knows that the object of the offense is defiled and that one has committed a grave offense oneself, it is not appropriate [to proceed with the recitation].

It may be permissible to perform it mentally; however, if one is with fellow students who have committed offenses within the same boundary and there is no pure monk present to serve as a witness, there is no hindrance to proceeding together.
In the question, there is a concern that if one were deemed unfit to act as a witness for another, then even if one were to personally undergo the purification, it would not be established.

In the response, the first part clarifies that although a grave offense has been committed, the remainder is still maintained as upholding the precepts, because the original vow was issued separately and the subsequent observance follows that separate basis.

The explanation is as follows: in the subsequent brief procedure of confession before a witness, even if one has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), one must still have a pure object [as a witness]. Only when both oneself and the other have confessed and repented, and there is no longer a lack of purity, is it permitted.

Regarding "one who rebukes" (*ākrośaka*): "rebuks" refers to the speech directed at the preceding witness to ensure the full details are provided; it does not matter whether they are staying or departing, nor whether they are human or non-human.

Regarding the two [categories], those who do not inquire about abiding and ceasing—ceasing is the Dharma while people are distinct; it does not cease with the person, for both person and Dharma are non-existent.

Alternatively, regarding the distinction between monastics and laypeople: the monastic is a distinct status while the layperson is of inferior flow; necessarily, when facing these two types of people, neither is included within [the category of] "persons."
Since the "Sangha of three" is actually four persons, it is called a "separate status"; alternatively, when facing two or three persons, it is also termed "unlawful.

Regarding the distinction between lawful and unlawful procedures, "omission" (*tuō*) refers to not reciting the names of the two [witnesses], while "error" (*cuò*) refers to failing to follow the essence of the formal act (*karmavācanā*).
The current recitation from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* deviates from its basis and conforms instead to the superficial characteristics; this is precisely what is meant by "error."

The Dharma is not that which omits the middle term or fails to list both names; if one’s own name, the name of the robe, or the designator and the designated are not distinguished—whether they are used together or interchangeably—it is called "non-Dharmic.
Such errors and corruptions are numerous; I have specifically cited those that deviate from the fundamental tenets to implicitly condemn their contemporary misuse.

Regarding the matter of what is improper: since these are dharma robes, they must not be indiscriminately dyed with the five colors; if they are dyed with superior colors, they are secular and not the Way.
Even if one wears them, they do not constitute a valid act, as they do not accord with the Dharma.

Matters that are neither central nor intermediate, as well as seeking wealth through physical appearance, are inferior to investigating the essence; those that deviate from the Dharma are all categorized as mundane matters.
The remaining four types, being interwoven and manifesting in mutual relation, may be understood as either present or absent accordingly.

Regarding the statement that one may designate another person as "not a monk" during a formal procedure (*jñapti*) before an assembly: this refers to cases where there is no *saṃgha* within the boundaries of the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, it is permitted to designate an individual;
the act of the assembly is not invalidated. One must also clearly understand the natural five-li boundary (*pañca-yojana*), and other boundaries should be known by analogy.

Regarding the section on the "person" within the initial category of the "confrontation before the assembly" among the various dharmas: previously the dharma-realm was explained, and subsequently the spontaneous [nature] was shown;
here, taking the *araṇya* (wilderness) as an example, others should be understood by analogy.
A person who is not in accordance with the Dharma is one whose conduct is defiled and whose essence is incapable of providing salvation.
Regarding the two types of conduct involving foul speech, they encompass both light and heavy offenses; provided there is a transgression, one is not permitted to accept the confession.

As for the person who reprimands, if they are capable of subverting the Dharma, this constitutes a separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha*). To set it aside and stop is not correct; even if one stops upon hearing the reprimand, though stopped, it is still not correct.
This is because the person is incorrect; however, if one does not stop, it is the person who is at fault, while the Dharma itself is not. One should simply rely on the Dharma.

If one falsely assumes a person to be vast and great, yet must abide in self-assertion, saying "I am," this is because of the cessation of what has been heard. To go forth from such a state is contrary to the Dharma;
to abide accordingly is as explained in the *Kṣānti-parivarta*: the meaning is not established in isolation, for such a thing is the ruin of the Dharma.

Among the three [types of persons], the first explains the *sahādhammika* (one who speaks according to the Dharma); one who can refute the person who speaks contrary to the Dharma is immediately called a *saha*.

Next, the second explains the *thapaniya* (to be set aside). This also has two parts: first, it clarifies that the method of setting aside applies when the person is not at fault, which is included within the present phrase;

second, it clarifies that when neither the person nor the Dharma are at fault, it pertains to both, and thus includes the subsequent phrase. As for "but merely," etc., this describes the reason for the fault: because one cannot endure [the situation].
To explain this, the text is cited for illustration:

the Dharma is not the same as the middle path, nor is it the same as the harmonious Sangha; because the various dharmas pertaining to individuals differ, they must necessarily be distinguished according to principle.

"Regarding the statement that 'the Dharma is not among the three [categories] such as neutral indifference' (*madhyastha*), this refers to the rules for returning robes after confessing offenses and relinquishing property.

'Harmony' (*sāmagrī*) means that one may reprimand the individual but not the *saṃgha* as a whole; "private" (*pratyeka*) refers to individual confession (*pratideśanā*). These apply to the three aforementioned positions.
As clarified repeatedly above, one must certainly recall [the offense] oneself; if one does not recall it, one must further investigate and examine it."

Regarding offenses committed against the nature of things that violate the Vinaya, one does not distinguish between whether the transgression is great or small; if it exceeds the limit, it is an offense.

Those who repent at present should simply confess what is "measurable" (i.e., appropriate). As for the rest that is "not measurable," this is called "non-offense. There is a sincere text in the treatises stating that although small and large [offenses] may both be defiled, one is not freed from them merely by confession.
One must universally undergo purification through repentance before the blemish and its consequences can be avoided.

The matter is not central; furthermore, I shall cite the case of an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) to illustrate the characteristics of what is improper. In the initial text, there is no distinction made between "large" and "small":

a large robe that exceeds the prescribed measurement constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense, while a small one that does not meet the requirements incurs a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the limit, this refers to the period beyond ten days. The following section refutes what is improper;
for the scriptural authority, refer to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātr̥kā* (the *Duolun*), as fully cited in the *Shan-chao*.

To repent for that which is not subject to formal regulation—such as items like wool or cotton that do not yet possess the characteristics of a robe, or heavy objects that do not qualify for forfeiture—is improper.

A small bowl is inherently not an object of formal purification; primary colors are neither received nor separated from [impurity]; and seeking through improper means is contrary to the correct teaching.

To store such things indiscriminately for personal use constitutes a downfall. All such matters are defiled and unfit for formal purification; how, then, could they be subject to forfeiture and repentance?
In the first section of the following classification, there are three parts: first, up to "shādiya" (offense of forfeiture), distinguishing those who have not committed an offense;

the phrase "long hair, cotton, and bedding that do not meet the required measure" and "heavy objects which are not permitted to be kept"; and the single phrase "small bowls," which includes both long-term begging and all instances where no offense has been committed.

The three phrases beginning with "correct colors" distinguish those who have not committed the offense of being separated from one's robes; they distinguish between correct colors and improper seeking, as well as between misuse and those who have already committed an offense.

Therefore, it is not permissible to remain separated overnight; as the following summary indicates, one should know that according to the Dharma, one may enter [the robe] and receive purification, but only then does the offense of "excessive separation" (*dīrgha-vippavāsa*) arise.

Regarding "not being in doubt about the excess": this refers to when robe-material has been scattered and its status as defiled or pure has not yet been distinguished; if one intends to bring it all together for relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), that constitutes an offense.

Therefore, in the Vinaya texts, those who are conscious of their transgression must repent, while those who have doubts must disclose them; even though concealment exists, it is not punished [as a separate offense] regarding the number of days.
Since there are clear precedents for this, there is no reason to apply overly strict restrictions.
Among the three [sections], the first restates and explains that for both transgressions under the prescribed teachings (*śikṣāpada*) and their confession, one must clearly recognize them;
harboring doubt and abandoning them indiscriminately constitutes an excessive fault. Therefore, the following cites scriptural evidence showing that confession is not permitted when there is doubt.

Although the subsequent section provides examples—such as when a doubtful offense remains undecided and the days and months are not counted—the treatment for concealing offenses (*paryuṣitaka*) can be used as a precedent: where there is doubt, one may not recklessly abandon the offense. Hence, it is said: "There is none."
The *Rongshen yuechao* quotes the Vinaya, stating: "If one does not recall [the offense], has doubts, or does not recognize it, in all such cases concealment is not established.

(The old interpretation—that the duration of concealment for a *pārājika* offense differs from that for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* in terms of the days and months of disciplinary treatment—is incorrect. In the commentary, it is judged that there is no offense where there is no awareness of the transgression;
rather, the presence or absence of an offense must be determined based on whether the mind was deluded by ignorance of the training rules or by confusion regarding the teachings.
The remaining text is self-evident.
Within the context of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the arrangement of positions is easy to understand.
The positions within mental attention consist of three dharmas, while the arrangement of positions consists of seven non-dharmas.

Regarding the confession of *duṣkṛta* offenses, one must understand the principles of the two types—light and heavy—as well as the distinction between those involving face-to-face confession and those that do not.

Among these, face-to-face confession before an individual (as in the case of the current rules for forfeiture) differs from the formal procedures found in other sections; it is not a matter of the Vinaya itself.
This [type of confession] is merely a mental recitation (*manasikāra*) and does not permit the disclosure of the offense to another person or the formation of a separate assembly (*gaṇa*).

However, because the initial explanation within the *cetanā* (mental recollection) provides a general indication, it is a heavy offense of *kṣudra-āpatti* (light misfortune), as previously established for the *pratyekamukha* (individual confession) performed with a mistaken mind.

This mental recollection (*cetanā*) is next explained: "person" and "non-person" here refer to the *pratyekamukha* being established as a non-offense, as illustrated below by the category of confessing a *pārājika* (defeat) after having concealed it;
this is identical to the *pratyekamukha* offense, yet it is a distinct category, meaning it is a matter of light misfortune (*kṣudra-āpatti*).
Regarding the offense of *pratideśanīya*, although it involves a gathering of people, because one has improperly assumed a superior rank, that person is at fault.

As for the other two types—*cittotpāda* and *pratyekasamgha*—they are likewise not permitted; they are exclusively for those who rely on the original [boundary] and are entrusted with the division of the realm.
The remaining texts offer admonitions and exhortations, fearing that one might enter onto a wrong path.

Next, regarding the other two [methods], the first provides a general explanation of the two dharmas merely indicating that they are not for oneself; the rest are easy to understand. For those who rely on the original [rules]:

the *pratimokṣa* (confession before another) and the *manasikāra* (mental recitation) are performed by returning to the *pratimokṣa* before a group; as for the *saṃghakarma-manasikāra* (mental recitation according to the monastic community rules), it increases according to the number of people.

If the number reaches two or three, one relies on the previous *pratimokṣa*; if it reaches four or five, one relies on the original *saṃghadharma*. This is determined according to the boundary (*sīmā*).
"Non-existence is not self-manifesting," etc., which explains the admonition and exhortation to prevent subsequent confusion regarding practice.
*Sifen lü shanbu suíjí jiémó shū jìyuán jì* 1.6;
*Sifen lü shanbu suíjí jiémó shū jìyuán jì* 2.1.
*Commentary on the Spontaneous Karmavācanā for the Compilation and Supplementation of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*,

Fascicle Two (from the section on the Binding and Unbinding of Various Boundaries to the Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras), composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Yuanzhao of Yuhang Prefecture during the Great Song Dynasty;
originally compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan at Fengde Temple on Mount Zhongnan during the Tang Dynasty.

Regarding the beginning of the main body of the treatise, one first seeks the characteristics through their meanings according to their sequence, and subsequently provides explanations following the chapters and their respective characteristics.
Within the eight chapters of this work, the reason why the *dhātu-dharma* (elements) occupy the foremost position is that all phenomena rely upon them;

since they arise based on the elements, they serve as the foundational support for the main body of the teaching. This meaning must be revealed first, so that once the various elements are recognized, [the rest may be understood].

One should earnestly practice the Way; among all practices, the primary纲 (fundamental guide) is that the precepts must not be disregarded. Therefore, following the reception of the Dharma, the second [category] arises: the formal acceptance (*samādāna*).

Once the basis of the precepts is manifest, one must establish the formal acceptance in accordance with their characteristics. As these are essential requisites for aiding the Path and supporting the times, the third category arises following the robes and medicine:

the formal acceptance. Relying on these characteristics, once the vows and practices are complete, the pure teaching is propagated through principle, and the various distinctions of the Sangha are maintained and sustained.

Therefore, the various *śīla-vastus* (rules of training) arise in sequence from the fourth: because one must rely on conditions to apply oneself to the cultivation of what has been heard through instruction;

the various *dharmas of dwelling* arise in sequence from the fifth: because there is fear of being defiled by faults during long-term cohabitation; the various *dharmas of formal accusation* arise in sequence from the sixth:

because once the summer retreat is concluded and one is pure, their merits must be rewarded; and the various *dharmas of giving* arise in sequence from the seventh: because the practices maintained in the preceding sections [must be formally presented].

Since the practice of cultivation based on the essential body necessarily involves the risk of arrogance and transgression, it is imperative that these be thoroughly cleansed; thus, the eight repentance rituals (sāṃghāṭī-dharmas) follow next.

Within the sequential order of the "Correct Main Section" (zhèngzōngfēn), this first section—wherein the Master has compiled the teachings and arranged the chapters—distinguishes itself from other versions;
therefore, it is said that within this single school’s text, eight sections are listed, and from the second section onward, each follows upon the preceding one.
The intent of the "Arising" (Shengqi) section: first, it introduces the first [chapter]; next, it introduces the second; following that, it introduces the third;
following "Receiving" (Shou), it introduces the fourth; following "Hearing" (Wen), it introduces the fifth; following "Together" (Tong), it introduces the sixth;

citing the Dharma, this refers to the *Prātimokṣa* (Self-Indulgence); following "Indulgence" (Zi), it introduces the seventh; following "Up" (Shang), it introduces the eighth; the above constitutes the first fascicle.

Taken together, these seven categories of supernormal powers (abhijñā) are correlated with one another: the first chapter is the root, while the latter seven are all branches; the former seven rely upon observance (*dhāraṇa*), while the final one concerns transgression (*āpatti*).
Furthermore, the third and second [categories] along with the eighth pertain to personal practice (*svacaryā*), while the rest are communal rules (*saṃghadharma*).
Additionally, the third and seventh concern the requisites (*pariṣkāra*), while the remainder are the actual practices (*pratipatti*); the fifth category encompasses both.

Regarding the arrangement of the ranks for monks and nuns compiled by Master Guang, while there is certainly a consistent logic in its sequence according to the Vinaya, the practice of returning those of the same dharma to their original categories and merely establishing separate positions for them is a vain expenditure of paper and ink.
Now, we shall simply follow the chapters to distinguish what is open and what is restricted;

based on the Vinaya, the five groups of practitioners are categorized under the same headings, and the principles governing their mutual inclusion and exclusion are fully exhausted. The titles at the beginning are adapted to the circumstances.
Thus it can be known.
In the first section of the following division, it is shown that in the *Karmavācanā* (ritual procedures), the methods for monks (*bhikṣu*) appear first and those for nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) appear later;

likewise, in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and the *Khandhaka* within the Vinaya, the monastic order (*saṃgha*) always precedes the community of nuns. Therefore, it is said: "According to the Vinaya, this is so."

Even if one grants that the subsequent passage is a refutation and exclusion—meaning that since the *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, and other rituals are taught as common to both monks and nuns, once one has emerged from the *saṃgha* (the male order), one may naturally be considered identical to them regarding the *bhikṣuṇī-dharma* (the rules for nuns)—it is nevertheless listed [separately] again; hence it says "returning to enter," etc.

Second, explaining the current point: this refers to the two assemblies (*saṃghas*) practicing together. If they are obstructed, then each side is restricted to its own respective rules. This should be understood according to the individual precepts (*prātimokṣa*).

In the Vinaya’s *Śīla-mūla*, following each individual precept, the similarities and differences regarding the transgressions of the five classes of practitioners (*pañca-saṃgha*) are listed side by side.

That [text] cites the characteristics of the precepts to encompass the individuals; this [text], however, lists the classes according to their respective legal positions (*dharma-sthāna*), while still retaining the original title to manifest its essential derivation.
Chapter Two: On the Binding and Liberation of the Various Realms (*Dhātu*).

In this chapter, as indicated by the title, because seven [topics] are contained within the three types of persons mentioned in the text, it is called "On the Binding of the Various Realms. This refers to the mind and karma.
If one resolves to abandon [the practice], one immediately relinquishes the original undertaking of the karma.

This section clarifies that within each realm there are many distinct categories, which are subsumed according to their respective stages; thus, the text lists three types of persons regarding food and clothing.
According to the Vinaya, the characteristics are manifested through the sequence of preceding and succeeding conditions; now, those who compile the Dharma provide examples following this order.

The commentary on the first section of the introduction first indicates the general position based on what follows; next, it clarifies the examples from the preceding and succeeding sections of the Vinaya.
Regarding the two boundaries of persons and robes: the former is taken from the *Poṣadha-vastu*, while the boundary of food is taken from the latter, the *Bhaiṣajya-vastu*.
As for the subsequent examples, since they share the same nature as a boundary, "example" here refers to a category by analogy.

First, it should be understood that the harmonizing of the Saṃgha is fundamentally due to the fact that the Dharma relies on persons for its propagation; yet such propagation has its basis. If there were no restrictions and regulations, how could one distinguish between harmony and discord?

Therefore, the prior establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) serves to encompass the substance of the Saṃgha as a whole, whereas this present practice of separate residence (*pṛthak-vāsa*) necessarily requires adherence to the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*).

As for the manifestation of these characteristics of harmony, nothing exceeds the three types of action (*tri-karma*). By means of these, the multitude is prevented from becoming divided; once they have collectively relied upon the community, [they attain unity].

The Dharma is distinguished by its provision of sustenance and its opening up of principles; once these tasks are accomplished, there are external garments and internal medicines, each with distinct requirements.
Therefore, the Sangha is next subsumed. These two conditions are established according to their respective titles so that the intent of the teaching may be clearly revealed in the text.

In the first section of the following division, the human realm (*manuṣya-loka*) is specifically described to clarify the fundamental principle of establishing the boundary (*sīmā*) and manifesting the distinction between a harmonious assembly and a separate group;
this must necessarily come first, as the essence of the Saṃgha is harmony. Next, the realms of food and clothing are described together;

since the matter of the Dharma precedes that of material things, these two are placed later. Furthermore, external requisites are for constant use, whereas internal medicine is required only occasionally; therefore, the former is mentioned first.
The latter two lines of each section regarding robes and food point directly to the sub-commentary.
Within the first [section], there are two parts: a general classification of the meaning into general and specific categories, and a detailed analysis through four gates.
First, a general introduction; second, the intention behind the formulation and binding of the rules; third, the enumeration and explanation of names; fourth, the classification of positions.

The fourth section, concerning the distinctions between the binding and releasing of the four types of *saṃgha-kṣetra* (monastic boundaries), both large and small, summarizes the general meaning in four gates. Regarding this fourth gate on the distinctions between binding and releasing, it serves merely as a topical outline (*uddāna*);

since there is no separate textual passage for its detailed explanation, the commentary concludes the explanation of binding and releasing at the end by stating: "This is the first meaning of the fourth gate."

The same applies to the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*); one should understand by analogy that this section generally encompasses all boundaries, as each individual boundary possesses its own procedures for formal establishment (*bandhana*) and dissolution (*mokṣa*), which constitute their respective distinctions.
Regarding the intent behind these regulations:

the formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), through which the True Dharma is maintained, can only be propagated far and wide by means of the Sangha’s extensive exposition.

The principle [of the *saṃgha*] must be universally applied and followed according to reason without limitation; however, because practical matters are complex, one must rely on the specific conditions and boundaries.
Even if there were cases where members of the same community gathered together in haste, it would merely waste one's primary practice and would not be effective for the preceding conditions.

The Noble Ones of the past, knowing the capacities of beings, opened up the practice by delimiting it according to the specific site and establishing distinct zones. Once this was opened, any ritual action performed outside of these boundaries is not valid. Therefore...

The establishment [of the precepts] and the honoring of harmony and benefit reside herein; the sequence of first opening [the path] and subsequently establishing [the rules] makes the underlying intent clear.

Within the intent of this establishment, the initial section describes how the monastic dharma is universally observed; however, the following two sections clarify how the teachings are formulated according to specific capacities.

Furthermore, these are divided into two parts: the first clarifies that among the various capacities, events arise and conditions emerge in manifold ways; thus it is said that "matters are diverse" within Jambudvīpa.

The objective realm (*viṣaya*) is subsumed under "nature" (*svabhāva*); the "elements" (*dhātu*) are treated as overlapping because they are pervasive; the "shadows" (*chāyā*) follow with difficulty because of their rapid movement;
and they "abandon and ruin the primary task" because the body responds to affairs like a shadow following a form—hence it is said they "follow like a shadow.

Next, regarding the establishment of the teachings: looking back at the preceding "natural" [state], the original regulations were generally gathered together; thus, the names are restricted by being established, while the opening [of the rules] is viewed from the perspective of that gathering.
Because subsequent actions must necessarily rely upon the specific realm (*dhātu*), the original restriction is restored.
Second, the explanation of the names and their enumeration.
First, regarding the name: the *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* on the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that the original sound is *catur-ma*; this is correctly translated as "separate dwelling" (*parivāsa*).
Furthermore, various editions refer to this as the "poṣadha boundary" (bǔsà jiè) or the "precept platform" (jiè chǎng), but these are not the original phonetic transcriptions.

It is called "separate residence" (bié zhù) because the ritual procedures for this residence do not interconnect with those of other residences, and because no formal consent (yù) is accepted from them; thus it receives its name.

In the first section of the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names), the initial citation of the scriptural authority translates the name; it correctly translates the meaning as "separate dwelling" (*prātimokṣa*), as explained below.

Furthermore, two names are produced: while "the boundary for the *poṣadha*" in various texts refers specifically to the original occasion for its establishment, "the *śīmaṇḍala*" (precept field) is a general designation for the collective conduct of the assembly. Neither of these is a literal translation.

Therefore, this term is specifically highlighted in the brief summary so that, when the meaning is shown below, one may know that this name comprehensively includes both the *kṣetra* (field) and the *sīmā* (boundary).

Now, following the *Vinaya-mūla*, it simply says "boundary" (*sīmā*); since the addition of the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) pertains to the location and excludes the other [the field] which is restricted to this [context], it is called a "boundary.
Thus, the text says: "A boundary (*sīmā*) is that which is established by a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*)."

The subsequent section indicates the names and their origins; the meaning is the same as explained above. Below, it cites scriptural evidence from the *Vinaya*, specifically the section on the "five present [factors].

Regarding the enumeration, there are two parts: first, concerning the natural [boundaries], there are four different types based on the realm (*dhātu*); second, regarding the determined measurements, there are six differences, as already stated in the section on conditions (*pratyaya*).
In our own school, these are established through ritual action (*karmavācanā*); briefly stated, they are threefold, which are further divided according to their respective stages.
Thus, the formation of the seven boundaries has already been explained in the section on mutual inclusion mentioned above.
Since the first among the enumerated items is naturally set aside, it is referred back to what was stated above; now, below, the actual method of construction is clearly explained:
three large and three small *śīmaṇḍalas* (boundary fields) constitute the seven. This refers back to the principle of "suspended" [boundaries] within the section on mutual inclusion.
Regarding the third point, the determination of the size of the boundary (*sīmā*):
there are three stages for distinguishing its size.

First, regarding the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), if it is small, it is determined according to circumstances; if it is large, it must be established as a four-part boundary (*caturbhāga-sīmā*). This refers to a great boundary that is vast and distant, where the monks...

In monasteries where the number of residents is very large, when it comes time for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, they should assemble in one place; those who are scheduled to recite on the fifteenth day should go there on the fourteenth.
Because of the appearance of the dawn, they must not accept *chanda* (consent) from others; based on this principle, one should travel even as far as a hundred *li*.

Regarding the first section of the initial part on the measurement for displaying the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): first, the four types are established by way of their meaning; next, they are determined according to the text.
Since it takes more than one day to reach a distance of one hundred *li*, the lower limit is taken from various texts as three *yojanas*, which is one hundred and twenty *li*.
As has already been shown above, one must not allow the boundary to span across two days.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "At that time, there were those who established boundless boundaries. The Buddha decreed that the maximum distance should be three *yojanas*.
A *yojana* is a measure used by the Middle Brahmans; its correct phonetic transcription is *yōu-shàn-yā* (yojana). This term has no direct equivalent in Chinese;

it refers to the resting station for a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) during his tours of inspection. Just as this ancient term "ting" (station) is not restricted to a mere number of *li*, so too should this be understood in its broad sense.
It is forty *li*; tradition holds it to be the measure of a *krośa* according to the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, the *Samantapāsādikā*, and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. That which exceeds this is not valid.
In the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the three *yojanas* are calculated by taking the measurement from corner to corner.

The subsequent section is divided into two parts: first, it demonstrates the maximum limit of the fivefold cause because of its potential for confusion, thereby establishing a fixed boundary; second, it explains the *yojana* by calculating it in *li*.
The "resting halls" (*stha*) of a Wheel-Turning King correspond to the ancient "halls" (*ting*) of this region, which are equivalent to today’s guesthouses or postal stations.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three grades of *yojana*: the superior grade is eighty *li*, the middle grade is sixty *li*, and the inferior grade is... [fifty *li*].

The perimeter is forty *li*; however, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is sixteen *li*. Taking the scriptural teachings as the standard and calculating the middle value, it is said to be approximately three *yojana*.

As cited in the *Shanjian* (Sudarsana) commentary, this is consistent with the *Mahāsāṃghika* school. Regarding the objection that "the measurement exceeds [the limit] and thus does not constitute [a valid site]," this indicates the established rule (*niyama*).
Below, the second section clarifies the measurement of the dharma-corners; the measurement of the corners is for the purpose of determining the four circles—if there are four...
Regarding the dimensions, there is a surplus at the four corners.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "I permit the establishment of a boundary for the sake of a unified *poṣadha*.

Whether it be one *goḷu* or even ten *goḷu*, if a monastery is situated on a mountain, one may establish a boundary extending ten *goḷu* down the mountain, and likewise dwell in summer retreat (*varṣā*) there."

The same applies to establishing the boundary (*sīmā*) for a monastic dwelling (*vihāra*) or entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*) on a mountain. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, the length and breadth [of the area] shall be ten *krośas*.
One must ensure that no doubt arises within this space during the performance of the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* rituals.

Even if there are rivers or great roads, it is permissible to establish the boundary together; however, one must first determine the characteristics of the banks before performing the formal act of demarcation. For nuns (*bhikṣuṇīs*), the maximum distance for establishing a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is one *krośa*.
This is because one fears the dangers of distant travel and the ease with which one might be insulted.
Regarding the third [point], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* both state that one *gavyūti* is two *li*;

according to their school, it stops at twenty *li* (the former interpretation of five *li* based on the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* is an error). Below, the mountain monastery is explained through the alternating clarification of its upper and lower sections. However—

Because within a *goḷa* (a ten-cubit space), all share the same *dharmadhātu*, one may reside there together during the *varṣā* retreat; however, fearing that doubts might arise regarding differences in height and the lack of mutual inclusion, this point is specifically resolved here.
(The old commentary’s explanation that "mountains and rocks above and below do not obstruct one another" is highly inconsistent with the meaning of the text. Question: This [space] is too narrow;

why is it cited? Answer: It is either to manifest the differences between schools (*nikāya*), or to prove that [the retreat] ought to be restricted, or to demonstrate that all schools establish [this rule].
The boundaries cannot be extended indefinitely; there may be a specific intention behind this, which scholars should further discern.

The first of the three sections of the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* initially demonstrates that the measurements are the same as before, ensuring that no doubt arises; this indicates the reason for not being overly expansive. Second, it clarifies the attainment of the riverbank.
Third, it clarifies the differences between the monastic communities of monks and nuns: the boundary for nuns is strictly limited to two *li*, beyond which they may not go.

The *Śāstra* states: "If there are inevitable circumstances of danger, one may utilize the three *yojana*s within the *Saṃghāṭī*-boundary (since the boundary is so vast, it is permissible to dwell in the midst of it to avoid such dangers).
Question: Within a boundary, if there are villages and rivers, is it permissible to combine them and establish a single boundary?"
Regarding the question, as much has already been clarified in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* above, this question is raised again in order to cite various scriptural passages.

The answer states that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says: "One must not cross by way of a rapid current"; this clarifies the prohibition (*niyama*). It continues: "Except when there is a permanent bridge, boat, or beam"; this clarifies the allowance (*anujñā*).
As stated extensively above, one should simply determine the characteristics of the bank; in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is sufficient to mark five locations on an island.
The *Jie* (Saṃghāvaśeṣa) is very clear and explicit.
In the initial response, the four divisions [of the Vinaya] state that "shī" means rapid or swift; the Liang dynasty version also uses "bridge," distinguishing between large and small.
The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] refers only to islands—solitary places in the water; that text clarifies five markers: two are in the water and three are on land.
As fully cited in the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya*, it states that "one may obtain [the robe] within the village.
This is clearly established by the four-part textual authority (*caturbhāga-vibhāga*), which excludes the area outside the village while permitting the wearing of the robe there;

the textual evidence makes it known that this applies to the Sangha's possession of the robe without distinction as to whether one is inside or outside the village. Furthermore, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, when laypeople construct new halls or dwellings for the sake of auspiciousness, or otherwise...

Because people were being troubled [by non-Buddhists], the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts therein; by this standard, one should know that the boundary (*sīmā*) encompasses [the village].

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The reason for generally establishing a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) that extends through the village is because, through the power of the boundary, various evils find no opportunity, it is protected by benevolent deities, and it is done for the sake of the donors (*dānapati*);
thus, the village is included within the general establishment. By this standard, [it is understood].

This is because the actions performed by the virtue of the Saṃgha result in the fulfillment of karma; being permeated by roots of goodness, they are protected by the deities of the realm and must not be treated lightly.

Next, the response has three parts: first, according to the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the distribution of robes, since the village is situated within the boundary (*sīmā*), it is necessary to formally announce it.

Excluding the preceding [case], according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, since the performance of the *poṣadha* in a secular dwelling is permitted, it follows as a matter of principle that the boundary must first be demarcated.

Subsequently, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clarifies that this [boundary] universally encompasses all things; thus, various evils—namely demonic, heterodox, and monstrous occurrences—are to be understood according to this.
Below, the commentator reveals the intent behind the divine protection based on this.

The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "If a sick bhikṣu within the boundary cannot seek to establish a single dwelling within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should first dissolve the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and establish a separate boundary;
then, having re-established the great boundary, those who do not carry their robes may enter [the area].

This also excludes the Buddha’s precincts, because the status of the Buddha and the Saṃgha differ and do not mutually encompass one another; thus, in the central lands, the Buddha’s courtyard is listed as distinct from that of the monks."

This indicates that the Buddha-ground, the stupa-ground, and the Sangha-ground each have distinct boundaries; since these practices have not yet been implemented here [in this region], how could they be intermingled?
In principle, they must be strictly demarcated.

Within the three distinct boundaries, the first section of the treatise first presents the conditions for opening them, then teaches the method for establishing them, and finally clarifies their protection.
Regarding robes, this discussion is based on the formal ritual procedures for handling them; if one were to speak of them according to their natural state, they would apply universally to both sides.

The three distinctions regarding the Buddha-ground are explained by the commentators of the lower [tradition] based on their own intent; however, they still criticize the confusion between the distinct grounds of the Three Jewels in the Western Regions (India), asserting that in this land (China) they are intermingled, which is precisely what is meant by "external."
Furthermore, as explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, for those practicing the separate retreat (*prātimokṣa*), one first performs three or four small separate retreats;

having completed them, one establishes boundary markers all around with a path left open on the four sides, which is then called an *araṇya* (forest) site. Outside of this, one performs a great separate retreat to encircle it, like the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) surrounding the four continents.
According to these authentic texts, within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), one may perform five or three [smaller boundaries] as appropriate.
It is established.
In the first section of the following division, a treatise is cited regarding the distinct dwelling within the Cakravāḍa mountains; this is one of the seventeen [points] cited below.

"Araṇya" is translated as "empty place," which refers to the natural space between [the mountains]. Below, a metaphor is raised to clarify the meaning of the name: the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
Master Ying states that the Sanskrit term *cakravāḍa* means "Wheel Mountain" (*lúnshān*), hence it is called the "Encircling Wheel.
This can be understood by referring to the definitive judgment below.

Second, regarding the dimensions of the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept platform): the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that it must accommodate twenty-one people; fewer than this is not permitted. This refers to the maximum limit.
This brief statement limits [the prohibition] to these cases because it addresses both the commission of the offense and the object of the action. That treatise further states:
"One must not establish a monastic residence within the precincts; a conscientious bhikṣu must dismantle it, leaving only the Buddha hall."

Within the boundary of the precept platform (*sīmā*), the initial explanation of the small measurement is based on the sufficiency for the proceedings of a single assembly; thus, reduction is not permitted.

If two assemblies are combined, it must accommodate forty-one persons. Next, the broad measurement is shown: since it is prescribed that the *saṃgha* reside there, it is evident that the space is not narrow.

The three kinds of small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*) have no fixed dimensions; they are established according to the number of those assembled, based on their seating. For receiving the precepts, the minimum is ten persons;
for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, four persons; and for the *Pravāraṇā*, five persons. Beyond these, the number may be increased as required by the occasion.

However, one must not extend [the boundary] outside the physical limits, for fear of someone objecting. Furthermore, this differs from the aforementioned [great boundary], as it is intended to be long-lasting and stable, serving only as a provisional remedy for specific circumstances.
The three [types of] small [kalpas] are performed simultaneously.
At the beginning of the first [small kalpa], the measure is shown; furthermore, by contrasting the latter with the former, the two realms can be understood as being opposites.
The remainder is as explained later.

Regarding the text on delimiting the *saṃgha-sīmā*, it is further divided into three parts. First, for the sake of those who are naturally weary and seeking relief from their burdens, the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) is established;

however, because its restrictions and regulations are complex and cumbersome, the *śikṣāpada-kṣetra* (precept field) is also permitted. Second, as for the usual practice where relief is difficult and there are non-essential matters, the *sūkṣma-sīmā* (small boundary) is permitted.
Each of these is as stated in the text and shall be analyzed individually below.
Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation of the general heading, each section is presented according to its original context;

the sequence follows the order of the boundaries and restrictions, as these matters must be assembled together. Because the events are diverse and numerous, and because the various instances arise frequently—yet are not always immediate or constant—the subsequent text is extensive, so I shall here provide only a brief indication.

Regarding the text for the first *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), there are again three types: namely, the original [boundary], the two shared [boundaries], and the other two established according to the procedure; their meanings correspond to their respective positions.
This can be seen in the annotations within the markers of the great boundary.
Regarding the first [section], there are again two parts, namely: the binding and the liberation.

Within the initial section on binding, it is the fundamental basis for the collective karma of all sentient beings, the excellent condition for generating goodness and extinguishing evil, and the pure ground upon which one dwells in the Dharma and relies upon the Sangha;
when these conditions are complete, one achieves what was previously mentioned—its characteristics are as follows.
To deviate from this is surely to overturn the tracks left by those who came before. There is one who establishes a doctrine and briefly sets forth four gates;

though these are intermingled and complex, making them difficult to comprehend, success lies in their underlying intent while failure lies in their outward manifestation. Therefore, I shall directly recount them to provide a thorough overview, so that by reading the text one may grasp the essential matters.

These are arranged into ten sections: first, the identity and non-identity of characteristics; second, the physical forms and appearances; third, the vertical delineation of boundaries; fourth, the proclamation of regional orientations.
Five: The Method for Assembling the Sangha; Six: Not Accepting *chanda*; Seven: Adding Methods and Explaining the Text; Eight: The Presence or Absence of the Dharma;
Nine: Revealing Faults and Failures; Ten: Concluding the Incompletion.

Regarding the first of these, the section on the method for binding [the boundary] (*sīmā-bandhana*) is divided into two parts. The first part, which describes the merit of the boundary, consists of the initial four lines.

The first phrase indicates the inclusion of the Saṃgha; the second phrase clarifies the accomplishment of the dharma; the third phrase elucidates the discernment of the matter; and the fourth phrase reveals the dwelling in the dharma of the superior place.
The reliance on the Saṃgha constitutes the two commonalities. The subsequent four phrases clarify success and failure.

The preceding words refer to the method of the initial formal act (*karmavācanā*); the "subsequent tracks" refer to the procedures performed thereafter. Regarding the section beginning with "There being persons," the following two [phrases] clarify the characteristics of the conditions. First:

In describing antiquity, the accounts were sparse and their texts have already been lost; since the established categories were few, the matters lacked systematic order, and thus they are said to be "confused.
Because figures appear both hidden and manifest, it is said that "gain lies in floating and sinking";

because their deeds are difficult to clarify, it is said that "loss lies in current practice. Therefore, below, the present [work] is fully detailed; searching through texts to recover facts is called "investigation" (jiǎn).

In examining the various teachings, one finds the matters appropriate for practice within ten categories. Of these, the first two concern the *sthāna* (loci); the third and fourth concern the *vastu* (matters);
the fifth and sixth concern the person (*pudgala*); and the remainder are all concerning the Dharma (*dharma*).

Regarding the first, the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi-lakṣaṇa*), the intent is to rely on the designations to identify the essence and to discern its similarities and differences.
Regarding the eight kinds of "good views," first is the mountain sign (*parvata-nimitta*): large ones are like Mount Sumeru, while small ones are like elephants.

If one were to use them as boundary markers, how could they directly indicate the mountain? This would fail to recognize the limits. According to principle, one should rely on the edges or the peaks to point to specific locations so that there are precise dimensions, as explained in the *Vidyāmātrasiddhi-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇābhidharma-śāstra*).
Second is the stone sign (*śilā-nimitta*): large ones are about the size of an ox, while small ones are three [units].
Ten *śata-māṣaka* scales may not be used; one must install separate weights as a standard. This is based on the principle that there are both general and specific applications regarding mountains.

Regarding the characteristics of the three forests: because grasses and bamboo are empty in substance and lack solidity, they are extremely small. Fourth, when trees are joined together, one must also rely on their borders;
they cannot be pointed out generally. Regarding the characteristics of the trees: being withered and decayed, they are unfit for use; they are extremely small, eight inches in height, and in form...
If it is as large as a needle, there is no self-arising; even a new seed may obtain the five-path mark (*pañcamārga-lakṣaṇa*), yet at a dead end, it cannot allow passage for carts or pedestrians.
Even those measuring three or four villages in length and breadth may be made to serve as the six-ant-hill mark (*ṣaḍvalmīka-lakṣaṇa*); the smallest of these reaches eight inches in height.
Those possessing the seven-river mark (*saptanadī-lakṣaṇa*) are kings who rule with excellence, where it rains once every five days; this is not considered a [defining] mark.
That which flows continuously without ceasing even when it has not rained for four months may also constitute the eight characteristics of water;
this refers to natural ponds, whereas water entering a field does not serve as such a characteristic.
Regarding the first gate, the characteristics of Mount Sudarśana (Sujāta) refer only to its general form; one must specifically point to its peaks, ridges, crags, and precipices.
Regarding the demarcation according to the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*: the "one zhang and five chi" cited below refers to the separate placement of stones and so forth;
the "two types of flat stones" refer to those without sharp edges. Based on what follows, the aforementioned mountain characteristics cannot be considered "flat";
this excludes the third and fourth characteristics as being unsuitable for the former [definition], while subsequently clarifying their dimensions. As for the trees, four or more constitute a forest.

1. A single trunk constitutes a tree; among the five [meanings], "extreme" (*kū*) refers to a road at its end where no further path exists. Because people have vanished and weeds grow over it, its original appearance is lost;
therefore, the character *ren* (任) is pronounced level-tone (even tone). 2. Among the six [meanings], when ants transport soil to form a mound, it is called an "ant-hill" (*yǐfēng*). 3.
Among the seven [meanings], when a benevolent king governs the world with the True Dharma, rain falls according to the seasons; thus, the depth of the water cannot be measured. Therefore—
One cannot use the eight types of fields as examples for the exclusion, because they are not constant; furthermore, these two characteristics are difficult to manifest in actual things.
Therefore, whether referring to embankments, riverbanks, or establishing distinct markers, one uses the general term "rivers" and so forth as the name.

If one were to enumerate the types of boundaries according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, there are more than ten kinds; such as those in open spaces, on bare ground, over mounds of grass, or at the base of stakes, none of which are permanent or stable enough to rely upon for long.
They are established for a single period of construction and are dissolved once the work is finished, following the standards of the Vinaya texts.

However, for a long-term residence where it is intended that the site will be revisited later, one may employ a boundary that accords with both the Vinaya and the Śāstras, so that both systems may provide mutual support.
The details of the four categories and more are as explained in the *Śāstra* and *Commentary*; here, four types are cited merely to clarify that [the dwelling] is not inherently fixed.
Furthermore, there are thorns, stagnant water, heaps of dung, and so forth—all of which are things that lack long-term stability.

First, the meaning is generalized by analogy: like the sky or dew, they can only be used temporarily; therefore, it is said that "one may rely on the Vinaya. However, the Vinaya lists forests and mountains [as dwellings].
Since [the views of] Master Yan and others are largely consistent with the treatises, it is said that they may be reconciled with both the Vinaya and the śāstras.

For instance, as stated in the treatises, how could small trees, anthills, or the ends of grass and bamboo on a desolate path be considered permanently stable? What prevents them from being used temporarily? Now, if one determines this by way of intention:
if the discussion concerns temporary use, all such objects are permissible; however, if one intends for long-term or permanent use, one must select materials specifically.
Regarding the shapes of the two realms, they may all be formed according to the cardinal directions, diagonals, or angles.
Thus, the *Sudarsana* has five characteristics: first, square; second, circular; third, drum-shaped; fourth, half-moon; and fifth, triangular.
The second realm’s shape is represented by the objects of the Sudarśana drum and the half-moon.
In the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra*, its seventeen shapes—such as curved, straight, overlapping, and so forth—are briefly categorized into five and three types to serve as a path for spiritual understanding.
First, the long and circular; second, the distinct abodes of the earth’s terrain, which are narrow and elongated with rounded ends. Following this [classification]:
Having erected stones at intervals of one *zhang* and five *chi* around the perimeter of the site, chant according to these stones. First, demarcate the *poṣadha* boundary;
subsequently, demarcate the two [boundaries] for not losing one's robes (*acīvarāpanna*) and so forth. These include:

1) the four corners, 2) separate dwellings, 3) water, 4) waves, 5) mountains, 6) cliffs, 7) the half-moon shape, 8) the natural state (*svabhāva*), 9) the surrounding circle, and 10) the two ropes for the fourteen sides—all of which are determined by these [stones].

The entities themselves are listed by name; how could there be only seventeen? Since the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are immeasurable, one ceases [naming] them once they are known. The rest is as explained in that treatise.
Regarding the *Abhidharmasamayaśāstra*, it mentions "long" and "round," or "ten feet" or "five feet," citing distance and proximity merely to illustrate the establishment of their characteristics.
The "water-wave" refers to the curved shape of the boundary markers resembling waves; its essential nature is that of a *araṇya*, an empty place.
The two ropes refer to the two boundary lines enclosing the space, with four walls connected in between—that is, there are houses on all four sides with an open courtyard in the center.
Furthermore, ten types [of enclosures] are enumerated, including those with a single gate, square earthen walls, nuns' quarters, laymen's (*upāsaka*) quarters, and fences.

The walls are full; those who are demented or insane are all as explained in the *Śāstra-ṭīkā*. All [the details] below are shown in summary by the commentators of the *Vyākhyā*, with the concise indicated and the extensive pointed out.
Third, regarding the vertical marking of the domain: the foundation of boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha*) lies in this one gate. If one attains mastery therein, all conditions will follow.
Those who possess mere superficial indications rarely enter the ritual procedures of the Dharma.
Regarding the initial point among the three upright markers, this is the essential method for establishing the Dharma; it correctly articulates the fundamental intent.
To deviate from this is for the mind to have no object of focus and for the Dharma to have no application; therefore, know that this is the vital requirement.

If one wishes to establish the boundary markers (*sīmā-sthāpana*), one must first recognize the three measures: first, the boundary sign (*sīmā-nimitta*), which is that upon which the proclaimer relies;

second, the boundary characteristics (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*), which are those recorded in the *karmavācanā*; and third, the boundary substance (*sīmā-dravya*), which is the ground upon which the ritual act (*karma*) is performed.

Whether the sign is identical to the substance and its characteristics and lies outside the sign, or whether the sign differs from the substance and its characteristics and lies inside the sign, as for their actual manifestation, they must necessarily exist [there].

To cite this externally while ignoring its substance—how could such a thing not fail? If one wishes to know the distinctions between summer retreats, robes, and medicines, merely understanding these three constitutes mastery of the boundaries (*sīmā*).

If one does not recognize their essential nature and instead points vacuously to mountains and forests, or relies on cities and towns without regard for the actual facts, yet happens to obtain the terminology, what can be done about such a lack of meaning?
In the first section of the demonstration of measurements, there are three parts. First, the perimeter markers for the object;
second, the outer surface of the four sides, as stated in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual motion): "within the four-sided boundary"; third, the interior ground enclosed by that perimeter.

If the boundary is defined relative to the exterior, then the marker is identical to the substance itself; if the boundary is defined relative to the interior, then the marker and the substance are distinct. Thus, the marker and the substance [are related in these two ways].

While there may be differences in their specific manifestations, their essence and characteristics are necessarily inseparable; therefore, it is said that "characteristics must exist outside of the essence.
Next, the following passage demonstrates that success or failure depends on light and darkness.
Now, establishing the standard: if one is in a village, one mostly relies on walls and boundaries; whether defined by the interior or the exterior, both constitute a location.
If one is in a wilderness, one should rely on many forests, springs, or designated trees to mark the boundaries; these serve as the signs by which the dimensions are ultimately recognized.

If there is already a *śīma* (ordination precinct), one should first erect three boundary markers around it, each distinct and not touching the others; if such a precinct does not exist, one may rely on a single prominent object to determine the distance and proximity.

In the first section of the "Establishing the Dharma" (Jùfǎ zhōng), the preceding part clarifies that when the boundary markers (*sīmā*) are established, both the *lān* and the *bié* must be clearly demarcated without exception.

Next, the following part clarifies the presence or absence of the *kṣetra* (monastic precinct) and the number of its boundary markers; regarding the three types of *kṣetra*, they will be explained in detail later.
Question: When two boundaries do not meet, can a single marker establish two distinct characteristics?

Some say that anything larger than one cubit (*hasta*) may be established as such, as stated in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī-ṭīkā*: "A single mountain or a single rock may be demarcated separately from both east and west.
Furthermore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there was a questioner who asked whether it is permissible to establish them side-by-side; the Buddha replied that they must be completely surrounded.
This refers to what is described as the "internal and external characteristics.
In the question-and-answer section, the ancient interpretation restricts the measurement and does not permit it to be reduced;

furthermore, it cites the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* regarding mountains and rocks from east to west to prove that the boundary markers must be broad, while subsequently citing the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regarding the demarcation of the perimeter to verify that the characteristics must be distant from one another.

Now, regarding the interpretation of this passage, if one does not permit the connection [of the two realms], it is feared that the two realms would interpenetrate; however, as long as there is a separation, what need is there to discuss whether they are large or small?

As for the previous mention of the two ropes—the ropes themselves constitute the substance—it may be said that they can be connected through the mind. As for the mention of "clouds, mountains, and stones," this too is likely due to mutual involvement;
one must grasp the underlying meaning.

Now, regarding the initial section of the *Madhyama-āgama*, it is consistent with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as explained below; furthermore, when interpreting the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, since it still employs ropes as markers, one knows that mountains and rocks do not necessarily have to be large.
Fourth, the directions for the boundaries (*sīmā*) are proclaimed.

The Vinaya prescribes that those who have long resided there should chant; being familiar with the local conditions and having established the sequence of divisions, even if they are long-term residents, they need not be hindered by prior circumstances if they do not fully understand the preceding matters.

It does not preclude new arrivals who are deeply conversant with both internal and external matters from chanting according to the designated markers. This principle applies equally to those who are considered "old" residents;

for the Vinaya regulations are capable of application regardless of whether one is a guest or a host. Furthermore, all must recognize the three types of markers—the substance, the characteristics, and the threefold distinction between the general and the particular.

Regarding the fourth section, "Singing the Characteristics for Selecting Persons": First, although the general principle of the Vinaya is broad, when determined according to its specific meaning, it remains essentially the same.

Since the Vinaya texts state that whenever a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed, it must be done by one who is "competent" (*dakṣa*) among the assembly, such individuals may be selected as witnesses.

Furthermore, the following demonstrates the characteristics of competence: the "general characteristic" refers to the essential nature [of the person], while the "distinctive characteristic" refers to specific attributes.
Among the five parts [of the ritual], one bhikṣu appointed as a messenger proclaims the boundary markers of the four directions;

he must also proclaim the exclusion of the interior land because it is necessary to exclude it for the purpose of establishing the *śīlā-maṇḍala* (precept-platform). Regarding the current practice of performing the formal establishment (*sīmā-bandha*), the internal and external markers are proclaimed separately, one after the other;
among these, the external markers of the area to be excluded are most clearly indicated as being empty ground. This shall be further explained in the relevant passage.
Next, regarding the initial citation of the text within the ritual procedure for chanting the boundaries (*sīmā*) to exclude the interior ground:
while the external marks are recited, the exclusion of the interior ground is mentioned therein, and thus the internal marks themselves are not recited. Now, below, the present method is shown;
one need only recite the two types of marks and there is no requirement to mention the exclusion, as will be explained in the relevant passage concerning the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept enclosure).

Fifth, the characteristics of assembling the saṃgha. The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "One must not perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) at night; even if it were performed, it would likely not be valid.

Furthermore, when intending to perform the formal act, one should mark the four corners and station people there to look on, ensuring that no one enters. If anyone enters, the act is not accomplished; therefore, one should first demarcate the boundary."

Regarding the *śīmaṇḍala* (ordination platform) and similar matters, because people are mixed and right and wrong are difficult to distinguish, they cannot be universally practiced. What harm is there in not counting them? It is simply that such numbers can be obstructed.
In the first part of the "Citation of Precepts for Assembling the Saṃgha" from the *Pañcavidyā*, there are three preliminary sections; the first establishes the time and season, lest it be improper.

"Manifest" means that in a secluded assembly, if the number is insufficient, it is difficult to discern in the dark; therefore, with the clarity of lamps and candles, it is logically appropriate that there be no impairment.
Furthermore, next, the inspection is clarified to ensure one does not enter into spontaneity. Next, the three periods of time are explained in sequence.
The commentary also clarifies the meaning of the timing and inspection for the preceding section. "Not by number" means that the full complement must not be reached.
If one who has not gathered [the required number] and has not suffered a loss attains fulfillment, the distinction constitutes an obstruction.
If, among the six kinds of natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*), the markers (*stūpa*) are narrow while the area is wide, it is because the natural gathering is complete;

thus, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, there is no offense for a separate assembly beyond seven trees, which can be understood by analogy. If the markers are wide while the area is narrow, it is limited to the markers.
Collect them.
Next, regarding the initial text within the collection, there are two cases: if the heading is narrow, the *xiang* (mark/sign) is outside the heading, and one must extract the heading to collect it;
if the heading is wide, the *xiang* is inside the heading, and one must extract the *xiang* to collect it.
