The distinction between the two terms is as follows: "enclosing the earth" is called a *maṇḍala* (壇), while "clearing the ground" is called a *kṣetra* (場).

The term "field" (*kṣetra*) refers generally to any enclosed area, whereas "platform" (*maṇḍala*) specifically points to a site where the earth has been piled up. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that in foreign lands, the *śīla-kṣetra* (precept field) is mostly located in the open air, much like a secular sacrificial altar.
This refers to what is known as a state-sponsored altar established outside the capital for the suburban sacrifice to Heaven (*jiaosi*).
Regarding the ascent of the steps and taking one’s place at the Round Mound (*cūḍāmaṇi*), the procedures are as prescribed in the *Jie tan jing* (Sutra on the Ordination Platform).

Question: As for the designation of a "site" (*kṣetra*), it is generally used when many ritual acts (*dharma*) are performed there. If that is so, why is the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) not also designated as a "site," since it too involves many ritual acts?
Why is it not called a "site"?
In the question-and-answer section, the interrogative phrase is intended to clarify the reason for the designation of the "field" (*kṣetra*).

Some say that the "great boundary" (*mahā-sīmā*) was originally established for the purpose of dwelling and not specifically for the eradication of evil or the production of goodness; therefore, it is not given the name "field.

Although the "small boundary" (*kṣudra-sīmā*) may temporarily produce goodness, because it lacks spatial limits and is neither long-lasting nor firmly established through formal ritual action (*karman*), its name is lost [in this context].

In the initial explanation, by merely describing the two realms— the Great and the Small— it is revealed that the *kṣetra* (precept-field) is specifically designated with this name because it is established solely for the purpose of performing ritual acts.

Some say that Yuan Jie’s "Great Boundary" (*mahā-sīmā*) actually encompasses the entire Dharma, yet because it creates two difficulties, it is not called a "field" (*kṣetra*). The "Precept Field" (*śīla-kṣetra*) is not like this;

it is established according to the assembly and is formed as it goes along, without any contradictions or difficulties, which is why it bears that name. Therefore, the fifteen legal acts (*dharmas*) must take place within the Great Boundary:

namely, the reception of the day, the relinquishment [of robes], the receiving of the *kaṭhina* robe, the dissolution of the boundary, the binding of the boundary, the binding of the clothing and food boundary, the begging for a bowl, and the relinquishing [of the bowl].

The four dharmas within [the *pravāraṇā*] constitute twelve; these three—[the *pravāraṇā*, the lost robe, and the boundary]—were originally established for the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) where it is difficult to open a separate *kṣetra*.
As for the remaining *karmans*, they are all performed together within the *kṣetra* because the number [of participants] is not difficult to assemble; thus, the location is designated as superior.
Alternatively, each may be based on a single position and cannot be manifested simultaneously; since that [previous case] was already called "great," this one receives the name "field" (*kṣetra*).

Next, the explanation has two parts. First, regarding the ease or difficulty of the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), the preceding section on the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is explained; subsequently, the *śīmaṇḍala* (boundary for the observance of the precepts) is clarified.
This reverses the two aforementioned difficulties: gathering the assembly as it convenes constitutes "ease of collection," and the absence of discordant obstacles constitutes "ease of harmony.

Among the fifteen formal procedures, the three methods of receiving a day’s leave, relinquishing [the robe], and the virtuous robe (*guṇavat-cīvara*) all depend upon the original summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Because the site of the *śīma* (boundary) is not a place of residence, the dissolution of the boundary must revert to the original location where it was bound; remote dissolution is not permitted.
Regarding the four dharmas of binding and dissolving robes and alms bowls: two bindings are based on the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), while two dissolutions cannot occur at a different location.

One begs for an alms bowl and performs the confession of forfeiture because the penalized bowl must be entered into the kitchen. The four dharmas that do not apply to the *śīma* site are as in the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa-dharma*.

Among the twelve [methods] of the middle and superior grades, even if there are difficult circumstances, they do not open the field; the three or two [methods] of the upper and lower grades and the distinct [method] are listed separately below.
Excluding these fifteen, the remaining one hundred and nineteen all open the field, let alone when combined with the distinct methods—the general principles can thus be understood.
Alternatively, the following section establishes names to clarify differences in interpretation; each side establishes its own [system], yet there is no fundamental distinction between them.

Therefore, the text states that the *Mātṛkā* clarifies the inner and outer, as well as the sequence of priority and posteriority, within the context of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). This is the meaning of the second section.
In the first sub-section of the second section, the text cites the *Mātṛkā* to clarify the fivefold distinctions between the inner and outer, thereby establishing their chronological order.

Because it is difficult to achieve harmony when a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is assembled, and because it would be burdensome to provide all the necessary requisites, the tying of the boundary is permitted. If it were outside the boundary, it would originally not have been a troublesome task, nor would it have caused fatigue;
however, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Shan-jian mu lun) clearly states that it must be within. Thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Si-fen lü) says:

"If there are four persons in the assembly, the assembly arises," and it further says: "The bhikṣus of this residence shall chant the boundaries for the Saṃgha. If [the boundary] were outside, then...
There is no fixed location.

Regarding the initial establishment of the internal and external boundaries (*sīmā*), the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, and the *Samantapāsādikā* all provide excellent expositions; these are as noted in the commentary on the text.

The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "One should first demarcate the *karmavastu-kṣetra* (the boundary for ritual acts) and subsequently demarcate the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary). If one has already demarcated the *mahāsīmā*, it must be relinquished."
Furthermore, the preceding text clarifies that the sequence of priority and posteriority still reflects the distinction between the internal and external.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when first establishing a *śīma-kaṇḍaka* (precept-field), it was originally located outside the boundary; later, due to the threat of bandits, it was permitted to be established within the boundary.

If one wishes to establish them, one should first establish the *śīma-kaṇḍaka* and subsequently establish the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary). If the *mahā-sīmā* has already been established, one should first dissolve it and then proceed as before.
Regarding the third point, the sequence of the initial section of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* is identical to that of the *Sārmavidhi-vinaya*, which clarifies both meanings.

Nowadays, there are those who follow Master Daoguang’s *Karmavācanā* and establish the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) first; although the Vinaya texts do provide for both sequences, [the former is not the primary intent].

Because it is based on the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination), one cannot rely on this to clarify the principles of the ritual procedures for binding the boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), just as one cannot rely on the person [who composed the text].
This refutes the ancient [view] in the first section of the middle [part], which first demonstrates that it is not the Vinaya;

below, it points out the adherence to the claim that the Vinaya text first binds the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and subsequently opens the *śikṣādattaka* site, establishing the sequence based on the original *nidāna*. The principle below definitively corrects the *Mandala-sūtra*.
This means that although clouds may temporarily open up a space in the sky, it remains ultimately a place where the Dharma cannot reside. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"If one directly establishes a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) without a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) existing outside of it, one may not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If one forgets to establish a pure kitchen (*śuci-karmasthāna*), one must first dissolve the great boundary, then dissolve the small boundary; first establish the pure ground, then establish the small boundary, and finally establish [the great boundary]."

Although the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that [the boundary] is outside, this regulation was established prior to that. The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states that it was established after the *sīmā-kṣetra* (ordination site) had been demarcated;
as Master Bei remarked, one fears there would be no benefit. However, originally not knowing [of the restriction], it was as if the rule had not yet been established;
by relying on this path, one gains access. This may be called a stroke of fortune encountered beyond one's merit.

In the first section of the citation from the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, it is stated that because the original regulations did not include the Mahāyāna, one first designates a pure area (*śuddha-bhūmi*), next designates the monastic quarters (which constitutes the small boundary), and finally designates the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

This corresponds to the "encircled separate residence" (*parimaṇḍala-pṛthag-vāsa*) described in the *Viniścaya-śāstra*. If one forgets the prior designation of the pure area, once it has been dissolved, one should designate them again in their proper sequence.
This proves that the principle of establishing the *sīmā* (boundary) for the ordination platform must necessarily be performed first;

it is external, as in the initial circumstances of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, and according to the oral instructions of Upāli in the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions), which state: "One fears that there will be no attainment in receiving the precepts therein.

This "fear" is because if the original establishment was not performed according to the Dharma, then subsequent receptions of the precepts would involve doubt. As for those who originally did not know [this], they have not seen [the source].

The established rules of the teaching are not intentionally violated; thus, it is generally permitted for those who rely on chance to obtain [the result], as "encountering fortune beyond one's merit" is precisely the meaning of relying on chance.

Question: Regarding the consecration of a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), must the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) be performed? If it is like the aforementioned natural boundary (*prakṛtistha-sīmā*), why would one forget to establish it? Answer: As stated in the treatise (*śāstra*).

The description above appears to follow the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), for its text states: "Within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), pure ground (*pariśuddha-sthāna*) is not permitted; that which previously existed must first be relinquished.

Now, if one is to perform the formal demarcation (*sīmā-bandha*), one should first establish a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), then formally demarcate the kitchen (*maṇḍapa*), and further separately demarcate the ordination site (*sīmā-maṇḍala*).

Subsequently, having delineated both the inner and outer markers outside of these two boundaries, one universally establishes the great boundary, as described in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*, here referred to as the *Mingliao lun*). This is like a surrounding circle."

Regarding the separate residence (*pārivāsika*): if it were not as described here, there would ultimately be no principle for its formal establishment within the natural state; while there might be a provisional arrangement, that is not what is being clarified here.

Next, the section [addresses] the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, which previously established the pure kitchen (*kalpiya-kutī*) as if it were in the natural state; thus, a question is raised to resolve this, and the answer follows.

In the first part of the middle section, the meaning is explained by way of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which prescribes the prohibition of "pure ground" (*śuddhasthāna*). Therefore, one first demarcates a separate boundary (*sīmā*), within which the "pure area" (*śuddhasthāna*) is established;

because this naturally creates a separation, it clearly manifests the monastic boundary (*saṃghasīma*). Since the kitchen is not separately designated as pure, it is said that this accords with the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.

If, in the following section, the demarcation is shown to be necessary, then although the designation of a pure area generally applies to what is natural, the explanation here clarifies its specific application.
The ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is not what is being elucidated here.

Third, regarding the section on the actual application of the rite (*karmavācanā*), the text is divided into three parts: first, the listing of the roles (*kartṛ*) and the establishment of the three positions;

second, the statement "the officiant says this," which refers to the proclamation; and third, the section beginning with "the *karmadāna*," which correctly clarifies the formal conclusion (*bandhana*).
The "untying of the three fetters" is also the fourth section of the aforementioned meaning. The commentary on the text states: "The meaning unfolds through the characteristics and positions;
thus, three headings are established and the three characteristics are distinguished.

In the first part, we provisionally cite one instance of a *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary); therefore, the three characteristics and three essences are listed. However, these must further depend upon various other boundaries.

Furthermore, the establishment of the boundaries (sīmā) may be inferred accordingly; one should understand that they extend naturally until they meet [another boundary], as no specific marker is mentioned.

This is because the size of the site does not exceed what is natural, and if it were made even more expansive, it would ultimately obstruct subsequent legal procedures, for such a principle is not permitted.

However, according to the Vinaya texts, when monks search within the site and are unable to find [the limits], this suggests the area should be expanded; thus, one should follow the established regulation.
In the first section of the sequential commentary, it is first explained that the three types of boundaries (*sīmā*) require various realms;

that is, assembly halls and individual rooms may all be established as either collective or individual boundaries according to their presence, and this does not stop at three layers. Next, the collection of the Sangha is explained by means of signs;
since we now rely solely on these signs, it is necessary to clarify the underlying intent. Below, the Vinaya text is cited, which indicates that the field boundary (*kṣetrasīmā*) was too expansive.
From the original regulations— that is, within the previously cited *Śīla-vinaya*— it is not narrow that a bhikṣu may be present on the site or seek [permission] there;

this is because the "characteristics of the small boundary" (*kṣudra-sīmā-lakṣaṇa*) mentioned in the text refers to it in relation to the external great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), and is distinct from the three types of small boundaries mentioned below.

Because the names of the two types of *śīmaṇḍala* (the large and the small) overlap in their essential characteristics, they must be specifically distinguished by explicitly stating the term "śīmaṇḍala.
This principle also applies to the definition of boundaries (*sīmā*). For now, this is explained with reference to a site facing south;

the commentary notes that "curves and angles follow what is called" because the boundary of a *śīmaṇḍala* need not follow the layout of the altar, as it may instead conform to the shape of the hall or building, resulting in bends and turns.
Regarding the section on the formal act of binding (*bandhana*), there are two parts: namely, binding and releasing. Question:

Why is it not stated that they share a single recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* within the boundary of the *sīmā* (monastic zone)? Answer: Originally, because it was difficult for a large assembly to gather separately, this specific opening was established to bind [the area].

Since the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is governed by a general rule based on the actual residence (*āvāsa*), and the *sīmā* is not a place of residence, it is not mentioned as a site for the recitation.

Furthermore, regarding the three methods for binding the *dharmas*, the questions and answers within the context of the conditions are all compared against the method for binding a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) to show their differences.

In the initial question and answer, because other methods apply specifically to distinct cases, it is permitted to hold the *poṣadha* within a *śikṣāpada-kṣetra* (training ground) to assemble the Saṃgha; however, the regulation necessarily requires a great boundary.
It is not the standard protocol for the opening of a *karmavastu* (formal act) to take place on a site (*sīmā*).
Question: Since both the site and the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) are distinct residences, one should possess both [types of] communal dwellings; why then is it that there is none? Answer:

The site was originally established for the purpose of performing ritual acts (*karman*), not for the settling of monks. Since there is no actual residence, it is said that there is also no [communal] dwelling.

The great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is not like this; it was originally established in contrast to the individual [boundary] because it concerns distinct benefits, thereby manifesting the two as having the same precepts (*samāna-śīla*). Since the *sīmā-kṣetra* (precept-field) has nothing to be contrasted with, both are absent there.

Next, the question explicitly clarifies the cause for not dwelling together (*asahavāsa*), while also being stated in conjunction with the "same" [category]; thus, the answer cites them fully. At the beginning of the response:

Regarding the two meanings for not recording the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (boundary of the precept field): first, it is not for the purpose of settling the *saṃgha*; second, there is no one to be confronted [by the announcement].
The intent behind recording the *mahā-śīma* (great boundary) below should be understood as the opposite of this.

Question: Why is it that the two dharmas of *pravāraṇā* (invitation/invitation-ceremony) require the assembly of the *saṃgha* at the site, while other dharmas do not? Answer: These two encompass [the entire community].

Because the *saṃgha-dharma* is established for those who occupy positions within the practice and possess purity, it is ordained that both inside and outside the boundary (*sīmā*) shall universally comply with it.

Since the various procedures of the *karmavācanā* and other dharmas apply to many paths and are not restricted to a specific time, if one were to restrict them to a collective assembly due to many incidental duties, it would merely cause mutual fatigue;

thus, while there was an initial opening [of the path], there would ultimately be no subsequent benefit. Therefore, when the ritual procedure is performed, if there are persons present in different boundaries...
Because the two groups have assembled together, there is no mention of the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) in the text.

Regarding the three inquiries, since the previous conditions for their assembly have already been clarified, the present intent of the teaching is now further set forth; although this is a repetition, it is distinct and can be understood by examining the response.
In the response, the first part clarifies the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation), while the subsequent part clarifies that the remaining dharmas apply to many [cases].

First, regarding the reversal of the preceding [point]: because it is exclusively for the purpose of performing purification (*śuddhi*), there is no restriction of time; this reverses the preceding [point] which restricts the time. Second, regarding the reversal of the preceding [point]:

because it involves many conditions related to separate affairs, it reverses the preceding [point]. Third, regarding the reversal of the preceding [point]: because it exclusively gathers the Saṃgha, it reverses the preceding [point].

Below, based on the common and specific two types of assemblies, the previous meaning is further resolved: since the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) has a common assembly, both [common and specific] are cited; whereas the Precept Platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*) is exclusively a specific assembly, thus there is no common [assembly].

Since it is stated that there is no commonality in the statement and no commonality in the cause, the fact that the two meanings of "commonality" are not explicitly mentioned becomes even more evident.

Some say that even when performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one may establish the two types of commonality, as seen in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding the text for establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*):
"dwelling together, performing the *poṣadha* together, and receiving offerings together."

Next, regarding the separate explanation within the section on the increase and decrease of the preceding *karmavācanā*, the meaning is clarified by five distinct points: it is evident that there is no [separate category] existing therein;
the three [categories] below are identical to the addition of the *śīla* (precepts); this is identical to the benefit of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*;
and the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that this universally encompasses both the view and the benefit, such that they are not separately designated again.
The latter clarifies the method for dissolution.

If one follows Master Guang’s earlier version, the dissolution of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is understood to encompass the abandonment of the *sīmā-kuṭī* (ordination site); his commentary states:
"This single *karmavācanā* applies universally to the dissolution of both boundaries, according to their respective sizes, as the text contains no restrictive limitation."

Regarding the method for dissolving [the boundary], the initial text of the "Method for Using the Great Boundary" (Dàjièfǎ) compiled by Master Guāng has already been lost; however, the version by Master Tì still exists in the current canon.

This method is suspected to have been compiled by Master Guāng using Master Tì’s text. As for "according to the large or small," the "small" refers to the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept platform), where one simply says "dissolve the boundary";
it is clear from this that both [large and small] are applicable.

If that is so, then when the *sīmābandha* (boundary-binding) for the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) involves two types of "concordance" (*samāna*) and their subsequent release, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) explicitly mentions the term "concordance.

Since the binding of the *śīlākṣetra* (precept-field) lacks this word "concordance," it is clearly understood that the release applies only to the great boundary and not to the precept-field. This interpretation is incorrect.

Regarding the two types of great boundaries (*mahā-sīmā*), the procedure for the simultaneous binding and releasing of both is consistent; however, since the releasing of a site (*kṣetra*) does not involve binding, it cannot be employed here.
Some say that because there was originally no binding of the site, the principle of simultaneity can be applied, and thus it is also valid.
Among these three [interpretations], the intention of this master is that although the conclusion does not explicitly state the two similarities, there is no lack of logical basis in the text;
thus he says, "the principle can be understood as non-existent. Now, to explicitly state the similarity when explaining the meaning also presents no obstacle.

Now, the explanation is that this is not so; for the binding and unbinding of the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) both possess two commonalities, while the binding and unbinding of the *kṣudra-sīmā* (small boundary) both lack these two commonalities, and thus they can be established [as analogous].

In the case of the field-binding (*kṣetra-bandha*), there is no commonality at the time of binding, whereas the unbinding occurs later; since the unbinding is not analogous to the binding, this [field-binding] cannot be established.
Among these four cases, the characteristics of tying and untying the boundaries—whether large or small—are cited as analogous categories to determine the field and its limits.

Although the act of untying does not constitute a formal ritual procedure (*dharma*), it must nonetheless be expressed through verbal instruction. How could one simply record the moment of untying based on the underlying principle of the tying ritual?

Some claim that this [boundary] can be resolved by using three minor boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*); however, this is also not correct, as the characteristics of these three minor boundaries are simultaneously absent.
How could a ritual procedure (*karman*) performed on a single mat be comparable to them?
Next, the critique of employing the three minor boundaries contains two inconveniences: first, they do not establish fixed boundaries; second, they are not long-lasting or stable.
Nor is it dissimilar.
Now, comparing the various realms to form a resolution against a bond, although this is not explicitly found in the Vinaya texts, there is an inference (*anumāna*) [to be drawn].

This demonstrates that in the initial passage of the middle section, the comparison with the various realms applies to all matters—whether large or small, food or clothing—and thus serves as sufficient [evidence].
It is called "inference" (*anumāna*) because it is based upon [a standard].
Regarding the text, there are two parts: first, the heading; the subsequent section on the formal procedure (*dharmakarma*) is clear. Question:

Since the boundary of the precept-field (*śīla-kṣetra*) does not permit the residence of the Saṃgha, why is this text cited? Answer: There are many kinds of "residence"; here, the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*) occur simultaneously.
The heading of this section need not be considered strange; it is just as when a site is first established, one still refers to it as a "dwelling place," let alone in the case of its dissolution.

In the explanation of the Dharma, the initial question contradicts the preceding answer, and therefore it must be resolved. Regarding the various types of dwelling, there are both permanent and temporary forms;
since the dwelling of the four modes of deportment is clarified as not being long-term, what is cited here is merely temporary.
The following passage cites the binding [of the boundary] as an illustration for the unbinding; from this we know that the method of binding is likewise merely temporary. Question:

Since the field for binding has already concluded and the requirement is to bind the entire realm (*sīmā*), why does the text clarify the "establishment of the Dharma" (*dharma-prajñapti*)? Answer: The establishment of the Dharma is necessary;
one may simply rely on the text to determine when to perform the procedures or conceal them. This principle applies to all subsequent cases by analogy.
Next, following the inquiry on the boundaries (*sīmā*), the sequence for establishing the method of liberation is clarified; this applies to all realms.

Therefore, this general resolution extends to all realms, which is equivalent to encompassing the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*). In the response, although the items are listed in sequence, their application depends on the time;
"practice" and "storage" refer respectively to what is used and what is not used.

In the subsequent section on the ritual for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), there are three parts: first, the introduction of the causal origin; second, the characteristics; and third, the formal binding.

Regarding the first, one must not bind the boundary across a river because water is unstable and subject to sudden surges that create obstacles. Since the conditions for the assembly are thus hindered, the purpose of the *saṃgha* cannot be fulfilled.
To merely assume the name of saving those drowning while ultimately losing the reality of exercising the power of the means (*upāya*) is futile, as there is no ferry.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a boundary cannot be established across a river; however, if there is an island in the water, one may establish it by taking five points as markers.

One should take three *yojanas* within the water on both sides, for fear that those holding the ritual objects might drift out of the boundary while crossing. On land, the size is determined according to the circumstances.

In the first section of the initial analysis regarding the subsequent establishment of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the correct explanation is divided into two parts. First, it demonstrates the intent behind the regulation:

since it obstructs the assembly of the Saṃgha, there is no means for the performance of necessary affairs; thus, the conditions and circumstances are blocked. Furthermore, because it contravenes harmony and unity, the meaning of "Saṃgha" cannot be established.

This is because the Tathāgata, employing skillful means (*upāya*) to establish the Dharma, rescues those submerged in suffering; yet [under such conditions], there would be only a hollow name, ultimately achieving nothing.
Because it is effective in practice, it is said that [the boundary] merely extends to the ferry crossings, namely the boats, bridges, and piers.
Following the *Saṃghāṭa-vastu*, the next citation from the five locations established during the Kaicheng era concerns those who demarcate a boundary based on markers:
at that time, because the forest monastery of Mathurā was separated from the hermitage village on the eastern bank by a river, the bhikṣus of both places together demarcated them as a single *sīmā*.

From the *sādhika* boundary up to a river that has islands, one should perform the *karmavācanā* at five locations (that is, establishing markers at these five places to constitute a single boundary, where the ritual action is performed at each spot and everyone must assemble).
These are: first, the Mātṛvihāra; second, within the water; third, on the island;
fourth, within the water again; and fifth, the Ṛṣipatana Vihāra. (This means two are in the water and three are on land. It is like the two sides of a path on dry land.
Each side [of the three locations on land] shall be twenty-five *zhǒu* (twenty-five *zhǒu* equals forty-five *chí*; markers are to be erected at both sides).

The same applies to the water [the width being equal to that of the land above]. Once, during the summer when the waters were overflowing, a *bhikṣu* who had come to grant his consent for the *karmavācanā* was swept away by the flood outside the boundary and nearly died before he could escape.
Upon reaching the other *bhikṣus*, he requested that they enlarge the boundary; this was then done accordingly.
At three *yojana*s downstream, one establishes markers to define the boundary (that is, one moves the two markers in the water further apart).
Question: Do the two boundaries of water and land encompass each other? Answer: As explained above, within the natural boundary (*jātīya-sīmā*), the two do not encompass each other;
the statement that "the *Mahāsāṃghika* obtains [it]" refers to the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).
In this dialogue, the question is posed to clarify the distinction between what is naturally included and what is not within the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).

The answer first points to "natural inclusion," which refers to the previously established conditions for the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) of the Saṃgha; subsequently, it addresses "inclusion through ritual procedure."
It is not permitted for two boundaries (*sīmā*) to meet, because the substance of a boundary is delimited and restricted to its own respective portion;

if they were joined, they would ultimately cease to be separate dwellings, and therefore it is thus prohibited. Regarding the aforementioned distance of one cubit (*hasta*), there is no explicit textual authority;

however, based on the principle that two ropes used to mark off a portion are considered equivalent, the matter is settled. Thus, the text states: "One should leave a space between them," which refers to an empty area.
In the first section of the following analysis, the intent of the regulation is first shown as follows; next, the division of space—its indeterminate width—is clarified.

Since the preceding citation of ancient masters restricted [the measurement] to one *zhou*, the errors of those ancients are pointed out and the correct interpretation is revealed through further textual evidence.
Regarding those who do not chant the boundary markers (*fangxiang*): there are those who perform the binding of boundaries at the last moment and become confused about the ritual;

those who chant the three layers of boundaries collectively while seated within the site; those who chant and bind both the site and the great boundary (*dajie*) collectively within the great boundary;
those who chant only the outer markers; or those who chant only the inner markers. Although they chant various markers, because they are not all-encompassing, these are all considered [errors].

If different realms were to encompass one another, the internal and external would become confused, the three realms would be disordered, and the fixed boundaries for ordination could not be established.

Regarding the second section on clarifying the characteristics, the first sub-section first provides a general heading; the following specific enumeration has five parts: (1) chanting from afar within a single precinct and binding each according to its respective boundary;

(2) chanting universally and binding universally across a Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*); (3) performing the remote addition (*dūre-āropaṇa*) to a *śikṣāpada-maṇḍala*; and (4) and (5), the two [remaining] items.

The two types [of boundaries] lack each other’s characteristics; although the five [types] possess them, there are discrepancies in their vocalized definitions. All these are summarized below as the characteristics of mutual inclusion across different realms (*dhātu*).
That is, the first two cases involve mutual confusion between the internal and external, while the latter three do not. Alternatively, the two phrases may collectively encompass all five faults;
because the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept field) and the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) are separated by the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*), they are referred to as "three realms."

Regarding the boundary (*sīmā*), the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) constitutes the signless; it is not a formal bond (*saṃyojana*), yet it is the true Dharma. Because it is based on reality, there is no confusion regarding "this" or "that. According to the text:

first, within the site (*kṣetra*), one assembles according to the designated signs and chants for the binding of the site. Once the ritual action (*karman*) has been performed, one may then establish the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

Only after this may the Saṅgha be summoned to go outside the *śikṣādattaka* site (the *śikṣāmaṇḍala*). Then, having exited the natural [boundary], they enter the Great Boundary and assemble according to the designated signs.

First, chant the internal boundary marks (*antarlakṣaṇa*) to demarcate the vacant space; subsequently, chant the external boundary marks (*bahirlakṣaṇa*) to sever connection with other territories. Only then, by relying on the formal ritual of binding (*bandhana*), will the dharma be established without fail.

Regarding the first section, the initial part describes the formal regulation; following that, the subsequent part instructs on the procedure for establishing the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (monastic precinct) according to the text. Once the boundary has been established below, [the subsequent rites may proceed].

Regarding the demarcation of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the marking of the boundaries, the gathering of the assembly, and the individual recitation and binding of the ritual: since these matters accord with the teachings, there shall be no failure in their accomplishment.

As for the method of binding not being present in the Vinaya, the practice of the gathered assembly must necessarily follow the recitation as it appears in the texts; its details are so comprehensive that they may be seen as if before one's eyes.
The remainder is as in the two previous [sections] regarding the same matter.

Among the three methods for binding the site (*sīmā-bandha*), the first clarifies the application of the legal rules (*vinaya*). Since there is no separate establishment [of this method] within the legal codes, it is applied by analogy to the method of binding a site without a formal assembly (*asabhya-bandha*).
This is not repeated here, but merely refers back to the preceding section; thus it says, "it can be seen in the text.

The *Chao* (the *Zichiji*) adds the character "internal" (*nei*), and according to this, the rest need not be cited. What follows is a brief reference, namely the explanatory passages from the previous commentary (*shu*) and so forth.

The principles of the method for establishing a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) within the Threefold Knowledge (*traividyā*) are divided into five parts: first, the origins of the teaching; second, the distance for gathering the Saṃgha;

third, the absence of boundary markers; fourth, the similarities and differences between establishing and dissolving the boundary; and fifth, the clarification of what is correct and what is erroneous.

To begin with, the principle that expedient teachings correspond to one another is like the relationship between medicine and disease: the deluded sentiments of ordinary people are easily bound, and the intention of the Sages opens them up.
Therefore, these three minor establishments exist solely to address difficult textual passages.

When the Saṃgha is not in harmony or when there are those who do not agree, these are all "difficulties of persons" that render the formal procedures (dharmas) ineffective; thus, separate establishments are permitted to accord with their intentions and wishes, as can be seen from this.

Regarding the first section of the initial text within the "Arising of the Teachings for the Three Lesser Realms," the phrase "corresponding like medicine and disease" means that the teaching is established in accordance with the capacity of the recipient;
it refers to the fact that ordinary sentiments easily form knots, resulting in stagnation and a lack of harmony.

In the subsequent text, the author next cites conditions to prove that people are difficult to harmonize—that is, human feelings and affairs are contrary to what is appropriate—and thus the response must correspond to them.

Question: If it is like the case of Kauśāmbī, where there was no common harmony, how can they be within the same boundary (*sīmā*) yet permitted to perform formal acts separately? Answer: This is not the same as that case.

In that instance, because the matter and the views were both discordant, it would not constitute the meaning of a *saṃgha*; therefore, separate formal acts were permitted. In this case, although the views are the same, the actions are different;
since they do not harmonize regarding the action, they may be censured separately, and thus separate boundaries are established.

How is it that the present case is also like this, yet requires a separate formal act (*karmavācanā*)? Answer: "Matter" (*vastu*) refers to the action performed. Whether one accepts or rejects [the view], that is the very attachment held. There may be agreement or disagreement in views; if there is discord, one loses [the path]. Thus, because their views are at variance, they must perform the formal act separately. If the six matters of harmony are disrupted, they obstruct the communal Dharma; since the former involves both affairs and views while the latter concerns only affairs, they are not the same.
The traditional transmission merely states that "evil bhikṣus" constitute the difficulty; based on what is clarified here, it is sufficient to know that [that tradition] is false and erroneous.
Regarding the second point, the place where the Saṃgha assembles:

according to the characteristics of the Vinaya texts, it refers to those bound together within the external boundary (bāhirima sīmā) at a forest hermitage (arañña), specifically during the ordination ceremony, provided that no one who does not consent has yet left the boundary;

this is the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*). The text on the recitation of the Prātimokṣa states "descending to the lower path," while the text on the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) states "different locations."

Although within this specific section there is no mention of a natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*), the text clearly states that "descending to another location" refers to the lower path; thus, the Way constitutes a single boundary, while the lower area is the *araṇya*.
If one wishes to rely on a collective boundary, it may be established according to the occasion, as described above, such that everything is naturally determined.

In the second fascicle, regarding the present intention for the initial determination of the boundaries for formal assembly (*saṃgha*), the text is as listed in the commentary. The ritual procedure for receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) is the point where disputes arise;
because one quickly establishes the boundary outside the precincts and it is immediately a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), it is known that the three minor [boundaries] do not apply to cities and towns.

Next, the instruction on the recitation of the *Poṣadha* follows. Below this, the gathering of the monastic community (*saṃgha*) is clarified in two parts: first, indicating the characteristics of the boundary for both the *Poṣadha* and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*).

Because the causal conditions were on the road, it was subsequently opened and demarcated; those who were "under the road" were thus below the path, and because they faced toward the road from the *āraṇyaka* (wilderness) side, it is said they were in a different location.

Regarding the phrase "although belonging to the same section," etc.: although the four locations and six characteristics previously mentioned during the assembly of the Saṃgha appear in other schools (*nikāya*), and although there is no explicit text in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the principle of the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) exists; therefore, this is specifically indicated.
The path constitutes one *dhātu* (realm/region), which is the practice of the Path; the area below it is the *araṇya* (wilderness), which likewise constitutes one *dhātu*.

According to the principle that the Path and the *araṇya* naturally correspond to one another, the following two points clarify their application according to the circumstances: either the Path or the *araṇya* each has its own defined boundary.
However, while the Path is general and applies to both wilderness and villages, this [definition] is specific to the location of the *araṇya*, as in the original source where there was no village.
This refers to the wilderness (*araṇya*).
Some say that since difficulties arise simultaneously, there is no need to rely on fixed boundaries; rather, one should establish the boundary according to the seating arrangement.
Therefore, the text states: "When the seating places are full, demarcate the boundary up to such a point."
Regarding the first interpretation among those cited from antiquity, it follows the text on the formal procedure for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish).

Next, regarding the explanation that whether [the boundary] exists or not, it must all be formally set aside (*nirdiṣṭa*) and removed, but that this principle of "suspended non-binding" (*pratyutpanna-anibandhana*) does not fully accord with reason and differs slightly from the present case, the following section refutes it.

The reason for setting aside what is currently suspended and not binding it is that because a village already exists there, the place being set aside is not the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). Since it is obstructed by the village, there is no way to apply the binding in advance.

Regarding the statement that "suspended [robes] do not constitute a formal bond, while present bonds are suspended and removed": this was because originally there was no village large enough to accommodate a universal bond;
fearing that another village might later arrive within it, [the boundary] was first set aside for the sake of common protection.

Now, the current interpretation is not so; since the bond is established based on a defined limit (*sīmā*), the interior land is universally designated as having the same inclusion of robes, regardless of whether another village arrives.

The boundary for robes is thereby dissolved; it is not because the village exists within the robe-boundary that the boundary is incomplete, but rather because the village is where men and women dwell together, which tends to give rise to lustful thoughts and slander, and since its nature is such that it brings reproach upon the conduct of bhikṣus, the rule was established to exclude it.

In the first section of the current exposition on this principle, the first part clarifies that the formal act of binding (*bandhana*) does not depend on being within a village or settlement; it occurs even in uninhabited places.

Next, the second part explains the citation of the exception regarding the original [monastery], which serves to encompass both the restrictive and permissive rules. By understanding these two approaches, one will see that the interpretations of the ancients and the moderns naturally differ.
Therefore, in the Vinaya, when first establishing the robe-boundary (cīvara-sīmā) within a village, it does not state that the village must be excluded;

rather, the village is only excluded later when circumstances or obstacles arise. This exclusion is for a specific reason and does not exclude the substance of the village itself. How is this known? According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Mahā-vibhāṣā*), the former interpretation states that if there is no village, it is not excluded;

subsequently, however, it explains: "The nature of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) is such that one need not inquire whether [a village] exists or not; in all cases, it must be performed."
If one must leave a village without having removed [the robe], one should gather the robes (*cīvara*) before departing.
Regarding the first section of this rule: the original Vinaya text did not initially prohibit leaving behind [a robe] due to subsequent obstacles;

it was established because a bhikṣu left his robe behind in a village and, upon going to a gathering, became exposed and felt ashamed. The following judgment, based on specific conditions, refers specifically to the case of sexual desire (*rāga*).

Regarding the doubt concerning the cessation of the *sīmā* (boundary): it is said that the village boundary (*grāma-sīmā*) likewise does not arise [in such cases].

To resolve this doubt, both are excluded; for there are five reasons for excluding the village boundary as set forth in the treatise. First, because a single settlement (*grāma*) is disordered and indeterminate, whereas the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) is determinate.
Second, to eliminate slander. Third, to eliminate strife and contention. Fourth, to protect the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Fifth, to eliminate... [the text ends here].
Because it serves to clear away suspicion and because there are no insentient objects in other realms, there is no need to exclude them.

Next, there are two questions: first, regarding the obstruction of a village (*grāma-antarāya*), when tying the robe (*cīvara-bandhana*), one must formally state its exclusion; if there is no village and universal protection (*sarvato-rakṣā*) applies, what benefit is there in stating its exclusion?
This clarifies that where there is no village, it is unnecessary to state it. Second, regarding places where there is no village and no formal tying [of the robe], is it not so?

Regarding the previous statement that "even if one recites the exclusion of a village, it still obstructs [the boundary] compared to one who has already established a village," this means that if one recites [the exclusion], it is ineffective;

this demonstrates that even where a village exists, there is no need to exclude it. The character "yu" (猶) here functions as "bi" (比), meaning "compared to. In the initial explanation of the response, the terms "within the enclosure" (*yuan-nei*) and "outside the enclosure" (*yuan-wai*) were inverted;

the characters for "nei" and "wai" have been erroneously transposed in the transmitted text. If the boundary has not yet been formally established, then naturally, trees and vehicles outside the enclosure each [constitute a separate boundary].

Because it is established, once the offense of leaving one's robes (*cīvarāpatti*) has occurred, the force of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) remains strong, whereas all other [offenses] are immediately extinguished.

Since the village boundary (*grāmamaryādā*) is self-contained, the village must necessarily be excluded. Next, the reason for this specific exclusion is explained through five points: first, it is difficult to protect; second, the rest invite public censure;
third, villages and settlements are subject to constant migration; fourth, the robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) requires fixed demarcations; and fifth, it serves as a standard of reference.
Therefore, it is said that [the boundaries] are either fixed or unfixed. Among the four types, the fourth protects oneself, while the other three protect others.

The above clarifies that village boundaries must exclude [certain things]; the following section distinguishes other boundaries as not requiring such exclusion, because trees, carts, and other insentient objects do not constitute defilement.
Regarding the phrase "whether the four fetters are pervasive or not":
in the preceding section of these four, it was stated that in terms of the delimitation or pervasiveness of the realms (*dhātu*), "pervasive" means universal and "not pervasive" means restricted;
though the terminology differs, the meaning is the same.

Some say that the boundaries are not universal because the text states, "except for villages and the external boundaries of villages. Since there are clearly things excluded, it is evident that they are not universal.
As for the ancient masters' initial classification, it refers to the aforementioned calculation of those who do not establish the boundaries beforehand.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Excluding the village and its boundary, one establishes the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) by taking the open space and the dwelling-place;
because [otherwise] the boundary would not arise. The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "Regarding the area outside the village boundary, it is that reached by a person throwing a stone and having it return.

A commentator explains this as follows: "In the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, when establishing the boundary, the exclusion is explicitly stated; however, the text says 'one takes the open space' (implying that the exclusion is already established by the act of taking)."
This refers to the boundary area outside the village; "and the dwelling place" refers to the substance of the village itself.
Since the village later moved out and there was no prior formal declaration regarding the fourfold [boundary], it is now excluded and not formally established as a suspended [boundary].
The next section cites ten *pādas* from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which are the textual passages for the removal [of boundaries] within that *karmavācanā*.

The first two lines are identical to those in the present *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; the latter two lines were added by that school. Regarding the phrase "village" (*grāma*) and below, it explains the first two lines:

"village" refers to the settlement (*sanniveśa*), and "extent" (*sīmā*) refers to the boundary of the settlement. Since the text explicitly states the removal, the boundary is not established; this is further supported by the *Śaikṣa-dharma*.
Regarding the instruction you have shown concerning the upper limit of the boundary: it is thirteen paces from the person below.

Next, he presents another interpretation, which states that in the four-line passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the first two lines refer to the present exclusion (*pratyutpanna-niḥsaraṇa*), while the latter two lines refer to the future suspension (*anāgata-bandhana*). The "suspended" [robe] is not subject to the [formal] tying.
Now, the explanation is not so; since it excludes the village, it clarifies that there is something excluded.

Regarding the "taking up of open space," this refers to the area outside the monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma*) and the "residence" itself, which means the monastic quarters. Within this, the robe is included; as for the rest, these are what is excluded, and therefore it does not apply universally.
Furthermore, in the first section of the current commentary, the initial explanation addresses the term "excluding" (*pratiṣedha*).

Since the text merely excludes the "aggregation" (*rāśi*), which is a definitive exclusion, how could one further apply a "conclusion" (*nigamana*) to that which has already been excluded? Following this, the subsequent section explains the application of the conclusion by means of the "boundary" (*dhātu*).

Since the *kaṭhina* robe is tied and gathered in a wide and narrow square shape, the external boundary of the *kaṭhina* area is termed "empty space" (*ākāśa*), while the monastic quarters within the *kaṭhina* area are termed "residence" (*āvāsa*).
Thus, one should know that the text in question is identical to the present *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; how then can it be said to differ?

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, within the single *poṣadha* boundary of Śrāvastī, there were nine monasteries (*vihāra*) that had not established a "robe-keeping" boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), and thus each was governed separately according to its location.
Later, when monks from Jetavana went to the Kāpilavastu forest to practice meditation or stayed there overnight, they feared losing their robes.

Consequently, the Buddha ordered that a "non-loss of robe" rule (*acīvaramuṣitaka-dharma*) be jointly established for Jetavana and the nine monasteries, so that they might dwell in peace and security.
This also excludes villages and the boundaries of villages.
Next, regarding the nine monasteries of the Saṃghāṭī [Vinaya], it says: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "From this day forward, [the following shall be designated]:
the Jetavana Monastery, the Āmrapālīvana Monastery (named after the grove), the Eastern Monastery, the Western Monastery, the Eastern Grove Monastery, and the Western [Grove Monastery]."

In the Araññavāsika-vihāra and the Rājārāma-vihāra, at the Salākāvatta-cetiya (identified by its stūpa), they returned to the Araññavāsika-vihāra and collectively established the practice of not losing one’s robes;
that Vinaya likewise merely excludes the *gāma* (village) from the current school.

Question: When there is no village (*grāma*) and the boundary (*sīmā*) has been established, it may be called "dwelling together" because it pervades the entire great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). The robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) is dependent upon the monastic boundary (*saṃghasīmā*), and thus it is called the "original dwelling. It is not necessarily the case that they must both be mutually pervasive.

While the robe may be contained within the pervasive boundary, the village acts as an obstruction, creating a separation. Consequently, while it is "universal" in terms of its original basis (*mūla*), it is "restricted" in terms of its conditions (*pratyaya*); thus, there are two aspects.
The commentary on the text is as explained above.

Regarding the initial question within the dialogue, since it cites "residing together," one must consider whether villages exist throughout the entire realm or not; if they do not pervade the realm, then the two types of "residing together" should be excluded.

In the response, the first part cites an ancient interpretation, which is the aforementioned position that the preceptor need not be formally appointed in advance; this view may not necessarily be acceptable.

Regarding the statement that it is not universal yet may still be called "compatible": the following section first indicates the present meaning. Since it is called "co-residing," their essence must necessarily be compatible;

however, because the fundamental realm is universally pervasive while [the specific manifestation] follows conditions and is not universal, it is described as "restricted. The following section points to the two interpretations—the ancient and the modern—found in the previous recitation.

Regarding those who fear fire in the forest hermitage, this refers to the *bhikṣus* dwelling in an *araṇya*. As it says in that [text]: "At that time..."
In the city of Śrāvastī, a fire broke out, and the people of the city carried their belongings out.

"Running from the city like moths toward a flame—what urgent matter could there be? Regarding the phrase "by means of mutual designation," it says:

The Buddha declared, "From this day forward, I do not permit the designation of a *sīmā* (boundary) that extends through a village; rather, one should designate a *sīmā* at a location where a *sīmā* already exists, or designate a village within a location where a *sīmā* exists, and so forth.

Regarding the sequence of offenses, this section first explains the reconciliation of the two Vinaya traditions (*dharma-skandha*) based on their formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), specifically concerning "monastic dwellings outside the village.

Because the *Vinaya* permitted monks to establish a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) at a pleasant cave in the wilderness (*araṇya*), the ritual formula (*karmavācanā*) for its exclusion specified "excluding the village," which thereby included the surrounding settlement.

This was the teaching of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* that was subsequently superseded. Next, the following section explains the mutual compatibility of the two traditions; since the [exclusion] has already been prescribed, [the boundary] is established.

The *Jian* (Simplified) [Vinaya] does not accord with that school’s tenets, as it precisely conforms to their own doctrine; therefore, it is not subject to rejection. Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika* (Mūlasarvāstivāda) established the boundaries later, yet they also prohibited [the inclusion of] villages, as can be seen from the preceding [text].

If the text states that even prior to the establishment of a village, down to the *Pañcavargika*, all share this intention, it clarifies that the establishment [of the boundary] follows the *sīmā* (demarcated area).
The details regarding the entire village are extremely clear and comprehensive in the text.
In the first section of the five-part division concerning the removal of boundaries (*sīmā*), one can see the intended meaning by examining the phrasing. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If there was originally no village and the boundary for not losing one's robes (*a-cīvara-apahāra-sīmā*) has already been established, then if a person enters after the village has subsequently appeared, it is not necessary to [re-establish] it again."

Because the previous boundary has already been established: if a village originally existed within the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) but later moves out of that area, then this empty space remains a robe-boundary where one does not lose one's robes.
If a settlement was small and subsequently expands, the entire area following the expansion of the village is no longer a robe-boundary.
If a village was originally large and the robe-boundary was established, and it later gradually shrinks, then all the remaining empty spaces are [still part of] the boundary.

The *cīvara-sīmā* (robe-boundary) follows this principle: it is "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) in relation to its prior conditions when not limited by the presence of a village, but it is called "non-pervasive" (*avyāpin*) based on the dharma following its original source.
Regarding these two [types], the first citation of the text first clarifies that where there is no village, one may currently establish a boundary while excluding the suspended [boundary].

Next, it clarifies that where there is a village, one currently excludes [the village] while establishing the suspended [boundary], which is further divided into three aspects: first, moving the village out of the boundary; second, expanding a small area into a large one.

The three [realms] contract the large into the small; whether they exist or not, and whether they are broad or narrow, they are indeterminate according to conditions. This is verified by knowing that, apart from villages, one merely excludes obstructive conditions.
Following the subsequent [case], the preceding meaning is determined accordingly; all of these have sincere scriptural authority.

The subsequent section on the actual addition of the ritual text is divided into two parts: first, the indication of the conditions (*pratyaya*) to reveal the meaning; second, the binding and releasing according to the ritual procedure.
Regarding the first, the term "disgust and renunciation" (*nirveda*) refers to the ascetic monk’s (*dhūta-bhikṣu*) aversion toward the world and his lack of delight in its perceptions.

As for "excluding rapid currents," because they are subject to tossing, surging, and turbulence, even though such places are included within the boundaries of the *saṃgha*, they still communicate with the outside.
Jizang’s interpretation thus lacks the sense of a "bridge," yet it is also generally acceptable.

Regarding the specific application of the term *pratītya* (conditioning) within the context of the *dhūta* (ascetic practices), *dhūta* is translated as "shaking off" (*dousou*). There are two types of worlds: first, the *bhājana-loka* (receptacle world); second, the *sattva-loka* (sentient world).
Since the three realms and six paths all lead to the fruit of suffering, one knows suffering and abandons its origin; therefore, it is called "loathing" (*yàn*).
The world and so forth are characterized by rapid movement; the text does not open up bridges and causeways because it follows the previous rules regarding the monastic boundary (*sīmā*).

Therefore, it is said that the principle applies universally (although the Vinaya clarifies that bridges and causeways are opened, and the commentary does not cite this, merely stating that they do not exist).

Regarding the text of the formal resolution (*karmavācanā*): if there was originally a village but it is now removed, one performs a "suspended" binding (*utsṛṣṭa-bandha*). This is because, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the village is included in the upper ground;

thus, it differs from the ancients who suspended [the boundary] without performing the binding. The ancients said that the *Caturvargika-vinaya* contains no text regarding the binding of a residence or of empty space, but this is not a correct interpretation.
Therefore, as stated above, if there was originally no village but one now binds a suspended removal, one should follow the procedure in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
Afterwards, one may not enter the village to store robes.
Next, according to the Dharma, one performs the binding and unbinding; this is the fourth section of the preceding *yìmén* (gate of meaning).

Regarding the first sub-section of the method for binding, which explains the two phrases "performing the *karmavācanā* to bind" and "removing [the boundary]": first, regarding the method for binding a village, the ground beneath the village is collectively treated as the robe [area].

Because it concerns the *dhātu* (boundary), it is said to be "included. The repeated citation of ancient criticisms is as previously shown. Next, the method for establishing a boundary where no village exists can be understood from the text.

Thus, one knows that within a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), the male and female attendants (*upadhivārika*) have separate quarters; these are not part of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), and those who enter at improper times must inform [the monks].
Those within the same village, as well as those who eat together and stay overnight in private or exposed places—such cases should be understood accordingly.

If there are only single men or women, they do not constitute a "village" (*grāma*); rather, they are merely obstacles to defiled passion. Thus, the text states: "A village is where men and women reside."

Next, regarding the specific indications, the first passage concerns the residences of laypeople (*grhastha*), all of which are objects to be excluded; therefore, they do not constitute the "boundary of clothing" (*cīvara-sīmā*).
