Section Three: The Meaning of Binding and Releasing the Food Boundary (*āhāra-sīmā*). The text is divided into two parts; the first meaning further consists of two sections, the first of which concerns the division of binding and protection.

Within the third section, the "Classification of the Realm of Gathering Food" (*āhāra-dhātu-vibhāga*), there is first the textual exposition of the meaning; next, within that meaning, there is further division into the "Binding and Guarding" (*bandhana-rakṣaṇa*).
This consists of six gates, which include the preceding textual exposition of the meaning; the "Guarding" (*rakṣaṇa*) consists of five gates, which are explained solely in terms of their meaning.

Regarding the establishment of the *śuddhika* (pure) boundary, there are six topical divisions: first, the intention behind the regulation and the definition of its name; second, the enumeration of its categories and the determination of its essence; third, the distinction between one's own and others' boundaries;

fourth, whether the enclosure is complete or incomplete; fifth, whether the ritual action (*karma*) is performed or not; and sixth, the differences in the methods of releasing and binding the boundary.
Within the section on the "Classification of the Pure Portion," there are four points concerning the underlying meaning and two sections explaining the text.

First, regarding the intent of the precept: it is because the three grades of life-sustaining retribution follow divergent paths that the application of transformation and the establishment of teachings are not uniform.
Thus, those with superior retribution possess robust physical strength and upright character; their discernment allows them to respond to begging so as to alleviate the suffering of the body.
Those who entrust themselves to the forests and valleys and rely upon the four seas as their home—such individuals do not require the accumulation of stores.

For those of middle capacity and below, whose physical endowments are sparse and meager, if they were restricted from seeking alms, they would ultimately perish in ditches and ravines. If there were no means to provide for them, they would fall away from the path of practice.

Therefore, because some might die from illness during the period of retreat, the initial prohibition was relaxed; although it was originally restricted, it was eventually established with three grades of allowances.
This teaching arose because it enables the alleviation of the suffering of illness regardless of whether one is healthy or frail, taking the preservation of the Path as its fundamental principle.

In the first section, "The Intent of the Initial Gate," the initial general exposition discusses the three grades of faculties and teachings; that is, the three types of roots—superior, middling, and inferior—are brought to satisfaction.

However, the subsequent section provides a specific account of the emergence of the teaching, which is twofold: first, it clarifies how those of superior faculties rely on the regulations so that their retribution becomes firm and strong.

Because their past roots of goodness have brought this about, their physical bearing and skeletal structure are upright; because their movements are characterized by propriety, they know moderation in their begging for alms;

because they possess internal integrity and fortitude, they are able to relieve the suffering of the body; because they have few desires and are content, they take refuge in forests and valleys, longing for seclusion and stillness;
because they regard the four seas as their lodging, they are not burdened by external things. One who possesses all these virtues is called a practitioner of superior conduct.
Next, the middle and lower capacities are explained as requiring encouragement. First, it describes their inferior retribution:

contrary to the aforementioned points, they are incapable of superior practice and die from the exhaustion of illness, thus perishing in ditches and ravines. Second, it explains the benefit of granting permission:

if such permission were not granted, they might either retreat out of fear or abandon the path midway; hence it is said that they would "fall from their spiritual practice. Below, the original source is cited.
This clearly demonstrates the benefits of the teaching. First, it shows how the teaching universally applies to all three faculties; second, it applies to both the healthy and the sick. Question:

Since one has already received this teaching, can one still be called a "superior practitioner"? Answer: At times, due to the conditions of illness, the meaning of the teaching universally extends to provide aid to all.

Regarding the explanation of the term: food and drink are manifold and complex, capable of producing defilement and impurity; when one dwells with them and guards them while their physical nature contradicts the rules of decorum, this is called "impure.
Once the formal ritual (kṣepaṇīya) has been performed, one is restricted to a specific location; since the accumulation of such things has been removed, no fault arises, and thus it is called "pure.

This is purity in relation to conditions (*pratyaya*); it is not called pure merely in contrast to impurity. Only when one possesses the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*) is it truly termed "pure."

First, by storing and accumulating [food], greed increases and pride grows; this is called defiling the pure mind. Second, it causes non-Buddhists and worldly people to give rise to ridicule and slander; this is called defiling pure faith.
Third, since one has already stayed overnight and cooked together [with others], it can generate many transgressions; this is called defiling pure precepts.
Fourth, it manifests the cause for future retribution of suffering, and as one consumes what is impure, one is forever separated from fragrance and purity; this is called defiling pure fruit.

In the "Explanation of Names" (*Shiming*), there are three parts. First, a general explanation of the preceding section: "That which gives rise to impurity and defilement" refers to faults such as keeping food overnight;
"that which violates ritual propriety" refers to what is unsuitable for a *bhikṣu*. Next, the meaning of "purity" is clarified, the opposite of which can be understood by implication.

Below this, the section on "distinguishing from the superfluous" explains that "arising from conditions" is said in view of being free from faults, while "not corresponding to defilement" is used to refute false views.
Regarding the explanation: it is said that by eliminating superfluous impurities and designating [the remaining] as "pure," one fully possesses the lower [levels].

To specifically reveal this, the name "purity" (śuddhi) is applied generally to encompass four meanings: defilement of the mind is affliction (*kleśa*); defilement of the precepts is karma (*karman*); and defilement of the fruit is suffering (*duḥkha*). These three are both self-defiling and, in pairs, defiling others.
Now, having completed the summary, these are inverted to constitute the four purities (*caturvidhā śuddhi*).
Now, I shall comprehensively cite the various schools to clarify the distinctions between permissions (*anujñā*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*).

Next, I shall clarify these permissions and prohibitions by correlating them, for since permissions and prohibitions appear interchangeably across the various sūtras and vinayas, it is necessary to discern and harmonize their underlying pedagogical intent.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that because rice-water flowed from within the monastery courtyard into the alleys, the people rebuked the monks, saying they were no different from laypeople; consequently, it was prohibited [to do so].

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that initially, after the ground had been demarcated by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), non-Buddhists mocked them, saying, "This is a house for shaven-headed householders;

there is no distinction between its storehouses, kitchens, and food supplies and those of laypeople. Therefore, they ordered that [the kitchen] be built outside the monastic quarters. Since it was then located in the open air, many people came to beg for food.
In the past, it was established as an offense of *duṣkṛta* (*gīla*) for one who did not designate a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*).

First, regarding the abandonment of what was previously bound: the first section clarifying the suspension [of rules] concerns the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which originally permitted pure areas where rice-water flowed outside;

"fan" (the character pronounced "fan") means to rinse grains with water. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the initial prohibition concerned areas outside the boundary because there were storehouses and kitchens there.

Having encountered criticism and disparagement, he realized that hoarding provisions was fundamentally not in accordance with the Way. Next, he clarifies his permanent renunciation of begging for large amounts while eating small portions;
this is because those who beg for food often find that their intake is insufficient.
Some rely on this textual passage to claim that one need not perform the formal ritual of dedication (*parigraha*) at all, as it serves to purify items for the sake of others.

In the subsequent refutation of this divergent view, the initial argument—since it relies on the preceding text—should properly result in the permanent abolition [of the ritual]; yet to treat items for the sake of others in such a manner is profoundly contrary to the intent of the teaching.
Now, this interpretation is incorrect. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) prohibits the construction of kitchens within monastic quarters to avoid external criticism;

if one were to permit food from another's pure kitchen, one would ultimately incur external reproach—this is the first impossibility. Furthermore, if it were food from another's pure kitchen, there would be no offense for overnight storage or reheating;

yet that Vinaya text explicitly mentions both offenses—this is the second impossibility. Thus, the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) states: "One must wait for dawn before seeking alms. This is the [third] point.

If there is no place for food preparation within the central monastery, then this is the same as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. How can these two [texts] differ? A verse from the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"If there is a monastery or temple where smoke does not cease and various kinds of food are constantly prepared for the sake of others, this is called impure food;
a practitioner of reality should not eat such food."
Now, regarding the first section of the initial passage of the refutation of the "Middle," there are two points of contradiction with what one's own position relies upon. First, it is untenable;

next, we cite the Sūtras and Vinaya to prove that [the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*] is not the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. Since the meaning of "a place where food is consumed" is absent, its prohibitions are identical to those of the *Caturvargika*;

how then can you falsely claim that the opening of [eating] other people's property is permitted? The first three lines of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* verse point out the error, while the following two lines indicate the name, because...
Because it was constructed by a bhikṣu, it is called "impure. The latter two phrases establish a prohibition based on the subsequent scriptural texts;
for how could other objects still be permitted within a boundary?

Now, according to the explicit teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, if a monastic dwelling lacks a kitchen, it is not permitted to designate it as a *śuddhasthāna* (pure site), as clarified in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Panyun said: "Regarding the śrāvaka saṃgha, they possess no accumulation of large or small grains, wheat, or beans.

If at times of famine their disciples find it difficult to obtain food through begging and no one provides for their needs, they may open themselves to receiving and storing [food] only for the sake of abiding in the True Dharma.
This must be based on the four dharmas of a donor; this is the correct teaching. To act contrary to the meaning of these scriptural passages is not permitted, much less..."
The *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, and the *Prakīrṇaka* clarify that renunciation does not permit [accumulation]; even when the Buddha was at Jetavana, there were no kitchen tents.

Ānanda prepared medicine outside the monastery, as can be sought in the texts; thus, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Āryacaryā*, and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is said that one should sustain oneself by begging for alms, with no storage whatsoever.
Since the initial reception of the precepts in all Vinayas must conform to the Four Reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), how can one abandon these fundamental principles upon reaching old age?

Although the practice of opening [the precepts] for the Sangha is established as a constant, this may refer to what was previously abolished; one must not follow one's own mind or indulge one's emotions in opening them.

Next, in the extensive refutation, first there is a general demonstration: if the Great and Small Vehicles are viewed in relation to one another, the Hīnayāna is the teaching of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*) while the Mahāyāna is the teaching of complete meaning (*nītārtha*).
Now, in view of the Pure Land, both the Great and Small Vehicles are abandoned, and all are universally understood as teachings of complete meaning. However...
In the case of the minor [teachings], the former is opened while the latter is discarded; in the case of the major [teachings], neither is established at all—this is the difference.
As for the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, specifically the passage from the "Chapter on the Four Reliances," the first three phrases cite the preceding section, which states in full:
"As for the śrāvaka-saṃgha, they possess no accumulations, namely: slaves, servants, laborers, treasuries, or stores of grain."
If one personally prepares food by grinding salt, sesame, or various beans, or by pounding them— performing such various unrighteous acts—

Third, within this section: first, "generally indicating" (what follows); below, there is a "specific explanation. First, "no internal cooking":

Fourth, when the Saṃgha performs a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to establish boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), if the site has been occupied for a long time and cannot be partitioned, one must harmonize with all parties and establish it in accordance with the Dharma.

According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, within the section on "Spontaneous Assembly," it is established that in accordance with the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, monastic affairs may not be conducted on ground where the formal ritual (*karmabhūmi*) has not been performed;
further details are as explained in the section on "Delineating the Boundaries" (*sīmā-bandha*).
Regarding the two [Vinaya] Mātṛkās, it has already been determined as before that the *Mahāsāṃghika* textual evidence must pertain to formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*).

furthermore, by treating the two [preceding categories] as distinct, there are six.

At that time, the brahmin Śreṇika, who wore matted hair, heard that the World-Honored One was coming;

he prepared a monastic dwelling and a clean kitchen, sent someone to invite the Buddha and his followers, and so forth, as detailed in the commentary. "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) is a general term for those who dwell in pure conduct.

Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) establishes that one must not exceed the prescribed time; this is because the phrasing of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) in the aforementioned limited [texts] was overly broad, so this [text] provides a definitive resolution.

(According to this, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also designates specific methods as *karmas*, not only those in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* [Ten-Recitation Vinaya] and the *Caturvargika-vinaya* [Four-Part Vinaya]).

Items three, four, and the first [of the six categories] all concern the selection of persons; the second concerns the matter itself; and the fifth [category], place, and the sixth, method, are all subsumed under the four conditions.
The formal acts (*karmavācanā*) for the distribution of the three, one, or many items at separate locations according to the time and quantity require a minimum of four persons;

these apply to both the monastic and lay communities. However, the formal acts for the distribution of the four types of requisites at separate locations pertain to all seven classes of followers, while formal acts restricted to the Sangha alone are limited to the monastic community.

Fifth, regarding the distinction of location: the distribution of territory (*sīmā-bandha*) applies to all realms (*dhātu*), whereas the formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*) is restricted to the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
Among these five, that which applies to all realms is the *svabhāva-kalpa* (natural method).

Sixth, regarding the distinction of the method of dissolution: the dissolution of the territory is performed through oral procedure (*vāc-kalpa*), while the dissolution of the formal ritual act consists solely of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion followed by one proclamation).

Regarding the sixth section, the explanation of the method for the division of the oral dharma concerning the intermediate locations, it simply states that at this location one does not construct a purified dwelling (*pariśuddha-veśman*).
Within the formal procedure (*vidhi*), the binding and releasing are divided into two parts.

In the first part, the causal conditions are indicated: because of life-threatening danger, the construction of a peripheral room or a secluded place is permitted; however, this must necessarily possess two conditions.

To untie the knots, one must entrust oneself to the Way through pure cultivation. While the conditions of food and sustenance are cluttered and complex within the secular world, even a man of integrity would still keep his distance from the kitchen;

how much more so for one who has transcended the world and is suddenly subjected to the service of common servants—this is truly unacceptable. Furthermore, my residence is in a remote borderland and situated in a secluded place;
the intent behind this is clear.

In the first section of the sixth gate’s conclusion, it first demonstrates the circumstances for granting an exception regarding "life-threatening danger. This refers to the original *nidāna* in the Vinaya:
while entering the city to seek gruel out of concern for a patient, the city gates had not yet opened, and he consequently died of hunger.

Regarding the "two conditions," these refer to the requirement for a peripheral room as well as a secluded place; the following explains the intent of the teaching for those who dwell in pure cultivation.

This means that the place where one cultivates the Way must necessarily be a pure and open location; it is not appropriate to share the same quarters as food or to be situated among the vulgar and lowly.
This is a figurative expression cited from Mencius, though while borrowing his words, the intended meaning here is distinct [from his]. [Mencius said:

"The gentleman, in his dealings with birds and beasts, cannot bear to see them alive and then witness their death, nor can he bear to hear their cries and then eat their flesh; therefore, the gentleman keeps the kitchen far removed. [In contrast,] I, a humble and mediocre servant, am now mixed among the base classes.
Furthermore, the lower boundary is established to manifest the desire to remain far from the monastic community; thus, it must also include a secluded location.

In the Vinaya, one should chant the name of the room, which serves as its defining characteristic. In current practice, one directly relies on the four lines of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion and resolution), chanting and establishing the boundary oneself.

This follows the literal text but loses the essential context of the proclamation (*ārocana*). If one wishes to rely on the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), it should be included within the *jñapti* (motion).
If the second phrase were added, its underlying rationale would be established. However, for the sake of following the current text, it has been omitted here;
I fear that those who adhere strictly to the literal teaching might offer further criticisms. This may be a textual omission by the compilers, or perhaps a lapse in recitation by Jue-ming.

Furthermore, one must reflect upon whether Zhu-nian’s manuscript was incomplete, as compared with other compendia of the Dharma, the meaning appears deficient. How can this not be a cause for reflection?

Next, regarding the first section of the initial chapter on manifesting the characteristics: first, the text is punctuated; now, following this, the deviations are refuted. First, the calculation of their views is presented:

because they do not establish a separate *karmavācanā* (formal motion) for manifesting the characteristics, but rather include it within the conditions of the *karmavācanā*, it is said that "one may personally announce and personally conclude.

Next, the current refutation is threefold: first, pointing out the error; since the *Vinaya-mūla-saṃghāṭi-dharma* (the formal method of concluding) consists of only four phrases, one must rely on the text as it stands to achieve the result.

However, since the *chàngxiàng* (the formal proclamation) was not established, the second sentence did not cite the original basis for the conditions; thus, citing the conditions was considered an error.
To provide instruction for rectifying this below, we now establish the *chàngxiàng*. Since the preceding conditions already exist, it is necessary to add a sentence.

Now, the following text first clarifies the reason why [certain schools] do not add [the sentence], which refers to those who adhere strictly to the literal teachings (*jùjiào*). The remaining words are as follows:
This is precisely a derisive critique of the following section where the text is incomplete.

First, it refutes the faults of the initial compilation, suggesting that either Upāli compiled it first, or that the *Dharmaguptaka* school divided the lineage. Next, it refutes the faults of the transmitted tradition:

Jue Ming—that is, Buddhayaśas—recited the original text from the West, while here in this land, Zhu Fonian translated it in correspondence with him and served as the scribe for the various rules on boundary-setting (*sīmā-bandha*) and the formal motions (*jñapti*).
Because these five phrases are uniquely missing here, it is said that "the sequence is deficient," meaning there is a loss of systematic order.

As for the text listing the dwellings of the five groups of practitioners (*pañca-varga*), how could this refer to the nuns? The three groups of female practitioners are those for whom the monks constructed dwellings intended for their own support;
they are named after their original builders, as in the case of Viśākhā Mātṛ, who said, "I reside here."
A "room" (fang) should be understood as being analogous to that which is endowed with blessings and abundance.

According to the subsequent section on the meaning of monasteries for the Saṃgha, there is no principle for nuns to reside there; therefore, this is explained by reference to the host of the room and by citing similar cases.
Furthermore, it is seen in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* that when the mother Viśākhā built a room and offered it to the Saṃgha, she continued to provide for it herself, saying, "This is my room."
It is clear that this belongs to its original owner and should be given to them for their abundance of merit; that is, by receiving offerings and gifts, they benefit me with merit.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* lists the characteristics and states that it applies generally to all [monastic dwellings]. Thus, in that text, it refers generally to monasteries (*saṃghārāma*), excluding only the actual residences of the monks.

This is because if fruit trees within the boundary are about to ripen and do not grow, there is a fear that they might become "overnight stored" (*antargrāma-sthita*) if one does not formally designate them early on. Furthermore...
It is said that if one performs purification on a multi-storied building or atop a wooden frame where the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is not permitted, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, one must not take earth from pure ground and place it on impure ground while claiming it is pure; purity arises based on the original site.

If the original site—whether pure or impure—is moved, there is neither purity nor impurity. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, [the boundaries] may be separated by a road on one side, two sides, or three sides.
Both sides consider the area on one side to be pure ground and the remainder to be impure; this means that purity is obtained according to the time and the measurement of the location.

When the mind follows its own purity, the vessel and the food are also pure. For instance, if one does not know that fruit or food is within the boundary (sīmā), it is precisely because of this "not knowing" that the mind is pure, and thus it is permitted as a condition for purity.

Among the three [sections], the first indicates that the method of binding applies universally to the monastic compound (*saṃghārāma*), as it cites two commonalities; "excluding those where monks reside" and below provide specific exclusions.
Below this, the intention of the allowance is shown. Furthermore, the section below clarifies what is not in accordance with the Dharma, which is twofold:

first, it clarifies that although the ritual procedure was performed, the location added was inappropriate; second, it clarifies that although the soil was moved, the re-binding was not performed on the impure ground.

That is, within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), one subsequently cites the *Saṃghika-vinaya* to clarify the intent of the formal act of demarcation (*sīmā-bandha*). Regarding the two sides: the boundaries are defined by being adjacent to one another, with a path separating them;
both sides face each other directly, as indicated below. The names are provided as cited in the proof-texts, which will be explained in detail later.

The passage in the text concerning "binding from afar outside the precincts" refers to the sixth section on the distinctions of ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) within the chapter on the meaning of "releasing.
Furthermore, the initial heading among the three types of "additional binding" is also the fourth section on the distinctions between binding and releasing at the beginning of this scroll.

Regarding the method for establishing the *saṃgha-sīmā* (monastic boundary) and the method for establishing the *bhojana-sīmā* (food boundary) within the same location: how is it known that the latter is established at a distance? Because the text states:

"Now, within these four boundaries, one establishes [the food boundary]"; and regarding the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), it says: "The Saṃgha now establishes [the food boundary] at such-and-such a place.

The reason for this is that while the *saṃgha-sīmā* and the *cīvara-sīmā* (robe boundary) encompass persons and share both the same Dharma and the same location, the *bhojana-sīmā* is not like them in its mode of encompassing.

Regarding the obstruction caused by food for the Saṃgha: when the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of boundary-binding is performed while people are eating in the same location, it is inconvenient within the ritual procedure; therefore, the binding is proclaimed from a distance.
Next, regarding this remote binding, the first section initially demonstrates that the monks' meals are not held in the same place;

below this, the text cites specific passages as separate proofs, all of which concern the conditions for the *karmavācanā*. Furthermore, each section deduces the underlying reasons: the first clarifies that the monastic boundary (*saṃghasīma*) shares the same location, while simultaneously encompassing the robe-territory (*cīvarasīma*).
Because they share the same status as the Saṃgha, the method for delimiting the food zone (*āhāra-sīmā*) at a distance is explained next.
Furthermore, some interpret this as necessarily being on pure ground (*śuddha-bhūmi*); yet what hardship is there in defining the location oneself? How could it be that one is unable to do so?

Once the delimitation has been performed, even if there is the fault of overnight contact (*rātri-sparśana*), it only destroys the eating utensils and does not damage the purity of the ground. There is a specific ritual for the delimitation and the subsequent lifting of these boundaries; [otherwise] there would be defilement.
When two parties with offenses are unrelated yet reside together, a formal bond (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is established; even if they are listed in some place, the documents state their mutual relationship.

Next, in the first section, the preceding meaning is reversed: "suffering" (*duḥkha*) refers here to harm. Therefore, the subsequent section contrasts the differences between the binding and releasing of prior contact.
Furthermore, the following section resolves the previously held positions.

Question: Why is it that the boundary markers (sīmā) are not erected within a consecrated pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*)? Answer: This is because the ancients did not seek out the textual authority for doing so, as has already been clarified above.
One must understand the necessary demarcations; otherwise, how could one avoid the faults of "storing overnight" (*rātri-vipravāsa*) and "cooking" (*pakva*)?

The ancients had a saying: "To look at food from the perspective of the Sangha is to view it as both a gathering and an obstacle. This refers to the dual perspective of the Sangha's food. The intention behind establishing a pure ground is to gather food while preventing obstacles to the Sangha; one fears [otherwise] that food might be obstructed.

Regarding mutual defilement, it is further said that when one *saṃgha* looks toward another *saṃgha*, it is neither included nor obstructed; this refers to when the *saṃgha* residing in an impure area looks toward a pure area.
When performing communal legal acts (*saṃghakarma*), all must assemble together; only the "overnight cooking" rule is included, while the "separate assembly" rule is not—could it not be otherwise?

Next, regarding the section on the characteristic of non-erectness (*an-ūrdhva-lakṣaṇa*), the initial question arises because it was not established by the ancients; thus, it is posed as a hypothetical inquiry and answered accordingly.

Within the answer, the first part refutes the ancients as shown below, while the subsequent part clarifies the present position by referring back to what was stated above—namely, that within the ancients' system of characteristics, there was a separate master who established a category to distinguish between the similarities and differences of the two realms (*dhātu*). Here, the evidence is taken to show that each [realm] is subsumed [within its own category].
The text is divided into two sections. In the first section, the initial two phrases cite the ancient view;

the subsequent portion provides the present interpretation, stating that when the *śuddhasthāna* (pure ground) is viewed in relation to the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary), each is contained within itself and does not interpenetrate. Furthermore, in the second section, the initial two phrases cite the ancient view;
the subsequent portion provides the present interpretation, stating that when the *mahāsīmā* is viewed in relation to the *śuddhasthāna*, the principle of encompassing the Saṃgha is identical.

Regarding the mention of the "kitchen courtyard of the eastern wing" in the text: if one were to follow the Vinaya texts, it would simply refer to a certain location, as in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, where it is situated in the southwest.
However, following the local customs of this region, there is no way to disregard them;

for in the various monasteries of Jambudvīpa, gates all open toward the east, because the Middle Kingdom still regards the direction of the rising sun as superior, and furthermore, because the prevailing winds blow from the east.
"Scattered" (*san*)—in this land, it refers to the quarters, which also begin with the east. This is because they honor the yang energy and take the North Star as the center;
thus, the east is designated as the kitchen. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "To follow worldly convention involves no fault; one must not treat day as night."

Third, the explanation of the eastern wing. First, it demonstrates the differences between the various Vinaya schools: the *Dharmaguptaka* is not fixed, while the *Mahāsāṃghika* is as previously described.
Now, following this, the next section clarifies the establishment [of the monastery] according to local conditions. The first two lines provide a general indication regarding Jetavana;

below, there is a specific explanation. First, it explains that in the Western lands, the east is honored: (1) because the sun rises in the east, and (2) because it faces the wind. Since the temple gate faces east, the kitchen is located accordingly.

Regarding the two luminaries in the southwest, this land still takes the east as the beginning for the four cardinal directions and the four seasons, concluding with the north to determine the North Pole (*beichen*).
The *Erya*, in its "Explanation of Heaven" (*Shitian*), states: "The North Pole is called the North Star (*beichen*).
Guo Pu comments: "The North Pole is the center of heaven, used to rectify the four seasons. Thus, "pole" (*ji*) means the center, while "star" (*chen*) means the time.
Furthermore, because it resides in the center of the heavens, it is called the North Pole (*Běijí*); because it rectifies the four seasons, it is called the North Star (*Běichén*).
However, since the gates of temples in this land mostly face south—following the principle of the "Correct Yang" (*zhèngyáng*)—the kitchen and latrines should be located in the northeast;
this is also because there is much southern wind. Therefore, the following citation provides evidence that even within the Buddha-dharma, one cannot avoid conforming [to local customs].
The mundane [convention] merely does not follow that view; for example, day and night are fixed laws of the mundane world—how could one not conform to them?

Question: Once the boundary of a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*) has been established, there is certainly no cooking within it; why then is "overnight storage" (*sāyāhna-sthiti*) not prohibited? Answer: "Overnight storage" follows the person, and thus it is not questioned here.
Whether the ground is pure or impure, one commits an offense if there is a person present, but not if no person is present;
however, regarding cooking, this applies regardless of whether a person is present or not—whenever it is within the great boundary (mahā-sīmā), cooking inside constitutes an offense.

In the initial question-and-answer regarding the distinctions between "storing overnight" (*antarā-sthāpana*) and "cooking inside" (*antaḥ-pāka*), the answer states that "storing overnight" depends on the person and constitutes an offense in both locations [the monastery and the village],
whereas "cooking inside" depends on the location and is restricted solely to the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

Question: What is the difference between not having formally demarcated a boundary (*sīmā*) and staying overnight [within it] after it has been demarcated? How is this exception established? Answer: Before the boundary is demarcated, one may commit an offense throughout the entire area;
once it is demarcated, the offense is restricted to where the Saṃgha resides. Therefore, there is benefit [in establishing the boundary].
Next, it is asked: what benefit is there in purifying the ground if one still does not escape the offense of staying overnight indoors?
Furthermore, since one may neither stay overnight nor supervise the cooking, what is the point? The answer is: supervising the cooking is not a causal condition for an offense;
rather, staying overnight is the primary prohibition, and thus they differ.
Regarding the three questions: it is said that one should not even briefly enter to look at the cooking. Question:

Once the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is concluded, if there has been no overnight storage, is it permissible to cook it oneself, even if it involves "bad contact" (*duṣṭasparśa*)? Answer: This is also due to different conditions;
"overnight storage" refers to the fault of keeping it for a night, while the other two refer to the faults of preparation. Such preparation is improper and is not permitted by the pure dharmas.
Prevention.
The four questions regarding the distinctions between the four offenses in the division of desire are all easy to understand from the text. Question:
Now, one who opens [the boundary] does so to avoid transgression; yet here, even while staying overnight, one still does not escape the offense. If that is so, how can it be explained?

Question: Once the purification of the added materials has been performed, should one not likewise be prohibited from keeping extra materials or constructing a dwelling? Answer: The rules of regulation differ because they are established for the sake of benefiting others;
since they open and close according to the proper measure, it is said that one must know the [disciples'] capacities.

Regarding the five questions: the first part summarizes the preceding section; the latter part formally raises an objection concerning the ritual for designating purity (*śuddhi-vyavasthāpana*), the rules regarding keeping extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), and the authorization for constructing dwellings.
In the response, the first two phrases directly answer that the establishment of these rules benefits sentient beings and thus cannot be treated as a single uniform case;
the final two phrases conclude by praising the Buddha’s title, noting that his excellence in knowing the capacities of beings is rooted precisely in this.
Regarding the interpretation of the text, although it is not part of the formal Vinaya rules, because it provides an explanatory opening, there is no fault in explaining it by analogy.

Second, regarding the interpretation of the method: since the Vinaya contains provisions for "opening" (allowances) where there is no explicit rule, one may instead establish a prohibition and interpret it as an opening; therefore, it is said to be explained by analogy.
The second major section clarifies the five gates of protecting purity. First, the overturning of defiled dharmas; second, the protection and maintenance of the precepts;
third, the universality or limitation of offenses; fourth, the concealment of transgressions and falling; fifth, the cultivation of the seeds of purity.
The second section concerns the protection of purity (*śauca*). The following five gates are explained and cited extensively in the *Datong Shichao* (Great Commentary on the Rituals);
here, they are merely briefly pointed out according to the text.

Regarding the first [of these five], there are four positions: first, impurity in terms of conditions; second, purity in terms of conditions; third, impurity in terms of substance; and fourth, purity in terms of substance.

The first [rule] must be reversed, while the remaining three do not require it. For instance, when encountering conditions that involve contact with overnight-stored impurities, the Vinaya regulations prohibit it;

however, in times of scarcity, seeking food is permitted. If one easily obtains food and privately complies with the general text by storing and cooking it overnight—even if this is actually based on difficult circumstances—if abundance is encountered, one must cease this practice.
Such persistence results in impurity due to these conditions; alternatively, one may occasionally partake of pure conditions to maintain the utensils.

For example, if one subsequently intends to still the mind but the activity does not cease, or if one indulges the mind and attempts to grasp it while claiming there is no fault or entanglement—knowing yet acting intentionally—all such cases must be reversed.

In the first section on "Conditions" within the first gate of "Impurity," there are five initial points: first, encountering conditions and being touched by past habits; second, [the text states] "The Vinaya... and so forth, ending with "none."

1. On account of [the rule], three [cases] were opened; 2. because of the subsequent cause, four [cases] were opened without restriction; 3. or, because the underlying conditions did not cease, five [cases] were opened;
4. or, because of ignorance, teaching, arrogance, and transgression.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there were various wooden vessels commonly used for serving food; when they became greasy and impure, they were scrubbed with tiles and stones until they broke.
A vessel belonging to the Saṃgha that has been defiled should be washed with boiling water and alkaline ash.
According to the subsequent section on the fivefold division, once it has been touched as described above, it must be washed and turned over.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Copper vessels should be cleaned thoroughly; wooden vessels that have absorbed grease should be discarded, while those that do not absorb it may be used by shaving off the affected portion."

If one has rice, flour, sauce, vinegar, or similar items, and uses a small amount of them by bartering among the six groups [of monks] until the original substance is obtained, it is called "pure" (viśuddha).
This is because the ownership is not fixed; since it belongs to whoever happens to possess it at that moment, it may be used.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the initial portion is translated as "utensils" while the remainder is translated as "food";

this means that when objects are numerous, it is not necessary to exchange them all, but rather one takes a small amount, exchanges it, and places it within [the food]. Even if one obtains the original substance, it automatically becomes pure.
This method is extremely essential and should be followed accordingly.

Regarding the two conditions for purification (*pratyaya-śuddhi*): as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one inadvertently touches or grasps the monastery’s roasted flour (*piṣṭaka*) due to forgetfulness or error, or if one encounters circumstances where one must stay atop a boat or carriage carrying goods, these are cases of purification through conditions.
In the first section on purification through conditions, both instances from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* are considered non-intentional.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) holds a cooking vessel or other utensils, he may provide assistance by supporting it, but he is not permitted to tilt or overturn it.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, such acts of assistance must cease once the task is finished.
Among the four categories [of food], touching impure food with a defiled mind causes one to incur offenses; however, touching it unintentionally or when using a clean vessel is not an offense.

Furthermore, in times of famine when people eat one another, the following eight matters are permitted: storing food overnight (*antarāgata*), cooking indoors (*antargṛha-pakva*), cooking for oneself (*svayaṃ-pakva*), touching food with a defiled mind, and consuming both monastic and lay food as well as fruits from both water and land without performing the *kṛtānna* (remaining-food) ritual. These constitute the combined meaning of the eight points.

Regarding the two offenses of consuming leftovers and consuming stored food, which destroy the single type of livelihood, the text permits eating [meat] internally for the sake of life-threatening danger;

however, it does not permit damaging [beings] externally, because such acts would provoke worldly censure and lead to confusion. This is not explicitly stated [as permitted]. Even if one encounters a year of plenty where alms are easily obtained, if one still follows the aforementioned permission, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
In the first of the three sections of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, it is judged that one who touches the Buddha with an evil mind incurs an offense, while one who does not touch him achieves purity.

Second, regarding covering vessels from below: the Vinaya states that if a jar of ghee or oil is not covered and there is no pure person (pariśuddha-pudgala) present, one may take the lid in one's own hand and suspend it over the top;
this constitutes purification by means of that circumstance. Third, during times of scarcity, eight matters were permitted. Furthermore...

Fourth, the initial narration of the circumstances introduces and lists eight matters: the first four distinguish the characteristics; the two types of food share the same result regarding the opening [of the rule];

and the "not making *kṛtānna*" (not preparing extra food) consists of five matters in total. The reason they are divided is that, according to the original *nidāna*, the four substances were brought separately. Here below, the characteristics of the offenses are shown:

"evil contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśa*) includes both "storing overnight" (*antar-śaya*) and "not receiving the remainder" (*apariśeṣita*); since "storing overnight" is already opened [as permissible], it is combined here.

The meaning of "cooking for oneself" includes both the destruction of living beings and the textual allowance for internal consumption; that is, while fruits and vegetables for food are permitted, external damage—namely the cutting and destroying of grasses and trees—is not.
If these were listed together in the text, it might be thought that both are equally permitted; therefore, it is stated that such a confusion would not be evident.
If, below, it clarifies that returning to the prohibition results in an offense despite following the allowance, then this belongs to the preceding category.

The full text of these matters is listed exhaustively in the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*). When the conditions for opening [the rules] arise, they must be opened; when the conditions for closing arise, they are immediately closed.
Although there was prior contact with what was previously forbidden, because it was opened due to specific circumstances, no defilement occurs, and thus there is no need to reverse the rule.

Regarding the second point, see the text of the *Chao*, which explains that the four medicines are opened or closed according to circumstances, which is largely the same as the previous case. This concludes the decision below.
The superior condition is pure and unstained, never inverted.

In the former gate, one should not do what ought to be done; in this gate, one does not do what ought to be done. These two ways of deviating from the net of the Dharma both result in a single offense.
Among the three [categories], the various conditions listed above pertain to both gates; therefore, they must be clearly distinguished.

For example, when an exception was granted during a time of famine, once a year of plenty had arrived, one should not continue to store or handle [food] in that manner. To do so would be "to do what should not be done.
Although it was previously permitted, it now requires re-regulation; yet if one fails to comply with this, it would be "not to do what should be done. The former...

Regarding these two types of offenses—those committed through preparation (*ārambha*) and those committed through completion (*niṣṭhāna*)—although they differ in their modes of transgression, they both result in the fault of "overnight contact" (*sāmiṣa-sparśana*); therefore, they are said to constitute a single offense.

Third, concerning the impurity of substance: as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vibhāṣā*, the sale and purchase of wealth for food and the pursuit of livelihood by a practitioner of the Path involve a transgression equal to that of slaughtering animals.
Although this does not constitute the fault of overnight contact, its use is nonetheless forbidden in principle; this extends even to the case of making images, which is likewise improper.

Even if one gives with a mind of reverence, it is improper to accept [the gift] from a monk; for as long as the intention follows through and continues without interruption, it is fundamentally not permitted to transfer [the property].

Even if it were transferred, it would ultimately remain defiled because the intention still persists. Only after the person has died may it be entirely received by the Sangha, because at that point the intention has ceased.

Regarding the impurity of the body, first, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited: although one has left the household life, if one engages in business for a livelihood, they are called a "merchant-monk" (*vaiśya-bhikṣu*).
If such a person uses the wealth obtained to seek merit by hosting assemblies, a precept-observing bhikṣu must not accept or use it;
the transgression is greater than that of a butcher. It says: a butcher harms only one lifetime, whereas those who trade in all manner of goods harm all living beings.
Therefore, one does not prostrate to images nor accept offerings from them; the following explains the intent of the regulations. First, it demonstrates that the physical body is impure;
second, it clarifies that after death, the body enters the Sangha.

Fourth, the body is pure [in its essence], as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, where after a bhikṣu has finished eating, he gives his bowl containing the remains of the meal to a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*).
Having finished washing it, he returns it to the monastic vessel; because it was given with a single-minded intention, it is called "purified" (*śuddha*).
Furthermore, if a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) carries food and, having received it, returns it to a monk—provided there was no prior agreement between them—the monk may take the food as an offering.

From the five portions, he eats the remainder himself and gives the rest to those who have been purified. Once this has been clarified, he may then accept what is offered back to him in accordance with the Dharma.
All [of these] are obtained because one has resolved to renounce [the bowl] and lacks any intention to keep it again.

Regarding the first section of the *Śarīra-viśuddhi* (Purity of the Substance), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* first clarifies the giving of pure food with an impure bowl; this refers to a bowl that has already been used for eating.
Furthermore, the following section clarifies the mutual exchange [of bowls], where one takes food according to what is offered to purify that [bowl]. Below this, there is the opposite case.
One must not say a single word [to the contrary]; if one had previously made an agreement, it would not constitute "purity of substance.

The fifth point, "returning the gift the next morning," means that if a pure person (a *śuddhika*) does not eat [the food] but returns it the following morning for the bhikṣu to receive, it is permissible. All these points below serve as a general resolution of the preceding text.
As the original text states: "A new, clean vessel, firewood, water, clothing, or silk are not inherently subject to the fault of being touched or stored with [impure things] for consumption;
water is a great opening [of purity]. How could there be defilement?

Next, regarding new vessels, the first section classifies various objects by distinguishing between new and old vessels; the rest are not discussed. This is according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*).
The water is called "of great capacity" because it need not be formally accepted (*paribhoga*).
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when a bhikṣu washes an oily vessel and places it in water to heat it over a fire, once the water has boiled up, he should have someone inform him;
then he places rice inside and must not heat it further, but rather instructs a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) to wait until it boils again, at which point he may proceed according to the rule.
After receiving it, one must re-boil it.
Next, regarding the first section of the "Citation and Demonstration," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a vessel not previously used for oily substances is a "new" vessel;
such a vessel may not be used [for cooking] again because it protects against self-cooking. Once received, it must be re-boiled, as this is equivalent to warming food.
Nowadays, many people with good intentions light fires, thereby coming into contact with monastic vessels; this is all for the purpose of cooking for themselves.
The Vinaya permits lighting fires only before rice has been put into the pot, and because the vessels are then clean. At present, however, the vessels are all greasy with the remains of food;
since any contact would cause the moisture and dust to become thoroughly defiled, it is not permitted.
Regarding the first of these two [points], it describes the presence of two faults: first, the fault of improper contact; second, the fault of self-cooking.

The *Vinaya* (specifically the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) clarifies these faults: although that text permits lighting a fire, it does not permit contact with or cooking by means of it; now, however, the opposite is done, which violates the teachings and constitutes an offense.

As stated above, regarding the Saṃgha’s vessels for water and so forth: if they are free of oily residue and pure, or if they are new and clean, touching them does not constitute an offense because they differ from those belonging to individuals;
since the substance is unstained by oil, what would there be to overturn? What is it that could be overturned?
Among the three [points], the first follows the preceding text; "the Saṃgha" and below resolve the new vessel.
The two phrases below explain the aforementioned "contact with substance," while the two phrases below invert the aforementioned "no inversion.
Some say that in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when a boat is in the water or a chariot is being driven by oxen, even if a bhikṣu touches them, there is no [offense].
The substance of the offense is pure; the current interpretation that it is not so is incorrect, because it arises due to the conditions of the cow and the water.
Once those conditions depart, it is no longer defiled, which differs from a water vessel whose nature is inherently pure and lacks such adventitious conditions.
