This is because the meanings of the foreign land are vast and manifold, whereas the names in this land are limited and narrow; thus, one must expand upon them to fully express the meaning. There are also cases where multiple words in the foreign land are condensed into a single word in this land, such as translating *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as "unsurpassed complete enlightenment" (*wushang zhengdeng jue*) or *tathāgata* as "thus-come one" (*rulai*). This is because the foreign land has many synonyms for a single meaning, whereas this land often uses a single word to encompass many meanings; thus, one must condense them to avoid redundancy. There are also cases where a single word in the foreign land is translated using a combination of both [name and meaning], such as translating *bhikṣu* as "one who has broken [evil]" (*po'e zhe*) or *śramaṇa* as "one who has exhausted [defilements]" (*jinmo zhe*). This is because the meaning of the foreign land is broad while the name in this land is narrow; thus, one must combine both to fully convey the sense. There are also cases where multiple words in the foreign land are translated using a combination of both [name and meaning], such as translating *mahāyāna* as "great vehicle" (*dayuan*) or *prajñā-pāramitā* as "perfection of wisdom" (*boluomi*). This is because the foreign land has many names for a single meaning, while this land has few names for many meanings; thus, one must combine both to avoid confusion. There are also cases where a single word in the foreign land is translated using a combination of both [name and meaning] with a descriptive term, such as translating *arhat* as "worthy of offerings" (*gongyang zhe*) or *upāsaka* as "lay follower" (*jushi*). This is because the foreign land has many names for a single meaning, while this land has few names for many meanings; thus, one must combine both with a descriptive term to clarify the sense. There are also cases where multiple words in the foreign land are translated using a combination of both [name and meaning] with a descriptive term, such as translating *bodhisattva* as "enlightenment-being" (*puti-sanduo*) or *dharmakāya* as "dharma-body" (*fashen*). This is because the foreign land has many names for a single meaning, while this land has few names for many meanings; thus, one must combine both with a descriptive term to ensure clarity. There are also cases where a single word in the foreign land is translated using a combination of both [name and meaning] with a descriptive term and a phonetic transcription, such as translating *mañjuśrī* as "Wondrous Virtue" (*wenjushili*) or *avalokiteśvara* as "Observing the World" (*guanzizai*). This is because the foreign land has many names for a single meaning, while this land has few names for many meanings; thus, one must combine both with a descriptive term and a phonetic transcription to preserve the original sound. There are also cases where multiple words in the foreign land are translated using a combination of both [name and meaning] with a descriptive term and a phonetic transcription, such as translating *samantabhadra*
There are cases where the names for things such as water and fire are identical across different languages;

furthermore, there are instances where meanings are translated by means of corresponding meanings, such as *śiṃśapā* being translated as *nyagrodha*, *sūtra* as *xiuduoluo*, *vinaya* as *pilini*, and *śīla* as *jiejie*, among others.
Similarly, *pāramitā* is translated as "reaching the other shore," and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated as "unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment," and so forth.
In the Central Indian Sanskrit original, the sound is transcribed as *bhikṣu*; this has been corrupted in transmission and changed to "Bhikṣu" (Biqiū).

Initially translated as "Terrifier of Māras," it was subsequently called "Beggar" (*yācanaka*), and later "Destroyer of Afflictions. Alternatively, from the perspective of its function, it means "causing Māras to fear";

those who clarify its fundamental intent state that it is for the purpose of terrifying Māras. The names of the Māras are as follows: there are four worldly Māras, the first being the Māra of Desire (*kāma-māra*), which refers to the lower realms.
"Staying at the summit" means that by means of the fetters of desire, one prevents [the mind] from arising so that it does not emerge [from concentration].

What is called the "demon of the aggregates" (skandha-māra) refers to the body's accumulation, which perishes moment by moment. What is called the "demon of afflictions" (kleśa-māra) refers to the three poisons of the mind, whose arising inevitably extinguishes the wholesome.

What is called the "demon of death" (mṛtyu-māra) refers to the brief duration of a kalpa, wherein even one who has gathered excellent wealth ultimately proceeds toward death. This person, out of fear of these four, leaves the household life and takes up [the path]."
His intention was to provide a literal translation of the name.
Regarding the first section of the analysis, he first presents the three names collectively: *bhikṣu* (pronounced *pi-bi-fan* when transcribed; also called *bi-chú*;

as for the character *shàng* [上], it is unknown what it refers to, and the common worldly claim that it is the name of a plant is erroneous). He then explains the etymological reason for the name *bhikṣu*, which is *arhat*.

The Chinese names for the fruits correspond to the three names in the causal stage: "Frightener of Māras" corresponds to "Slayer of Thieves," "Bhikṣu" (Beggar) corresponds to "Worthy of Offerings," and "Destroyer of Afflictions" corresponds to "Non-arising.
Alternatively, the first name is explained in detail below as being the function that serves as the root of virtue; "will" (*citta*) refers to the mind of renunciation.
The name "Māra" has already been fully explained above in the section on the Three Refuges; here it refers to the "desire-māra" (*kāma-māra*).

The celestial Māra resides at the summit of the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); when beings seek liberation, he conceives distress and manifests various transformations to disturb them and cause them to remain attached to sensual desires;

therefore it is said, "by means of desire," and so forth. As for the *skandha-māra*, it refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which shift and pass away, preventing one from abiding in peace.
Regarding death as a *māra*, it means being oppressed by the suffering of death and having one's wholesome thoughts (*kuśala-citta*) snatched away. Thus, below this...
Regarding the conclusion that clarifies the meaning of the name: although both explanations are applicable, the original intent favors the latter; therefore, it is concluded with that alone.
For instance, in all the sūtras and vinayas, every renunciant—regardless of whether they are practicing a heterodox or orthodox path—is collectively termed a *bhikṣu*;

this is the general designation. In this land, the term *shamen* (śramaṇa) originally refers to a "Daoist practitioner" (*daoshi*), which is the correct etymological interpretation for those such as the Li and Zhang families.
Originally named Zhìtóu (治頭) and Guǐzú (鬼卒), the name was later gradually expanded and changed to Lànshàng (濫上). Then, Zhìshǐ (致釋) was changed to Chí (恥) and subsequently to Dàorén (道人).
In ancient translations from the Jin, Western Jin, and Han dynasties, it was translated as Dàoshì (道士), which also implies possessing virtue.

Nowadays, it is no longer translated at all, but simply called Bhikṣu to preserve the original sound. While this differs from the term used by the Li family, it does not prevent it from being identical to the "heterodox paths" of the five Indic regions.
Furthermore, this is based on the consensus of those who know [the matter].
Among the three points, the first clarifies that in the Western Regions (India), although the names "heterodox" and "orthodox" are distinct, both are considered monastics;
therefore, the following section next clarifies the confusion of names in this land (China). Jin Xizhi’s letter to Xie An states: "Recently, I have seen Shi Dao..."
Because he was peaceful, he was far superior to the Daoists who follow the Way of Impermanence; thus we know that "An" (Peaceful) was originally a name of the Śākya clan.
"Li" (李) is simply the surname of the Lord Lao (Laojun); his courtesy name was Boyang, and his posthumous title was Nian.

"Zhang" (張) refers to the Three Zhangs of the Han era—the leaders of the Yellow Turbans (namely Zhang Ling, Zhang Lu, and Zhang Jiao, known as the Three Zhangs). According to the *Hongming ji*, the state appointed him as their leader.

He who governs the people under his jurisdiction is called a *zhītóu* (formerly mistranslated as "one who combs the hair and guides the qi"). Because he drives and commands ghosts and spirits, he is called a *guǐzú*.
He who performs *jiào* offerings to the stars is also called a *jìjiǔ*; this title was later changed to *dàoshì*, which is why Buddhists do not use it.

Regarding the three characters for "ancient" (*gǔ*) and "modern" (*xià*) below, they indicate that the translations of antiquity and today differ. First, I shall describe the ancient translations; among them were those who possessed great virtue.

The preceding section reversed [the order] of the intent; now, the following clarifies that we do not translate [these terms] today. Although this [method] avoids redundancy for this land, it still overlaps with the conventions of that region, making it impossible to achieve perfection in both respects;
therefore, it is said that we provisionally rely on a single aspect.
As for the remaining terms that have been translated, they are relegated to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, lest this general treatise increase the proliferation of various views.
The preceding text in the main body only explained the term "terrifying Māra," whereas the names such as "mendicant" (*bhikṣu*) are fully contained in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts);

therefore, it refers back to them here. This is likely because some who fear the proliferation of various views might claim that these two accounts do not correspond or are redundant, or they might criticize this school for being overly verbose.
Thus, [the author] warns students against becoming attached to the literal words to demonstrate that the meaning is not merely about the quantity of the text.

Second, regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*), there are five distinct stages; briefly, these are analyzed through five topical sections: first, enumerating the numbers to manifest their characteristics;

second, the differences between the universal and the specific; third, the distinctions in the performance of the ritual; fourth, whether the teaching is directed toward ordinary beings or sages; and fifth, the amount of conditions relied upon.

Next, regarding the explanation of the five stages listed under the heading "Enumeration of Conditions," these refer to the "Welcome" (*svāgata*) and other categories cited in the commentary. Below, five gates are set forth;

as the capacities of sentient beings (*jñeya*) differ, the teachings (*śāsana*) are likewise not uniform. Therefore, it is necessary to establish propositions to distinguish their specific differences.
The enumeration at the beginning and middle of the text may be understood according to the literal wording; including the five types of ordination for *bhikṣuṇīs*, there are ten in total.

In the first section, which provides a general indication, the phrase "including the five for *bhikṣuṇīs*" refers to the eight *gurudharma*s, the ordination by messenger from a group of twenty, and the ordination before a group of ten for those who are young or living in border regions.

As for the *bhikṣuṇīs*, there are seven types of ordination, such as by the "Come-hither" (*ehi-bhikṣuṇī*) or by the destruction of fetters (*āsravakṣaya*); these two are identical to those of the *bhikṣus*, and therefore they are not included here.

Regarding the number [of ordinations], first, as for "coming well" (*svāgata*), its characteristics are manifested as follows: this person, having planted superior causes in past lives, early on received awakening and severed delusions;

having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) through the path, the Buddha personally summoned him. Because he received the precepts through the response to that teaching, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "Come well."
The deportment of a bhikṣu is dignified and orderly; holding his alms-bowl in hand, he appears like one who has studied the Dharma for twenty years.
Furthermore, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that once the cry of "Welcome" (*svāgata*) has been proclaimed, the eight requisites are all provided for him to carry with him.

Regarding the first section of the initial fivefold exposition on the formal ordination (*upasampadā*), there are two parts. First, the formal exposition of planting the seed—“seed” is pronounced with an upper tone;

the two delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *vicikitsā*) are like the two wheels of a chariot. Since the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) destroys the delusions of views, it is said that one wheel has been broken.

Because the precepts are induced by the teaching—specifically the "Come-hither" (*ehi-bhikkhu*) invitation—the following citation provides proof. First, it clarifies the possession of complete dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*), as in the second [case].

Regarding the "ten years," the *Vinaya* states that even if a bhikṣu is a hundred years old, if his seniority differs from another's, they are both regarded as equals based on their shared status as venerable elders.
Next, to clarify the acquisition of the necessary requisites: in addition to the six articles, a needle, thread, and a small knife are added, making eight items in total.
Second, regarding the "one who has destroyed the fetters" (*paryavasthāna-prahīṇa*): this person has cultivated wisdom such that delusions are exhausted;

having realized the path and attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they have mastered the correct principle and naturally acquired the precepts. They are named for what was destroyed, hence they are called "one who has destroyed the fetters. The Vinaya states:
"If one is able to cultivate the path and become an Arhat, this is termed 'leaving home' and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*)."

In the two [stages], when the afflictions of the wisdom-path are exhausted, this refers to the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); that which can destroy is "wisdom" and that which is destroyed is the "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).

Therefore, it is said that names are established from the perspective of what is destroyed. Below, the Vinaya is cited as proof: since the precepts arise in accordance with the fruit, they are called "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) and need not be received again.
Question: Do all those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who have destroyed their fetters obtain the precepts? Answer: There are many distinctions in this regard.
If one has already received [the precepts] within the cause, they will increase and become more excellent as one progresses through the various stages of the Path; they will not be received again.

If one has previously never made a formal resolve (samādāna-citta) to reach the fruit, then upon reaching the fruit, both the fruit and the precepts are simultaneously obtained—this is what is meant by "receiving [the precepts] by breaking the fetters.

If there was originally no resolve to obtain the fruit, there would be no precepts; therefore, there are white-robed Arhats. [Question: Is it because of the precepts that one attains concentration? [Answer: Because of...

Question: Since concentration gives rise to wisdom, how can one enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*) only after subsequently receiving the precepts? Answer: It is because the five and eight precepts must necessarily serve as the foundation for entering the Path;

until one has received the full set of precepts, one cannot attain the fruit. Question: Having realized the state of a noble one, one is free from evil; why then is there a need for the precepts? Answer:

Because one’s merit is not yet complete and one’s deportment (*īryāpatha*) is not fully established, if one does not receive them, there is no way to join the assembly; ultimately, such a person remains "white" (an ordinary worldling).
The robes were not yet fit for use on the path.
Regarding the third case, the "three-fold speech" (tri-vācika): this refers to a person whose accumulation of practice was not yet extensive and who had not yet attained the stage of an *ārya*.

Because such a person relied upon specific conditions and took ordination through the three-fold speech prior to becoming an *arhat*, it is so called. The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* (*Shunzhenglun*) states that among all *arhats*...

Those who wish to receive the teachings of the Mahāyāna should bared one shoulder, cross their robes over the body, shave their hair, don the dyed robes, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and rely upon them with a sincere mind;
within these teachings, they shall immediately generate the full precepts.
Among the three [points], the first correctly demonstrates that, in comparison to the preceding stage, it is inferior; thus it says, "the accumulation of practice is not far-reaching," etc.

In contrast to the subsequent conditions, which are superior, it says, "toward those Arhats," etc. The citation from the *Mātṛkā* below regarding "baring one shoulder" and so forth refers to the formal ritual (*vidhi*), such as taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
"Relying on the mind" is the cause that gives rise [to the vow]; "endowment" is the essence (*svabhāva*) that is produced.

Regarding the fourth case, the "five persons who uphold the Vinaya in border regions": because these remote areas were desolate and dangerous with few monks for them to travel among, it took three years before they could receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This provision was granted as a special concession based on these circumstances; the specific number [of five] is established to clarify the rule.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga* and the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*, if there are many monks in a border region, one may obtain the precepts through the original method of opening [the restriction], yet one incurs an offense [for violating the standard]. In this land of China (Chixian), prior to the Cao Wei dynasty, all...

The practice of not conferring full ordination continued until the Jiaping era, when the Dharma-time śramaṇas followed the *Fazhengbu* (Section on the Correct Dharma) to perform the *karmavācanā* ritual for the ten-person ordination,
as is detailed extensively in the *Monks’ Biographies*.
Regarding the "four remote regions," this refers to the area outside the boundary marked by white wooden strips.

Initially, when the śrāmaṇera Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa wished to receive full ordination, he waited for three years until the number of monks reached ten; he then requested that the Buddha grant him an exception.

Next, it is distinguished whether the assembly is sufficient or insufficient; because the assembly was large, an expedient exception was granted, but since it was subsequently restricted, the record remains open.

One incurs an offense because of violating the regulations for receiving the precepts. Below this, the three [sections] investigate this region: its primordial beginning was the "Red Prefecture" (Chixian), which is another name for Zhendan (China).
The *Hetu* states that five thousand li southeast of Mount Kunlun is called "Shenzhou" and is also termed the "Red Prefecture.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, prior to the Cao Wei period, the Dharma flowed into this region; at that time, there were only monks.
Although the shaving of the head and donning of the dyed robes had occurred, the formal reception of the precepts had not yet been established.

It was during the Jiaping era of the Cao Wei dynasty—the time of Emperor Qi—that the Indian monk Dharmakāla (alternatively transcribed as Kāla), translated as "Dharma-Time," first instituted the practice of receiving the precepts.
The *Shao* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states that he was the very beginning of the Vinaya tradition in the Central Kingdom and the second patriarch of our present school.

Regarding the "ten-member assembly" in the Middle Kingdom as the fifth [category]: because the Sangha was numerous while faith was scarce and the capacity for awakening gradually declined, ten persons had to be assembled before it could constitute a superior environment;
it is so called because this number serves as the defining standard for the assembly.

Among the five [regions], that which is called "the Middle Kingdom" refers specifically to within the Five Indias; there, the monastics are numerous while the faithful are few, and their veneration is meager.
Their spiritual faculties are gradually declining, and their receptive minds are light.

Some maintain that the destruction of the fetters is not the breaking of the precepts; this name "breaking" applies generally to those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), and thus it differs from other forms of undertaking [the precepts].

The text enumerates persons, dharmas, and the destruction of fetters; it does not merely list empty names. If one were to consider the acceptance [of robes], begging, and cutting [the cloth] as being the precept itself, then these too would have to be considered the precept.

This refutes misconceptions and leads to understanding. In the first section establishing the principle, it is also said that the initial fruit is a case of "name-overlap" (ming-lan), which is not the same [as the actual fruit].

Regarding those other types of "receivers of the human dharma" listed [in the Vinaya], they are as explained in the commentary concerning the "Come-hither" (*ehi-bhikkhu*), the "three-fold speech," and so forth;

these are all referred to as *bhikṣu*. However, these individuals have merely destroyed their fetters (*saṃyojana*); because they are designated by the name of the defilement destroyed rather than by the dharma they receive, this is a mere empty name.
In the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, eight kinds of *bhikṣus* are enumerated: first, the nominal (*nāma-bhikṣu*); second, the similar (*pratirūpaka-bhikṣu*); and so on.

The eight types of ordination are: (1) self-proclamation, (2) the four requests, (3) the five donning of cut-and-sewn robes, (4) the destruction of the fetters, (5) "Welcome," (6) the formal motion and three announcements (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), (7) that which they call [ordination by] the two lower [vehicles], and (8) from receiving [the precepts].

He argues that only the latter two are designated by names derived from the act of receiving; all others are not so designated because they do not involve such receiving, and thus he uses this to refute [the validity of the other seven].

If that is so, why does the Vinaya text state that one who has attained the path of Arhatship is called "fully endowed"? This refers to one who attains the path before the formal ritual (karmavācanā);
even if their age is not yet full, they may still take the place of an Arhat.
In the subsequent section on the Vinaya, there is the case of one whose age was not yet full at the time of receiving full ordination, yet who attained Arhatship and thereby obtained the precepts;

this refers to one who had already realized the state of a noble one (*ārya*) prior to the formal *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, whereby the fact that his age was not yet full was waived, and he obtained the precepts through the severing of fetters.

Now, the explanation is not so. If one is of young age, they may open the *garbha-vyūha* (the womb-intercalary) as in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, where there is no mention at all of an Arhat opening it because [the time] was not yet full;
thus we know that those who attain [enlightenment] later do not open the small [period] by receiving the *karmavācanā*.

Therefore, in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when there was someone who had not yet completed the full ordination (*upasampadā*), the Buddha consequently established the rule: "One who has attained the stage of *Srotāpanna* is indeed [qualified]."

The first form of full ordination (*upasampadā*) is not called the "fourth motion" (*jñapti-caturtha*); this applies even to those who received ordination at a young age, as there is no opening for them to attain the fruit [of the path].
Since this is identical in principle, the establishment, refutation, and conclusion [of the debate] concern the act of receiving the precepts.
Now, regarding the initial exposition of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* within the refutation [of the opponent's view], its intent accords with the preceding Vinaya:

the Vinaya permits [ordination] for those of young age, provided there are only three factors—conception, the intercalary month, and the *poṣadha*—whereas the established principle posits four factors by adding the "frequent" (*abhīkṣṇa*) and "great" (*mahat*). Thus, we know that "attainment later" refers to cases where the recipient has not yet reached the required age;
once the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, they realize the noble path and thereby receive the precepts, which is not a case of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

Because it is attained [through realization], the following section next cites evidence from that Vinaya showing that the attainment of the precepts through the destruction of views (*dṛṣṭi-prahāṇa*) at the first fruit differs from our own school;

it merely serves as proof that, prior to this, the precepts were not obtained through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Because one perceives the True Reality (*tattva*), it is called the "first" full ordination (*upasampadā*);
the three stages for those of young age are likewise the same as in our own Vinaya, and thus the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are severed below.
Among the list of the five categories within the community of nuns, the first clarifies the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
When women’s spiritual capacities were awakened, they developed a profound weariness with birth and death and sought to leave the household life under the Buddha;

however, because there would have been no great benefit for the propagation of the Way or for distant transformation, [the Buddha] suppressed their request and did not permit it. Later, while returning to Śrāvastī, they shaved their own heads and donned the robes themselves.

When the Sangha establishes a prayer for the reception of the precepts, one makes three requests; the Dharma of Reverence is then bestowed. If one practices it fully according to the rules, one will immediately realize the attainment of full ordination (upasampadā);
thus, this is the origin of its name.

Regarding the nun’s reception [of the precepts], among the five types of reception, this is the first section. First, it describes the arousal of the capacity [for practice]: Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred [women]...

The passage beginning with "As for women" and following clarifies that the Buddha did not permit the ordination of females because they are of inferior and weak nature and possess little reverence or faith;
thus, there would be no benefit for the propagation of the teachings, and instead, they would further bring disgrace upon the True Dharma, reducing its duration by half.

Furthermore, the subsequent section explains how the nuns, having been refused permission by the Buddha to shave their heads and dye their robes, returned to the city where they arbitrarily transformed themselves and went back to the Jetavana Monastery, leaning against... [the wall].

While they stood at the gate making their request, Ānanda of Siming on the lower ground petitioned the Buddha on their behalf, requesting that the teachings be transmitted so that they might practice the eight weighty precepts (*gurudharma*) and thereby receive ordination.
Upon hearing this, Mahāprajāpatī and the others immediately attained full ordination (*upasampadā*).

The second, the "receiving by a group of twenty," is intended to clarify that women’s retribution for afflictions is deep and their wisdom shallow; they are prone to conceit and indolence, and thus necessarily require the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Because both the monks and nuns must each manifest a superior resolve from the ten directions, it is named after these two assemblies.

In the second case, because their delusions are deep, they are largely stagnant; because their wisdom is shallow, they have little faith or joy; and because of pride, they do not respect the *saṃgha*.
Each of these involves ten mental states that vary according to the superiority of the object.

Third, regarding those who send messengers: their appearance is elegant and refined, and they are already steeped in worldly desires. When they leave the monastery to visit the monks, they fear falling into arrogance.

Because he was defiled, he sent a messenger to the Sangha to request ordination; when the formal ritual was performed as usual and the messenger returned to report this, he immediately attained the precepts.
Consequently, he was named [after the messenger].
Among the three, Master Huan’s return was excellent. "Yi" refers to those who are frivolous and whose minds are defiled by worldly attachments; there were various thieves [among them].
Because they waited for them to emerge, they dispatched messengers; this refers to the sending of envoys.
As for the fourth category, those who returned at a young age, having already served others and being deeply familiar with ritual propriety, are able to endure affliction and humiliation;

because they possess the capacity for upholding the precepts, they may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) even if they are less than eight years [of standing]. They are so named based on these temporal conditions.
Among the four [categories], "woman" refers to one who has been married as a "returner. Because she receives [the precepts] at twelve and expects them by twenty, eight years are subtracted.
Regarding the conditions of time and circumstance: "young age" is the time, and "having previously been married" is the circumstance.

Regarding the fifth point concerning the establishment of a group of ten for border regions: in great monastic centers where the community of monks is small, the rule for nuns is relaxed when there is a specific need;
furthermore, by relying on the monks, even if five are present on either side, it is appropriate that they receive ordination based on the principle that both sides must possess ten members.
Regarding the first of the five sections established here, it is based on the fact that there is no explicit textual authority in the Vinaya; rather, the *saṃgha* is taken as the precedent.
Because this opens the way for teaching and engaging with sentient beings to generate wholesome roots, it is said to be "established by principle" (*yìlì*).
Some do not establish it, arguing that since the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts do not permit traveling through frontier regions where there is danger, even if one were in such a place...

It is not appropriate to reduce [the number of precepts]. If that is so, since the Vinaya restricts the Saṃgha to a minimum of four members and does not permit fewer, yet the Saṃgha can confer ordination even with as few as five at the borderlands—how is it that this case is not analogous? How could it be inappropriate?
In the first section of the "Refutation of Ancient Views," ancient calculations regarding the *niḥsargika-pācattika* rules are cited. Therein it says:
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels among people in a border region where there is doubt or fear, she commits a *pācattika*. Here, the text below directly refutes the rule;
since the *vinaya* prescribes that even a *saṃgha* commits a *duṣkṛta* offense in the detailed explanation (*vyākhyāna*), this is used as a counter-objection to re-establish the previous position.
Regarding the meaning:
if one examines the monastic histories prior to the Song dynasty in China, it appears that the community of nuns received the eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*) as prescribed in the various Vinayas;
however, they were exclusively devoted to the path of women, and thus the five hundred nuns received the full ordination through the assembly of eleven groups. Therefore, Guṇavarman...
The Venerable One said: "If there were no two assemblies, but only one assembly receiving [ordination]—as was the case with the precedent of Mahāprajāpatī—it would be permissible.

How is this known? According to the discussion of the fundamental method, it stops at the preliminary preparations; since nothing could yet be accomplished, it refers back to the *karmavācanā* within the Saṃgha, which then brings about the subsequent [ordination].
This is the case for the eleven nuns, such as Tiśyarakṣitā of Sīhaladvīpa, who studied the Song language and became proficient."
The two assemblies receive [the precepts].

In the first section of the following chapter, it clarifies that one assembly receives them; this refers to the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha), specifically the account in the *Liang Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks of the Liang Dynasty) regarding Guṇavarman’s arrival during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty and his conferring of full ordination upon nuns.
According to various Vinayas, such as the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, and according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if [the candidate] desires...
Five hundred [monks] together with eight [nuns] who received the eight respects, and one nun, constituted the assembly of eleven; this one nun was also originally from the Western Regions.
Guṇavarman—translated as "Armor of Merit"—[is mentioned]. As for the phrase "how could they be equal," this explains why [the nuns] followed after the monks.
Next, the receiving of the precepts by the two assemblies is clarified; previously, it was explained that this occurred during the seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
Next, in the tenth year, there was Saṃghavarman, translated as "Multitudinous Armor.
Subsequently, when the various bhikṣuṇīs in this land wished to receive the double ordination from both assemblies, there were already eight bhikṣuṇīs from Siṃhala Island present here.
Soon after, three more bhikṣuṇīs, including Tiexuoluo (Aśokā), arrived at the capital, making eleven persons in total; however, for the actual performance of the ceremony, only ten were used.
The term "Ren-tie-suo-luo" (人鐵索羅) is a Sanskrit word for which no Chinese translation has been seen.
Since these five types of ordination (*pañca-upasampadā*) also include the "well-coming" (*svāgata*) and the "breaking of fetters" (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*), they constitute seven types of ordination.

Among these seven, the "well-coming" and the "breaking of fetters" encompass both groups [of monks and nuns]; therefore, while there are only five when restricted to specific cases, there are seven when including those that apply to both.
Question: As stated above, in border regions it is permitted to have fewer than five people; furthermore, since the Vinaya is empowered [to be effective], how can it be called a "permission"?
Some say that in the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa) ten people are required for the formal act (*karmavācanā*): four who are well-versed in the Dharma and Vinaya, and six who serve as the quorum.

They claim that in border regions, while five may be permitted, one must necessarily possess mastery of the Vinaya. This interpretation is incorrect. How could the term "possessing mastery of the Vinaya" be so restrictive?

Among the monastic community here at the center, those who know the Dharma are numerous; it is not difficult for them to rely upon the teachings and conditions, and their purpose will surely be accomplished.

However, since the monks on the borders are few, those who know the Dharma and practice accordingly are rare; I fear that if we were to restrict our numbers, they would not be exclusively proficient in the teachings.

Now, the performance of karma depends upon conditions, and if conditions are lacking, the karma fails. Without relying upon the observance of the Vinaya, how could success be achieved? Therefore, to dispel this doubt, this text has been composed and presented to those of virtuous conduct.
This excellent foundation for rescue and deliverance is not established in vain.

In the initial question and answer, the first question asks why [the rules] are reduced by five and are less strict than those in the Middle Kingdom; this is to open the way for the observance of the Vinaya, which is strictly regulated in the Middle Kingdom.
Since opening [an exception] does not constitute a valid opening, it is necessary to ask for an explanation. The subsequent answer is twofold: first, citing ancient precedents.
The error of the [previous] interpretation can be readily understood. Now, in the explanation provided here, the first three phrases offer a general indication of the "Middle" (Madhyadeśa);

that is, the "Middle Country" represents the "Outlying Regions" (Pratyantaka). Below this, there is a specific explanation: the previous section explained the Middle Country without further qualification, whereas the subsequent part clarifies that for the Outlying Regions, one must possess the virtue of preparatory application (*prayoga*), namely the phrase "upholding the Vinaya.
This is the excellent foundation, which refers to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*).

Question: When performing an action, whether good or evil, if the agent and the object are equal, why is it that for [acts like] giving or receiving precepts, the retribution is felt only when the result returns;

whereas for killing or stealing, one incurs the offense as soon as the deed is accomplished? Answer: These cases cannot be treated as identical. Receiving vows depends on conditions; the vow is fulfilled when the conditions arise and the volition is complete.
Evil, however, exists within the object; once the object is damaged, the offense is incurred immediately.
Next, the question concerning instructing others to kill or steal without waiting for a report, and dispatching a messenger—since the circumstances are identical, there should be no distinction;
the text of the response can be understood as being fully complete.

The second major section concerns the differences between the universal and the specific, categorized into four points: first, regarding the recipient; second, regarding the retribution; third, regarding the time; and fourth, regarding the direction.
Fifth, [the classification] is according to the gradual and the sudden;

sixth, it is according to the various schools. First, regarding the types of ordination: the "Come hither" (*ehibhikṣu*), the "destruction of fetters," the "three statements," and the "eight respects" are restricted to specific conditions (*dharmapratyaya*) and do not mutually interpenetrate, as can be understood from their respective characteristics.
Regarding the five groups, ten groups, and twenty groups: the "sending of a messenger" and the "formerly returned" establish the ten-group [ordination]. This...
Regarding these six types of receiving [precepts], their various names differ according to their conditions; yet, in terms of the formal dharma, they all proceed from *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

If these various forms of receiving are grouped together, they constitute five, based on their essential nature. However, when distinguishing between the specific and the general, since *karmavācanā* encompasses all six, there are ten in total.

Second, regarding the distinction between the general and the specific within the context of "receiving" (*pratigraha*), first it clarifies that the four types of receiving have both their *dharmas* (objects) and *pratyayas* (conditions) restricted to the formal ritual (*kriyā*).

That is, the conditions for the *dharma* are the conditions for the ritual, which are the conditions for receiving. Next, it clarifies that while the six types of receiving have their conditions restricted to the *dharma*, they are pervasive [in application]. Below, this is shown collectively by grouping them into five through the combination and separation of categories;
specifically, the six *karmas* of receiving are combined into one. To demonstrate their restriction, the preceding four are enumerated.
If one includes the "manifestation of supernormal powers" (abhijñā-prakāśana), which opens the way for the subsequent *karmavācanā*, there are ten [methods].
Second, regarding the classification by way of the fruit (*vipāka*):

according to the Vinaya, there are five ways of receiving ordination; the "welcoming arrival" (*svāgata*) is one such method, and it applies generally to both monks and nuns. The Vinaya enumerates eight types, clearly indicating that the "welcoming arrival" is common to all.
They possess both types of ordination.
Regarding the "welcoming" (*svāgata*) category within the retribution [ordination], the first section of the Vinaya lists eight kinds;

that is, the eight kinds of *bhikṣu* mentioned above, as well as the eight kinds of *bhikṣuṇī* from the *Prātimokṣa*, whose enumerations are not distinct, all of whom possess the "welcoming" and the "destruction of fetters" (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*).

Therefore, it should be known that these two [categories] apply universally to both assemblies (the old interpretation—which excludes three of the ten precepts and eight *gurudharmas* from among the ten types of ordination—is incorrect).
As stated in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Buddha did not ordain nuns in order to stop slander;

had he ordained non-Buddhists by the "Come-hither" (*ehi*) formula, one would have to say that they were originally palace ladies who amused themselves, and that having left the home life, they returned to ordain themselves for their own pleasure. This is as compiled in the *Śata-sāhasrikā-vinaya-saṃgraha*.
In sūtras such as the *Bhadra-varga* and the *Mūḍha-varga*, it is said that those whom the Tathāgata personally addressed with "Welcome" (ehi-bhikṣu) all attained arhatship;

how is this not contradictory? According to the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-śāsana*, one who is a noble being (*ārya*) is addressed by the Buddha with "Welcome," whereas one who is not a noble being is not ordained.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the purpose of stopping slander lies in the fact that while ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) must necessarily be noble beings to dispel false attachments, this [method of ordination] is not the formal teaching [for others].
Limitation.

The next section is divided into two parts: first, citing the contradictions between the sūtras and śāstras, and using the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* to stop slander; second, [showing how] the sūtras enter the path, such as the words "Tathāgata, etc.
which are from the *Śatavastu-vibhaṅga*, and the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, which says: "The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was addressed by the Buddha with the words 'Welcome' (*ehi-bhikṣuṇī*)."
The meaning of "crossing over" (du) is as explained below, where the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* reconciles this with the sages, namely those from the first fruit (srotāpanna) onwards.
Second, it clarifies that the destruction of fetters applies to both monks and nuns, as textual evidence for this exists within both of the eightfold enumerations.
Regarding the "breaking of the bonds" (*pārivāsika*), the eight types for monks and nuns are explained as above.
As for the rule that "three utterances and one acceptance" apply only to monks and not to nuns: at the beginning of the establishment of the Path, the method of three utterances was employed;

however, because nuns had not yet appeared, this was prohibited for eight years by regulation. It was only after fourteen years that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) was instituted, and only then did they begin to shave their hair.
Seeking to receive the Eight Respectful Precepts is not a condition for receiving ordination because the time limit has expired;

as for the three verbal [proclamations], they are restricted to the Saṃgha, for since the fault of the three verbal proclamations was prohibited by regulation, it was only after five years had passed that nuns were first ordained,
and thus the time limit has expired.

The eight points of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) and the single formal acceptance (*ekopasampad*) are restricted to nuns; this clarifies that the path between teacher and disciple must be established for there to be the capacity for broad benefit.
Because the nuns rely on the monks to be refined by the Dharma, they practice these respects as an act of subordination. If this were reversed, it would lead to the confusion of social ethics;
therefore, these rules do not apply to the monks.

The eight points of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) are for the purpose of honoring the Bhikṣuṇīs; they are to be revered by those above and respected by those below. In principle, there is no mutual interchange between them.
"Order" (*lun*) refers to sequence.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), the single reception of the precepts applies to both genders; whether the procedure is singular or plural depends on the law, while the full realization of the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) arises from the purity or thinness of one's wisdom.
At the conclusion of the ritual action (*karmavācanā*), it is precisely the designation (*nāman*) that is expressed.

Within the *karmas*, based on the legal requirements for single or plural assemblies, the monks have only one [voting] while the nuns have an additional fundamental rite (the old interpretation—that among the six types of *karmas*, "single" and "plural" refers to the number of monks being fewer or more than the nuns—is incorrect).
Because wisdom is either pure or thin, these designations corresponding to the aforementioned "single" and "plural" are all termed *karmas*.
Because it involves the refinement of the precepts.

Third, regarding the distinction between temporal universality and restriction: the "Come hither" (*ehi*), the three-fold recitation (*tri-śaraṇa*), and the eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*) are restricted to the period when the Buddha was in the world.

This is known because the attainment of the precepts through the destruction of fetters (*saṃyojana*) is universal, applying even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; as the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states, this was possible five thousand years prior [to the end of the Dharma].
Because of his threefold super-knowledge (*trividyā*), he knew that the fruit was accomplished and the precepts were fulfilled. While the *karmavācanā* ritual generally applies to both time periods,

the case of receiving ordination by the "Come hither" (*ehibhikṣu*) formula— such as Ānanda’s subsequent ordination of the seer (ṛṣi) mentioned in the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*— is a special circumstance and cannot be taken as a general rule.

Regarding the statement "among the three [periods], it refers to the time," this means during his lifetime and after his parinirvāṇa. Three are restricted while two are universal, as stated in the text.
"Five thousand years ago" refers to the first millennium. Thoroughly penetrating the three periods of time is called the "threefold penetrative knowledge" (trividya).

However, below, in reconciling differences, the *Dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (Fu-fa-zang zhuan) relates that Ānanda, at the moment of his own death, saved five hundred [monks] within the waters of the Ganges.
The sages all welcomed him and received the precepts; however, fearing that this might lead to obstacles, they specifically communicated their words. As for the distinct conditions:
first, the capacity resided in Ānanda and did not extend to others; second, it was for use at that specific time and did not extend to later times.
Regarding the four bases of address (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) and their specific or general application:
the "Welcome" (*svāgata*) and the "Eight Respects" (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) are restricted to Jambudvīpa, because the Buddha himself presided over his enlightenment there.

Why, then, did he not travel to the other three continents during his entire lifetime? The answer is that Jambudvīpa possesses four unique conditions: namely, seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, going forth (*pravrajyā*), and attaining realization.
The statement that the other three continents lack the conditions for seeing the Buddha is a judgment made based on one particular aspect;

as for Śrāvastī, where nine hundred million beings neither see nor hear [the Buddha], this does not preclude the possibility that other continents possess all four conditions. This is spoken in terms of the majority, and it is not the case that it is otherwise than described above.
The fourth section clarifies the three continents. Within the first sub-section, there is first the formal presentation of the question, followed by the explanation of the inquiry.

Regarding the answer, the first part explains according to the specific [circumstances], stating that the four types of superior conditions—such as seeing the Buddha—are distinct from those of other continents;
hence, it is called "distinct. Next, the second part discusses them generally, concerning the people of Śrāvastī.

There are nine hundred million and three hundred million who see the Buddha and hear the Dharma; three hundred million who see the Buddha but do not hear the Dharma; and three hundred million who neither see the Buddha nor hear the Dharma.
On the other continents, all four conditions are present—meaning that [the Buddha] responds universally according to individual capacities without restriction of place.

Generally speaking, all four continents possess these conditions, though they may be complete or deficient in varying degrees; however, from the perspective of what is most prevalent, Jambudvīpa possesses them more fully and lacks them less often.
The *karmavācanā* for breaking the *saṃghabheda* applies to all three [continents] without doubt; the three proclamations and one acceptance were established eight years ago.

Since [the Buddha] had not yet expelled Piṇḍola, and since there was no Dharma in the two continents [Pūrvavideha and Aparagodānīya], how could it apply to them? Therefore, the *Vinaya* states: "I now expel you; you shall not attain *nirvāṇa* for the rest of your life.
He then vanished from this place and appeared in the Western Continent (*Aparagodānīya*), where he spent the summer retreat, saved sentient beings, and greatly promoted the Buddhist teachings. 10.

The recitation is largely the same, with the addition of "establishing the monastic community. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In the Eastern Continent (Pūrvavideha) as well, it is because there exists the teaching of the Buddha-dharma that the fourfold assembly is established.

In the first section of the following analysis, it clarifies that *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) and so forth apply only to three continents; this is based on the exclusion of the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) mentioned below. The subsequent three [sections] follow accordingly.
In the *Madhyama-āgama*, Piṇḍola manifests his supernormal powers by taking a sandalwood bowl from atop a pole;

having been expelled by the Buddha, he went to another continent (*dvīpa*). Since the existence of the Buddha-dharma there occurred eight years after [the Buddha's parinirvāṇa], it is clear that the three mentions [of other continents] are restricted to the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa).
In the *Vinaya*, it merely mentions the Western Continent (*Aparagodānīya*) and does not state that monasteries were established there; therefore, the *Daśottara-sūtra* is cited.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* continues [the discussion] following this.
Because the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) is a place of hardship, it is not discussed here.

Within the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), the Northern Continent is one such difficulty; furthermore, the Dharma-teaching does not reach it, and the five faculties of feeling are entirely absent there. This is also for the time being...
This is stated merely from the perspective of a single characteristic. Regarding the five points:

first, the distinction between the gradual and the sudden, and the universal and the specific; second, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles; third, the specific discussion regarding the Small Vehicle.

First, the universal encompasses the Small while the specific is limited to it, as stated in the *Śīla-sūtra*: "Those who wish to receive the Bodhisattva precepts should first purify their minds and then receive them."

Regarding the precepts of the seven assemblies for those who aspire to the bodhisattva path and wish to know the great precepts (*mahā-śīla*): these are received gradually and apply to both the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna.
The five modes of receiving [the precepts] in the Hīnayāna each have their own specific applications, as will be explained below.

Regarding the fifth section, "The Scope of the Great and Small [Vehicles]," the first subsection has two parts: first, a general indication that the Great [Vehicle] encompasses the Small because it is broad and includes the small, whereas the Small is limited as it does not include the great;
this will be explained separately below. First, regarding the Bodhisattva Precepts of the Broad [Vehicle], there are two schools of thought:
according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which belongs to the Avataṃsaka division, both monastics and laypeople—not excluding animals—may receive them.

Thus, [the teachings] encompass both the gradual and the sudden. For instance, the *Śīla-sūtra* (Good Precepts Sūtra) belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sections; it holds that only bhikṣus may receive [the full precepts], and thus it represents only the gradual path, not the sudden.

Here, however, we shall clarify this based on the *Śīla-sūtra*: the precepts for the seven classes of followers comprise the fifty [precepts] of the *Upāsaka-śīla*, as these encompass all seven classes.
Therefore, that text states: "One who wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts must first receive the five precepts of an upāsaka."
The ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras and the full precepts for bhikṣus are like a four-story tower:
it is impossible that one could reach the second story without the first, or the fourth story without passing through the third.

Following the fivefold ordination of the Hīnayāna, this next section clarifies its limited scope; that is to say, there is no principle by which the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle can necessarily penetrate the Greater Vehicle.
"Comprehensive" (*tong*) refers to the fact that the full precepts (*jùjiè*) of their respective categories extend across all fifty fingers, as will be explained in the following section.
Question: To receive the Bodhisattva precepts, one must rely on the seven groups of practitioners (*qīzhòng*) as a preliminary practice (*qiánfāngbiàn*) before obtaining the Great Precepts (*dàjiè*).

When the physical body perishes, do the minor precepts (*xiǎojiè*) not also cease? Someone says: "The former precepts are restricted to a specific rebirth and perish along with their allotted duration; thus, when the Bodhisattva precepts end, [the minor precepts also cease]."

Regarding the future limit, it coexists with one's vows; some say that by receiving the Mahāyāna precepts, one causes the five, eight, ten, or full [precepts] to endure until the end of the future, so that neither is lost.
If this were so, and the original precepts remained throughout successive births, then committing evil would constitute a transgression.
The answer is: because one is unaware of possessing the precepts, there is no mind of contravention.

In the question-and-answer section, the intent of the question is as follows: It is held that the Great Precepts (mahā-śīla) persist through future lives and are not extinguished, whereas the Minor Precepts (kṣudra-śīla) coincide with the physical existence and must be lost at the end of life.
However, since the Minor Precepts serve as the preparatory means for the Great Precepts, the Minor Precepts should likewise follow [the Great Precepts] and not perish.
There are two explanations for the answer; the first explanation is based on the fact that the two vows do not interfere with one another, and therefore the Minor Precepts...
From the moment one loses the appointed time, one makes a vow. Next, the explanation of the essential nature shows that the Small Vehicle is brought back to the Great Vehicle;

therefore, it grows together with the Great Vehicle until the end of the future. If this is so, the following section below addresses an objection regarding the separation of lives: since [the offense] exists in principle, there should be a transgression.

The answer in the text clarifies that there is no transgression by focusing on the fact that [the person] did not know [of the offense] at a later stage. If this is so, it must depend on past traces; for there may be those who do know.

Regarding whether there is an offense or not, the answer is that both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna precepts and prohibitions are spoken of in reference to what one has previously received according to this present report;

even if one were to know [the rules], in principle there should be no offense. As for the two interpretations above, the former is limited to the specific teachings, while the latter is universally applicable;
each has its own merits, and thus neither should be rejected or adopted.

Second, regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of the Hīnayāna: the first [ordination], the reception [of the precepts], is restricted to the gradual method and not the instantaneous; the remaining four [categories] are common to both the gradual and the instantaneous.
Next, the general presentation according to the Hīnayāna is easily understood.

Thus, because the Vinaya states that one who receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) without having been granted the śrāmaṇera precepts obtains the precepts [for the higher stage] yet incurs an offense, we know this was established as a regulation.
The gradual method involves first receiving the five precepts and then the ten precepts before the full ordination; as stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*,

one who does not receive the fifty-two precepts but receives the full ordination directly obtains the three types of precepts simultaneously, whereas the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) restricts the process to the gradual method—
this is a clear textual authority.

In the first section of the gradual explanation of the separate *karmavācanā*, first, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one relies solely on the ten precepts as the preparatory means for full ordination.
Next, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*, five additional precepts are added to make ten preparatory means.

If one follows the *Bhikṣuṇī-niyatārtha-śāstra*, it is also permissible to receive the ten precepts directly without first taking the five precepts; however, this incurs a fault according to the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra*.
Since the three precepts are obtained simultaneously upon receiving full ordination, we know that in a single *karmavācanā* ceremony,
there is no one who does not receive all fifty precepts. Therefore, if someone in recent times wishes to abolish the five precepts, how could this clear judgment not be deemed reckless and arrogant?

Question: Since one may obtain all three [precepts] at once, why is it necessary to receive them in succession? Answer: It is said that to cultivate and habituate oneself to the Buddha-dharma, one must follow a sequential order.
First, one receives the five precepts to discipline oneself; as faith and joy gradually increase, one next receives the ten precepts, whereby the virtuous mind further increases.

Only then does one receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) to attain the flavor of the Dharma. Thus, one’s aspiration becomes firm and steadfast, making it difficult to fall back, and one’s majestic deportment remains unbroken.

If one receives them all at once, it would conversely result in losing the proper sequence and violating the rules of decorum (*vṛtta*), just as one gradually encounters deeper waters when traveling across the great ocean.

Furthermore, it is said that sentient beings attain the Way through conditions that are not fixed; depending on whether they rely upon the ten precepts or even the full set of precepts, the Tathāgata has thus taught this sequential order.

In the first part of the subsequent section, there is an initial question that challenges the preceding point regarding the simultaneous reception [of precepts]. The sequential response contains two meanings. First is the meaning of defiled habituation;

furthermore, it is said below that the attainment of the Way is not fixed. Within this, the first part first describes the benefits of receiving [the precepts] in succession—namely, obtaining the flavor of the Dharma and so forth—which means that one’s resolve does not change.
"Not breaking the majestic deportment" means that one's conduct is free from transgressions. This concludes the first sub-section. The second follows.

It clarifies that by combining the two types of harm and reversing them to form the two benefits, one subsequently attains the two fruits; this can be understood through the analogy of the ocean provided for comparison.
Regarding the subsequent meaning, it is said that because the inclinations and joys of sentient beings differ, they may enter the Way by means of whichever precept is appropriate;
therefore, a sequential order is required.
Question: When one first receives the five precepts and the ten precepts, and later receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*), does one abandon the five precepts? Answer: One does not abandon them;
however, one loses the status of an *upāsaka* and a *śrāmaṇera*. One sequentially attains the status of a *bhikṣu*. These two sets of precepts are ever-present;
they are designated according to the occasion, just as the leaves of a tree are green in spring and summer, yellow in autumn, and white in winter.

Next, regarding the question of "abandoning the five precepts" (where the characters for "ten precepts" are omitted), "abandoning" means losing [the precepts]. The answer states that they are not abandoned, which refers to their essential nature (*dharmatā*).
However, what is lost is the sequence, which refers to their names and positions. Below, the analogy of leaves is raised: although they change, they still persist;
this can be harmonized with the meaning stated above.
He asked again: "When one receives [the precepts] at a single time, are there three distinct precepts? He replied: "They are all fully possessed as non-informative action (*avijñapti*);

there is no distinction. (Fifty. The third question feared that [the recipient] might doubt whether they could be divided into three separate entities; therefore, in the reply, it was stated that they are "all fully possessed as non-informative action," meaning the entity of non-informative action pervades all three, and "there is no distinction" means they are merged into one.
If that were so, it would follow that there is only one precept; why then was it stated above that one "immediately obtains three types"? The answer is:

although a bhikṣu receives the physical form [of the precepts], his non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is identical to that of a śrāmaṇera and a layperson; therefore, it is said there are "three. In reality, there is only one essence of non-informative action that extends to all three persons.

Thus, it is frequently said that receiving the five precepts constitutes the lower grade, receiving the ten precepts the middle grade, and the first five [of the bhikṣu precepts] remain the lower grade, while the latter five constitute the upper grade.

Regarding the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Essentials of Receiving the Precepts): when receiving the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), the layperson remains below the śrāmaṇera; it is only those other than these who are placed above. Thus we know there are not three [levels].
In the initial formal response to the difficult question, that which is the same as for the śrāmaṇera and the layperson is as follows:

for example, the five precepts are prohibited for all three [categories]; the subsequent fifty precepts for the śrāmaṇera and the full precepts for the bhikṣu are likewise uniform. How could this not apply to all three? Therefore, [the layperson] does not receive them.

The essence of the five precepts is received directly; the essence of the ten precepts is common to two types [of ordination]; and the essence of the full ordination (upasampadā) is received directly by those who do not receive the fifty intermediate precepts, as it applies to three types of persons.
Therefore, the following passage cites scriptural evidence for that school’s position that the three grades are permanently fixed and their essence does not involve a repeated increase:
when one receives the five at the lower grade and the ten at the middle grade, the final five of the ten are themselves the middle grade; hence it says "the former."

Fifth, furthermore, the higher grade of receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*) consists of only two hundred and forty [precepts], which is indeed the higher grade; therefore it is said that "the others" are then superior to this.
This is based on the sequential reception of the three grades of the threefold precepts as being combined into a single entity.

If their substance were three, they would have to arise separately; thus, one can prove that there is no third [possibility] regarding instantaneous reception. If the *Tattvasiddhi* school [is followed], the lower five...

Regarding the ten precepts of the middle grade, five are cited as constituting the middle; as for receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of the superior grade, fifty are cited, equaling the upper limit.
Question: When receiving the three sets of precepts all at once, how does one relinquish them? Answer: There are both sudden and gradual methods of relinquishment.

If, according to the gradual method, one directly relinquishes the full ordination to become a *śrāmaṇera*, then the full ordination is lost, while the *śrāmaṇera* precepts remain, and so on down to the five precepts and the three refuges.

For example, you also hope that one might receive the precepts all at once; this is identical in principle to the laity and śrāmaṇeras preventing evil. If one abandons them according to one's own mind, they are abandoned;
if one retains them, they remain.

Among the four questions, there is a gradual sequence for receiving and abandoning [the precepts], yet if there were abandonment both gradually and suddenly, there should be no gradual abandonment when one receives them all at once.

In the answer, the first phrase provides a general response; the subsequent sections provide specific explanations. Since the meaning of "sudden" (*tun*) is easy to understand, it is not further clarified here, and only the "gradual" (*jian*) is explained, up to the point where it says "and so forth.
This refers to cases such as abandoning all ten precepts to become a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or abandoning the three [precepts] while retaining only the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*).
The reason for this is stated below, as the meanings of the "three" and "one" have already been demonstrated in the preceding text; thus, it says, "it is also considered from that perspective."
The preceding section clarified that regarding the reception of the *karmavācanā*, there are both gradual and simultaneous methods for its relinquishment;

this is to be understood as before: while the reception is restricted, the relinquishment is general. As for what is called "simultaneous relinquishment," it refers to directly becoming a layperson (*avadātavasana*) without retaining anything whatsoever.

The three phrases of "Welcome" (Svāgata) break the fetters; although these three texts do not explicitly clarify this, according to their meaning, they all involve first receiving the five precepts before proceeding to the threefold refuge, which constitutes the gradual approach.
The case where a layperson directly approaches and receives the Dharma is restricted to the sudden approach.

In the text concerning the eight respects and the single reception [of ordination], the five precepts are listed, which indicates the gradual approach; as for the other five hundred women, it is not certain that they had previously received [the precepts].
Receiving the precepts through hearing and reverence should be considered instantaneous (*tun*).
Among the remaining four types, the first three—the *svāgata* (welcoming), the three-fold formula, and the ten precepts—are explained together;

however, as for the five precepts and the severing of fetters, they involve receiving two types of precepts simultaneously. In the text of the Eight Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), the five precepts are listed, which is precisely what the Vinaya clarifies.
Āryā Ānandā first received the five precepts for the sake of Upāli; as there is no textual record regarding other women, it is said that this was not necessarily the case.

Sixth, regarding the opening or closing of the various schools: based on the original *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part Vinaya), five types of *karmavācanā* are briefly explained. Within the "receiving" [precepts], six types are distinguished from the "separation.
If one distinguishes between the general and the specific, there are ten horizontal categories, which account for the presence or absence across the various schools.
The sixth section, the first sub-section, generally consists of five parts, but specifically comprises ten. "Horizontal" (*heng*) means lateral;
it refers to comparing different fundamental categories with one another to reveal their presence or absence.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are ten kinds of precepts: first, the precept of spontaneity without a teacher, which refers to the Buddha not relying on a teacher.

Because the principles of the Teaching are fully exhausted, one attains the precepts through inspiration; as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One who relies on the natural [dharma] does not depend on external instruction.
This is not to say that he does not rely on others at all. Sitting cross-legged beneath a tree is the teaching of the body (*kāya-śāsana*).

To say to oneself, "By this sitting, I have attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*)," is the teaching of the mouth (*vāk-śāsana*). Subsequently, when the outflows are exhausted, the precepts are also simultaneously attained; these two are both self-vows.

As recorded in the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (or *Dharmakṣaya-śāstra*), at the time of his self-vow, his physical and vocal discipline was fully perfected. Regarding those who attained the Way, there were five such as Kauṇḍinya;
regarding those who debated the Dharma, there were four. As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha commanded Sūdaya to explain the meaning of "permanent form" and other such doctrines;
he preached the Dharma without impediment and without timidity. Furthermore, the *Samyukta Āgama* (*Sudarsana*) states that at the age of seven, he engaged in question-and-answer sessions.

The six modes of receiving the precepts—namely, through being welcomed as a "Welcome One" (*svāgata*), the three refuges, the fivefold assembly, by messenger, the eight heavy rules, and by formal motion (*jñapti-karman*)—are all encompassed within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

In the section on "Natural [Receiving]" in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong), it first cites the Vinaya to demonstrate that when the Buddha attained enlightenment, severed delusions, and realized the Truth, he naturally induced the precepts;
as the following citation from the Śāstra clarifies, this natural induction must arise from conditions and does not depend on the instruction of another.
It is not that there is no teacher, nor is it that one does not rely on others; rather, it means that the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti*) arises through the teaching.

By this principle, the attainment of the precepts within the fruit-stage of a Tathāgata is likewise. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the attainment of the precepts during the causal stage varies according to individual capacities, as explained in detail in the second section of the *Yìchão*.
"Self-vow" refers to Mahākāśyapa, while "the forest-like multitude" refers to the great assembly that gathered.
Regarding their appearance: among the three groups, the five Kauṇḍinya were those first converted at the Deer Park.
Kauṇḍinya was the leader among the five; this is translated as *Mūlapariyāya*, which refers to Kauṇḍinya.
Second was Aśvajit (also called Aśvabhī); third was Mahānāman (also called Mahākauṣṭhila); fourth was Bhadrika (also called Bhaddiya); fifth was Bhadrayāna (also named... [text truncated]).

(10. Daśabala-Kāśyapa): If one receives the precepts by relying on a "well-seen" (*sudarśana*) or "well-come" (*svāgata*) [invitation], it differs from this. Regarding these four [cases], that sūtra states:
When the Buddha was in the country of Magadha, on Mount Paṃśa, he arose from his quiet chamber at dawn and was walking in meditation outside when the novice Śuddha was walking behind the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "I shall now ask you a question regarding the meaning of 'permanence' (*nitya*)."
"Are 'form' (*rūpa*) and 'impermanent form' one and the same meaning, or are they different? He replied, "This meaning is not one. Why is this so?
Because permanent form is internal, while impermanent form is external. The Buddha said, "You have well explained this meaning;
I now grant you the status of a great *bhikṣu*. Therefore, it is said that your preaching of the Dharma is unhindered," and so forth, as detailed in the [relevant] chapter.
In the twenty-second fascicle, the Buddha of Good Vision asks, "How old are you? and [the disciple] replies, "I am seven years old. The rest is the same as in the *Ekottarika-āgama*.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are eight [instances]; one is restricted to the age of seven, while one is general. This refers to the "self-perfection" (*svayam-aṅga*) also called "self-awakening," which refers to the Tathāgata.

The remaining cases of "Welcome" (*svāgata*) are fifty-eight; those sent by messenger are twenty; those who have previously returned are seven; and those who receive [ordination] together with four others are as in the *Dharmaguptaka* school.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika*, it is self-sufficient, which is naturally as stated above. Five refers to the border regions, ten to the Middle Kingdom, and eight to the Eight Respects (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*);
the rest may be understood accordingly.

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are twelve types of ordination that mutually involve both general and specific applications: first, natural ordination; second, ordination through a single utterance, which refers to taking refuge in the Buddha; third, ordination through two utterances, which refers to taking refuge in the Dharma;

fourth, ordination by a group of ten—one such assembly refers to the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs among the ten monks, with Mahāprajāpatī serving as the preceptor; fifth, ordination by three persons; sixth, ordination by a single person;

seventh, the destruction of evil views; eighth, the reality [of the fruit]; ninth, the status of an Arhat; tenth, the supreme Dharma; eleventh, [ordination] by a group of five; and twelfth, [ordination] by a group of ten. These are the twelve types of receiving the precepts.

The six types of first-time full ordination (*upasampadā*) are: the first fruit, the youth, the "Come hither" (*ehi bhikṣu*), the three statements, the eight respects (*gurudharma*), the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), the twenty-member assembly, and the dispatch of a messenger.
These six modes of receiving ordination are the same as those in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* clearly explains that within the Middle [Truth], there is mutual pervasion and limitation, meaning they are each half. According to the following questions and answers, five are limited and seven are pervasive;
this differs from the *Caturvargika-vinaya*. To destroy evil views, "substantial evil" is precisely the afflictions (*kleśa*), while "substantiality" is precisely the principle (*tattva*).
Furthermore, the "First" also refers to the True Principle, as it is the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).

Question: Regarding the formal procedure for receiving the precepts through the three utterances (*tri-vākya-upasaṃpadā*), how can it be established if the text is incomplete? Why is it permitted to receive them even when there are deficiencies? Answer:
At the beginning of the Dharma’s transformation, the capacities of sentient beings reached the point where the names differed though their essence truly converged into one.

As clearly elucidated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the original basis was revealed; because it was opened up according to conditions, it may also be attained by returning to that basis. Therefore, the two modes of receiving the precepts are not the same.
The initial question cites the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states that if there is a deficiency in the three refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*), the dharma is not established.

In the response, it is said that while the names differ, the essence is identical; that is, the principle-essence is a single entity, and whichever name is invoked, it is fully present. Although the capacities of sentient beings (*sattva*) differ, the principle remains eternally the same.

Nevertheless, when the seven thousand bhikṣus, including the brothers who were "ox-chewers" (gomayakhādaka), all received the precepts through the threefold formula, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely states that they took refuge in the Triple Gem and went forth following the Buddha; there was originally no mention of formal binding by the ritual.
In the initial section of the question-and-answer, the "method for long-term practice" refers to the three utterances.

"Lì" (漓) means "thin," which is why the text below cites a passage from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* as proof; "past karma" refers to past conditions. The Three Refuges are likewise [governed by] past karma.
In Sanskrit, he is called Gavāmpati, which translates as "Cow-chewer" (*niuxi*) or "Cow-track" (*niuye*). In the past, he was...
Because he was formerly an ox, his mouth has the habit of ruminating and his feet bear the marks of an ox; "chí" (呞), pronounced "shī," the *Shuowen* explains as "to regurgitate and then chew.
It says that seventy thousand brothers went to where the bhikṣus were, and each of those bhikṣus conferred the precepts upon them using the threefold formula.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the threefold formula also includes the addition of the formal binding [of the precepts]. Now it is said that originally there were none.
