In the next section, explaining the general heading, first the text points out that "relying on conditions" refers to the five conditions mentioned below;

under each condition, the respective obstructive functions are revealed to establish the text according to the Dharma. In the subsequent commentary where the text cites and explains them, "Middle and Extremes" refers to the directions, while "monks and nuns" refers to the [disciplinary] groups.

Regarding the phrase "the positions are all inclusive," etc.: among the six types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) for receiving ordination, if one distinguishes between the Central and Border Regions, a group of ten persons or twenty persons who have previously returned [to the faith] belong to the Central Region;
a group of five persons, or ten persons established by formal motion (*jñapti*), belongs to the Border Regions.
If one distinguishes between monks and nuns, groups of five or ten persons belong to the monks, while the remaining twenty persons and so forth belong to the nuns.

Furthermore, regarding the following presentation from the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, the many explanations cited for the third and fifth conditions among those corresponding [to the object] are from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
As for the first and third conditions among those corresponding to the subject who receives [the precepts], this is based on the distinction between cause (*hetu*) and condition (*pratyaya*).
Alternatively, taking the arousal of the thought [of awakening] as the cause, all others are conditions; these are not fixed according to the occasion, so do not remain stuck in one interpretation.

Firstly, regarding the initial category of those capable of receiving [the precepts], there are five further divisions. Because the term "capable" is used interchangeably with others, it does not clearly distinguish them;

furthermore, while one’s primary duty lies in the state of being born [into the path], if the precepts alone are held in high esteem yet lack the necessary conditions, one will fail to obtain them despite having received them. Therefore, it is necessary to point out and expose their characteristics as clearly as one's palm.

Therefore, at the beginning, he was able to receive what others set forth; in the middle, he first demonstrated the general and the specific. "Able to receive" refers to the general [capacity], while the "five kinds of characteristics" refer to the specific.

"Confusion" means that the general is confused with what follows below; thus it is necessary to list them. "The meaning is as clear as one's palm" uses a metaphor for its ease of perception, like something laid bare.
This is like a demonstration.

First, "only humans" excludes those in the four miserable destinies; as for the heavens, although their retributive fruits are superior, they are mostly attached to pleasure and lack the seeking required for the cultivation of the Path.
Asuras harbor doubts regarding the Path; those in the assemblies are correct, whereas non-humans, ghosts, spirits, and animals are characterized by flattery, deception, unreality, and ignorance.
The retribution for those who are foolish and ignorant lies in their failure to grasp the Way through sincerity and straightforwardness;

their wisdom remains far from elevated, and though they receive the precepts for the sake of the Way, obstacles to the Way constantly afflict them, causing the suffering of hell to perpetually assault their minds. Therefore, the Treatise says:

"Like a mass of molten iron, how could such a person cherish the Way and receive the precepts? Only such a person—whose suffering in the lower realms is light and whose joy in the superior heavens is inferior—possesses a strong capacity for discernment.

The power of mindfulness can exalt one’s spiritual practice; as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Duo lun) quotes regarding the taking of refuge and precepts, there is a sincere dedication that brings results.

Within the initial section on the human realm, first there is a general heading for all under heaven, followed by a detailed explanation. First, other destinies are excluded and the five paths are presented;

when the text mentions four destinies, it combines the asuras with the various realms, because those among the devas who are attached to pleasure—as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states—[are included therein].
As Maudgalyāyana exhorted Śakra, saying, "The appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter; why do you not approach him frequently to hear and receive the True Dharma?

Śakra replied, "In the heavens there are various palaces and towers, countless celestial maidens, divine *sudhā* food of a hundred flavors that appears spontaneously, and hundreds of thousands of musical performances with which we entertain ourselves. Although I know that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult," [he nevertheless went to the Buddha].

Encountering the True Dharma that is difficult to hear, yet being bound by defiled pleasures and lacking self-mastery, they are like asuras—or alternatively, "doubting deities" (*āśura*), for doubt is an obstacle to faith and thus prevents entry into the Path.
The first four lines below clarify the lower realms of ghosts and animals;
the latter four lines clarify those who oppose the Path through their lack of straightforwardness, contrasting them with the spiritual wisdom of ghosts and spirits.
"Contrary to the nature of beasts, they soar far aloft" refers to being high and remote. The verse cited regarding the hells is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Its full title is "The Intermediate Existence (*antarābhava*) Body within the Hells" (referring to the retributive aggregate within hell). It is like a mass of molten iron; its burning heat and affliction are such that suffering cannot be illustrated by any metaphor. "Only next...
below clarifies that while the suffering of the human realm is light, the lower realms possess the suffering of impermanence, whereas [the higher realms] possess pleasure.

"Inferior heavens lack superior realms"—these two phrases differ [from the previous discussion]. "The power of cognition differs from that of animals" and "the power of mindfulness differs from that of ghosts.

Regarding the latter, it refers to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states that while speaking of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), only humans can obtain the precepts, whereas the other four destinies cannot. This is what is meant.

Second, those who possess all their faculties are distinguished by a dignified and upright appearance that delights the minds of others; whatever they propagate and elucidate is easily received upon seeing their countenance.
If they were not concise and refined, they would bring disgrace upon the ranks of the Sangha. Therefore, the Vinaya texts state that only those whose six faculties are pure should receive the Dharma;
for instance, if the eye focuses on more than twenty forms at once, it is incapable of such reception.
Second, regarding the examination of the faculties, the first section states that for one who leaves the household life to propagate the Dharma and benefit all beings,

it is essential to possess the proper physical appearance to inspire faith in others. Below, citing the Vinaya texts, this section briefly mentions the faculty of the eye and enumerates the various prohibitions,
numbering more than one hundred and forty types, including twenty-two specific characteristics such as blue, yellow, red, white, mottled, crimson, and crystal-like.
The details regarding the extremely deep triangular [eyes], the wide-open slanted glare of wrath, the *mīla* (slit) eyes, and so forth, are fully explained in the *Zizhi*.
However, in this present age of turbidity, both merit and wisdom are deficient; although there may be some who study and practice, they are mostly mixed with unwholesome conduct.

Consequently, those who receive such retributive forms are rarely able to be complete in their observance of the teachings. Regarding the general principles for the secular world, there are allowances and prohibitions: prohibitions serve to prevent worldly censure, while allowances provide for practical necessity.
To accomplish the task of the Way, these two serve as the fundamental basis, sufficiently encompassing the preceding conditions.
In the next section, first, the narrative describes the degenerate age and inferior retribution; "learning and practice" refers to cultivation and observance.

Following the teaching, it next clarifies that the teachings are both general and specific, opening up allowances and establishing prohibitions to prevent censure, thereby protecting against external influences; through transformation, one leads those of inferior capacity toward the Way.

As for the faculties, the three of ear, tongue, and mind are superior aids to the Path. Because one listens to the Dharma with the ear and contemplates what is correct or erroneous with the mind, doubts can be resolved;

it is not that the tongue lacks clarity. Since these three must be fully present to constitute the very foundation of the precepts, it follows that those who are insane, deaf, or mute—whether the deficiency pertains to themselves or both themselves and others—are excluded from the count.
This may be inferred regarding the mind. As for the eyes, nose, and body, minor deficiencies are generally permitted.

Regarding the ritual for receiving the precepts, although the capacity to request and maintain them applies generally to both prohibited and permitted cases— as extensively cited in the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*—
one must carefully assess the individual's faculties and not grant ordination lightly.
Among the three [sections], the first clarifies that if the three faculties are deficient, the lower [categories] are not opened;

this is cited to prove that it is not a case where the function applies to both oneself and others—namely, the agent and the recipient. Next, regarding the eyes and so forth, it clarifies that if the three faculties are deficient, it is generally permitted as explained below;
for details, see the *Jìkāo* (Commentary), specifically the section on Receiving the Precepts (*Upasampadā*), which is extensive and not recorded here; one should seek it in the relevant text.
Truly, this careful deliberation intends to ensure precise selection.

Regarding those whose body, speech, and mind are pure: since they serve as vessels for the Way, their utter purity makes them fit for it—just as a clean house can serve as a model [for receiving guests], or as a clean cloth easily takes dye.
Therefore, one first purifies defilements so that later, when receiving the precepts (*vinaya*), they may be successfully established.
The thirteen types of persons listed above all constitute obstacles to the precepts, as will be explained by their subsequent characteristics.

Regarding the first section of the three [subsections]: first, the house is illustrated through a metaphor, thus following the principle of "law first, then metaphor"; second, the clean garment follows the principle of "metaphor first, then law.
Next, the specific individuals to be excluded are indicated below, where they will be explained in detail.

The author of the *Wenlue* (Textual Excerpts) and others maintain that the five, eight, ten, and fifty precepts constitute the foundation of the complete set of precepts (*upasampadā*). Since this foundation has already collapsed, there is nothing further to be added;

how much more so for one who destroys the complete set and turns away from the Way—such a person cannot be re-ordained even if they undergo the formal reception again. Regarding the citation of various karmic actions below:

although those such as the offenses of a defiled nun or the grave sins (*ānantarya*) do not involve the violation of specific precepts, their karma results in retribution in the present life. The obstruction of the precepts regarding the three miserable realms (*durgati*) corresponds precisely with these.
Because it contradicts [the established rules], it constitutes a formal objection (*codya*).

In the first section of the following chapter, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* explains the "offenses involving immediate retribution" (*ānantarya*) only in reference to those possessing full ordination; therefore, it cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to extend this principle to other precepts.

However, according to what constitutes a formal objection, one must rely on the four grave offenses (*catasraḥ pārājikāḥ*); although the five, eight, and ten precepts do not distinguish between gravity and lightness, they may be applied by analogy.
Taking the *Mahāsaṃghika-bhikṣu-piṇḍa* as an example, it describes the collapse and ruin [of the precepts]. Below, the text sequentially explains the gravity of the karmic offenses;

for now, this is discussed with reference to laypeople who have not yet received the full precepts at all. The commentary lists śrāmaṇeras, those who have defiled nuns, and those who commit parricide or regicide, noting that these are still subsumed under the category of "borderline" (*prānta*) offenses.

However, those who merely "dwell as thieves" (*caura-vāsaka*) will be clarified later. Since the retribution in the three miserable realms (*trāya-patha*) occurs in this very life, they are not obstructed by the precepts; therefore, [they are included here].

This is contradictory. One who possesses the four characteristics is one whose form is identical [to the Buddha]. Below, the distinction between covered and exposed garments shows that both are not the true marks of the Way; they remain detached from the two extremes.

At present, the three robes (tricīvara) are actually identical to the original: the *biānshān* (tunic), the *zhèngbèi* (square-back robe), and the *fāngqún* (square skirt). The *jìzhī* (waistband) is likewise.
None of these are from the Sūtras or Vinaya; nevertheless, they accord with the textual principles of the Vinaya, being neither mundane nor heterodox.

Regarding the first of the four [points], the text states that "having the same physical form" means severing the conditions for [external] characteristics. The subsequent items, such as "the following categories," explain the exclusions of what is not [appropriate]:
mundane people’s adornments represent attachment to the extreme of existence, while the nakedness of non-Buddhists represents attachment to the extreme of non-existence. This is also [the case].

The *Zhuan chang er bian zhi lun* (Treatise on the Wisdom that Severs the Two Extremes of Permanence and Annihilation) states: "Because the noble disciples of the Buddha abide in the Middle Way, they wear the three robes.

Next, we shall determine their usage according to the time. First, it clarifies that the characteristics of the three robes are identical to those of the Western regions of India and not different from them.

Following this, it indicates the other garments: the *zhengbei* (front-and-back robe) and the *fangqun* (square skirt) described in the *Jiaochao* (Commentary) resemble the modern-day *weiqun* (curtain-skirt).

To drape [the robe] over the left shoulder and tie it under the right armpit is called "fastening the *kāṣāya*"; this is named after the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, though its manufacture deviates from the Dharma.
Although these various garments are not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtras or Vinayas, their substance and color still preserve the appearance of the Way;
thus, they may follow the Vinaya texts. The Vinaya states: "From this day forward, [I prohibit] all laypeople and those wearing the robes of non-Buddhists."
In all cases, it is not permissible to wear these.

Regarding those who have attained a small portion of the Dharma, this refers to the identity of the Dharma; the ocean of the Dharma does not open through sudden or gradual means, but employs skillful expedients to cause them to have faith and joy, so that their observance of the precepts may become firm.
Among these five [points], the first concerns the severing of the conditions and characteristics of phenomena; next, the underlying intent of the teaching is revealed.
Above, the various conditions are listed so that they do not become dualistic: the first four must be complete, for if they are incomplete, they do not constitute a condition;
as for the last one, whether they are complete or incomplete, both the precept and the offense are incurred.

Regarding the summary of the simultaneous attainment of both the precepts and the offenses: one attains the precepts because they accord with the Dharma, and incurs an offense because one violates the regulations.
In the second major section, concerning the objects of focus, there are seven points.
First, regarding the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā*), which must be accomplished: since the teachings cannot be established without a defined boundary, one must thoroughly master this principle.
One who receives [the precepts] based on conditions of this life hears and accepts the ritual procedures and recites them immediately, without observing the conditions at all;

they merely memorize the text and do not require the *sīmā* (boundary). Even if one knows there is a *sīmā*, one must understand how it was established for people; yet many are confused and muddled by its complexity, thereby failing the original purpose of the *sīmā*.

One must therefore thoroughly inquire into the essential nature of the initial establishment—its definition, its separation, and its conjunction. If later generations do not know this, it is merely a hollow pointing toward something that does not exist, as described in the preceding text.

Since the intermediate abandonment of fetters is extremely easy, why do you disparage yourself? Having grasped this, you should directly establish it as a matter of fact to test whether people's minds are sincere;
future generations will likewise be so—why worry that it will not be thus?

Second, regarding the boundaries for the *sīmā* (ordination precinct) discussed here: first, the circumstances are recounted, and now, below, the errors are refuted. First, the failure to establish the boundary is refuted.

The reason is that receiving the precepts is not achieved merely by being able to recite the words, nor is it attained simply by chanting the *karmavācanā*. Even if one proceeds to the next section, the following critique points out the errors:

first, one must clearly investigate the boundaries and limits of the *sīmā*; second, one must examine whether the person performing the formal act (*karman*) is clear or obscure regarding their training and conduct.

As for the reference to the preceding text, it refers to the "Chapter on Establishing Boundaries" (*Sīmābandha-varga*); regarding the subsequent general reprimand, it concerns the two faults of the mind.
That which is unreal does not serve to deliver others, because it results in a similar retribution in future births. Second, regarding those who uphold the Dharma and the Saṃgha:
the proclamation of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) is not appropriate for those who are not members of the Saṃgha.
In the general discussion of the two [assemblies], it must reach four people to be capable of upholding the communal *saṃgha* dharmas.

Regarding the third point, the number of the *saṃgha* must be complete; although the two types of ordination—those of the Middle Kingdom and those of the borderlands—are listed as fifty different categories, one must not recklessly participate if the required number is not met.
As the treatise distinguishes the individuals, it says "pure, pure. In what context does this term "pure" not apply? Could it possibly refer only to the precepts?

Furthermore, the purity of the precepts depends upon the clarity of wisdom; one must thoroughly understand the permissions and prohibitions regarding phenomena and matters, like a mirror, before the essence of the ordination can be pure and untainted.

Among these three [stages], the specific requirement for full ordination (*upasampadā*) is that the number [of witnesses] must be complete; since the two conditions may overlap, they are first distinguished here according to their general and specific aspects.

The first section of the *Kō* (Exegesis) explains the fulfillment of the number [of precepts] and correctly clarifies the actual reception [of them], while concurrently indicating the peripheral allowances as follows. Next, the *Muron* (Mother Treatise) is explained:
if one merely guards the precepts without wisdom, the teachings on what is maintained and what is transgressed will remain obscure; such a person ultimately cannot be considered pure.
Now, if someone says that as long as one does not break the precepts, they are sufficient to be counted [among the Sangha], this statement is erroneous.

Generally speaking, "not breaking the precepts" applies equally to those who are unattached yet still defiled and to those who specifically do not break them at a given time. This includes those such as those in deep sleep, the mentally dull, the deaf, or the insane;

though they exist, they are as if non-existent. Those who merely endure and remain silent, relying on empty formalities, cannot be called a complete assembly of monks (*saṃgha-pūrṇa*). Now, in these border regions, we shall employ the original dispensation.
Regarding the five things that are inevitably impossible to fulfill, one should understand that even if they are not practiced, there is no offense.
In the first part of the subsequent section, it cites those who are not such [as the case in point];

below this, it refutes the claim that those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have eternally exhausted their afflictions and are thus called "ultimately liberated," for while they are entirely free from transgressions, it is said they are "not broken" because they may still commit errors through negligence, and thus are described as being "still stained."
If it is said that "provided one does not break the precepts," then even if a noble one (*ārya*) mistakenly breaks them, they should still count [toward the quorum];

yet since ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) still possess afflictions and karma, their status is distinct, and because there is both transgression and non-transgression regarding the *Prātimokṣa*, it is said that "individually, they do not break [the vow].

If it is said that "provided one does not break the precepts," then as long as ordinary monks do not break [the vow] due to conditions such as sleep or meditative concentration, they should suffice for the quorum; this is what is resolved below.
Regarding the *tuyong seng* (monks employed for local duties), since such monks must mostly rely on those from China where the Dharma is difficult to obtain, five persons may be used;

in principle, they should be free of offense. The *Ten Recitations Vinaya* and its commentaries state that one attains the precepts or incurs an offense based on whether the location is one where [the requisites] are easily obtained.

Regarding the fourth, the "Gathering of Realms" (*dhātu-saṃgraha*): by means of the realms, persons are subsumed; together they eliminate the inversion of self, all conforming to a single Dharma to accomplish unimpeded practice.

Among these four [categories], the "restricted realms" (*prādeśika-dhātu*) manifest harmony so that attachment and contention do not arise. According to the immediate teaching, this ultimately eliminates the inversion of self.

If one takes the Mahāyāna as the distant standard, one accomplishes unimpeded conduct; by clarifying the *dhātu* (element/realm) according to this principle, how could it merely serve to distinguish between "self" and "other"?

Fifth, regarding the clarification of the teachings: the terminology of the *karmavācanā*, the Great Dharma, and the Saṃgha can be easily harmonized and understood, provided they are entrusted to definitive resolution.
This *Mātṛkā-śāstra* rightly distinguishes the non-Dharma from the Dharma. Since its words are concise while the matters it covers are extensive, how could one possibly record them all in detail?
It is appropriate to take four key conditions and apply analogical reasoning to the preceding and following sections; in this way, one will achieve mastery.

Among the five [sections], the first describes whether the conditions for [ordination] can be obtained; because human affairs are difficult to harmonize, it provides a general resolution by entrusting the merit to the Dharma.
Thus, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* comprehensively includes all four conditions—person, dharma, matter, and boundary—whether taken singly or in combination.
By enumerating these seven propositions (*saptavākya*), it universally subsumes all conditions; hence it is said that they are "compared and matched" from top to bottom.

Regarding the six conditions of material support: internally one delights in the sublime Dharma, while externally one relies on a sublime appearance. Body and mind depend upon one another like a fish and water;
whether these conditions are absent or borrowed, they are neither one's own resources nor the true Dharma.

Regarding the six [points], the first two lines concerning body and mind are like the metaphors of fish and water; that body and mind have no mutual dependence and that both are non-Dharmic (a-dharma) will be clarified later in the text.
Seventh, as for the restriction to the period when the Dharma abides:

because the capacity of sentient beings has declined and the conditions have come to an end, and since the present time has not yet reached [the end of the Dharma], it is not explained in detail here.

Regarding the extinction of the Dharma within these seven periods: based on the single dispensation of Śākyamuni, during the kalpa of decrease, the lifespan increases again until it reaches sixty thousand years, at which time the Dharma will be completely extinguished.
When the lifespan is seventy thousand years, Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world; when it is eighty thousand years, Maitreya descends to be born.

The seven external conditions mentioned above are likewise grouped into four: first, the seven are explained in terms of location to clarify the formation of the fundamental realm; second, three or four conditions together establish the meaning of the *saṃgha*;
third, the formal act of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; fourth, the six matters concerning the resources for renunciation and their combination, which may be examined in detail.
In the first section of the *Liaojian*, it states that "external conditions" are mentioned because they are contrasted with the aforementioned internal retribution which is the recipient;

as for the seventh being categorized by location, this is because the dharma of boundary-delineation (*sīmā-bandha*) has not been lost, so when separated, there are seven, but when combined, they reduce to only four.
Success and failure constitute two [opposites]; other instances of contradiction or incompatibility need only be discussed in terms of the facts.
In the subsequent section on the general classification, "other contradictions or incompatibilities" refers to the six conditions being incomplete, which constitutes failure.
Since such matters require extensive explanation, it is said that they "must be discussed."

Regarding the various differing explanations concerning robes and alms bowls, some interpret them according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, asserting that even if one lacks these items, it is permissible to receive the precepts, though one incurs an offense.
Others say that since the Vinaya schools differ, how can one case be used as an analogy for another?

For instance, if one lacks a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), one cannot follow that precedent. Still others say that if one lacks robes and alms bowls, it is entirely contrary to the Dharma and thus cannot be permitted. If...
One who borrows [the precepts] had them at that time, but it is hoped that they will inform the Sangha; if they do not state that it was not the Dharma, they shall not obtain the precepts.

The meaning is based on the four propositions regarding a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) who has broken the precepts; such allowances and prohibitions are thus established. Although there is indeed textual evidence for this, ordinary minds find it difficult to believe.
Fortunately, if one relies on the scriptural teachings, then there are no [other] precepts.

In the "Separate Simplification," there are four interpretations of ancient and modern masters. The first master, following the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, clarifies that while one obtains the precepts, it is not proper conduct (*airyāpathika*), and thus one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
The second master merely refutes the former interpretation but does not produce the correct principle;

he clearly indicates that one must judge according to the precedent of one's own school (*nikāya*), allowing for cases where the *upādhyāya* is not present before one or where there is no *upādhyāya* at all.
The *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) does not clarify that the attainment of precepts is restricted to specific schools (*nikāya*) such that they must not be used indiscriminately;

this is the second master’s view. There is no case where one may borrow [precepts] entirely without obtaining them. This is seen based on the four propositions concerning what is known or unknown regarding the *upādhyāya*: in the first three propositions, if one is unaware [of the transgression], all are permitted;
in the final proposition, because one is aware, it is not permitted. Such are the distinctions between what is allowed and what is prohibited, as established by those who have passed judgment below.
The Master has now judged that the first two lines of the verse deprecate the first and last of the two interpretations, while the latter two lines adopt the second master’s view;
thus, the "Teaching of Sound" (śabdavidyā) refers to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

In the third section on the "Great Conditions," it clarifies that the mind must receive this [teaching], which is the primary cause for the fundamental meaning; therefore, it must be presented beforehand as listed in the text.
"One who does not claim [ordination for themselves] has no intention to receive it and is forced to appear on stage against their will.

One who does not name their preceptor (upādhyāya) holds someone else in high regard and treats the preceptor with slight. One who says they do not 'beg' (for ordination) does not desire this and distinguishes themselves from the rest of the assembly.

Although they may remain silent together with others, even if they have something to say, since it is not their original intent and what they beg for is not what is being requested, it is not called 'receiving' [ordination]."

Regarding the first of the three types of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*), it demonstrates the causal characteristics: the mind is the primary cause for the arising of the precepts and the fundamental basis upon which the Dharma relies;

thus it is called the "causal basis. As will be explained below in the three sections that follow, this refers to not requesting [the precepts]. Although the meaning of the preceding section is settled even if one were to request them, it is still not [a true generation of the mind] because there is no sincere intent;
the *upādhyāya* perceives this lack of respect as being without the mind to receive and accept the teachings from the *upādhyāya*.
Therefore, in the commentary, the inclusion of "sleeping drunk" and other such states all refers to the absence of consciousness. Regarding the fourth case, where the mind and the object coincide:

although the boundaries are established, the *saṃgha* is complete, and the formal requirements (*dharma*) and the primary conditions are assembled, the intention is directed toward something else and one does not bring to mind the root precepts;

thus, the mind does not correspond to the object. Even though the mind is earnest and present, if one is unaware that the boundary has been established, then despite the assembly and the formal requirements being complete, [the act is nonetheless invalid].
It is not that the conditions have converged but the objects have diverged from the mind; other cases should be judged accordingly.
As for those whose conditions are not uniform and who do not correspond with one another, their karmic offenses coincide such that they cannot be separated from each other.

Within the four mental states (*citta-vastu*), one distinguishes the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) by contrasting the aforementioned two and three conditions. First, the initial heading indicates the permutation where both are associated;
below that, the second permutation is explained: regarding the conditions of the Saṃgha and the Dharma, the "conditioned object" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) refers to the actual phenomena (*vastu*).
Among these four objects, those that are "individually conditioned" (*pṛthag-ālambana*) lack the mind that seeks the Dharma as its object, even if [the object] is present.
Other wholesome conditions are likewise not congruent; although the mind may be inferior, the third phrase is explained by reversing the above, which makes it clear.
The remaining cases are to be inferred accordingly: that is to say, other non-congruent factors do not arise from the mind-object relationship as previously described.

Regarding those capable of receiving [retribution], obstacles, and supporting conditions, they are all included within the categories of "existent" and "non-existent," as can be seen. Both being inferior explains the fourth phrase: when sinful karma and its corresponding signs coincide.
Because past evils have converged, one cannot separate the two; thus, both mind and objects are non-existent.

Regarding the five factors being identical: phenomena are produced through conditions; they do not accord with or conform to the eight characteristics, nor is there any confusion between their beginning and end or their prior and subsequent stages.
For example, to prepare a single meal, five conditions must be fulfilled; if even one is lacking, it cannot be accomplished. Phenomena are likewise so.

Regarding the five matters within the section on the "Establishment," the first correctly explains the eight characteristics, which are the eight dharmas mentioned below. These are illustrated by analogies:
the analogy of food represents the essence of reception (*pratigraha*), and the analogy of the five practices represents the eight dharmas.
As for the preliminary conditions prior to the performance of the ritual act, the eight [dharmas] are listed as they clearly appear in the text, each being distinct from the others.
The first section, "The Ritual Text for Requesting the Master," consists of two parts: first, explaining the causes and conditions that led to this request; second, cultivating reverent devotion.
Within the first part, there are again two sections: the former clarifies the circumstances that prompted the request, while the latter establishes the ritual procedures and confers empowerment.

The initial statement that "a disciple has no teacher's instruction" implies that those of middling or superior capacity must rely on the guidance of a teacher; otherwise, they will inevitably fall into corrupt conduct.

Since there are truly no virtuous friends [to provide such guidance], the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom must have something upon which to rely; therefore, the office of the Upādhyāya (Preceptor) was established.
Next, regarding the practice of requesting a teacher, the *Zhongke Shangzhi* states that among the nine grades of human capacity in Confucianism,
those of superior intelligence do not require instruction, while those of inferior stupidity cannot be taught; only those of middling capacity can be instructed,
and thus a teacher is necessary.

Therefore, following the terminology of this region:

first, regarding the names for the disciples, the title "younger brother" (*di*) is used because they follow [the teacher] from this point onward, and the title "son" (*zi*) is used because they are born from him. Next, regarding the names for the teachers:
since the Dharma of renunciation originated in the Western land of India, the title *upādhyāya* (Preceptor) did not originally exist in this land.

Below, I cite secular etiquette to clarify the meaning of "not translating. Since the time of the Han dynasty, the state has frequently established positions for *boshi* (doctors) of the Five Classics and the various schools of thought (*zhuzi*), who serve as teachers for scholars.
The *Liji* states: "The gentleman knows the difficulty and ease of reaching the ultimate learning, and he knows its beauty and flaws;

only then can he provide broad analogies, and only then can he become a teacher. Regarding the practice of *shuxiu* (the offering of a fathom-long roll of silk): *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
In antiquity, dried meat was used as the ritual gift for visiting one's teacher; nowadays, however, the term has come to encompass items such as gold and silk.

Regarding the mutual guidance between teacher and disciple, what is called "reverent respect" means that although one may have left the secular world and their physical form may occupy a lowly position, because they harbor the Way within their hearts, they are revered before being instructed;
thus, there is no coming in vain. When both self and other maintain such mutual respect, the True Dharma arises from it, becoming magnificent and far-reaching;
all in the world rely upon this for enlightenment, which leads to profound attainment.

Among the three [sections], the first clarifies the intention of the teacher’s reverence for the disciple through the text, so that they may mutually respect one another; fearing that [the reader] might doubt this and act perversely, it specifically demonstrates [this principle].
Respect based on status relies on physical appearance, whereas respect based on the mind arises from the heart; because one harbors the Way within, one must not treat others lightly.
Thus, there are no who go in vain—this means that the disciple must certainly receive the teaching. Next, the following section explains the successive benefits of these practices.
The realization of enlightenment arises in succession without ceasing, reaching infinity.
One who perceives well should not allow faults to arise unbidden; rather, one should bind oneself to adverse conditions and restrain them, ensuring that the precepts are never abandoned.
Other instructions on the Dharma are as extensive as those found in the *Shoujie* (Receiving the Precepts) and the *Xingshi Chao* (Manual of Ritual Practice).

Regarding the explanation of the rules for requesting [a preceptor]: first, because there was no formal method for requesting, transgressions arose; the Upādhyāya rebuked them, saying, "Who requested you? Consequently, he established the regulations for requesting.

This was done to restrain those with evil conditions so that they would not commit further transgressions. As for the phrase "requesting the bond," it means forming the relationship of father and son.
This refers to the matter of *niśraya* (reliance) immediately following the reception of the precepts; the *Shishi Yaoyong Chao* (Essentials for Teachers and Disciples) concerns this very point.
Section.
The text lists the request for the Dharma within the assembly so that the recipient may observe the signs and give rise to reverence.

It is certainly not harmful to require this one year or one month prior to the reception. Some say that the addition of the ritual to a single session should not be protracted; this is likely out of fear [of the aforementioned].

This is due to mental indolence; in terms of the meaning, it seems to lose the proper sequence. However, following the ritual, since ordinary people generally have many habits of arrogance and the precepts require reverence and caution, one must first subdue the physical body and seek the pure Dharma.
Only after this will one reflect upon transgressions; I would never rashly bestow them.

In the section on "Cultivating Reverence," the first part explains the Sangha. Within this, the initial passage clarifies that the present interpretation applies to both the communal (Sangha) and the private;

"previously requiring one who receives" refers to a prior private invitation. Next, regarding the individuals, the following portion refutes the view that it is restricted to the Sangha alone, as it does not apply to those invited beforehand.

Since the relationship between teacher and disciple lasts a lifetime, how could one allow the mind to become lax? Thus, it is said that while it appears to be a loss, in reality, there is no such loss. Next, the following portion provides the explanation.
Having performed the universal prostrations, one first ensures that the spirit of reverence is fully established and maintained thereafter.
Within the ritual application (*adhikāra*), the invitation may be divided into two parts. First, regarding the rules for the invitation:

according to the Vinaya regulations, one should be instructed by a companion in a secluded place to recite and master both the text and its meaning; subsequently, one proceeds within the assembly of monks.
To extend the invitation in accordance with the Dharma is also part of the ritual protocol.
Regarding the first section of the second part, "The Ritual for Establishing the Invitation," the instructional text directs that the meaning be taught to others and recited by oneself;
as for observing whether the faculties of the recipient are sharp or dull, there is no fixed requirement for either.
The petition contains five points: "Venerable Sire, please attend" requests that you focus your mind; "acting as preceptor" clarifies the object of one's prayer;
"I pray that you will act as such" expresses the hope for your compassionate compliance; "I rely on you for full ordination" indicates that the three trainings arise from this;
and "out of the fivefold compassion" restates one’s inner sentiments and requests your permission.
In the subsequent section on the text for the invitation, there are five parts: the first phrase constitutes the first part; the two phrases beginning with "I, [Name]" constitute the second part;
the two phrases beginning with "May" constitute the third part; the two phrases beginning with "I rely upon" constitute the fourth part; and the final single phrase constitutes the fifth part.
Next, regarding the response: if there were no words of reply, there would be nothing for which to feel joy and exultation.
Within the heading of the response, it is because one knows permission has been granted through the answer that joy and exultation arise.
There are four types of responses; first, "So be it," which generally accepts the request and agrees to act as the teacher. "I shall instruct you" [is the second].

It is not only that the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* contains extensive teachings on the phenomena; those who seek purity should likewise revere the *Prātimokṣa*, for it governs and sustains the three types of action (*trikarma*).
As for the injunction "do not be heedless," since all faults originate from heedlessness, one must restrain the faculties of the emotions and distance oneself from the five desires.

The commentary lists four sections: first, responding to the request; second, granting the teaching; third, admonishing regarding action; and fourth, focusing on the mind. Regarding the first, "responding to the request," there are two parts:
the initial response of "yes" (*k'e-er*) and the subsequent agreement of "so be it" (*k'o-shih*). "Yes" is the response of assent; "so be it" is the appropriate reply for those of superior station.

To say both "yes" and "so be it" together indicates that one has not yet fully mastered the terminology and is entirely unsuitable. As for the response regarding repentance and upholding [the precepts], its meaning encompasses both of the preceding points.

Because those being addressed include both juniors and seniors, among the three [explanations], the first interpretation—which accords with the text—is acceptable. That is to say, it refers to receiving instruction from those who have not yet mastered the terminology;

this is a critique that overturns the traditional transmission. As for the subsequent [explanation], it reconciles the repentance methods found elsewhere, which combine two types of addresses, stating that one may address a senior when facing a junior.
This is because the former applies to both juniors and seniors and may thus be designated in two ways, whereas this case concerns only requesting a teacher and should not be listed as a pair.
Some explain that although the Vinaya lists four [answers], the intention is that they constitute a single answer collectively, as they are common to all four.

As explained above regarding the initial passage of the text, the first part consists of words of concession, while the latter three parts comprise the sequential classification of the encompassing meanings.

Regarding the invitation of Preceptor Wenlie and the assembly of other masters: according to principle and the requirements of the matter, one must not arrive arbitrarily;

Among the various masters’ expositions, the first section relies on principle and the requirements of the matter. "Principle" refers to the principles of the Path, while "matter" refers to the ritual procedures.
At present, ritual practices have become thin, deficient, and increasingly superficial;

One must require the original master to provide detailed instruction, enabling the recipient to understand the application of the Dharma so that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) may be established.
When the entire assembly shares in the merit equally, how could the three masters alone receive its benefit? Although the text opens with a request, the meaning conforms to the preceding section.
In the next subsection, the initial description of "erroneous grasping" (*nòu*) refers to seizing and pinning down the cloth, which is like arranging it;

The section on "Desire" (*kāma*) below correctly refutes the Master’s original instruction, which refers to the Upādhyāya revealing the name and virtuous deeds of the *karmavācanā* instructor so that [the candidate] may know these individuals who have performed the labor of presiding over the rite; thus it is called "knowing the application of the Dharma.

When merit is attributed to the entire assembly, one does not receive the gift from the three masters alone. In the text below, the term "Dharma" is indicated, with only the word "Upādhyāya" being changed.
It is still used for the term *ācārya*.
The term *ācārya* originally followed the oral transmission and was also subject to corruption and abbreviation;

However, the title "Teacher" (ācārya) applies generally to both light and heavy [offenses], as six types of ācāryas are set forth in the Vinaya:
first, the tonsure teacher; second, the renunciation teacher; third, the scriptural teacher; fourth, the instruction teacher; fifth, the *karmavācanā* teacher; and sixth, the reliance teacher.

Only the latter teacher provides lasting stability from beginning to end, whereas the others are titles applied collectively for the duration of a single session. Further details are as explained in the *Shuochao*.

Regarding the first section of the three [parts], the initial part explains the meaning by translating names; this refers to those who translate the *Prātimokṣa* and *Vinaya* according to what they hear, without investigating the original phonemes.

Regarding the "monks outside" (the external community), those who perform the ritual procedures in unison with others are titled "Venerable Persons" (zūnrén) or "Venerable Teachers" (zūnshī);

Second, as for "peacefully accepting," the commentary provides a detailed and explicit explanation.

The terms "robes" (*cīvara*) and "alms bowl" (*pātra*), as well as "name," are general expressions used to facilitate communication.

that is, one should exit the assembly with dignified deportment in accordance with the *Vinayavibhāṣā*. Having completed the announcement, the text continues: "One should rise and pay homage to the Saṃgha," then proceed according to standard decorum to the place of the recipient.

Since this passage is omitted from the *Karmavācanā* manuscript, it should be cited and added here. Regarding the section on the objects of focus (*ālambana*), the text subsequently provides an exegesis of the names and the request (*yācana*).

This may be called "Harmonizing with the Questions. From this point downward, it indicates that while the general harmonization is simply stated as "receiving the precepts," the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is distinct;
