Next, regarding the mind (*citta*): the mind is itself the formations (*saṃskāra*). As the *Cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra-saṃgraha* asks, "What is the nature of the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*)? The answer is: its nature is the root of non-attachment (*alobha*), which is one of the three roots of goodness.

When discussed in terms of its retinue (*parivāra*), it is of the nature of the five aggregates of goodness (*pañca kuśalaskandhāḥ*). (The root of non-attachment is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); as the primary factor, it is the mind, while the others...)
Because these four aggregates together constitute this practice, they are called its "retinue.
Fourth, the sequence:
clothing is that which is required at all times to sustain the body; as it is the most essential, it is explained first. Once the body is covered, internal afflictions [are stilled].

Because one must cross over [suffering], begging for food comes next; although the body may be sustained thereby, its dignified deportment (īryāpatha) must depend on external support. Thus, the third is explained as sitting under a tree.

Since there is no capacity for treatment if illness arises and is not remedied by the three aforementioned supports, the fourth is established as "medicines from rotting matter" (pūtimukta-bhaiṣajya).
In the fourth section, the formal explanation, the sequence in which the preceding leads to the succeeding is easily discerned by following the text.
This is presented according to the first person who possesses the four distinct types of ascetic practices (*dhūta*) during the stage of the practice of enjoyment;

while these characteristics are listed individually for many people, it is only when they are combined that they are fully realized—just as the "leaving the seat" [practice] is divided into five, yet cannot be separated from the whole, so too may this be understood.

Regarding the initial section of the *Jianzhong* (Simplified Commentary), it does not provide a specific distinction to exclude [the following], fearing that one might think they are identical to those twelve *dhūta* practices;

therefore, it specifically characterizes them. As for the "enumeration of the characteristics according to the faculties and the teachings," it means establishing the teachings based on the faculties [of the practitioners]. Regarding the separation from sitting, there are five categories. The *Chao* states: "Five types are established regarding location: first, the *araṇya* (wilderness);
second, the charnel ground; third, at the foot of a tree; fourth, sitting in the open air; and fifth, sitting wherever one happens to be. This refers to the following.
It is clear that the practices performed by many individuals cannot be condensed into a single person across five locations (namely:

being separated from one's robes as two cases, [the practice of] wearing cast-off robes as the third, being separated from food as the fourth, and the practice of begging for food—consisting of eating only one mouthful at a time while remaining seated in one posture without performing the ritual of leaving food behind—which constitutes the fifth; this refers to the practice of constant sitting. This does not apply to those who walk together, and the reasoning is as explained above).
Regarding the opening and closing [of permission] for the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*):

it is because the Great Sage, having thoroughly understood the faculties and natures [of beings], bestowed medicine according to their capacities. Through the superior power of his transformative influence (*adhiṣṭhāna*), he prohibited the first four dharmas;

this was so that those with superior strength might sustain their bodies and advance on the Path to obtain benefit. However, for those of middling or inferior capacity whose power is weak, matters depend upon various conditions; thus, if these were not permitted, [they would be unable to practice].

If one were attached to wearing robes and so forth, there would be a regression from the Path; how then could one endure traversing hardships? If there were only prohibitions, the capacity for a superior rebirth would be severed;

if there were only permissions, one might become arrogant and seek only the higher practices. Because the three types of persons—those who are permitted, those who are prohibited, and those who possess both—are all fully equipped to realize the truth, they are called the "Noble Lineages" (āryavaṃśa).
In the first section of the fifth gate concerning the True Dharma (*saddharma*), first the intention of the Sage is set forth as a response;

next, the permissions and prohibitions are clarified. "Prohibition" here refers to the established rules (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*). First, the four prohibitions are set forth as being specifically intended for those of superior faculties; next, the four permissions are clarified, which encompass those of middling and inferior faculties.
For now, the offering of robes is cited as an example, with the other three categories explained accordingly. Finally, the third part clarifies the relationship between the two teachings.
When all elements are complete and not lacking even one, and they are combined and applied correctly, this is precisely the realization of the fruit.

Thus, one knows that the teaching of the Sage possesses four meanings: first, benefiting sentient beings with a compassionate mind; second, prescribing medicine according to their capacities; third, skillfully understanding what is permitted and what is prohibited;
and fourth, it is not only permitted for those of middle or lower capacity to wear various fine garments, but it is also permitted for those of superior capacity when they are ill.
The wearing of refuse-rags (*pāṃśukūla*) is permitted for receiving offered robes because it follows the original path; thus, this allowance was made. Therefore, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* states:

"If the Saṃgha is in harmony, they cause [the practitioner] to transcend and rise above the stage of 'leaving birth' (*vitarāga*), to attain the fruits [of the path], to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), and to engage in the activities of seated meditation, study, and reflection.

The remaining three supports may be inferred by analogy with this example. Fourth, the Buddha taught that the four practices, such as alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*), are conditions capable of generating the Path.
The eight factors beginning with right speech are the causes capable of producing the Path; speaking in accordance with the Dharma, they are free from the fault of error or confusion.

In the first section of the following chapter, there is first a general summary, followed by a specific enumeration: first, the original vow; second, the discernment of capacities; third, the ability to master the teachings.

Having opened [the teaching], it subsequently applies universally to those of the three faculties. This is further demonstrated by citing the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, which shows that the permission to hear [the Dharma] must necessarily be granted.
One must maintain harmony among the monastic community and a countenance free from contention; only then can one advance on the Path and attain its fruits.

Regarding the contrast between transcending and ascending versus the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), and the contrast between departing from birth and the higher realms, the previous discussion on the gift of robes was intended to show that the other three [requisites] are no different in their underlying intent. These four [requisites] manifest the benefit of supporting the Path through the four reliances (*catur-yoniśaḥ-pratiniḥśraya*).
Therefore, they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*); because they facilitate the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path, they are termed "causes of the Path" (*mārga-hetu*).

Devadatta imitated the Buddha by teaching five dharmas that were restrictive rather than open—namely, wearing patched robes, begging for food, dwelling under trees, and abstaining from butter and salt.
First, these do not possess the four meanings [of the true dharma] as explained above;

second, they constitute a perverted teaching that leads others into false views, asserting that the eight factors of verbal karma are the conditions for the Path, while the five practices such as begging for food are the causes of the Path.
Exceeding the Eightfold Noble Path, he extensively expounded a counterfeit delusion regarding the true basis, causing the ignorant to become entangled;
those who still study this path are the faction of Devadatta.
Regarding the establishment of his [counterfeit] doctrine within the false dharma, Devadatta—whose full name is Devadatta—is translated as "Heavenly Heat" (天熱).
At the time of his birth, because the hearts of the various devas were afflicted with feverish distress, they established false Triple Gems and destroyed the Buddha’s True Dharma.
The five things are the Dharma Jewel itself. Regarding "butter and salt": they boiled salt with butter-fat, and because it was considered a rare delicacy, the word "etc.

is used to include fish and meat by analogy. Next, the faults are revealed as lacking four qualities: first, a lack of a compassionate heart; second, [a lack of...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.*
1. Misunderstanding the capacities of others; 2. Not understanding the three [types of] teachings; 3. Lacking benefit; 4.

Preaching the Dharma in a perverted manner—taking causes for conditions and conditions for causes—and thus employing the five factors to disparage the Eightfold Noble Path. "To exceed" means to go beyond.
As for "resemblance," the first three of the five are similar speech, while the latter two constitute false speech. Even the ignorant and the dense masses continue to study them to this day.
The vestiges of these traditions still remain in India.

Therefore, if it were said within the *Samprayukta-citta* that the five factors are not the eightfold noble path, the earth deities would proclaim their birth, and throughout the entire trichiliocosm—the sphere of the Buddha’s transformation—meditation and recitation would cease;
the rest is as explained in the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Precepts).
In the first section of the following division, it is explained that once the schism has already occurred and become accepted by people, the Wheel of Dharma cannot turn;

this is followed by the explanation that meditation and recitation are themselves the contemplation of the Dharma. The *Vinaya* states: "It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when the Saṃgha is divided at the time of the morning meal, it must be reunited by evening;
during that interval, no humans or devas can realize the Path. Therefore, it is said that [the Wheel] does not proceed. The remainder below refers to the abbreviated explanation.
One should consult the *Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra* regarding the precept on schism (*saṃghabheda*).
Following the text, there are two parts: first, the causal conditions (*nidāna*), and second, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Within the causal conditions, first, regarding the basis (*āśraya*): because one is weary of one's original training, the subsequent [precepts] are opened up; based on this basis, according to principle, the original [vows] remain intact.

My practice of the Way is mediocre and my understanding shallow; thus, I fear that the previous instructions may be forgotten as I later decline. Knowing that the primary precepts are not in vain, I have come to this.

Second, regarding the explanation of the conditions (*pratyaya*) according to the text, there are two sections in the sub-commentary. First, providing an explanation based on the initial conditions for the establishment of the precepts.

The last two lines explain the reasons for the subsequent conferral [of precepts]: out of a desire to cause those of external paths (*tīrthika*) who have become weary of their original practices not to turn back from the Way.
Based on what follows, this demonstrates the intent of the regulation; according to principle, it refers to the logical foundation for establishing the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*).
"Ordinary and coarse" refers to those of dull faculties who, having regressed, later realize their initial error and thus do not abandon their pursuit of the fundamental source.
Second, regarding the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), first the fundamental thesis is stated: "A bhikṣu relies on rag-robes. Below this, four characteristics are enumerated.

The reason why both the prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) and the prescriptions (*vidhi*) are presented together with the previously cited three titles of the Tathāgata is to briefly demonstrate that he is not a heterodox teacher, but a Great Sage.

Because they were personally admonished, they were raised together [with the others] so that their instruction would be treated with gravity; thus, when they act according to the teaching, there will certainly be no negligence or indulgence.
Next, regarding the initial passage of the section on "Essential Nature and Characteristics" (*tǐxiàng biāojǔ*), its subtle intention extends to both the preceding and following sections.

Briefly stated below, the general explanation demonstrates that those who are not heterodox—namely, the non-Buddhists (*bāiwài*) and Devadatta—both establish reliance upon the Dharma; therefore, they do not lightly transgress, as there is no negligence or indulgence.
Therefore, the text states: "Those who leave home based on this depart from the conditioned; those who receive full ordination ascend to the wishless;
and by perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣu, they accord with the sublime ritual."
Next, among the three realms of existence (*tribhava*), all are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); because one transcends these conditioned states, it is called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*).
As for "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*), it means there is nothing sought after. Regarding "conforming to the noble conduct," this is so because all three vehicles (*triyāna*) are likewise.

Previously, it was explained that if one commits the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), one loses the source of the noble ones (*ārya*). Now, it is taught that the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) involve performing actions that accord with the causes for the work of the Path.
Regarding the third point, "abstaining from and undertaking," abstaining from what obstructs the noble ones and undertaking what accords with the Path constitutes following the Path.
"Because of the cause" (*yin yin*) means "relying upon" (*yi*).
Regarding the stages, the first part is divided into two sections. The section from the beginning up to "is able to maintain" constitutes the fundamental regulation.
The section from "if one obtains long-term benefits" onwards is the provision for exemptions, as it would otherwise be impossible to endure what was prescribed previously.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe), the initial section on the fundamental regulation is intended primarily for those of superior faculties;
the opening of the time limit for distribution is intended for those of middling and inferior faculties, according to the extent of their respective capacities.
The previous section was divided into four parts.
In the first subsection of the "Detailed Explanation of the Original Rules," this initial section provides a brief demonstration.

Regarding the phrase "one who relies on rag robes" (*pāṃsukūlika*), this raises the name to illustrate the subject; according to the Vinaya, ten types [of robes] are listed, all of which are common in the world.

The metaphor of discarding things like refuse and sweepings refers merely to what is held in contempt by the world; that which the world deprecates is what the Way prizes. This statement is made with respect to ordinary people. Thus, the *Lunyu* says:
"The gentleman does not feel shame over coarse clothing or poor food; if he were to feel shame, he would not yet be fit for discussion.
Liu Zi said: "Food is sufficient to fill the void and sustain the breath; clothing is sufficient to cover the body and ward off the cold. These are his words.

This is so. As for such things as wearing the *guanzhangfu* cap and the *fengye* robe, having fine delicacies before one’s eyes, and hearing elegant sounds filling one’s ears—the glory of a single moment is truly not worth esteeming.
The Book of Documents says: "High positions and rich flavors cannot both endure for long.

Therefore, the gentleman maintains the way of humble radiance; to endure what others cannot endure is called the overcoming of hatred and love, and to cut away what others cannot cut away is the severing of worldly attachment.
Desire is what people practice, while non-practice is benevolence and righteousness; if this is so regarding desire, how much more so for one who harbors the Way?
This is because they are ignorant of the fact that these are merely elaborate branches and worldly customs.

According to the Vinaya, the detailed explanation below is divided into three parts. First, the names and essences are shown. Regarding the ten types [of offenses]: first, chewing like an ox; second...
1. Mice-gnawed; 2. Burnt by fire; 3. Washed by water for four months; 4. From a woman who has recently given birth; 5. From a temple of the gods;

6. From among graves; 7. Obtained through prayer; 8. Gained through bartering; 9. Received as a royal gift; 10. Discarded in the Western lands (these ten types were collected because they were abandoned there, and thus taken to serve as clothing). The common world deems these lowly while the Way regards them as noble, demonstrating their apparent opposition.
Below this, we shall next discuss their names: ordinary people call them those of shallow understanding, whereas a distinguished gentleman would [view them differently].
How could one consider rags as mere refuse? Therefore, the following three passages cite analogies.

First, regarding the *Lunyu* (Analects), it says one "cannot yet discuss [the Way] with him," implying that such a common person is not worth speaking to about the Way. Liu Zi refers to Liu Zhòu (it is not the case, as some say, that it refers to Liu Xié or Liu Xīn).
He authored two fascicles and fifty-five chapters; being impoverished and having no means to promote himself, he carried his book and waited upon Shen [Yi].
He met [Liu Xun] before his carriage and presented him with this book; having read it, Liu was struck by its uniqueness and immediately invited him to ascend the carriage to establish a friendship.
People of the time called this work the *Liu Zi*. Now, citing the "Preventing Desires" (*Fangyu*) chapter, it says:

"The wise person carves away their passions to cast off entanglements and restrains their desires to maintain integrity. Such statements as "only then can one receive food and be sufficient" are correct, for they praise his possession of virtue.
This is the principle. At the very end of the passage, the two characters "yān-róng" (厭榮) and "guàn-yī" (冠衣) appear;

"zhāng-fǔ" (章甫) refers to the cap worn during the Yin dynasty, and "féng-yè" (縫掖) refers to a robe with wide sleeves. In the *Jiayu*, Confucius replied to Duke Ai: "When I was young and lived in Lu, I wore the féng-yè robe;
when I grew up and lived in Song, I wore the zhāng-fǔ cap. "Exquisite delicacies" (*jiā-yáo*) refers to a variety of prepared dishes, not merely grain.
Food is called *yáo* (delicacies), and "fragrant sounds" refers to the music of songs and performances; high status is considered noble, and rich flavors are considered wealth.
It is unclear from which scripture this is taken, as both are impermanent. Power inevitably declines. Therefore, the following clarifies the ease of turning toward the Way:
the *Qián* hexagram states that the way of man hates fullness and loves humility. Humility is honored and radiant; though one may be lowly, one cannot be surpassed.
Regarding "The culmination of the noble person is to endure what others cannot": this means that as for what the multitude is unable to do, I shall exert my strength to perform it.
This text originates from the *Jingzhuzi* (Son of Pure Abiding), which originally contains only three phrases; the commentary adds correlations and explanations to assist in clarifying the text.

Using the secular to illustrate the Way—where the secular is shallow and the Way is deep—the principle must surely surpass it; how could it possibly fall short? How much less so regarding their mutual relationship?
The passage beginning with "In contrast to knowledge" [refers to] the lower three points of intention.
Second, "relying on this to leave the household life" clarifies the fundamental aspiration for receiving full ordination; one must not forget this as the primary point.
Among these, secondly, the substance of what is received is the foundation for establishing practice, while the four reliances are the beginning for initiating all practices.
The third [point] concerns the question regarding the gravity of retribution, asking how one could ever transgress again after having vowed to "exhaust one's life" [in upholding the precepts].
The fourth is the establishment of the vow and the proclamation of the words, "How could I later commit a transgression?
These three questions and four answers are easy to understand according to the text.

Question: Since the substance of receiving [the precepts] actually resides in the *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), why is it that the question is instead directed toward the agent? Answer: In reality, it is as you have asked.

However, because those with dull faculties require explicit instruction, they would otherwise remain ignorant; thus, the agent must be designated. For those of superior faculties who skillfully comprehend the purport of the teaching, there is no need for such formal indications—as was the case for the "Come, O Bhikṣu" (*ehi bhikṣu*) formula or the "Three Words" (*trivācika*).
For those of dull and turbid dispositions, however, it is necessary to provide clear and manifest instruction, as in the case where the text simply states "one receives" without further elaboration.

Regarding the precepts, since one knows what the objects of the precepts are, the first four objects are established; subsequently, the four characteristics are practiced so that they may be clearly understood and explained.

If this is still treated with contempt, how much more so when there is neither speech nor a formal vow? For who would know that [the precept] has not been transgressed? Therefore, it is not established in vain.

In the question, the sequence—first receiving [the precepts] and then inquiring about their meaning—seems inverted; therefore, in the answer, the first part generally explains that both types of practitioners require them, praising [the precepts] as an aid for those of dull faculties.
Next, it specifically clarifies the necessity for practitioners of dull faculties: "There are births" refers to being attached to existence;

"sentient beings" refers to *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts), which is a general term and not explicitly listed here. If one commits an offense even when following this [general rule], how much more so when one does not?
Regarding the opening section on robes, it says: "Excessive benefit" refers to that which exceeds the original regulations; all else is considered excessive.

As for robes offered by donors (*dānapati*), one may accept them regardless of whether the donor is a layperson or a monastic, because they are brought forward as pure offerings (*śuddha-dāna*). Regarding the cutting and damaging of robes:
the former applies generally to both secular and monastic clothing, while the latter specifically pertains to the characteristics of the monastic path; thus, these two are listed separately.

Regarding the opening of the *Zhong* (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kaṭhina-vastu*), it first mentions "long-term benefit" (*chánglì*), which is a general reference; "the alms-offerings of donors and so forth" is the specific enumeration of what is accepted.
Within the context of the two types of food, the initial prohibition and the subsequent allowance are both explained as before.

Within the first of the two general divisions concerning begging for alms, there are two major sections: the initial prohibition and the subsequent allowance. Within the prohibition, there are also four parts:
(1) stating the name, (2) showing the basis of practice, (3) the question, and (4) the vow; these are all as in the preceding section. The latter two [sections] are likewise.

If the Sangha has been appointed, it refers to an invitation according to the monastic order; for the sake of liberation, one who has left the household life and received the precepts is permitted to go and offer condolences.
To act contrary to this is improper and is termed "theft. Next, regarding those who deliver food, they shall provide meals at the monastery on the eighth and fifteenth days of the month.
As for the term "food on the [first] three days of both the white and black fortnights," it means that during these two months, there are three days each—excluding the fourteenth day for nuns.
The Vinaya specifies three such "inauspicious days," for which one must provide offerings and observe the fast as described for the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*).

On the first day of the month, food is highly esteemed in that country; furthermore, on the occasion of special ceremonies, many items are displayed at monasteries and temples, following local custom.

One should also be aware of the first day of the first month, the third day of the third month, and the ninth day of the ninth month. As for the monks' regular meals, they are provided according to what is available.

The amount [of food] is determined by the standard of one’s age. If one is invited to a meal at a layperson’s home, that constitutes a separate invitation. The commentary on the six sections begins with the first:

explaining the "monastic assignment" (*saṃgha-kṣepa*). This specifically excludes those seeking liberation; according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, because such a person does not act for the sake of liberation, they deviate from the principle of the Saṃgha.
If one goes [to such a meal], it constitutes theft. By this standard, one should know that one must not arbitrarily accept an assignment in the monastic order. Next is the explanation of...
Regarding the offering of food, it is customarily prepared and sent into the monasteries on the three fasting days for the Śramaṇas and the three for the laity;
thus they are called the "Six Fasting Days" (ṣaḍ-upavāsa). It is likely that fourteen characters are missing from the text, as the *Vinaya* of the Bhikṣuṇīs contains a full account as cited below.

Because spirits and deities gain power on these days and consume the vital essence (*ojas*) of humans, they are called "evil days. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these correspond to the days of the Four Heavenly Kings.
5. Regarding the dates for the various festivals: On the first day of the four seasonal festivals, those considered important in that country are likewise observed in this land;

this follows local custom, using the three seasons as a comparison. The first day of the first month is celebrated throughout the empire. As for the remaining two days, they must surely be those favored in the capital of Jingzhao;
although they are used in the southeast, they are not formally cultivated there, serving merely as occasions for banquets. This concludes the fifth explanation regarding the monks.

The "Constant" refers to the eternally abiding; it excludes the six types of invitations and the separate invitations found in the Hinayana teachings, while the Mahayana remains forever closed [to them].
Following the characteristics [of beings], there are many [levels], yet the pure mind is the foundation. Those who are partially defiled are not permitted to calculate [the merit];

thus, the *Buddhapiṭaka* and the *Lokadhāri-sūtra* state that those who do not eliminate the notion of self are not allowed to receive even a single cup of water or a single garment of cloth. Each must recognize their own portion.
The measure is not otherwise; how could it be a false word that one’s body is wrapped in glowing iron sheets and molten copper is poured into one’s mouth?
Among the various aspects mentioned in the *Jiegao*, the abundance of descriptions indicates that they are not exhaustive. Pure speech is universal, yet here three types are shown:

first, being free from seeking through improper means; second, being free from greedy indulgence; and third, being free from nourishing the body for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path—these are the same as the five [previously mentioned].
If even those who are partially liberated are thus subject to defilement, how much more so for those who possess both [defilement and liberation]?

Below, scripture is cited as proof that those who do not seek liberation are unworthy of the offerings of the faithful; each should recognize their own measure and be cautioned to reflect upon themselves.
For if one does not know their own measure yet presumptuously accepts the offerings of others, they will inevitably incur bitter retribution. Thus it is said: "Otherwise... Let students examine this.
This cannot be read over lightly; rather, one should reflect inwardly upon one's own mind: for what purpose do I sit here receiving the offerings of others?
If it is not for the sake of seeking liberation, then this very robe I wear is already an iron cuirass, and this very food in my bowl is already molten copper.

Since the cause and its fruit are as inseparable as a form and its shadow, how perilous it would be—let alone if, lacking wisdom, one commits evil and violates the precepts! How treacherous that indeed would be!

The statement in the *Shùxià kāizhōng* (Opening of the Space Under the Tree) regarding "separate rooms" (*biéfáng*) refers to the practice of requesting the allocation of the two types of rooms—the large and the small.

Alternatively, it may refer to the case where the seven groups of followers establish separate quarters within a monastery for the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* (the Sangha of the four quarters), so that those who come to reside there have distinct offerings provided for them.

Thus, the Vinaya says: "How many rooms are endowed with abundant merit? This refers to these [separate quarters]. "How many rooms lack abundant merit? refers to the general monastic community (*saṃgha*).
Regarding the "permanently inhabited gabled houses": in the Western Regions (India), most buildings are flat-roofed multi-storied structures, sometimes reaching four or five stories in height.

Such gabled forms are rare in the peripheral provinces of the northern borders of this land (China). As listed in the text, these are buildings that are high in the center with four eaves at the sides.
Therefore, the Vinaya states that "the great halls of kings are all opened for use," referring either to small huts with crossed-beam roofs or to those with rafters.

Regarding "the head resting on the ground": this refers to small rooms where rising does not obstruct the head and sitting allows for the knees to be drawn up; they provide a barrier against wind and rain from the front. Regarding "stone chambers":
these are mountain dwellings consisting of rock caves or grottoes with two rooms and one door arranged according to their natural features; this can be verified by actual observation.
The practice of sitting beneath the three trees can be understood through its original formulation; however, the commentary on the opening text divides it into five parts.
First, it explains the distinction between large and small separate rooms (*vibhāṣā*). A "separate room" is a term from the Sanskrit *vibhāṣā*, which here refers to a private chamber.

"Generosity" (*dāna*) means that a donor constructs a room to provide for visiting monks and personally supplies their needs. Those who possess abundant merit are those who receive [these offerings] as members of the Saṃgha.
This is for the purpose of bestowing merit and benefiting those donors; as for those who do not receive such benefit, they remain in their permanent residences and are not provided for elsewhere.
[The second explanation: The eaves of the pointed-roofed house border on regions inhabited by barbarians and others where [such structures] are rare;

it is high in the center with four galleries (xià) on the sides—what is nowadays called a "unicorn pavilion" (dújiǎo tíng). It is cited that the appearance of the King’s Hall in the Vinaya may resemble this, and thus it is called a "King's [Hall]."
Because it was given as a gift to the Saṃgha, its use is permitted; "joining the palms" refers to crossing the ends of the rafters so that they are interlaced at the center.

Third, regarding the small room, the measurements for the horizontal and vertical dimensions are explained according to principle as being very narrow; furthermore, citing the absolute minimum as merely requiring enough space to contain the body is not necessarily the case.
Fourth, the explanation of the right chamber; fifth, the explanation of the two rooms sharing a single door—these are listed according to their physical characteristics and do not stop there.
This is it. Regarding the four types of putrid medicines, these are things discarded by the world but are actually usable; they are namely excrement and urine.

According to another source, "medicines discarded due to being old" refers to the dregs and residue left over from worldly decoctions that are fit for disposal; these should be taken and boiled again.
Once cured, one stops; why is it necessary to inquire about the origin?

Regarding the four types of medicinal decoctions for suppressing [diseases], there are two interpretations. In the first interpretation, cow urine treats *lao* (exhaustion) and human excrement relieves heat;

this is called Huanglong Tang (Yellow Dragon Decoction), which has a purgative effect. In the second interpretation, it refers to a general category of medicines that people do not commonly use; hence the term.
"Discarding and rotting" are merely different names for the same thing; it means that one should simply use them to treat the illness without investigating their origin.
Therefore, why must one inquire into their source?
Regarding the classification of the five medicines, *sarpis* (clarified butter) and honey are divided into two [categories], whereas oil is not so divided; this can be explained as follows.
Regarding the division of clarified butter (*sarpis*), raw honey, and cooked honey, there are bees; however, petroleum (*taila*) is not divided. This can be explained as follows:

although clarified butter is a single substance, its flavors differ when raw or cooked; whereas for oil, even if it is raw or cooked, its substance and flavor do not differ, and thus it cannot be divided.

Third, regarding the summary, the text is divided into two parts: first, from the beginning up to "the coming and going," which clarifies the instruction given while seated to the two disciples during the three periods of the day;
second, from "later" onwards, which clarifies following them on their travels after they have risen.

The threefold exhortation to study consists of: first, the provisional division while seated; second, the instruction after having received [the precepts] but before dispersing; and third, the admonition regarding the rules. Regarding the first, there are two parts:
first, up to the point where it says "you should ask the Upādhyāya and Ācārya to provide you with detailed guidance"; second, the instruction that one should cause [others] to receive [the precepts].
"To go before those who possess [the precepts] is to exercise deep restraint.
This means that during the ritual of sitting and distributing [the precepts], the recipient should be positioned in front while the preceptor follows behind;
fearing that there might be a lapse in decorum, one must establish this precautionary standard in advance.

The preceding section is further divided into six parts: First, from "You have already received the full ordination" down to "the assembly of monks is complete," this records the conditions for receiving the precepts and establishes their sufficiency;
it exhorts you to guard and uphold them, ensuring they do not become deficient, and warns against neglecting the substance of the precepts by committing offenses after having received them.

Second, from "You should properly receive the teachings of the Dharma" downward, this clarifies the karma of samādhi through both self-cultivation and the transformation of others. Third, "Harmonizing the high and the low" clarifies the service of the Dharma and the service of the Sangha.

Regarding the practice of righteousness, it must be in accordance with what is called "in accord with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*), which excludes teachings that are not in accord with the Dharma; thus, practicing without transgression constitutes the fourth [point].

Regarding "one should study," the preceding section clarified self-cultivation and the transformation of others; now that this initial stage of cultivating merit has long been completed, one should cultivate the portion of wisdom.

Therefore, the two wheels of merit and wisdom possess a virtue equal to that of heaven and earth. Fifth, regarding "you who have first resolved your mind," this is an exhortation to uphold what precedes.
The teaching on cause and effect is thus: the ripening of results is inevitable. Sixth, regarding what remains unknown, this reveals that the Dharma depends upon persons;
its essential principles must rely on the transmission of a teacher to be fully realized and perfected.
Next, the explanation of the first section, which provides a general overview, begins with a brief indication of the overall intent, as will be explained later.
Second, "receiving the teaching" refers to the cultivation of merit; one must first practice for oneself and only then transform others.

The activity of samādhi refers to the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), both of which belong to the category of meritorious deeds. Samādhi is also called *samāpatti*, or translated as...

Regarding "for the sake of concentration" (*samādhi*), or alternatively "equal holding" (*samādhāna*): among these three, that which accords with the Dharma refers to what is consistent with the principles of the Law;

that which does not accord with the Dharma is the opposite. Among the four [categories], this text follows the second to clarify its meaning. The metaphors of the two wheels and the two instruments signify that they must be possessed together.

This applies to all five points, as cause and effect are universally so. Generally speaking, all evidence confirms that following the teachings now will certainly not be in vain. As the text says: "Tang."
"Discarding" (*dāna*) means to waste or abandon; "sixfold" refers to the six types of [monks]. If *vāsa* is interpreted as "assistance," it pertains to the two masters;
if interpreted as "taking," it pertains to the disciple.

Within the first section, "you have already received the precepts" generally clarifies the substance of the reception, while "the formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) was performed according to the Dharma" constitutes the conclusion.
Regarding the attainment of the teaching and the securing of its locus: being within the ritual boundary (*karmabhūmi*) is not merely natural.

The "Preceptor who acts according to the Dharma" clarifies the fundamental teacher as the condition for entering the precepts. The "Acarya" refers to the two teachers at the time of receiving [the precepts], and is not what is being asked below.
"The assembly of monks being complete and full" establishes the supporting evidence (*aṅga-sādhana*), ensuring that the reception is not erroneous. All of these are for the purpose of...

The four conditions—the person, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the boundary—are fully present; when life ends, one shall uphold [the precepts] without concern for receiving them in vain. This concludes the summary and entrustment;
may you rely upon and practice this.
In the initial section of the separate explanation, six phrases are cited and explained. The first is the "person who receives," which encompasses both the essence and the supporting conditions.

The matter is in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the second point on the Dharma, the third point on the locations, and the three sections beginning with the Upādhyāya, these all concern the community’s management of receipts and expenditures;
"receipts" (shou) refers to what is received together. This concludes the fourth section on conditions, wherein the person is the very matter itself.
When the time comes, one may adapt according to the occasion; it is sufficient to take these points as the basis for discourse, though it is not necessarily required to recite them verbatim.
In the concluding summary, the first two lines of the verse indicate the increase and decrease [of the teachings], while the latter two lines demonstrate the preceding text.

Regarding the two disciples, they descend three times daily; this explains the method by which master and disciple mutually sustain one another. I have briefly set forth its essential points, while the details are as found in the *Chao* (Excerpts).

As for the subsequent section on "arising and following in practice," it clarifies the two masters; within this, the first subsection briefly sets forth its essential points, specifically indicating the annotations.
The "Excerpts" (鈔) refers to the "Chapter on Teacher and Disciple" (師資篇).

It is divided into two parts: first, the original teacher (本師和尚) clarifies the method of mutual inclusion; second, from "Requesting an Upādhyāya" (請依止) onwards, it reveals that when there are obstacles to the formal circumstances, one must further rely upon another teacher.

Next, regarding the section on circumstances involving obstacles—such as passing away, ceasing one's practice, or departing for distant lands—the reason why the two masters are explained immediately following the reception [of the precepts] is this:
having newly received the Great Dharma, one possesses only the aspirational mind;

yet, when it comes to the myriad practices that encompass all preceding realms, if one’s conditions conflict with the Dharma, the transgression is self-imposed. One cannot claim exemption on the grounds of ignorance.
The fault lies solely in the fact that, with the exception of relieving oneself, all other matters must be reported; therefore, this is clarified here to prevent negligence.

Among the three [sections], the inquiry and explanation are presented to expound the intent of the teaching: first, the nature of the vows received is described; next, the mutual pervasiveness of the conduct is explained.
According to the Vinaya regulations, with the sole exception of minor urination or defecation, everything else must be announced to the teacher.

Second, regarding the request for dependence (*niśraya*), the explanation of the conditions for avoiding transgressions states that one must separately request [a teacher] to serve as a *upādhyāya* (preceptor) to remedy the commission of unrighteous acts;

this is because the original *upādhyāya* has either passed away, ceased the path, or departed with a settled intention to leave the boundary. Regarding the explanation of the conditions for requesting dependence, "avoiding" refers to cases where the teacher has died or ceased the path, while "transgressing" refers to when the teacher has resolved to go beyond the monastic boundary.
Alternatively, it may be that both terms encompass all three conditions.
Thus, the statement that one with five years of *kṣānti* (summer retreats) may leave their *niśraya* upon attaining knowledge refers to the formal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) of the teaching;

whereas the statement in the *Vinaya* that one becomes independent of others once the five divisions are established refers to the essential substance (*svabhāva*) of practice. Each has its own intended meaning, and they are not contradictory.

In the first section of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, there are two passages that at first glance appear contradictory; however, by distinguishing them according to their teaching and practice, one finds they are consistent in their underlying intent and thus not in conflict.
The *Pañcavargika* refers to the five factors—precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—which constitute the body [of the path];
therefore, it is called "varga" (division).

Regarding the statement on "possessing virtue" (*guḍe*), it says: "Knowing what constitutes an offense means that one understands how transgressions are established through their causal conditions; knowing what does not constitute an offense means recognizing one's capacity for governance.

Knowing what is light refers to the lower four categories of offenses; knowing what is heavy refers to the upper two sections. To know them exhaustively by name and type, and to understand their characteristics thoroughly without the slightest confusion, is what is meant."

Regarding the first section on "Distinguishing Virtue" (*jiande*), the four categories—such as offenses and so forth—are all found in the Vinaya texts; because they cannot be understood without study, [the Buddha] established them so that one may thoroughly recognize what constitutes an offense and what does not.
These apply generally across the various chapters and clusters (*pian-zu*), while their lightness or gravity is specifically divided into the upper and lower [categories].
Their names, types, characteristics, and three aspects are distinguished as in the "Chapter on Repentance."

Regarding "ten years of seniority," this refers to one who, by secular reckoning, has reached the age of maturity and established his character and resolve; such a person can exercise judgment according to circumstances and is free from the net of evil.
Selecting the middle age for ordination, one receives the precepts at twenty; being now ten years [in seniority] after that, it constitutes thirty years of age.

Therefore, it is called "mature adulthood" (*zhuangshi*). The *Book of Rites* states: "At thirty, one is mature and has a household. "Established character and resolve" means possessing integrity and the ability to judge and remain detached.
It is an exaggeration to claim that he alone possesses such capability.

There is no one who does not rely on virtue; reliance arises from reverence and respect. Since his conduct and understanding have repeatedly failed to meet the expectations of human sentiment, it is only natural that there is no one toward whom people feel a sense of loyalty or inclination.
Therefore, although he remains solitary and independent, this is not a cause for reproach.

Regarding the initial section on those lacking virtue, the first part describes those who may be relied upon, while the subsequent sections demonstrate those who cannot. If the word "zuò" (作) is read with the rising tone (*shēngdì*), it refers to those whose conduct is contrary to the Dharma;
if it is read with the departing tone (*qùhū*), it refers to those who themselves are not pure and white. Both cases betray the disciples' feelings of reliance.
To claim that being solitary and independent is not a fault is incorrect, for it is permitted not to rely on others only when one is without a teacher.
Second, regarding the section on receiving [ordination] from a *bhikṣuṇī*, the text is divided into two parts, which mark the actual reception.
In the first part, the conditions for the designation and the explanation of the name are as follows in the text: "Mā" is a phonetic transcription of a heavenly (Sanskrit) term;

here it is translated as "mother. It is called "heavy *bhikṣuṇī*" (*guru-bhikṣuṇī*) because Mahāprajāpatī was the foremost among *bhikṣuṇīs* and was the mother of the Buddha; thus, she is preeminently associated with her kindred class and designated as "Mā."
In this world, these refer to figures such as the Emperor’s paternal aunts and maternal uncles.

Regarding the second point, "The Nuns’ Dharma," in the first section of the introductory commentary, the text refers to the Buddha Suśīma (Good Vision) calling upon the practitioner of the Way named Āyuṣmat (Loving Person);

this indicates that he subsequently followed the Dharma and joined its ranks. (The character "māra" [demon] in the note is a scribal error. As for the examples provided below, "huang" (皇) is explained as meaning "grandfather."
Because the maternal kin are held in high esteem, they are so designated.
As for the arrangement of the ritual procedures, those that are inconvenient have been revised based on the discussions arising from the defilements of men and women;
furthermore, because they frequently encounter one another in their respective ranks, the three groups [of nuns] have been placed after the śrāmaṇeras.
The subsequent section concerns the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, which states that regarding the arrangement by rank: this refers to the sequence of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If men and women were placed alternately, they would appear like pairs, thereby inviting the censure of the world; hence it says, "consequently, their forms frequently meet.
Here, "frequently" (*lǚ*) means "nearby," and "their forms meet" (*jiē xíng*) refers to the intermingling of men and women.

Those who cite the *Āryā-Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* argue that because women are by nature weak in character and their intellects are limited, if they were not restrained, they would follow their inclinations and drift into dissipation;

thus, the inception of the Eight Respectful Rules was the very condition for them to receive the precepts. According to the Dharma, the method of respect has remained consistent for a thousand years, demonstrating a profound understanding of human capacity.

Among the three [sections], the first describes the inferiority of the retribution; the second reveals that one must rely on [the precepts] because of drifting and wandering—that is, being unrestrained and negligent;

and the third below demonstrates the benefits. Regarding the "Eightfold Respect" (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*): first, Ānanda initially requested it for the sake of Mahāprajāpatī, and thereby the Dharma of the Precepts was established.

A thousand years later, the *Samantapāsādikā* states: "If women are ordained, the True Dharma will be reduced by half. The Buddha commanded that the Eightfold Respect be transmitted; if this can be maintained, [the Dharma will endure].
Receiving and practicing [the precepts] again for a thousand years, those who deeply understand the underlying principle (ji) praise the Buddha’s skillful means (upāya-kauśalya).
Within the subsequent section on receiving [the precepts], they are divided into three groups according to the assembly.
In the explanation of the heading regarding receiving, the phrase "according to the assembly" refers to the three assemblies of nuns.
The initial procedure for conferring the precepts upon the lower assembly is the same as that previously set forth and is not repeated here.

In the first section of the detailed commentary, the method for *śrāmaṇerī* (female novices) receiving the precepts within the lower assembly is identical to that in the *bhikṣuṇī* (nun) community; therefore, it is omitted here for brevity.
Second, regarding the six dharmas: first, *śikṣā* means "training" (*śikṣā*), and *maṇā* means "female" (*mānā*). This indicates the category of the dharmas, which is divided into two.
Within the designation of the six dharmas, the Sanskrit term is *śikṣamāṇā*, which is translated here as "female trainee in the dharmas."

Within the section on the conditions for ordination (*pratyaya*), both characteristics are fully enumerated. First, regarding those with pure minds: because women’s wills are weak and they are often ignorant, they frequently commit transgressions in accordance with circumstances;
moreover, due to their shallow learning, the Noble One specifically established increased stages of training to encourage them in study. Men are not like this;

they are generally capable of enduring difficult conditions, and even when faced with obstacles and hindrances, they do not immediately succumb to ruin. Therefore, within the ranks of the Sangha, no such restrictive regulations were imposed upon them.

Second, regarding the purification of the body: because she had previously been betrothed and spoke of returning to serve her husband, yet later followed the path [of ordination], became pregnant while observing the precepts, and gave birth;
due to these circumstances of pregnancy and the resulting reproach, a two-year period is established. Thus, one should know that defilement and purity are determined by the origin [of the pregnancy].

It should be understood that the study of the Dharma is for the purpose of purifying the mind; the "lifelong" (yixin) mentioned in the original text refers to this. Regarding the regulation of the period [of training], it is for the purpose of purifying the fetus. This is the fundamental principle.
The mention of "two years" refers to this very point; the two ways in which the ultimate goal is established each have its own source.

Regarding the explanation of the three points within the heading: first, the heading itself; second, the subsequent [explanation]; and third, the detailed interpretation. First, regarding the explanation of the pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*):

previously it was stated that there is an increase in the status of the *bhikṣuṇī*, meaning she is separately established as a distinct community (*saṃgha*) and exhorted to train by being further burdened with six rules. Next, the male [monk] is explained below. Following this, the second point is clarified.

The nun has no [return] to the *saṃgha*; she may be seen as two distinct [categories]. The "purification of the body" (*śuddha-kāya*) is immediately explained as "going to take refuge," which is like a woman being married.

Regarding "following the path after death," this refers to those who leave the household life (*pravrajyā*) upon the death of their husband. "Giving birth" (*janman*) means producing a child. "Carrying" (*avaṣṭabdha*) means holding or embracing [the child]. These three subsequent knots clarify the first knot;

the "purification of the mind" (*citta-śuddhi*) introduces the subsequent explanation of its characteristics, which are universally applicable throughout one's entire life. This constitutes the proof.
Knowing that the training is discussed according to the subsequent [rules], the next section concludes the purification of the body and introduces the method for concluding the subsequent rules;
since these are restricted to two years, it is evident that they each have their origins, namely the two preceding texts.
Regarding the analysis of the dharma, there are three parts.

To explain the general classification of the dharma, there are three: first, the conditions (*pratyaya*); second, the dharma itself; and third, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). In the following text, only the conditions and the characteristics are explained.

In the first section concerning the conditions for begging [for ordination], ten types of women are listed: those who have previously returned [to lay life]—meaning those who were married—and eighteen-year-old virgins.
"Regarding 'one who resides in the chamber but has not yet returned': there are these two conditions. For two years, she has been a fellow student.

Within the first section of the preliminary conditions, the first point demonstrates that the conditions differ: 'residing in the chamber' means a maiden who has not yet returned, that is, one who is unmarried.

Next, it clarifies that the training is the same. (Note: The character "jiā" [marry] in the commentary should be "guī" [return]; this can be verified by the text cited in the sub-commentary, as the current version is a scribal error.)
These female practitioners of the Dharma possess no formal precept-body (*śīla-avasthā*); they merely receive the status of the separate teaching (*pṛthag-dharma*) that exceeds that of a śrāmaṇera.
As explained above, I state this again for fear of forgetfulness. People do not understand that while there is a division into three assemblies, there are not three distinct precept-bodies;

in reality, they are identical, differing only in that [the latter] increases the training. How is this made clear? By relying on the practice of the six dharmas, one may listen to and receive them without transgression, as they are divided according to their respective categories.

If one commits an offense by again following the rules for beginners or rules not for beginners, or if one's training is incomplete, deficient, or not practiced, these are all termed "unlawful" (*adharma*) and are censured by the Buddha;
in principle, they must not be accepted.
In the first section of the following division, the substance [of the precepts] is determined through its meaning to be the same as that of a śrāmaṇera, with no distinct precept-substance;

this refers to the explanation found at the beginning of the second fascicle. Below that, it refutes the view that they are actually identical, stating that while the substance is one, there is a difference in that the six dharmas are added, which constitutes the meaning of "receiving" by examining conduct as a preparatory means (*upāya*). It is not [the case that the six dharmas are the essence].
Regarding the initial exposition of the essence of undertaking [the precepts]: some are "in accordance with the Dharma," while others are not explained as being "not in accordance with the Dharma.

As for those who are "not learners" (aśaikṣa), this refers to those who have not received the training at all or whose training is incomplete. Although these individuals may have previously received the precepts, their term has not been fulfilled; they are deficient and do not practice them.

Furthermore, there are those who, having already received them, have committed an offense and no longer act from the beginning. This is as described in the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, where the prohibitions were established because of specific transgressions that occurred, rather than being decreed by the Buddha as a general rule.
This refers to what the Buddha rebuked.
Nowadays, those who perform the rites mostly rely on their own subjective opinions and do not follow the established regulations;

consequently, some grant the training rules (*śikṣamāṇā*) at the end of the year and confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) at the beginning of the year, or they fail to observe many precepts during the two years of training and ought to be re-ordained, yet this is neglected and not carried out. Or...
Whether few or many, they are disordered and difficult to explain.

Third, regarding the clarification of ritual procedures and the refutation of worldly views: the first section of the initial text provides a general refutation; below, specific items are listed. At the end of the year, one receives instruction;

at the beginning of the morning, one proceeds to full ordination (*upasampadā*). Thus, these two days are treated as equivalent to two years. One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): [one who has been ordained for] one year, etc.

1. Deficient in conduct but complete in years (as in the first two days above, combined with the following: having few or no transgressions). 2. Deficient in conduct but complete in years (as in the second year above, where there were intermediate transgressions, combined with the following:

having many, meaning exceeding two years). 3. Deficient in both conduct and years (the first three phrases are all contrary to the Dharma). 4. Complete in both conduct and years (only this phrase qualifies for ordination).
To suddenly fail to practice is to show contempt for the teachings.

There is also one master who maintains that the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations) accomplishes everything in its entirety—namely, the six rules for śrāmaṇerikās, the fundamental rules, and the full ordination (*mahā-śīla*).
They collectively refer to these as the "wooden pestle precepts" (*mùpò jiè*), though it is unknown from whence this term originates; what further discussion could there be of it?

Next, regarding the "four dharmas within the *koṇi* (corner/section)": because one receives [the precepts] through a single motion (*jñapti*) followed by a formal act (*karma*) consisting of four parts, it is said that they are "entirely" [received].

This is a colloquial expression equivalent to saying "all at once. The character for *mùn* (木*圂*) is pronounced *hùn*. (When wood has not yet been split, it is called *mùn*, referring to a rounded log. The character for *pǔ* (樸) is pronounced *pǔ*.

(When wood is in its natural state, it is called *pǔ*, meaning the material before a craftsman has fashioned it into a vessel. This means that one receives the precepts through a single dharma; being like a whole log or raw material, there is no need to further divide them into gradual stages.
This is overly prolix. The preceding sentence refutes [the opponent] by showing they have no basis for their claims; the following sentence clarifies that there is nothing therein worth adopting.

Now, in establishing the True Dharma, one should follow the scriptural texts and strive to adopt what is superior and excellent; thus, even across a hundred generations, there will be no antiquity that cannot be followed.
This reveals the first section of the present middle [treatise]: first, it must accord with the teachings; second, its principles must be extensive and superior—that is, excellent;
third, it may be transmitted through a hundred generations, remaining ever new despite the passage of time. This is truly because there is a basis for examination, leading to inexhaustibility.

Among the six classes of women, if one has not received the precepts at all, or if she has received them incompletely, or if she is under age—these cases are treated identically to those who have not received them;

they are ineligible for the advancement to full ordination (*upasampadā*). Since the rank of *śrāmaṇerī* (novice nun) is missing, how could there be a *śrāmaṇera* who proceeds directly to receive full ordination from nuns?

Next, in the section on distinguishing what is not the correct explanation, first are listed those who do not receive [the precepts] due to deficiencies; this refers specifically to deficiencies in practice.

The passage beginning with "All those below" provides a general judgment that there is no principle for a *śrāmaṇerī* to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*); therefore, it is judged by analogy that such cases are invalid.

If that were so, the response regarding why a śrāmaṇera does not receive the full ordination would differ [from the case of a woman]. First, there is no scriptural authority permitting a woman to receive the full precepts after having already received them.
Second, because a man’s vital energy is firm and upright, he possesses the capacity for upholding [the precepts].

Third, because a woman is weak and cannot uphold the precepts, a distinct stage [of the śrāmaṇerī] was established as the foundation for practice; if she lacks this foundational practice now, how could she receive [full ordination] later? Fourth, men do not...

One may attempt [this practice] because it pertains to the physical body and womb; thus, it is not restricted by time or month. For women, the case is the reverse of the former, and therefore they must study it fully.

Regarding the resolution of the objection: why is it that a *śrāmaṇera* who does not receive the ten precepts yet directly attains full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) incurs only a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), whereas this is not the case for a *śikṣamāṇā*?
In the response, first there is a general synthesis, followed by a detailed demonstration in four parts. First:

First, this implicitly reveals that for śrāmaṇeras there is scriptural authority permitting [the immediate reception of full ordination], whereas for the two [groups of nuns] there is none. Second, it reveals that if the male stage is permitted, it is beneficial;

third, it clarifies that while the śrāmaṇera stage lacks the fifty [precepts] which serve as the basis for practice when one possesses full ordination, this is not the case for nuns, and thus this stage is added for them.
Fourth, it is easily seen that by analogy one knows the immediate reception is permitted only within the *saṃgha* of monks, and is not permitted for the assembly of nuns.
Question: Is it possible to receive the six dharmas directly without first receiving the fifty [precepts]? Answer: No.
Since the *śikṣamāṇā* takes the ten precepts as its essence, if one were to receive them directly, there would be no basis for support; therefore, it is not permissible.

Now, regarding the principle that the two girls—one ten years old and the other eighteen—receive instruction and then receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon reaching the required age, this must be inferred as follows:
if the eighteen-year-old becomes a *śikṣamāṇā* at the beginning of the year, she receives [full ordination] the following year when she is nineteen, and the year after that when she is twenty;

thus, having completed exactly two full cycles, she certainly attains the precepts. This applies equally whether it is from the second day of the first month up until the final day of the twelfth month. All such cases are valid.

Receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) may take place alone on the first day of the first month; this does not preclude the youngest *śikṣamāṇā* from receiving the training rules on the last day of the twelfth month.
This constitutes one day of receiving the dharma within the eighteen years [of training] as a *śrāmaṇerī*.

When the next day arrives at the beginning of the year, she becomes nineteen years old. After completing one cycle of training, when she reaches twenty years of age, she is granted the Great Ordination.

The judgment regarding the precepts states that one has attained [the fruit] without contradicting the scriptural evidence concerning the purity of the fetal body; how could this possibly be mentioned as being the same as the previous reduction?
Now, in the present exposition, first there is a general indication, followed by specific illustrations. First, it is stated: "When both the year and month are complete," and so forth.

Next, regarding those for whom the months are full but the days are not yet complete—the minimum duration being one year minus one day—since the final day of the twelfth month constitutes a full year, those who do not violate the teaching may have their years fulfilled because the count of years has been reached.

Thus, one may verify the state of the body and the womb based on the passage of time; how could this differ from the ancients? Even if it is reduced as previously refuted, although it is now reduced...
"To speak of them as being entirely different from the ancients means that their words differ from those [ancient ones].

As for those who do not practice [the rules], when it comes time to receive [the precepts], they are questioned by the monks whether they are complete; yet the nuns feel no shame and proclaim themselves pure and clean.

They deceive themselves and lack understanding—what is the use of receiving [the precepts] in such a way? Moreover, having personally attended upon the Buddha, how could one's own speech be so full of falsehood? Why are you in such a hurry?"
I fear you may lose the state of a noble one (*ārya*); yet that noble fruit is not obtained through empty words—be warned!

Among the three [sections], the first describes errors; within the section on the *saṃgha*, it is stated that for formal reception (*prātimokṣa*), one must first inquire of a nun regarding the six rules.

"Full" refers to the completion of years, and "pure" refers to the completion of conduct. Below this, there is a direct refutation: first, the refutation of deception, which means not understanding for oneself.

To understand this clearly, let us next censure those who deceive the Buddha. Below, we further censure those who act with such haste that they seek to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) without practicing the six preparatory rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*);
because such lying obstructs the Path, it is judged that they have not attained the state of an Arya. Now, all are like this:

to receive the fifty-six rules all at once and thereby claim to have received full ordination is utterly devoid of principle; there is no possibility of attaining the precepts, which is precisely what is meant by "the land of the Middle Kingdom."

Now, regarding the five formal procedures for requesting the Dharma: first, placing both knees upon the ground is what constitutes *jang-kwi* (long kneeling); this means that the toes and the kneecaps rest upon the ground.

According to the Vinaya, because [the Buddha’s] body was weak and flexible, he would sometimes kneel crosswise and fall to the ground; thus, the Buddha prescribed the standing posture as distinct from the practice of the *saṃgha*.
Even in the present day, squatting on the ground is superior to sitting cross-legged before the Buddha.

Regarding the first section of the "Requesting the Dharma" (qífǎ), the initial part provides a general overview of the five modes of deportment, while the subsequent two parts provide specific explanations.

In the case of *chángguì* (long-kneeling), it further cites the original source material to clarify its difference from the monastic community; *tǔ* (pronounced *tuǒ*) refers to lying with the thighs upon the ground. This, however, is not based on the formal protocol for kneeling.
Furthermore, regarding the *śeṣaka* (formal sitting):
prior to the formal practice, one must first request the *upādhyāya*, because within the procedure for requesting the Dharma, both [the request and the formal act] are performed simultaneously.

Since the subsequent section of the text does not mention requesting the *upādhyāya* but instead records the request within the formal act itself, it is required that one first requests [the preceptor] in accordance with the monastic regulations.
Regarding the phrasing:
when the text lists "Elder Sister" (Dajishi) for the bhikṣuṇīs to listen, this is used in contrast to other monks; it is certainly not a loss to follow the convention of addressing them as "Sister.
As for the titles "Brother" (Xiong) and "Sister" (Jie), these are all ancient and elegant designations; the true meaning is found within these very characters.
Among the three [phrases], the first clarifies the distinction from the "monks" (bhikṣu) who necessarily follow; the next indicates that the meaning applies universally, as it returns to the Sangha.
This refers to addressing the Venerable Ones (bhadanta) with the intent of expressing praise; saying "Venerable Sisters" (bhagini) now deeply accords with the original intention.

Regarding the phrase "established at the place where one’s view is manifest" in the text, there is concern that this might constitute *caura-vāsa* (staying like a thief). Following the aforementioned method for receiving full ordination, it is also permissible to pray while kneeling upright with palms joined and facing toward [the preceptor].
Of the four parts, the first indicates the intent of the regulation; the latter part follows the ritual procedure for making such a request.

Regarding those summoned from among the assembly to be identified by name and appearance: although they may have received the Dharma from afar, they do not know which specific precepts they have violated;
therefore, their characteristics are listed and made manifest so that their offenses may be adjudicated according to the Vinaya.

In the first section of the exposition on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because this applies even at a distance, it is necessary to demonstrate the characteristics; however, since it does not involve a violation of the regulations, the Vinaya does not establish an offense (*āpatti*).

This section on characteristics is divided into three parts: first, the heading that provides a general indication; second, the prohibition against committing impure conduct (*abrahmacarya*), which demonstrates the gravity or lightness [of the offense]; [and third, the specific enumeration].
Regarding the third point, the Buddha’s words distinguish between the specific stages and the general application of practice, whether they exist or not.
In the first section, the person is shown to be honored and the Dharma to be supreme; how could one fail to revere them?
In the subsequent section, the three titles of the Buddha are presented as a general indication, intending to demonstrate the honor of the person in order to manifest the supremacy of the Dharma.
Within the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*), there is no distinction between the general and the specific.
Within the first characteristic, two parts are distinguished: the prohibition against committing impure acts up to the case of the Śākya maiden explains the essential body of the precept;
the citation of the original [case] to provide a further exhortation is not the essential body of the training itself.

Next, to clarify the initial signs of lightness and heaviness: the explanation of the precepts correctly elucidates that the four offenses—sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth—are the fundamental ten precepts;
thus they are called the "primary substance. Because these were already established previously, they are termed "repeated exhortations" regarding what is heavy.
Question: When a śikṣamāṇā who is training in the precepts is told to "reiterate what was said before," does this mean she does not understand? Answer: It does not mean she does not understand;

rather, it is a means of admonishing her to intensify her training. It is like when a teacher instructs a student morning and evening, reiterating what was previously said—where else would there be a separate method for this?

In the question, the intention of restating the characteristics after they have already been set forth is revealed. In the answer, because the ten precepts have already been explained, it says "previously mentioned";
because they are now recounted once more, it says "restated. "Exhorting to increase learning" means citing the previous fundamental rules to encourage subsequent methods of study.
The following citation of the teacher’s instruction serves as an example of this general principle of restatement; "exhorting" (*xù*) is also synonymous with "admonishing" (*jiè*).

Second, if one touches a defiled male, this is precisely what the school of training (śikṣāpada) regards as a transgression; the mind must be pure and clearly aware, for since it must necessarily be performed, a deficiency would entail receiving the precepts again from the beginning.
Thus, how could it be that the finality of the physical form is not so?
Next, regarding the correct study of the Dharma, the "correct school" refers to the right precepts currently received;
"purity" means upholding them without transgression, and "clarity" means a thorough understanding of the characteristics of the teachings.

...up to the precept against intentionally speaking falsehoods among the assembly; this concludes the section on the specific characteristics of the training rules for the devas. Fifth, regarding eating at improper times;
sixth, regarding drinking alcohol: these have no counterparts [in the higher realms] and are therefore presented as fundamental trainings to be practiced throughout one's entire life.

Regarding the explanation of the remaining characteristics, the first example applies to the subsequent three groups. This is because within the latter three groups, the heavy precepts are first cited and the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) are subsequently explained;

thus, it is said that the characteristics of the training in the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*) are discussed separately. As for the division of the heavens, this refers to the fact that the high and low of heaven and earth are easily perceived.
Next, the latter two [groups] are explained individually; since they contain only the rules of training, there is nothing with which to pair them.
Third, regarding the analysis of conditions:
because the precepts to be studied by a *mahāśramaṇī* increase the original number of stages, the characteristics of their training are likewise the same.
Third, within the section on the commonality of practice and dharma, the initial text states that "increasing the original number of stages" means surpassing the *śrāmaṇerikā*.
If that is so, then since a *śrāmaṇera* also has access to the ten thousand objects of the sensory realm, he too should be called a "scholar" (*śaikṣa*).

Answer: Learning is gradual or sudden, and the regulations are lax or strict. A "scholar" is defined by his ability to guard against objects; thus, even if he commits an offense, it does not constitute a grave transgression. Furthermore, a female practitioner is easily corrupted by external conditions, and her status is elevated as she advances through stages.

When a *śrāmaṇera* commits an offense, he simply restores what was lacking. However, the Great Monks (the ordained *bhikṣu*) possess high conduct and profound virtue; therefore, their discipline is more rigorous.

Because there are many things to be guarded against, while the other four [precepts] are progressively more remote, it is appropriate that their status be lowered accordingly; thus they can be understood through mutual illumination. Question:
Since the *śikṣamāṇā* is the same as a *bhikṣuṇī*, she receives the name "learner" (*śikṣamāṇā*); should the *śrāmaṇera* not likewise follow the example of the *bhikṣu*? Answer:

The first two lines of the verse provide a general indication for all practitioners, while the subsequent lines answer specifically. First, it clarifies the reason why a *śrāmaṇera* is not so named: because...

If viewed in light of the full precepts (*mahāśīla*), it is considered gradual; if viewed in light of not advancing to a higher status, it is considered sudden. Thus, one studies the sudden while the regulations are gradual.
According to other texts, this is also called "elementary training" (*kṣudra-śikṣā*), but as it is not the primary designation, it is omitted and not explicitly mentioned.

Next, regarding the female [novice], the meaning of the name *śikṣamāṇā* is clarified: she studies the gradual while the regulations are urgent. This is further illustrated by citing the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*).
The extent of what is prohibited serves to reveal the differences in status and the distinct names of the two ranks of śrāmaṇera and śikṣamāṇā.
