Regarding the exception for taking food with one's own hand or giving food to others, some interpret this as referring to two specific conditions; however, that is not the case here.

All other practices are identical to those of the bhikṣuṇīs, except that the śikṣamāṇā is permitted to receive food directly from a person without it being formally offered, whereas the bhikṣuṇī must receive it from another person before she may give it away.

The nuns have this distinction alone; however, if one considers that they do not experience unpleasant touch, how could it be that they lack the precepts? As for the offenses of the four lower assemblies, their listing is not in vain;
the principle follows from the person, and only then can one proceed further.
Next, regarding the explanation of the differences, first, the ancient interpretation is presented as having two conditions.

That [interpretation] maintains that "except for taking with one's own hand" means that one is permitted to eat even without having received it oneself; and "giving food to another" means that one is permitted to act as a donor for the sake of another.
Now, next, the present interpretation is shown. First, it explains the general meaning of the text by way of a single condition: the case of a nun who has not received [the food] herself.
Once the Great Nis (bhikṣuṇīs) have received [the precepts], they may bestow them; this follows the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*, which also permits it only when no one else is present.

As for the subsequent point regarding the refutation of ancient erroneous views, one can verify from the section on the precept against receiving food that the four assemblies are subject to the same regulation, and thus there is no reason to arbitrarily grasp [the bowl].
Regarding these two methods of training for women, the three dharmas they must fully master are listed below; their three aspects are extremely clear.

However, because those who recite this now generally do not recognize the training in the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*), I have divided them [into separate sections] so that there may be no further confusion.

Regarding the first section of the three dharmas: first, the text explicitly points to the passage; next, it demonstrates the intent of the division, stating that "for those who do not understand, the words are easy to see.

However, according to the tradition of the ancient masters regarding the reception of the six dharmas, they added the five-strip robe (*pañcaka-cīvara*) to correspond to the lower assembly’s wearing of the plain robe (*sāṃghāṭī*).

Therefore, in the initial section concerning the differentiation of attire, since their status now exceeds that of the minor assembly, their clothing ought to be distinct; although this is an ancient tradition,
it is acceptable from the standpoint of principle.
Regarding the conduct of people in recent times, it is customary for śrāmaṇeras to wear the five-strip robe; yet when it comes to the six rules of training, they revert to their original attire.

This is the collapse of the Vinaya and the ruin of the Dharma, a gradual process of corruption and decline. Both teachers and masters practice flattery and sycophancy, secretly luring in śrāmaṇeras without realizing they are extinguishing the Dharma.
According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, a śrāmaṇera has two robes: one is the *antarvāsaka* (inner garment), which serves as a substitute for the [upper robe].
The *saṃkakṣikā* is for constant use; the *uttarāsaṅga* is intended for entering the assembly. If these were formal garments, one should not say they are "intended for" [specific occasions].

Therefore, their status is distinguished as superior or inferior by means of the differences in their clothing. Since the Vinaya does not provide explicit determinations, there is this gradual development.

In the first section of the initial division of "Rebuking Excess" (*Chilang zhong*), the first part describes the errors of novices (*śrāmaṇera*): wearing five strips [of cloth] is an usurpation of the superior style;

being identical in dress to the fundamental [monastic] robes is a degradation to the inferior. This section below directly rebukes those who flatter and attach themselves—meaning those who serve their own private interests—and secretly entice others—meaning those who tolerate such usurpation and excess.
Below, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-mātṛkā* is cited to prove that this is not the Dharma. The character "dai" (代) should be pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*).

Therefore, the following section concludes by examining the transmission of the Vinaya and investigating the reasons for its corruption; thus, there is this gradual degeneration, which refers to the process of such corruption.

Furthermore, there was one master who maintained that the robes worn by a śrāmaṇera were entirely identical to those of one with full ordination, asserting that the original purpose of the three robes was merely to ward off the cold.
Since the Great Sangha receives [provisions], it is permissible to exclude those of lower standing; therefore, three [meals] are provided equally.

Regarding the initial section of the classification: it describes the fault that the Great and Small [Sanghas] do not wear the same robes; the original regulation was for the purpose of warding off cold, and thus there was no principle for excluding those of lower standing.

Now, this interpretation is incorrect. The *Pratimokṣa* regulations for the Saṃgha apply to those of lower status; that which is not regulated must be understood as being permitted according to the times.

If one who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*) already possesses the three robes, it is improper to further display the three names [of the Saṃgha] when receiving the great precepts. The bowl is likewise:

its substance is intended for the service and offerings of those of lower rank, and since the monastic utensils are sufficient for personal use, even if one possesses them physically, they serve as a support.
The Dharma has not yet reached its ultimate fulfillment; logically, one must receive the robes and alms bowl at the time of major ordination, as required by the texts.
As for the ten precepts of renunciation, they are not part of the formal regulations and thus are not discussed here; these refer specifically to the three robes and the alms bowl.

Next, regarding the explanation herein, the first section narrates the origin of the rules for the Saṃgha; specifically, the *Cīvara-khandhaka* establishes regulations for bhikṣus concerning seasonal requirements—namely, the alternating use of single or double-layered robes according to the cold or heat.
Following this, the next section clarifies that small groups are not permitted [to perform such formalities].

First, the argument is refuted through reasoning: by means of the interrogation regarding full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is first demonstrated that one must necessarily receive and accept the robe and bowl (*cīvara-pātra*). How could this be otherwise?
The subsequent demonstration serves to verify that there was no bowl previously; this principle applies by analogy. One may rely upon and hold [the bowl], yet it must not be used immediately.

It should be employed as a substitute for monastic utensils. Although the subsequent demonstration appears to deviate from the formal principles, the subsequent demonstration actually represents the correct ritual procedure.

At the time of the "Great Acceptance" (*mahā-upasampadā*), one must state that the full precepts (*upasampadā*) are being received, for it is only then that the requirement for possessing the full set of requisites is established. As for the items listed in the text, these refer to the mention of the robe and bowl within the *karmavācanā* (formal motion).
Therefore, at the bottom [of the text], ten counter-examples are taken to clarify that the items not inquired about are not necessarily all required;
specifically, the "three robes and bowl" are explained as the matters not inquired about regarding the ten precepts.
Third, the method for conferring the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is divided into two parts according to the text.

In the initial section on the formal conditions (*pratyaya*), the characteristics of various types of *kṣānti* (reception/approval) are listed; briefly, there are four kinds, and in detail, seven or eight:

[1] *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), [2] *jñaptidvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), [3] *jñapti-karman* (the formal act consisting of a single motion), and [4] *anujñā-karman* (the formal act of obtaining consent). The first three have already been explained above. The latter one is further divided into four types, as clearly indicated above.
It should be understood that this *karman* is what has been practiced in later generations, and its underlying legal principles (*dharmapratyaya*) must be known.

In the first section of the "Conditions Marking the Three Great Nīs," the four [types of ordination] are abbreviated because the first three are restricted to a single *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), while the seventh is expanded;
the latter four all refer back to the former, which constitutes the general meaning.
Although the term "abbreviated" (*lue*) above specifically refers to the abbreviated form, the phrase "initiating the *karmavācanā*" mentioned below encompasses all four types of ordination.
Regarding the method for sending a messenger to receive [a nun]: it was permitted for Dharmapālā because her practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) was difficult;
however, it is closed off now because the circumstances are not comparable.

In the initial part of the instruction on sending a messenger, the original causal context is shown: "Dharmapālā" is the name of the nun, and "worth half the kingdom" indicates that she possessed such value.
Her beauty is now surpassed; henceforth she shall not be permitted to attend [the assembly]. As for those of a different class who possess physical charms, they certainly cannot equal her.

Those who have returned [to the path] at the age of ten, having been provided with service according to the scriptures, and who are capable of upholding the precepts and furthering their studies, shall at twelve advance to receive the Great [Precepts].
Regarding these precepts, there are mutual discrepancies in their explanations.

In the initial passage of the *Zhonggui* (The Return to the Middle), the original intent of the opening is presented; it appears that the capacity for such mutual discrepancies in explanation is precisely as cited below.
As the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states regarding those who obtain the precepts at age twelve:

"Because they endure the hardships of being employed by their husbands and develop a distaste for their original domestic affairs, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says that since those previously married can endure suffering and possess sufficient wisdom, it is permitted for them to receive the precepts."

Next, the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, and others all rely on the twelve-year rule, taking those who are capable as qualified; this is the same as the present *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
"Wise" refers to one who has already become weary of the world.
According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, for a girl married at ten years of age, after she has been ordained, she studies the śrāmaṇerikā precepts for two years, and then another two [years].
After the years have passed and the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts have been fully completed, one may receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*); calculating this age, it is fourteen years.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* adds two more years; thus, there are differences in the reckonings of the various schools.
I recall having seen a treatise stating that for a woman who has been married and returned home at the age of ten, once she has completed twelve years and mastered the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*),
she may receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). I also remember seeing a text— though I have recently forgotten which school it belonged to—
in which a master from the country of Miśākṣa (Mahīśāsaka) came from China and said that one should grant full ordination at the age of twenty-two.

In the introductory section of the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, the account of what was heard regarding marriage and returning home appears redundant; I suspect it is a scribal error, as I once saw it but later forgot to show it to others.
Thus, the subsequent passage cites "taking another person" as evidence.

According to the intent of the Mūlasarvāstivāda—one of the five divisions of the Sarvāstivāda school—the meaning is that because one has previously married and been defiled by worldly conditions, twelve years must be added to the period of training in the Dharma.
This may well be so.

Since such differences exist, one must examine the matter with great care; however, according to many texts, at the age of twelve, one should wait until the time has arrived to observe whether one is capable of upholding the precepts.
Among the three [sections], the first concludes the preceding [topic] and below indicates that which is to be grasped;
down to the end, it exhorts one to observe the capacities of the practitioners. Thirty-eight young girls proceed as usual;
eighteen young girls are as clarified in the text.
Regarding the principle of establishing five groups each for monks and nuns in the four directions, historical records prior to the Song dynasty do not mention it;
subsequently, when Yang Jian returned [to the capital], he followed the Chinese system as previously explained.
According to the established tradition, after Buddhism was introduced during the Later Han dynasty, it was during the Cao Wei period that the formal ordination of monks and nuns was instituted;

however, for nuns, the dual assembly (*ubhayasaṃgha*) required for full ordination was received only from one of the two assemblies. In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Saṃghavarman arrived at the capital of Yangdu and requested the assembly of Western nuns to establish the dual assembly for ordination.
Thus, it is said that the practice of relying once again on the Chinese system began from this point; from this, we may know [the historical development].
Prior historical records do not mention the term *ratha* (palanquin); it refers to the capital of the Son of Heaven, as indicated previously in the General Meaning (*Sūtrārtha*).

Within the section on formal reception (*samyak-pratigraha*), this is further divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the fundamental method (*mūla-dharma*); second, the method of receiving [ordination] from the Saṃgha.
Within the section on the formal reception (*samyaksamādāna*), because Śreṇika first received it, it is called the "Fundamental Dharma";
subsequently, the expedient means for the formal reception within the Saṃgha were also established as gradual stages due to the weakness of their karmic retribution.

Regarding the first type of *bhikṣuṇī*, the prior conditions are no different from those for a *bhikṣu*. The subsequent addition of the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) is largely the same as in the *bhikṣu* community;
the differences will be explained again below, while the rest can be understood by extension.

Within the text of the fundamental rule (*mūla-dharma*), the initial section on prior conditions refers to the eight factors beginning with the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). The subsequent addition refers to the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
Regarding the reception of the precepts, the two cases are not identical; their differences must be explained in detail.

In the previous section on maintaining a following, the fact that a nun acts as a preceptor and is required to have two years more seniority than a monk reveals that her resolve is weak and she has accumulated merit over many years.
Women possess many dispositions and delight in maintaining a retinue, which is still a remnant of their original habits; according to the Vinaya, they act as superiors in maintaining disciples.

The Master established more than twenty precepts for ordination; because those who ordained others year after year were unable to instruct them and thus committed many transgressions, he accordingly established the rules for maintaining a following and commanded the community of nuns to measure their capacity before ordaining.
In the first section of the commentary on the text, "addition" (*āgama*) is explained as being different from [the addition] for the *saṃgha*; "cumulative" (*anubandha*) means still many.
Regarding women, next, the regulations for requesting [ordination] are clarified; however, since their practice remains contrary [to the rules], the Vinaya text is cited to manifest respect.

This refers to the preceding and following passages within the *Pratideśanīya* (Singular Offenses) chapter of the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa*. Now, the names are briefly listed: first, a pregnant woman; second... [text fragment].
1. Ordaining a woman who has recently given birth; 2. Ordaining a girl under twenty years of age three times; 3. Ordaining forty-eight girls; 4.

Granting full ordination (*upasampadā*) immediately after granting the two-year training in the Dharma; 5. Granting full ordination without first granting the training rules (*śikṣamāṇā-śīla*); 6. Granting full ordination when the six years of training have not been completed; 7.

Granting full ordination to a young girl who was previously married and is under twelve years of age; 8. Granting full ordination to a young girl who has completed her training without informing the assembly.
1. Granting the full ordination (*upasampadā*) while knowing that the candidate has not been formally proposed (*ajñapti*). 2. Granting the full ordination to more than ten disciples at one time. 3.

Not instructing disciples for two years in the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), nor employing the two methods of guidance to receive them. (That is, ordaining people year after year. 4. Ordaining someone who is not yet two years old as a follower of a preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
5. Bestowing the precepts upon another without the consent of the *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha. 6. Being less than twelve years of age oneself.

14. Having been a preceptor for fourteen years, one does not personally confer the full ordination upon others without the consent of the twelve-member assembly (that is, one does not request to maintain a retinue).
15. A nun who has been ordained for fifteen years does not confer ordination without the consent [of the assembly], yet she slanders the Sangha as being partial and so forth.

16. One who grants ordination despite the disapproval of parents or a husband. 17. One who ordains a woman who is afflicted by grief or anger. 18. One who encourages a śikṣamāṇā to abandon her training.
19. Studying the *dharmas* while receiving the precepts; 20. Seeking robes from a *śikṣamāṇā* while receiving the precepts; 21.
Bestowing the precepts upon another when less than one year has passed since one’s own ordination; 22.
Bestowing the precepts within one's own *saṃgha* only after having stayed overnight [since the previous ordination] (the latter case is cited below during the section on "Timing").
Regarding the term "Ācāryā" (A-ye) used within the context of requesting the Dharma: it is because she is a heavy *upādhyāyī* (preceptor) that she is treated with the same reverence as Ānandā;

she was the sister of the Buddha’s mother and is thus called "Āmā" (A-mo), which means maternal aunt. Next, the character "Ā" (pronounced "an" with the *ge* tone) is a word for respect and superiority, equivalent to the name of the Buddha’s maternal aunt; its significance as a title of honor can be understood from this.
The two matters mentioned in the commentary are precisely the dharma-food (*dharmāhāra*).

Regarding the conditions for entering formal meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), five points must be addressed: first, the time; second, the assembly; third, the realm (*dhātu*); fourth, the establishment of the rite;
and fifth, the detailed analysis.
From the beginning, the Vinaya regulation stipulates that one must go among the Saṃgha on the very same day; if one stays overnight, one incurs an offense.

Regarding the section on the formal reception (*sammukhībhāva*), the first sub-section of the text is as previously cited: "incurs an offense" means that one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
Question: Is the original *dharma* lost? Answer: It is not lost. Because the *dharma* is suspended by the act of relinquishment, the lapse of a day does not constitute its dissolution.
Regarding the question, the first part of the answer states directly that an offense is incurred without mentioning whether the *dharma* is lost or not;
the latter two parts indicate the intention that even through dissolution, it is also relinquished.
If that is so, one may simply use the original object to receive the formal act (*karmavācanā*); although the text of the response does not explicitly state this, one may take it as granted.
Even though the original object remains, the Buddha’s regulation contains points where doubt may arise; therefore, one should relinquish it and receive [a new object] according to the Dharma.
This is because all such signs of doubt are permitted by the Buddha.

In response to the question of whether it is unnecessary to receive the original *dharmas* again when those received during a difficult transition have not been lost, the answer first provides a general reply applicable to both cases:
that is, one may either receive them again or not, and in both instances it is permissible. Although [the text says] "next," it then provides a reply regarding re-reception;

because it is not determined whether one incurs an offense against the prohibitive rules (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*), it is said to involve doubt. As for the phrase "relinquishing and receiving according to the Dharma," it means:

Regarding the ritual procedure for confessing before another (pratideśanīya), one must relinquish the previous formal act and receive it anew; this applies to cases such as raising a doubt regarding the disciplinary treatment (*vinaya*).

For example, if a monastery does not know the location of the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), or if the boundary enclosure (*sīmā*) was established first and the ritual site (*kṣetra*) was established later, or if the markers for establishing the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) were improperly set or have become indistinct—in all such cases, one must dissolve the previous boundary and re-establish it. This is the rule.
Second, regarding the number of the assembly:

there are those who, having performed the preparatory rites for the formal procedure (*dharmakarma*), take two or three nuns to the *saṃgha* to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and then establish the following position:
"Since the nuns are entirely not presiding over the ritual within the *saṃgha*, what need is there for the assembly to go? Furthermore, the boundary (*sīmā*) need not be established."
Even though the text enumerates twenty assemblies, their arrangement before and after indicates they do not exist simultaneously.

Second, citing an ancient source reveals three errors: first, not knowing this dharma; second, not knowing that when two assemblies perform the rite together, each acts according to its own *dharmadhātu*;
third, erroneously conflating this with the Vinaya texts, which specify twenty assemblies for comparison.

Regarding the bhikṣuṇīs, it is said that because their fundamental dharma (*mūladharma*) and formal undertaking (*samādāna*) together constitute twenty items, they are listed both before and after [the bhikṣus].
However, this calculation is not correct; for a bhikṣuṇī’s reliance on the *saṃgha* consists in receiving [the precepts] from either one or the other [of the two assemblies].

When a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the complete method for its performance must be clarified within the assembly of both divisions (*ubhayasaṃgha*). Whether eight persons or forty persons preside over the *karmavācanā*, this is the domain of the *saṃgha*.

Regarding the question of whether the meaning of "harmony" and "patience" applies to both assemblies, how could it be permissible for them to reach the point of ordination and yet distinguish between "this side" and "that side"?

Therefore, in the Vinaya texts, when it speaks of the two assemblies of monks being fully complete, it explains this within the context of the *bhikṣu* (male) assembly; how could this be the same as the previous case?

Furthermore, the main text of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that ten *bhikṣuṇīs* should go [to the male assembly], and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* also says that those *bhikṣuṇīs* should be led there.
Within the Great Saṃgha, nothing may be omitted or abbreviated.

Now, in explaining the first phrase, I shall directly refute [the position of] the Bhikṣuṇīs and below, and then present the correct principle. First, it clarifies the necessity of the assembly and the boundary;

Chapter Four: The Section on Receiving and Purifying Robes and Medicines.
This section explains the rules for receiving and purifying robes and medicines.

Regarding robes, there are two general types; regarding medicines, there are four types. Within the category of robes, "receiving" applies to both those that are regulated and those that are permitted, namely the three robes and the hundred [other garments].

While the methods of receiving them differ according to whether they are taken by hand or by mouth, the purification lasts for only seven days and pertains solely to the extra medicines.

The above clarifies the ritual for receiving precepts; as for the principle of internalizing the Dharma within oneself, one must protect it. Since the preceding state of the object is pervasive and indeterminate, it cannot yet be [fully determined].

Because they are manifested according to circumstances, we define them by their forms and include them within their functional aspects; yet the burdens of body and speech are heavy during one's lifetime.

Since receiving and maintaining [the precepts] largely follows the deluded mind and allows the defiled spirit to run wild without being thoroughly purified, the Great Sage established the Dharma to prevent this, desiring that the physical form be fully equipped with the ritual decorum of the Dharma, while the mind maintains right contemplation, thereby subduing arrogance and dispelling base attachments.

The intention behind the initial turning of the Wheel of Dharma was that at the outset, the rules for later robes were already complete;
why, then, were they further codified? The following explanation clarifies this: first, it describes how over time circumstances changed and the teaching declined;

second, it reveals the reasons for those changes—namely, that people became overly eager for meditative realization and attainment, neglecting the proper form of the robes so as to merely cover their bodies, which eventually led to corruption and laxity.

Regarding the scriptural citation concerning the insignia of the noble ones in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the Vinaya states: "One who wishes to correspond to the dharma-robes of the *kāṣāya* must subdue the fetters (*saṃyojana*);

therefore, these are not garments to be worn by ordinary people. Furthermore, in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, when the King of Beasts, Firm Vow, was encountered by a hunter, it is because he wore the *kāṣāya* that the hunter did not shoot him.
Once he had been struck by the arrow, he endured the pain until death; however, the text simply says "one who wears the *kāṣāya*."
One shall swiftly attain liberation from birth and death.
In the initial passage of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, a verse from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is cited to demonstrate that this is not the attire of an ordinary person. The first two lines state:

"One who harbors the fetters (*saṃyojana*) should not wear the *kāṣāya*; the 'fetters' refer to the essence of the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), which are the three poisons. Next...

The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "In the distant past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, in the mountains and forests of this Jambudvīpa, there was a lion named Caṅkara-vi (in the language of Qin, 'Firm Vow'), whose body was golden in color and whose radiant marks were clearly manifest.
At that time, a hunter—having shaved his head and donned a kāṣāya robe, yet secretly carrying a bow and arrows smeared with poison—"
Struck by the arrow, the lion was startled awake and immediately intended to charge and harm him. Seeing that he was wearing a *kāṣāya*, he thought:
"This person will surely attain liberation before long. Why is this? This dyed robe is the emblem of the sages of the three periods of time;
if I were to harm him, it would be to harbor an evil mind toward the holy ones of the three periods. He then spoke a verse, saying: "Ya..."
"Rāra vaśa saha," and so on, up to the hunter who flayed his skin and offered it to the king. The king requested the seer to explain these words.
[The seer] said: "Rāra means one who has shaved his head and wears dyed robes;
such a person shall swiftly attain liberation from birth and death. Vaśa means that those like this man all possess the marks of the worthy and the holy."
"Approaching Nirvana" (saṃhā) means that such a person shall be seen, revered, and honored by all devas and people of the world, and so forth.
The rest is as extensively cited from scriptural proofs in the *Shishi Yaoyong Chao*; at the appropriate time, one should draw upon and arrange the phrasing to mutually elucidate them.
It is best to encourage others to listen to and faithfully uphold what is beneficial, rather than being dogmatic; how could such narrow-mindedness not be contrary to the Way?
To cling only to one's own views without attachment is the very root of delusion—be aware of this.

Regarding the second section: first, it points toward extensive vision; from the "Chapter on the Two Robes" onwards, the encouragement to "lead and pull" refers to citing and invoking [scriptural authority].
The first two lines below refute the attachment [to the object], while the next two lines refute the attachment that seeks to eliminate it.

This is like a medicine that eliminates a disease; once the disease is gone, the medicine remains and itself becomes a disease. Because this subtle and esoteric view of dharmas is difficult to eradicate, it is called "supreme.
The final line warns the practitioner: when you reach this point, be careful not to force an intellectual understanding. You must now...

If you have not yet attained mastery in your studies due to indolence, how can you dispel [delusions]? Moreover, if you attempt to dispel them by means of further dispelling, that will certainly not be within your own capacity.

Unless one possesses the illumination and penetration of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding names and characteristics (*nāma-rūpa*) as being entirely dependently originated, then even if one speaks of the profound mystery all day long, one has not uttered a single word;

even if one holds a scroll all day long, one has never looked at a single character. This is like waving one's hand in empty space—it may be called "suchness" (*tathatā*), but it is nothing more than that.
If immovability is such as this, then toward what destination would its propagation not reach?
As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, five points are most excellent for explaining the Buddha’s words, for they mostly follow reason. Thus, it first says:
"A single robe cannot ward off the cold, whereas three robes can. This is because those who lack shame and remorse are excluded, as they constantly dye themselves with only a single robe.
1. Purity of conduct: By wearing the robes with a sense of shame and dread of blame, one does not give rise to [unwholesome states], as each of the three functions has its own prescribed method;

whether in private or in public, one maintains protection so as to generate a virtuous mind. 2. Threefold [function]: By means of the *saṃghāṭī*, one dresses according to the assembly and place, thereby able to inspire faith in sentient beings. 3. Fourfold [function]:

If traveling on a road, one wears it folded back over the shoulders like a high banner, reverently protecting it as if it were a stūpa; thus both the hidden and the manifest cherish its virtue. 4. Fivefold dignity: [The remaining points follow].
Regarding the purity of deportment (*īryāpatha-viśuddhi*): the four modes of conduct and their respective enjoyments each have their proper place.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* first sets forth and praises these; then, citing the initial intent, it shows that: first, it obstructs the forms of mental hindrances;

second, it extinguishes evil; the remaining three produce goodness in others; the fourth produces goodness in oneself. Thus, the latter four follow the preceding pattern, and all state: [the following].

A single robe cannot [fulfill all needs], whereas the three robes can; therefore, according to their respective functions: the *antaravāsaka* (lower robe) is for manual labor and traveling on the road; the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) is for entering the assembly and for eating;

the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) is for preaching the Dharma and entering villages. One who gives rise to wholesome thoughts should wear these during this life for one's own benefit and in future lives for the benefit of others.

When wearing them with the folds turned outward and tucked high, it is for those living outside the boundaries of a *cāturmahārājika* village; the Saṃgha shall order such a person to wear the robe with the folds turned inward.
As for those who do not wear [robes], when they fold and lift their patched garments, they appear non-human in the dark and human in the light;
their deportment is pure and their speech is without fault.

The above explains three points; one must recognize the three names as detailed in the *Shishi Yaolan* (Essentials of the Vinaya), but here I provide a brief explanation for those who have not yet seen that work.
Based on this, one may briefly understand it.

Regarding the explanation of the name, the first phrase of the heading concludes the previous three points; that is to say, the intent of requiring these three is to indicate the detailed meaning through the brief, so as to allow for mutual comparison.

As explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, these three names are used because they manifest phenomena never before seen; since none of the ninety-six non-Buddhist paths possess such names, [the Buddha’s teachings] are distinguished.

For instance, regarding the term *antarvāsa* (安陀會), its original Sanskrit sound has no corresponding name in this land [of China]. Since the essential characteristics of its substance and form are unknown, from what could it have been translated?
Thus, many of the ancient translations differ, and it is precisely for this reason that there have been no [standardized] transmissions.

Regarding the section on "Non-Translatability," the initial passage cites a treatise to demonstrate that [the Buddha's teachings] originate from the Sage’s mind and cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings;
as follows, one name is briefly cited to illustrate the many translations, with the other two cases serving as examples.
Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*), they are collectively designated as *kāṣāya*. This term does not exist in the vernacular [Chinese] script, but is produced according to its phonetic sound.

During the Liang dynasty, Master Seng'an stated that it refers to "the clothing of the Way" (*daofu*). However, *kāṣāya* originally translates as "dyed color" (*rañjana-varṇa*); it is not actually the name of a garment. Therefore, the Vinaya texts state:

"One should make it the color of *kāṣāya," which refers to "ruined color" (*kaṣāya-varṇa*). Why then would one [confuse] the name with the substance? Among the six flavors, there is the flavor of *kāṣāya*.
*Śāmi* refers to clothing; as translated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is rendered as "reclining equipment" (*pariṣkāra*), meaning that the three robes are square like felt mats.
As for the translation in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is taken to mean "bedding," such as modern quilts and covers. As stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*:
"Bedding" is a name for the three robes, as explained in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). Ultimately, this is not their original meaning; it is unclear [how they arrived at this].
What is its name?
In the first section of the following analysis, it is shown that the name applies generally to all three robes, hence it is called a collective designation. The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:
"The robe worn by the Tathāgata is called *kāṣāya*. The "Pure Conduct" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "When wearing the *kāṣāya*, one should make this aspiration..."
Regarding the term "wuzi" (無字) for sentient beings and so forth: in the Sanskrit original, this is a transliteration of the sound *kaṣāya*, which later came to be called "yi" (衣, robe).

Therefore, in the dictionaries (*pianyun*), the character "yi" is conventionally added. Furthermore, beneath the character "liang" (梁), there are two sections. The first introduces the words of others; these should be those of the Dharma Master Dao’an of Xiangyang.
However, since Dao’an lived during the Jin dynasty, the reason for referring to him as being of the "Liang" period remains unclear. Alternatively...

I fear that there may have been another Master An during the Liang dynasty; however, the statement evaluating his "Dao-fu" (robe of the Way) is entirely inconsistent with the term *kāṣāya* as used in translation.
The name and substance of the dyed robe are completely different. He cites the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to demonstrate what is improper, yet he uses the "six flavors" to counter-argue.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the six flavors are sweet, bitter, acrid, pungent, salty, and bland; it does not say there is a "flavor of the *kāṣāya*."

It is unknown from whence [this term] originated, as seen in the following citation of scriptural texts. Both Vinayas adopt the "square shape" (fangxiang) to translate the name *saṃghāṭī* as explained in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*.

It remains unclear from what the *kāṣāya* derives its designation; I therefore refer to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), specifically the section on the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, which states:
"It is simply that the three robes are collectively termed [this]; since this land previously lacked it, it is not known [what it refers to]."
Since objects that share the same dimensions of breadth and length are treated as identical when spread out, they are conversely termed "bedding" (*śayanāsana*) and so forth;
the rest is as explained there.
Now, following specific distinctions to clarify their usage, they are like the common *shān* (shirt), *kuà* (trousers), and *yīshāng* (robes); yet when it comes to explaining their names, it says:

The Emperor said: "That which is worn above is called an *āśuka* (upper garment), and that which is worn below is called a *paridhāna* (lower garment). Knowing what these objects are, one should simply accept them as they are.

Furthermore, since the devas of the various form realms practice the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), they all wear these garments; they are originally not human clothing, so how can one know their specific names?"

In the first section of the "Distinct Manifestation," the initial part provides a general indication, while the subsequent citations from various texts each rely on a single characteristic; hence it is called "distinct manifestation.
Because these lack a substantial entity (*vastu*), their names cannot be definitively examined; thus it says "slightly known. "Slightly" means briefly.

"Function" (*vṛtti*) refers to efficacy, such as the defiled states and so forth. As examples are raised below, the first cites conventional names to illustrate that they lack reality, thereby providing an explanation.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* was compiled by Liu Xi of the Han; this applies to all characters and is not limited to a single instance. Since objects originally have no names, names are established arbitrarily according to their meanings.
Furthermore, when one distinguishes and examines these names in search of their referents, their origins remain unfathomable; hence it is said, "To know these things...
Next, the text cites celestial garments to further illustrate their unknowability.
The *Mahāsannipāta* is titled "Detachment from Defilement" (*vairāgya-vastra*);
the *Bhadra-kalpika* and *Mūrkha-paṇḍita* are titled "Transcending the World" (*lokottara-vastra*).

The next section is collectively named the *Mahāsannipāta* and *Bhadra-kalpika-mūrkha-paṇḍita*; though their names differ, their principle is the same as the "Dust-Free" (*viraja*) of the subsequent *Miśraka-vyākhyāna*.
The emaciated lotus and other such metaphors all signify the intent of liberation through detachment.

The four parts [of the robes] are called the "three dharma-robes" (tricīvara), which is a term for their ritual application; when worn, they cause the mind and conduct to accord with the True Dharma. Thus, the text states:
"Though one may wear the saffron robe, if it cannot eliminate resentment, it does not deserve to be this robe."
The *Caturvarga-vinaya* establishes the names and clarifies the meaning; the mental application toward the True Dharma does not transcend the two types of upholding.

To further provide textual evidence, the verse from the *Kauśāmbī-khaṇḍa* of the Vinaya states: "Though one wears the saffron robe, if one harbors the fetters (*saṃyojana*), one cannot eliminate enmity and harm;
such a person is unfit for the saffron robe. Only when the fetters have been extinguished and one is adorned by the upholding of precepts is one truly fit."
One who subdues their enemies is one who should wear the *kāṣāya*.
According to the *Nine-Scroll Miscellaneous Records on the True Dharma*, the *kāṣāya* is the general name for the three robes of foreign lands;

it contains many meanings. It is called the "Dust-Avoiding Robe" because it severs the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). It is called the "Emaciating Robe" because it cuts away and diminishes [defilements].
Because it is free from afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "Lotus-Colored" (*padmavarṇa*); because it is free from attachment (*saṅga*), it is called "Clothed";
or it is called "Intermediate-Colored" (*vicitravarṇa*) because it is composed of the three types of dharmic colors.
In Paramārtha’s commentary, this refers to India, hence he says: "The foreign name contains many meanings; it is shown that it is not to be translated."
Thus, "leaving behind dust" refers to destroying karma and emaciating the body, while "breaking through delusions" is likened to the lotus flower;
these two correspond to the former two [aspects], and the latter one corresponds to the color.
Furthermore, as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Those who wear the Tathāgata’s robe are those whose great compassion is like that of a bhikṣu who is identical to the Buddha."

From what has been explained above, we know that for one who practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the robe—four inches wide as cited in the sutra—is worn upon the body so that strife and contention are both stilled;

is this not indeed the power of loving-kindness enveloping them? Furthermore, the aforementioned statement that Brahmā practices the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) and thus constantly wears this robe makes the meaning even more manifest.
Therefore, this robe is also called the "Robe of Loving-Kindness and Compassion" (*maitrī-karuṇā-cīvara*); this is also the intended meaning of the verse in the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the scripture is first cited as follows: "If these good sons and good daughters enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat, they shall then extensively expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly.
The Tathāgata’s chamber is great compassion toward all sentient beings; the Tathāgata’s robe is a mind of gentleness and patience."
This "seat of the Tathāgata" is the emptiness of all phenomena;

one dwells therein and, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expounds this sutra for the fourfold assembly of bodhisattvas—this is called the three modes of propagating the sutra. Now, as for the robe corresponding to compassion:
perhaps it is because the principles of compassion and patience are not different. As for those bhikṣus who wear the same robes as the Buddha, they are the ordinary beings of the lower realms.

To have one's living body clothed in the Buddha’s robe—how could one not rejoice? Below are two citations as proof. First, regarding the citation from the *Shuochao* (Commentary on the Śāstra), specifically the "Two Robes" section which quotes the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*:
"When the Tathāgata made his vow for Buddhahood in the presence of Ratnagarbha Buddha, he said:

'My kāṣāya shall possess five merits. First, even a person who has committed grave offenses or holds false views, if they show a single thought of reverence toward it, [shall surely attain liberation].'"
1. One obtains the prediction of attaining the three vehicles; 2. gods, nāgas, humans, and ghosts revere even a small portion of it; 3.
those who have not yet attained non-retrogression in the three vehicles, as well as humans and ghosts, obtain sufficient food and drink from as little as four inches [of the robe]; 4.

when the four classes of sentient beings are in mutual conflict, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, they immediately give rise to compassion; 5. if one carries even a small portion of it while in the midst of battle, one will always...
If my *kāṣāya* lacked these five powers, I would be deceiving the Buddhas of the ten directions and others.

Furthermore, the next section below specifically points to the previously established four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), namely: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). The final three lines conclude the name of the *vinaya* verse;
that is, the aforementioned instruction to eliminate resentment is itself nothing other than loving-kindness and compassion.
The world calls this the "field of merit robe" because it possesses the characteristics of a boundary for the Dharma. Just as worldly fields use ridges to hold water so that fine seedlings may grow,
thereby nourishing the physical body and life, the field of the Dharma robe vastly expands the benefit of the fourfold welfare and increases the three wholesome states of mind,
thereby nourishing the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body.

Regarding the initial indication in the tradition of the world: at the time of shaving the hair and donning the robes, because no verse has been transmitted [from that specific moment], it is said, "The world calls it 'Dharma'.
"Dharma" (fa) refers to the boundaries (wei), which are the ridges of a field; this can be understood through the analogy of the world and the Dharma. "Mí dà" (彌大) means exceedingly great.
The "four benefits" refer to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). The "three virtues" refer to non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion (*alobha, adveṣa, amoha*).
When it comes time [to explain], one must cross-reference the *Śāstra* (Commentary) and the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Precept Text) to ensure mutual consistency.

Regarding the first section of the "Distinct Names," the *Śāstra* refers to the "two robes" (*dvivastuka*), while the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* omits the character "commentary" (*śu*) and reads it as "offense of forfeiture" (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Therefore, it is traditionally said that the *antarvāsaka* is the inner garment (*nīcavastra*), and the *uttarāsaṅga* is the upper garment (*uccavastra*);
because it is worn constantly upon the inner garment, the *saṃghāṭī* is the "exalted and superior garment" (*abhyudgatavastra*). Such explanations of the names are based on their functions.

Alternatively, some say that the lower garment is so called because it is worn when walking within the monastery grounds, while the middle garment is so called because it is worn when entering the assembly.

The upper garment worn at all times is named for entering villages and subduing external groups; thus, the term *saṃghāṭī* is translated as "subduing" (*li*), which is a translation based on its function.
Alternatively, it may be derived from its appearance, referring to the five-, seven-, or nine-striped patterns.
It may also be derived from its value and quantity, or from its suitability for cold or heat, and its lightness or heaviness.
The subsequent section has five parts. First, regarding the inner garment (*antarvāsaka*): because it is worn closest to the body, it is superior;

it is worn when entering royal palaces or villages to preach the Dharma. Second, regarding the lower garment (*nivasana*): it is used for walking within the monastery grounds or performing manual labor;
these three occasions constitute its use. As for the upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*), two uses have been cited; the other names may be understood by reversing these [functions].
Alternatively, the three lower [robes] follow the [distinction of] characteristics, while the four lower [robes] follow the [distinction of] value; the *Chao* states:
"The seven-strip robe is called a robe of medium value" (the other two may be inferred accordingly). Alternatively, the five lower [robes] follow the seasons—cold and heat, light and heavy;
the *Fenbie Gongde Lun* states: "Because there are three seasons, three robes were prescribed: one wears the heavy in winter, the light in summer, and [the medium] in spring."
This refers to the middle [case].
The text states: "One must not use an article subject to forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) for [making] lower [robes]. This is the meaning of the second section:
because the substance of a Dharma robe must be pure, and wealth that has incurred the offense of forfeiture is unfit to receive the ritual of acceptance, it is not permitted.
In the first section of the initial division within the second gate concerning begging, the primary point is to indicate that among the various rules on robes within the *Triṃśaka*,
if an offense has occurred and not been confessed, the addition of [the robe] will not be valid.
Furthermore, regarding those who speak briefly while harboring ulterior motives, why is it that "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*) does not encompass all such matters?

It is because the term refers specifically to cases where one engages in greed and defilement with a corrupt mind for the sake of profit—selling the Dharma, performing prostrations, reciting sutras, or engaging in any such acts to obtain bribes.
All such gains are termed "wealth of wrong livelihood," as they directly contradict the Buddha’s transformation of beings; therefore, they are strictly prohibited.

Next, regarding the section on the signs of the examination, first the matter is introduced as being vast; below, the essential points are briefly shown by enumerating four types of methods for seeking profit:
namely, lecturing for payment, abstaining from food, and inviting gain while fasting.
To speak briefly, if there is even the slightest expectation of reward, whatever one employs will all fall into deviant conduct, defiling one's own mind within and manifesting it outwardly.
Because they are reviled as ugly, they deviate from the Buddha’s transformation; nowadays, such people fill our eyes—alas, who can escape this?
As it is said in the Sūtra: when a bhikṣu wearing rag-robes went to a river to wash them, the devas took the water and used it to wash their own bodies, not shrinking from its impurity.
When an outsider holding a clean woolen blanket came next to wash it, the devas blocked him from afar, saying, "Do not!"
A pond becomes foul because it receives offerings from those of wrong livelihood; this passage serves as proof that mental purity is the fundamental basis.
In the initial section of the cited text, the first source mentioned is the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*, concerning the śrāmaṇera Cunda, whose name is also found in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Because this is a minor matter, it is said that from the bhikṣu downwards, the distinction between purity and defilement depends on the mind and does not reside in external objects.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five types of wrong livelihood (*pañca-mithyājīva*): first, manifesting an air of authority with a loud voice for the sake of gain;
second, forcibly predicting good or bad fortune; third, inciting others to give by provoking them; fourth, altering one’s usual dignified demeanor; and fifth, practicing and learning incantations.
These arts are all for the sake of profit; thus, the "four perversions" (*catur-viparyāsa*) refer to the four cardinal directions, the zenith, and the nadir.
The next category is the "five perversions. Regarding the first [of these], it is for the sake of gain and offerings; this single phrase encompasses the following four types.

The fourth is the perversion of the body (*kāya-viparyāsa*), while the remainder are all perversions of speech (*vāk-viparyāsa*). Among the four perversions, only their names are briefly mentioned. As the *Śāstra* says: "The celestial maiden Viśuddhanetra..."
Question: Śāriputra, there are four kinds of food for a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). Cultivating medicinal herbs and planting fields is called "downward-facing food" (*adhomukha-bhojana*).

Gazing upward at the stars and constellations is called "upward-facing food" (*ūrdhvamukha-bhojana*)—[as stated here, "upward" refers to looking up]. Skillful speech in the four directions is called "four-directional food" (*caturmukha-bhojana*).
Divination, incantations, and calculations are called "intermediate-point food" (*vidig-mukha-bhojana*)—[it is said that these are improper]—all of which are for the sake of seeking sustenance.
Because the mouth craves base matters, it is called "mouth-food.
Although one seeks pure wealth, its substance must accord with the Dharma; since silk, brocade, and embroidery are all inappropriate, the world generally uses plain silk and gauze.

This is because their substance involves the taking of life, and thus they are also subject to prohibition. Currently, neither the monks of the Five Indies nor those from the various Hu regions possess them.
As for those who use silk to make *kāṣāya*, this practice arose here in this land of China simply by following local custom. I personally asked them about it, and they replied:
"Silk is indeed available; however, out of compassionate consideration, we use cloth for our monastic robes (*brahmacarya-vastra*).
To know clearly that one is killing [the silkworms] yet still wear such garments is, in principle, improper."

Regarding the substances of wealth, first we exclude those that are ornate, light, fine silk, gauze, hemp, coarse *ge*, and *zhu* grass; these are not in accordance with the Dharma for the sake of the world.
Next, we distinguish between silk and cloth. First, we show the intent of the prohibition:

although the Vinaya prescribes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for obtaining [silk] from a silkworm-keeper, it remains permissible according to the Vinaya when it has come through successive transfers from one who is not a silkworm-keeper. Now, following the Mahāyāna, we seek its meaning deeply.
In all cases, these are not permitted, as is extensively analyzed in the *Zhangfu yi* (Ritual for Robes).

Now, the following citations provide evidence that "Five Heavens" refers to the four directions and the center—that is, the five regions of India—and that "various Hu" refers to those outside the five regions of India. This can be verified through direct observation and inquiry;
it is not false. The passage below consists entirely of the words of Hu monks; because they were composed by those from the Brahma Heaven, it is called "Brahma" (*Fan*).
[The text] says: "Wearing [robes]. The third instance states: "If one uses brocade robes," which clarifies the characteristics of color and form; this is the meaning of the third section.

One follows the Way with the Dharma-robe (*dharmakāṣāya*), yet the colors of brocade are variegated and ornate, dazzling and stirring the mind and spirit. Blue, yellow, and the five primary colors, as well as true purple and superior hues, are what the common world values.
Because of greed, they were pared down and reduced.
Regarding the first section within the third category of "unlawful matters," both the ornate prose and the formal structure deviate from the Way.
For instance, when Master Tancheng was in Zhao, he wore silk and brocade; this was a case of employing divine means to establish transformation, acting as a temporary royal regulation.

It is not that they do not follow the common people in their harsh punishments; rather, it is because the sages exercise discretion regarding the sovereign’s intent that they transmit and record [these matters].

Regarding the two stones, it is said: "The Great Master did not know how to manifest his virtue; he ought to have been placed before the princes and dukes. To clothe him in silk and brocade is improper.
As for this practice of "expelling" [based on such criteria], why does Master Tancheng not study the marvelous manifestations of the divine? Why does he fail to learn from them?
In the first section of the following chapter, the *Shenyi* (Miraculous Powers), it is recorded that Zhu Fotucheng was a man from the Western Regions whose family name was Bo.

He arrived in Luoyang during the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty. He was skilled at reciting divine incantations and could command spirits and objects; by applying a mixture of sesame oil and vermilion to his palms, he could see events occurring thousands of li away.
Furthermore, by listening to the sound of bells, he could declare whether matters would be auspicious or ominous. This took place in the fourth year of the Jianping era.
In the fourth month of that year, when the sky was calm and windless, a single bell atop the stupa rang out alone. Daorong said to the assembly, "The bell says the state will suffer a great mourning;
it shall not pass this year. In the seventh month, Shi Le died and his son Shi Hong ascended the throne.
After a short time, Shi Hu deposed Hong and established himself as ruler. He devoted himself entirely to Daorong and issued an edict stating: "The Monk is the great treasure of the nation."
Honorific titles were not bestowed upon him, nor did he receive high emoluments; yet how could his virtue be signaled without such honor and reward?

It was fitting that he be clothed in brocade and silk, and ride in an ornate carriage. On the day of the imperial assembly, the Monk ascended the hall while the Attendants and those below them all assisted in lifting the palanquin.
The Crown Prince and various dukes supported him from the sides as he ascended, while the presiding official proclaimed, "The Great Monk! as the assembly took their seats.
All rose to show their respect; the details are as in his original biography. "Zhao" refers to the Shi clan who usurped the title [of king];
both of its two rulers were tyrannical, hence the phrase "cruel punishments. The "two Shis" are Shi Le and Shi Hu. This serves as a warning that one must not emulate them.
As for wearing robes, it is appropriate to study their spiritual anomalies; since people today lack such spiritual anomalies, they merely imitate [the outward forms].
To wear the skin of a tiger while having the nature of a sheep—what is there to be valued in that?
Regarding the *kāṣāya*, various Vinayas frequently state that it should be one of three lawful colors: blue, black, or madder-red, as described in the *Shu* (Commentary).

Next, regarding the first section on the various Vinayas within the "According to the Dharma" (yathādharma) chapter: the *Dharmaguptaka*, *Daśabhāṇavāra*, and *Mahāsāṃghika* share the same name as the *Dharmaguptaka*;

the *Daśabhāṇavāra* refers to it as "blue mud rafters" (*nīlapaṅka-khaṭvā*), differing slightly in wording. Below, it refers to what is seen in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* (Rǎo) under the section on the two robes.
However, while *kāṣāya* is simply translated as "dyed," it is not established unless it is of various colors; thus, one knows that there is no fixed characteristic [regarding its hue].
Now, according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, the robes of the *svāgata-bhikṣu* (welcoming bhikṣu) were identical to the color red.
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states, "I wear robes of red color," and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also says, "The garments worn are all red. This refers to the present-day Indian monks (*brahmacārin*).
All wear the color red; Zhen Di states that although there are five schools of monastic robes in China, they are all uniformly red.
Using this fact as evidence, it appears that dyeing the *kāṣāya* red is quite close to the historical reality.
Next, in the section defining colors, first the name is indicated; now, the following two citations clarify the characteristics.
*Sudṛśa* is fully called "Welcome Bhikṣu. A clay alms-bowl is dark blue, slung over the left shoulder; the *kāṣāya* robe is a vivid red, bright and magnificent. Regarding the cause:
when a bhikṣu was begging for food at a certain house, there was a pearl there that had been swallowed by a goose. The owner suspected the bhikṣu [of stealing it].
A thief struck him nearly to death, yet he said nothing; when he subsequently struck a goose to death, the bhikṣu only then spoke.
The owner asked for the reason, and the bhikṣu replied: "I was wearing a red robe which reflected the pearl like flesh, so the goose swallowed it. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
When the Tathāgata entered the city to beg for alms, King Ajātaśatru released a drunken elephant intending to harm him; [the elephant] saw him...
The attendants were dressed in red garments; they called this "blood," yet it was seen again as something moving toward them, which is what is meant by "now personally seeing.
The citation from Paramārtha relies on what has been transmitted. The following three points are stated as a formal announcement.
However, among the five colors, there is also the color red; while their names are the same, their characteristics differ.

Just as with blue and black, these may be identical in substance, whereas red is dyed with *mūlana*. It slightly involves a tinge of black, much like the bark of the *kandha* tree found in the southern seas of the world.

In the *Jianzhengse* (Simplified Rectification of Colors), the first section demonstrates that the names are identical; since this is also the case for blue and black, it cites them as a point of inquiry.
Regarding red, the next section clarifies the distinctions between their characteristics. The *Zhangfuyi* (Rituals for Robes and Garments) states: "The single color *múlán* exists here in this land;
it is predominantly red with a small amount of black, and is what is meant by the 'Gandhāra' color."
The text states: "Listen; [the robe] is two cubits long," which refers to measuring the garment by laying it out—this is the meaning of the fourth section.

According to the various schools, the minimum size is only that prescribed in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, as this is the constant rule for those who have left home and are impoverished. Furthermore, how could one fully possess the formal requirements for covering the body?
The characteristics of the other two robes are similar to those in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. To measure the body most effectively, first take the cloth from the shoulder down to the ground.
Four finger-widths above the ankles should be used for the body of the robe; the remaining leaf-patterned sections should be proportionate to it.

Among the four [treatises], the first provides the general indication, while the subsequent ones provide the detailed explanation. First, regarding the specific measurements of our own school (the Dharmaguptaka), the *Mahāsāṃghika*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* each have three grades of measurement that are broader than those of the *Dharmaguptaka*.
This is as fully cited in the *Sengqishi yaoyi chao* (Essentials of the Sengqi Vinaya) under the section on "Leaving Home" (*pravrajyā*), etc.

This refers to the emergence of the smallest possible measurement for the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*). Taking five parts from the remainder, according to the initial text, one should rely on the use of the lower garment;

as it is appropriate to be small, it simply mentions "two garments. First, below, the method for measuring the body is shown: the ankle is the protruding bone on the outside of the foot; from the shoulder to the ankle is the width measurement.
Horizontal ridges and vertical strips are all termed "leaf-patterns" (*pattra-lakṣaṇa*); if the width is excessive and does not correspond [to the body], it is specifically [noted].
Regarding the demonstration of the proportions for the *dufa* (outer robe): since there is no hindrance in making it long, it was not specified [in the original text].

However, if one simply ensures it covers the body and provides convenience, nine chi as stated in the text seems quite excessive. Nowadays, people do not exceed five chi in width, yet their length exceeds one zhang two chi;

to stubbornly cling to the text regarding the "five parts" measurement of the body—does this not indicate that the measurement was not conducted with sufficient precision? Having been practiced for a long time, it has become a custom, and in the end...
The dharma-robes have long been subject to the decay of their proper regulations, making them difficult to explain.
The text states: "If one makes a new robe, it shall be single-layered," which clarifies the distinction between single and double layers; this is the meaning of the fifth gate.

While the various schools generally agree on these two [rules] regarding seasonal adjustments, when it comes to the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe), it must be double-layered. That many nowadays make it single-layered is an error.

Regarding the rules for obtaining, practicing, receiving, maintaining, and wearing the Dharma robes, one should understand the examples of offenses by inferring increases and decreases from these cases.
Among the five sections, the first subsection initially indicates the various [rules], while the subsequent parts correctly clarify them.

Because the two [robes] below are permitted to be worn either singly or in combination according to the occasion, whereas the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) is strictly regulated and not allowed to be worn alone, the condemnation of improper conduct and the determination of offenses are based on the measurements of length and width as specified in the following section.
Because they are reduced, they are called "comparative" (*bi-liao*).

The reason they are exclusively double-layered is to simplify matters and propagate the Way, as there is no need for further additions. Regarding the lower two garments, since they are permitted [to be single-layered], one may wear upper garments during the spring and summer;
this is the regulation. If the garments are thin and light, the mind is easily disturbed, which is not the mark of one who cherishes the Way with sincerity.

The formal robes are heavily layered and possess grand proportions; such is the holy regulation. There are reasons why ordinary minds do not understand this, and furthermore, at the time of receiving the robes, the regulation is applied across all three periods [of the day].

Regarding the first section of the subsequent analysis, the initial inquiry is posed, followed by the explanation below. First, the general intent of the application is shown: because "repetition" leads to deterioration, it is called "simplifying affairs."

The following sections further clarify the principles of permission and prohibition, which are again divided into two parts. First, regarding the restraint of the mind, there is a question in the text:
"Master Wenzhang said, 'How extreme it was! The ancient ways of making robes, caps, garments, and shoes—how plain they were and yet how functional!
[The Master] replied, 'Are not the ritual robes of the former kings profound? One wears the cap to dignify the head; one wears the shoes to honor the feet.'"
Robes and garments are draped and flowing (the term "chanyu" describes their fullness), and swords and pendants ring with resonance; these are all means for restraining restlessness.
Even when the people are restrained by such means, there are still those who gallop recklessly upon the roads.

Now, to discard them and say they are not right is like casting a fish into the deep abyss or placing a monkey in the trees—how could the common people of the world refrain from racing wildly through the vulgarities of custom?
If this is so, how much more so for the supramundane noble path—could it possibly be otherwise? Second, regarding the explanation by way of the seasons, the *Vibhaṅga-śāstra* states:
"The three robes were established for the sake of the three seasons: one wears the heavy [great robe] in winter, the light [five-strip robe] in summer, and the medium [seven-strip robe] in spring.
Since the great robe corresponds to winter, it must be made of double layers. This refers to the robes in relation to the seasons.
The regulation does not mean that one specific robe is fixed for each of the three seasons; the *Zhangfu yi* states: "Since change resides in human sentiment, one need not seek its ultimate source.
The source lies in warding off the cold; a single, coarse garment is sufficient and not excessive."

The text states, "It should be five strips below," which refers to the number of strips on the robe; this is the meaning of the sixth section. In the Vinaya, the three robes are distinguished by name;
the five-strip and seven-strip robes have not yet been seen distinguished by their physical appearance.

Interpreting the text according to its underlying intent, as in the nine grades of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Duo-lun), the *saṃghāṭī* is clearly established according to the preceding examples. Thus, it is certain that the five-strip robe is the lowest grade and the seven-strip robe is the middle grade.

Regarding the first section of the six [parts], the initial exposition of the *Mūla-vinaya* simply mentions the *antarvāsa* and so forth, without dividing them into five or seven types to distinguish between middle and lower grades.
However, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the upper garments (*uttarāsaṅga*) are of nine grades, with the lowest being nine strips;
this may be taken as a precedent for the present case.
Regarding the statement that it reaches a maximum of twenty-five categories, some say this is because one wishes to act as a field of merit for all realms of existence;

thus, "twenty-five existences" refers to the four realms of form (*rūpadhātu*), the four evil destinies, the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—including the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*)—as well as the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the four dhyānas. This is what is meant.
Next, at the beginning of the text, the phrase "the person indicated" is introduced because [the person] fundamentally has no origin; thus, the following section provides a further explanation.

All "existences" (*bhava*) are briefly categorized into three existences, namely the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness. Alternatively, it is said there are nine existences, as each of the upper two realms contains four.
This is stated in reference to the *niśraya-vipāka* (the objective environment or receptacle world); here, however, the primary [subject] is used to manifest the dependent [environment].
Subdivided into twenty-five items, they are summarized here in verse from the *Abhidharma-śāstra*.

The first line collectively encompasses the five destinies and four modes of existence (*bhava*) of the lower realms within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), namely the four continents. The second line, according to the treatise, combines them as "Brahmā-rāja and the six heavens of the desire realm.
The heaven of Brahmā-rāja is the third heaven of the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*). There are six heavens in the desire realm.
(The Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa devas dwell upon Mount Sumeru; the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas dwell in the sky.

Regarding the third section of the treatise, it discusses the five Pure Abodes and the non-percipient beings, totaling eighteen heavens within the four dhyānas: the three heavens of the first dhyāna (Brahmapārṣadya, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā);

the three heavens of the second dhyāna (Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara); the three heavens of the third dhyāna (Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna); and the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna.

(Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala—these three are the abodes of ordinary beings; Asaṃjñisattva—one day of the non-percipient realm inhabited by non-Buddhists; Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha—these five are the abodes of those who have attained the third fruit.
Asaṃjñisattva is the fourth heaven of the fourth dhyāna. From the fifth level upward, they are collectively termed the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes);

these are what the *Abhidharmakośa* calls the five Anāgāmins. These four [groups] of four and the sixth [group] together constitute twenty-two. The remainder are the three [levels] within the fourth dhyāna.
There are those among the heavens who reckon this [state] to be the ultimate fruit of Nirvana; therefore, it is specifically singled out so that they may know it is not.

The reason it is negated alone rather than in pairs is that the practice of the śramaṇa takes compassion and benevolent nurturing as its foundation, which accords with the transformative influence of the world’s yang energy.
The number is not even; however, those who wear the robes understand compassion, as explained in the *Shō*.

Among the three [types of clothing], the single is an odd number and the double is an even number. Since yang represents life and yin represents death, one adopts the meaning of the yang number to encourage inward reflection.
The text states that "rice fields conforming to the Dharma" clarifies the characteristics of the *khaṇḍa* (cut-and-sewn) robe, which is the meaning of the seventh section.
The Vinaya states that the three inferior aspects of a śramaṇa’s robe refer to its cutting, its color, and its substance.

Regarding the first passage among the seven, the Vinaya is cited to demonstrate that [the robe] is "lowly" because it is cut into pieces for its blade, dyed with inferior colors for its hue, and made of coarse, discarded rags for its substance.
The reason for demonstrating its length and breadth is that, according to the world, rice fields vary according to the high and low levels of the water. [This applies to] the śramaṇa.
Regarding the manifestation of long and short garments: this is also because the field of respect (guru-kṣetra) benefits all who are noble, while it diminishes for those who are ordinary;
this is analogous to how the length is greater while the shortness is less.
Among these two [points], the first clarifies the reason for the long and the short: where the water is high, the furrows are narrow; where the water is low, the plots are broad.

Following the extensive discussion on śramaṇas, the following section demonstrates the differences in quantity and length; while the long robes increase in stages, the short ones are fixed at a single measure—a rule that can be seen through both dharma and metaphor.

Furthermore, it says that "mutual contradiction constitutes the taking [of robes]": the act of taking relies upon the teaching, which necessarily requires the three robes; even if they are present, one must not fail to wear them according to the rules.

Because violating the precepts at night constitutes the offense of separation, one must certainly receive them; the ritual procedures for their reception and observance are established to generate wholesome roots in sentient beings.
Since deviations in length or brevity contradict the spirit of compassion and purity, a distinct offense is incurred for every step that transgresses the ritual protocol.

Among the three [sections], the first clarifies the completion of the acceptance and the establishment of the robe’s count; therefore, it is placed next. The following clarifies the offense of usage arising from transgressing the established regulations.
The text states, "It should be made according to the Dharma with four borders," which clarifies the method of its construction—this is the meaning of the eighth section. Because it is circular...

Because it is held by means of [the waistband], it does not quickly deteriorate. Regarding the "five strips and ten partitions," these refer to the characteristics: there are only five [strips] when considering the general form, yet they are distinguished by length and shortness.
One should wash and dye them oneself; these six matters are all tasks for completing the robe.
Of the eight [sections], the first division is threefold: first, the explanation of the perimeter; second, the clarification of the specific characteristics of the five [robes];
third, the illustration by analogy, which should state that the seven strips and twenty-one sections, etc., are characterized by only five [types of robes].

This is because while the five and seven [striped robes] have fixed characteristics, the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) and others differ in length—being either one unit short or one unit long—and thus are termed "general" and "specific. Below this, the six matters regarding washing and treatment are explained as in the commentary.
Regarding the three characteristics of cutting, pleating, and folding, there are none that do not follow these regulations;

however, the permission to follow one's own original [garment] or to reduce the plain [sewing] is granted solely on account of poverty, and thus this concession exists. If one intends to cut the original [garment], it may be permitted if one originally lacks [the means].
As for the width of the pleated sections, the text is indeed as specified elsewhere; yet nowadays they are mostly oversized, which reflects the spread of decadent customs.

In the first section of the following analysis, the regulations regarding the folding (*saṃvartana*) of leaves are shown: "folding with outer leaves" refers to folding the leaves upon a seamless robe (*avikṛta-cīvara*);
