Among the three [categories], the Dharma of Correctness is the primary section; once the school’s tenet has been established, the collection of the principles of the Dharma must necessarily be complete.
*Sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemoshu ji yuanji* (Commentary on the *Sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemoshu*), Part 4-1;
*Sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemoshu ji yuanji*, Part 4-2.
Second, it clarifies that listening to the teaching is equivalent to the purification (*pariśuddhi*) regarding robes and medicine.

In the heading of the section on "Listening," the items such as robes and medicine correspond to the preceding title; however, for robes, one must specifically apply the purification, while additionally including the extra bowl (*atireka-pātra*).

Regarding medicine, one only accepts it for seven days, yet this applies to both types; furthermore, when gold and grain are included, the "timely medicine" (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) likewise applies to both.
Medicine sustains the physical body and life at all times; therefore, it is explained first. Regarding the preceding internal support of the four medicines, there are two parts:
first, the conditions, and second, the method.
Within the initial presentation of the four medicines, the sequence is first indicated, and then the text is divided below.

Regarding the listing of the names and characteristics of the four medicines within the section on conditions (*pratyaya*), this is explained extensively in the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*). Here, however, because only the application of the methods is addressed, it is not elaborated upon at length.

In the first sub-section concerning conditions, the *Chao* indicates that all four medicines are named according to their temporal limits, categorized as either "primary" (*bhojana*) or "non-primary" (*abhojana*).

At that time, clear gruel was designated as "non-time" (vikāla) medicine; butter, honey, and so forth were designated as "seven-day" (saptāha) medicine; and those unfit for consumption were designated as "life-long" (yāvajjīva) medicine.

Regarding the textual basis, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* (Wǔyì) establishes five principles to prevent the characteristics of theft, which serves as the foundation. The remainder is as explained in the second section of the *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts).

Furthermore, citing oral tradition, it is held that these are added to extend the duration of practice, thereby permitting them to last until the time limit expires. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "These are the three kinds of medicine."

Holding food overnight and receiving it while not ill are both impermissible; conversely, one may receive them if the opposite conditions apply. Next, the section on receiving with the hands involves five intentions:
first, to sever the conditions for theft; second, to seek verification; third, to prevent slander; fourth, to practice few desires and contentment; and fifth, to cause others to give rise to faith.
Receiving by word of mouth allows for a delay in time for the sake of treating illness; thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* permits holding food overnight.

Storing two nights' worth of impure substances, storing two [nights'] worth of boiled [food], or [receiving] that which has been touched by what is unwholesome—these are called defects in the medicine.
It is not permitted except in the case of illness; if the medicine is defiled, it is not permitted even for one who is ill, and if the medicine is pure, it is prohibited even for one who is healthy.

Regarding the enumeration of "timely medicines" (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*): when the hands and mouth mutually obstruct one another, the method applied by the mouth serves to prolong [the validity of the acceptance].

One may receive [food] with the hands and pass it over [to the other], yet for "limited-time medicines" (*yāmika-bhaiṣajya*), it is inherently improper to consume them after midday. Although there is no need for the mouth-method [of acceptance] as it cannot be prolonged, the mouth-method is nevertheless employed as a separate concession;
this is because, due to others' displeasure or being constrained by difficulties, one is unable to perform the hand-acceptance and must apply the method from a distance.

Regarding "receiving by mouth," the *Vinayamātṛkā* states that there are times when, due to specific circumstances, one receives while placing the food on the ground; this refers precisely to such a case.
Thus, it is said that "hand and mouth mutually exclude [the other].

Among the three types of medicine, the term "mutual exclusion" regarding *kālāhāra* (timely medicine) means that while originally one receives only with the hand, one may, due to circumstances, receive by opening the mouth to substitute for the hand.

Receiving [the precepts] through any one [of the three modes] constitutes [the completion]; it does not allow for mutual inclusion. First, the explanation of the non-requirement of oral methods; next, the clarification of the conditions for opening the allowance of oral methods.

Regarding those who do not rejoice [in the teaching], this refers to outsiders (*tīrthika*); regarding those who are pressed by difficulties, this refers to the *Pañcavargika* account of the fire burning the horse-stable.
In both cases, the food is placed at a distance on the ground, and the bhikṣu adds the three receptions orally; this then corresponds to [receiving them] with the hand.

Regarding the formal act of receiving (*pratigraha*): according to the Vinaya, the causal conditions do not go beyond the two aforementioned cases. Furthermore, if one sees a woman while eating from a precious vessel and lust arises, one must likewise perform the formal act of opening the mouth (*mukha-vikāra*).

As for the other three medicinal substances, if they are consumed immediately, the formal act of the mouth is not required; however, if one intends to keep them for a period of time, one must first receive them with the hand.
Regarding the subsequent oral consecration (*mukha-dharma*), it must necessarily involve both types of reception (*paribhoga*).

As for the other three medicinal substances, they cannot be established through oral consecration unless they have first been received by hand; logically, there can be no partial application of this rule.
Within the category of subsequent reception, the four types of medicine are divided into four sections.
Regarding the *kālāpāna* (medicines for the day), there are two divisions based on their nature as objects (*ālambana*).
First, concerning the five types of "proper food" (*bhojana*) as listed in the text: if one consumes these five, it is called "proper food";

this constitutes an invitation (*pravāraṇā*) and is sufficient to give rise to a subsequent offense. Next, the five types of *khādaniya* (solid foods) are listed; these are "improper" because their substance and strength are slight, and although one may consume them...

Because they are opened [by the formal act], these five are not "invited" (*pavārita*), not "formal" (*yathāvutta*), and not "sufficient food" (*paripuṇṇa*). This is explained in detail according to the individual precepts in the *Śāstra* (Commentary).

Next, regarding the section on the "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*) among the legal procedures, it states that the five types of "formal food" (*yathāvutta*) are "invited" and "sufficient," because they are contrary to the rules of "invited" and "sufficient food."
In both cases, since the offense is established based on the five types of *pañcamūla* (fivefold) medicines and there is no offense when they are not *pañcamūla*, the opposite applies accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding the two methods of administration, four distinctions are made: first, observing whether the medicine is pure or impure; second, determining whether the giver is qualified or unqualified;
third, clarifying the method of acceptance; and fourth, measuring the time. As it is with the *kālika* (timely) medicines, so it is for the others by analogy.
Regarding the "various faults" mentioned within the initial section on defilement and purity: these were already fully set forth previously in the section on the Pure Grounds;
here they are briefly cited because faults arise constantly.

In the first sub-section of the explanation of the contemplation of the defilement and purity of phenomena, "faults arise constantly" means that there is no time when they are not required [to be examined].
1. Not "staying overnight" (*antarāvasita*): This means knowing that it is not food for human consumption, as clarified by the *Samavasthāna-vibhaṅga*.

2. Not "cooked inside" (*antargrha-pakva*): This means not cooking food within the same monastery grounds. 3. Not "cooked by oneself" (*svayaṃpakva*): This means it has not been purified by fire from oneself or another.
4. Not "defiled by contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśa*): This means not grasping it oneself before it has been formally accepted. 5. Not "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*).
"Overnight" (sukha) refers to when a bhikṣu, whether for himself or another, has already taken possession [of medicine] and it remains until the following morning.

Sixth, "trading" (paṇāpana) refers to when one, whether for oneself or another, possesses impure medicine; that is, those who provide for themselves through such improper livelihoods and unlawful means, as described above.

This concludes the seven offenses involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). Regarding "residual" (śeṣa), this refers to the remaining three types of medicine which, having been accepted, exceed their limit, and are not gifts from others.
And they take and eat them. The next section consists of seven items;
their names and characteristics are easy to understand. Of these six types [of offenses], all are based on the actions of fully ordained monks (*bhikṣu*).

Only the second, "cooking within," applies to both the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as to monastics and laypeople alike. The seven offenses are concluded. Regarding medicinal substances, there is also a prohibition against keeping them for oneself or for others.
Because one must first undergo seven transgressions before being eligible to receive the Dharma, all [previous instances] are said to be incorrect.
Second, there are three methods for bestowing food.
First, regarding "discrimination": since food is that which constitutes a proper meal (*bhojana*), non-food does not constitute a proper meal; or rather, it may be edible.
That which is edible is not "food" [in this context], such as grass and wood; that which is inedible is what is now being offered.

To say it is food would not be an obstacle, yet at the time of taking possession, it is actually the five types of formal meals (*pañca bhojanāni*). Because the mind and the object are distinct, the formal act of acceptance (*paribhoga*) is not established.

Acceptance must necessarily correspond between the mind and the object to be valid according to the Dharma. If one accepts erroneously, it is not [valid] and therefore not established. Thus, the Vinaya says: "If one intends..."

If one receives this [food] but mistakenly receives that [other food], it does not constitute a formal acceptance (*paribhoga*), nor does it involve contact (*sparśa*), and so forth; this may be inferred from other examples.

Regarding the "giver" (*dātṛ*), in the first section of the initial analysis of the distinctions between what is permissible and what is not, both meanings—what constitutes food and what does not—are presented together.

First, they are distinguished based on whether the food is "proper" (*kalpa*) or "improper" (*akalpa*): if it is proper food, there is an offense for eating to satiety or for accepting multiple invitations (*pātrapūra*).
Because there is no offense when it is not the proper [time], the text next explains this by means of what is edible and what is inedible.

Below, it first judges what is unlawful and then demonstrates whether an act is established or not; the *Vinaya* can be consulted for these points. As for "mutual contact," this refers to the section on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) found below.
Because that [case] involved a light mind, it is compared here to the distinct conditions [of the present rule]; thus, it says, "know by analogy."
Second, if one who possesses the intention to give entrusts food to another, even though it is accepted, it does not constitute eating because it is held for the purpose of being kept;
since it is clearly permitted to eat it later when given, it is evident that if there is no intention to give, even if it is accepted, the act of eating is not established.
Regarding the two [cases], if one first entrusts [the food] and subsequently gives it, one knows that although the previous mind accepted it, the act is not accomplished.

Third, "giving according to the Dharma" means it is not with a disrespectful mind; as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one touches [the food] with a disrespectful mind, the hand does not accomplish the giving of food.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (or *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*), one must know that a bhikṣu is the recipient of the food; if [the recipient] understands, the act is accomplished.
The details of the conferral are as explained extensively in the *Śāstra* (Commentary).
Among the three [types of ordination], in the case of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one must reach a state of sincere understanding through the treatises to achieve comprehension.
Regarding the third, the method of self-acceptance (*svīkaraṇa-dharma*):

First, it clarifies that for both the giver and the receiver to be mutually understood, their physical forms must not be mistaken or even slightly discrepant; otherwise, the rite will not be accomplished.
This is evident in the first section of the third part, which provides a specific explanation of the formal reception.
Second, if one intends to eat it oneself or gives it to those of lower status, although one receives it, the reception is not valid.

As stated in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, when a bhikṣu received alms food covered in dust and grime and gave it to a śrāmaṇera upon arriving at the monastery, the śrāmaṇera later returned it; the bhikṣu then received it again according to the Dharma.
From this, we know that the previous reception was not called a valid reception.
Regarding the second point, "seeing well" (*sudarśana*): because one forms the thought that the dust and dirt belong to another and does not accept them as one's own, it is called "giving back.
This refers to a *śrāmaṇera* returning what he has received to a *bhikṣu*.
Third, "receiving in accordance with the Dharma": as stated in the Vinaya texts, items such as robes and bowls are mutually exchanged; these ten phrases are explained in detail therein.
One may indeed scoop up food with the hand, but one must look upward toward the heavens at the proper time and ensure there are no signs of theft.

If one reaches out to snatch the food and places it on the ground to eat, such an act is contrary to the Dharma. Although placing food on the ground is permitted, it is only for specific reasons. To divide the food and eat it arbitrarily without such a reason constitutes an offense.

This is like the practice during years of famine when one would personally grasp and cook food; since the present situation lacks such a reason, one must abandon the karma of hunger, for the mind is not yet satisfied.
One may trust only in the Dharma; this is explained in detail as in the precept on not accepting food.
Regarding the three [categories], the first indicates the Dharma. In the first four sections, five types of hands and held objects are enumerated to form four permutations:
two mutual, two both, and fifth, throwing from a distance. Furthermore, there are five types: body, robe, elbow, vessel, and returning.

Regarding the four types of receiving [food] and the placing on the ground with conditions: if it is placed below, it manifests as improper. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, a general indication that it is not the Dharma;

although the following section provides a specific explanation of the "placing on the ground" portion, it remains subtle. Below, the opening regarding times of scarcity serves as proof that this is not the permanent Dharma.

As for the phrase "it is not [permitted] now," etc., this is an exhortation to rely upon the teachings. To eat while not having received [the food according to rule] will result in the retribution of hunger; therefore, it is called "hunger-karma."

Regarding the fourth point, the practitioner of contemplation should briefly employ five methods. When a bhikṣu makes use of robes, food, dwellings, and bedding, he must certainly practice observation.
As the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu of sharp faculties receives offerings, he should attend to them as they come to his mouth, as they touch him, and at every moment of their entry and exit;
he should maintain mindfulness at each instance. If he does not maintain such mindfulness, he falls under the influence of the gift. This is not the case for one of dull faculties."
If one eats while maintaining this mindfulness, both the giver and the recipient, as well as the act of giving, will avoid falling [into evil realms].

If one does not practice this, the abdomen will burst and the food will be expelled; yet because there is still a karmic retribution for having eaten, it does not happen immediately. Other citations are clarified in the *Shuochao* (Excerpts from Commentaries) regarding the cultivation of merit through the act of giving.

The fourth section, "Clarifying the Practice of Contemplation," provides a general overview of the four matters at the beginning; these are set forth as follows, with the text cited to illustrate them.

First, it clarifies that one must perform the appropriate mindfulness while eating, while wearing robes, when entering or leaving, and when facing the dwelling. The text is brief regarding bedding and requisites; because those of sharp faculties possess strong mindfulness, there is no need for such intervals.
However, for those of dull faculties who easily forget, the practice is restricted to the initial moment, as explained below. Next, it clarifies the [practice of] non-... [text fragment].
Because those who practice giving are unable to bestow it effectively and thus fail to provide relief, both fall into this retribution from the future.

Wearing tattered and coarse *kāṣāya* robes that have detached from the body is a retribution manifest in the present life. Because there is the fruit of the future and because the retribution in the present is slight, it is said that they do not "immediately" [experience it].
Regarding the initial calculation of labor, as the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* states, it takes a hundred efforts to produce this single grain;

as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, from the initial plowing, sowing, weeding, and reaping, up until the food in one’s bowl—when calculating a single bowl of food, the laborer sweats profusely while eating little.
How could a wise person not contemplate such dependent origination?

The separate explanation of the first contemplation concerns the labor of sowing, harvesting, cooking, and serving the food in one’s alms bowl. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, a single grain involves a hundredfold toil, and many grains are beyond calculation.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that one must trace the beginning and end of the process from plowing and weeding until it reaches the bowl. "Sweat" refers to the blood of one's own body;

this text mentions rice as an example, but all other foods are to be understood accordingly. The commentary instructs that one should contemplate the source [of the food], reflecting upon how it was obtained through the sacrifice of others.
With what intention does one give to me?
Second, regarding self-examination, as stated in the *Sudarśana-sūtra*, there are four ways of utilizing gains and offerings: first, using them like a thief; second, using them like a debtor;
third, using them like the property of a son; and fourth, using them like one's own property. To eat without such reflection and to accept alms while violating the precepts is [unlawful].
The first person is one who upholds the precepts; the second group of seven refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*).
When one reaches the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) and receives offerings, they are regarded as if receiving their own possessions. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"If an ordained bhikṣu receives food without mindfulness and with a mind that relishes its flavor, he will die a firm death and enter the Copper Spikes Hell, where he shall suffer the two torments of swallowing iron balls and drinking molten bronze for countless eons."

Of these two [sections], the first cites the *Sudarsana* (Good Vision) Sūtra to clarify what may or may not be used through theft; the analogy of having a debt with its attendant guilt; the analogy of needing to repay borrowed goods;
and the analogy of needing to apologize for one’s own property. These three results and four stages of the path constitute the seven types of learners (*śaikṣa*).

The first two are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), while the latter three are noble ones (*ārya*). Only those who have realized the four fruits are worthy of the faithful offerings of students. Upon hearing this, the learner is able to...
Regarding "no concern," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further cites that the "copper stake" mentioned as the retribution in the future life is the name of a hell.
Third, concerning the prevention of mental faults, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "We observe that sentient beings are born from impure matter rather than from solid rocks;
this is due to the fault of craving flavors. Furthermore, there are three kinds of food: the excellent, the inferior, and the mediocre.
Furthermore, based upon the three objects, three perceptions arise; next, the three feelings arise; and subsequently, the three formations arise. Thus, suffering is accumulated:
following the pleasant feeling from delicious food, the formation of greed arises; following the painful feeling from bad food, the formation of hatred arises;
and following the neutral feeling from mediocre food, the formation of delusion arises. Consequently, one proceeds to the three paths—the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals—necessarily.
One should cultivate the contemplation that the three evil realms do not arise from one's own actions, for good and evil are experienced by oneself without being deceived.

Thus, the popular proverb says, "Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned only by man," which is indeed true. In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, four contemplations should be cultivated: first, the contemplation on the fault of intoxication through food;

second, the contemplation on the fault of attachment to joy and pleasure; third, the contemplation on the fault of craving for beauty; and fourth, the contemplation on the fault of excessive adornment of the body. One should develop these.
Because of the defilement of greed, this [text] specifically cites its remedy.

Among the three [sections], the first briefly introduces the cause of impurity: on a clean spot of ground, one sees few insects arise from a flat rock. Next, the main body clarifies cause and effect; this also has three parts:

first, a general indication of the mind and its objects as causes, wherein consciousness arises based on objects; second, the subsequent arising of the three aggregates (*skandha*); and third, their accumulation and integration.

Ultimate suffering thus constitutes the three poisons and the five aggregates are fully present. As will be shown below in the specific correlation of cause and effect, the method of contemplation is first presented;
it begins by exhorting practice to prevent the three [defiled] minds. "Qi" (cheating/deception) means emptiness or unreality. Below, secular evidence is cited from the *Zuozhuan*:
"Calamity and fortune have no fixed gate; they do not exist beforehand. It is only that man summons them through his own actions—whether right or wrong."

This also corroborates the previous statement that "good and evil are generally derived from one's own mind. Although the phrasing may appear similar, one must understand the varying depths of meaning.

To clarify this, the following citation demonstrates that being able to abandon the four faults constitutes the four contemplations: (1) greed for satiety, (2) craving for flavor, (3) desire for luster, and (4) delight in plumpness.
While these four remedies for greed apply generally to all three poisons, anger and delusion are rarely associated with them.
The fourth [simile] is that of excellent medicine: it merely sustains the body to eliminate hunger and thirst, providing strength and stability so that one may attend to one's affairs;
what else could be sought from it? Thus, a sutra says: "This body is like a carriage;
it makes no distinction between good and bad, for fragrant oil and foul fat are equally used to provide smooth lubrication. This is precisely what is meant.
Among the four [types of] medicine, those used to treat illness and hunger and thirst are treated by means of food and drink. This is transcribed below in the verses of the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*.
It concerns how the King tested non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) with two kinds of food, coarse and fine;

the non-Buddhists’ minds gave rise to attachment and aversion. He then tested the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus answered the King with verses. Thereby, the King came to know the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, as it is said: [The verses follow... *Note: The specific verses are not provided in the source text.*

Regarding the oil applied to the axle, how could one discuss whether it is fragrant or foul-smelling? This is as fully cited in the *Zizhi* (The Essential Support). Fifth, concerning the practitioner who seeks to achieve the Way:
the Buddha established the contemplation of food for the purpose of cultivating the Path. If one performs ordinary meritorious deeds, they do not accord with the supramundane intent. Why is this?
Because the merit of the ten wholesome actions of a Wheel-Turning King is merely transformative. As the *Dhāraṇī of Holding the World* says: "If it is not for the sake of eradication..."
Those who have extinguished the afflictions of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") are not permitted to accept even a single cup of water from others, let alone other forms of giving;
this is stated in detail in the text and will be cited when the time comes.

Of the five points, the first clarifies the work of the Path (*mārga-karma*): it means that those seeking liberation do not regard ordinary merit as the Path, and therefore such things are not permitted. As it says:
If, upon being shown next time that [the food] is unfit and cannot be removed, we do not recognize this as the practice of the Path, it is because the text of that sutra is extensive;

therefore, it is referred to below. How could it be merely a matter of verbal recitation? It must necessarily involve holding the alms bowl before one's chest and focusing the mind with intense contemplation on the food; only when the mind becomes distressed and surges with agitation does one truly know [the practice].

How unbearable! One should close one's eyes for a short while and wait until it has settled before proceeding to insert the spoon. Only after inspecting it beforehand should one place it in the mouth; what intention could there be in putting it in?

Those who know through experience that they crave such things will spit it out in an instant, their eyes unwilling even to look at it, let alone endure the foul stench of the flowing filth as it is poured out.
This is not worth craving; it is only because of delusion that one does not realize this. If one obtains such poor food, one should wait until the anger subsides.
Later, she ate them. According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, if one does not practice contemplation, a rākṣasa will seize [the body] and devour it until it is fully satiated;
only then does one remember the previous contemplation. This karma having already been completed, regret is of no avail. One must certainly be aware in advance: what is it that causes delusion?
In the first section of the *Jiegao* (The Exhortation), the initial instruction on holding the bowl before the chest demonstrates the proper deportment.

The note states that "concentrated observation of the food" means to restrain the mind within its object. "The heart is stifled and surges up" refers to the intensity of craving and indulgence. "Knowing it is unbearable" means that one's power of restraint is insufficient.
"Closing the eyes and waiting for composure" means gradually bringing oneself under control. *Di* refers to the bowl; *didi* is the sound of the bowl.
"Looking" means observing individually. "Internal" refers to entering. What is meant by "internalizing the mind"? It is to distance oneself from the three minds and four faults.
To "know one's greedy cravings" implies that one has not yet been disciplined; it is like vomiting above while flowing out below, which is loathsome.
Above, this corresponds to delicious food; below, it corresponds to foul food. This section below cites a text to provide proof through the analogy of the rākṣasa eating with the three minds.
If one looks back later, it cannot be pursued;
the words are brief but the matters are vast, and it is only upon reaching the moment of eating that one knows the measure. What station is this?
Since a great man cannot commit a grave transgression to enter hell, how could he sink into ruin for the sake of a single mouthful of food? To undergo suffering is...
Consequently, one's conduct becomes extremely weak.
Regarding the first part of the subsequent section: at the outset, one is made to reflect upon oneself; at other times, lofty talk is beyond reach.

When facing food, one finds it difficult to restrain and pacify [the mind], which clearly shows that one is but an ordinary person—this can be known by oneself. Next, the following section demonstrates the application of encouragement regarding those who commit various evils.
To undergo suffering without complaint and instead do so for the sake of food and drink, falling into hell for kalpas on end— how pitiable that such extreme weakness is so base and inferior!
Second, receiving [the offering] within the gruel.

The initial section of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If one does not cause intoxication, drinking at improper times is permitted. From this, it is known that what causes intoxication is the immediate medicinal substance [meant here].
Nowadays, there are various grasses and trees blended and fermented to create a liquor that possesses color, fragrance, and flavor no different from ordinary wine;

yet, because it does not cause intoxication, the Buddha permitted its consumption in a private place. However, if it possesses the color, fragrance, and flavor of wine and causes intoxication when drunk, one must be dealt with according to the law.
Offense.
Regarding the first section of the initial analysis of the conditions for "improper time," first the substance of the medicine is established; now, below, the timing and circumstances are indicated.

If the three qualities of color, fragrance, and taste are complete but it does not cause intoxication, drinking it is permitted. If the qualities are incomplete yet it causes intoxication, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (light offense), because the objective conditions are not fully met.
One must not arrive late.

One should not accept a beverage on this day and drink it on the following day, because by doing so one transgresses the proper time; furthermore, drinking what remains from the previous night constitutes the offense of consuming what has been touched overnight.

Regarding the two [types of] *dvitīya-kāla* (afternoon) transgressions: if one has already consumed [the food], touched it, or further failed to receive [it as a formal gift], yet does not drink it, there is no offense.

The text states that "it is clear like the color of water"; this refers to fruit juice (*pāna*) because it fears being mixed with dregs and sediment. Thus, among various fruits, there are naturally clear juices;
when first pressed and filtered, they are not without admixture, but after settling for a long time, they become pure and clear, distinct from the [impurities] of the improper time.
Among the three [types of liquids], "dian" (淀) is pronounced "dian" and also means dregs or sediment.
When water drops are pure, they constitute a "pure flavor"; thus, although the text mentions them in the context of fermented liquors (*jang*), their meaning extends to all four medicinal substances.

Just as clothing must be folded and marked with dots to change its color, and food must have water drops added to it for the sake of a pure flavor, so too must footwear have [a mark] made by a person.
To wear [robes] is for the purpose of destroying what is considered "good"; thus, all such things are nothing other than skillful means for destroying the self.
Otherwise, if the afflictions were powerful, independent, and habitually indulged in, how could one achieve the state of forgetting the self? Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:
"Just as sugarcane is not purified by fire and its clear juice is not purified by water—one falls into transgression for each [instance of failure]."

Among the four [purifications], the first indicates the purification of the mind; while the text is specific, its meaning is universal. All four medicinal substances must be purified with water drops.

As an example provided below, new clothing must be sprinkled with drops, and new sandals must be worn for seven steps. As shown below in summary, this demonstrates skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the forgetting of attachment;
"attachment" here refers to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). As cited below as scriptural proof, failing to purify with fire results in the destruction of life and falling into ruin.

Regarding the second addition, the phrase "receiving [permission]" is missing from the text where it should be heard and permitted; now, judging by the meaning, since both the medicine and the illness are present, it may be understood according to the text.
However, if there is no illness, drinking a beverage at an improper time constitutes the offense of taking food at an improper time.

Second, regarding the addition of methods: first, "indicating what is missing" (*chishi quejin*) refers to the textual points that must be added; second, "preventing confusion" (*dianwen bi xia zhelan*) refers to the necessary additions to avoid ambiguity.
Third, regarding the method for receiving seven-day medicine, the *Pratyaya* (contextual conditions) section lists five types each of ghee (*sū*) and fat (*zhī*).

This is also based on the meaning of the text, which adds the method for receiving medicine as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "For wind disorders, one consumes oil; for cold disorders, honey; for heat disorders, ghee; [and so on] in equal portions."
The methods for preparing stone honey (śarkarā) and its extensive administration are detailed in the *Śīlavisara* and the *Karmavibhāṣā*.
Within the seven-day period, the initial conditions are shown: five types of ghee and fat each, namely the five starting with ghee and honey;

as for the five fats, they are those of the bear, badger, pig, donkey, and fish. Furthermore, below this, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clarifies the four types of illness in relation to the four medicinal substances, distinguishing the various types of ghee.

"Raw and cooked" constitutes five [categories]. "Equal portions" refers to the simultaneous outbreak of all three types of illness; this is seen in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) under the section on long-term medicines, and in the *Shichao* (Manual of the Precepts), in the chapter on the four medicines.

Regarding the fourth type of medicine, that which is taken for life (*jinxing-yao*), although various flavors are listed among its causes and conditions, those unfit to be used as food are collectively excluded from the category of lifelong sustenance.
Regarding the addition of medicinal ingredients that correspond to specific illnesses, this is permissible; since these are for life-long use, they are permitted to be pre-cooked as described above.
Because this has been explained extensively in the *Jìngdì* (Pure Ground) and the *Cáo* (Digest), it will not be repeated here, but may be cited when the occasion arises.

Regarding the four offenses— storing overnight (*antarā-sthāpana*), double-boiling (*dvir-pāka*), impure contact (*duṣṭa-sparśana*), and the fourth [offense]— the first section explains the conditions for the formal act (*karmavācanā*) throughout one's life, while the subsequent sections demonstrate the methods and clarify the rules concerning internal storage and the two types of cooking.

As for the ritual for the purification of robes (*cīvara-śuddhi-dharma*), its meaning is divided into six gates, such as the intent behind the prohibition, and so forth, as extensively cited in the *Śāstra*.

Regarding the six sections concerning the designation of the second robe (*dvitīya-cīvara*) for purification (*śuddhi*), they are: first, the intent of the regulation; second, the distinctions among donors;

third, whether the allowance for designating it applies universally; fourth, the ritual application of the designation; fifth, the survival or demise of the donor; and sixth, the differences in the loss of the ritual efficacy.

Now, regarding the term "extra robe" (*atireka-cīvara*) mentioned in the text, it refers to any garment remaining beyond the "one hundred and one" [allowable items]. It is not restricted to whether the dimensions are standard or non-standard;
in all cases, they must be formally dedicated (*paryavadāpana*). The text states that the length is eight finger-breadths and the width is four finger-breadths.

Using the Buddha’s finger-breadth—where the surface of a finger measures two inches—and measuring according to the scale of the Zhou dynasty of the Jiji period, this results in a length of one chi and six cun, and a width of eight cun. Anything less than these measurements [is considered an extra robe].
As stated in the text, it is also explained that there are merely differences in the degree of the offenses.

Regarding the first section of the "Explanation of the Conditions" (*yuan*), within the "Correct Explanation" (*zhengshi*), the first part demonstrates the meaning of the names: those of superior capacity require only three robes; those of middling capacity receive one hundred and one;

and those of inferior capacity are permitted to keep extra robes. Below this, the substance and measurement are clarified. First, the text provides a general heading; below that, there is a detailed explanation.

The first clarifies that which is of proper measure (pramāṇa), while the second clarifies that which is not of proper measure. "Proper" refers to an offense of expiation (pāyattika); "improper" refers merely to a transgression of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)—this is the distinction.

When people engage in such matters, they speak only of what is of proper measure; as for the rest, which is not of proper measure, they discard it and do not discuss it, even if it happens to be of proper measure.

Regarding measurements using the Tang *chi*, those that fall short are not mentioned; furthermore, while one may grasp their terminology through mutual contamination, one loses their actual substance.
Eight *chi* make one *zhu*, six feet make one pace, and three pecks make one *bō*—these are merely recited words. One must recognize the changes of the times.

In the initial section of the "Refutation of Errors," three faults are generally set forth: first, the reduction of measurements; second, the failure to mention the use of the *cubit* (*śa*), because one Chinese *chi* contains two additional inches;

and third, the lack of knowledge regarding the offense of transgression when the measurement is reduced. Regarding the fault of exceeding the day, if one says that what exceeds the measurement should be measured, that statement is likewise invalid.
Below this, there is a specific refutation of the *cubit* scale, noting that one has merely heard of its length and breadth.

Regarding the numerical values for measurements, one must understand that the length of a *chi* (cubit) differs between ancient and modern times; otherwise, one speaks of the form while losing the substance.
One should likewise take the examples of the *zhou* (forearm), the *bu* (step), and the *bo* (bowl-measure) as necessary illustrations to be understood.

In the text, the phrase "excluding the *pālikara*" (translated into Chinese as "auxiliary robe") refers to the one hundred and one articles of monastic equipment (*ekottarikapratyaya*) which must be maintained;

because they are not subject to the rules of pure giving (*śuddhadāna*), they are excluded. If one does not accept the one hundred and one articles but keeps surplus property, then according to the count of those one hundred and one, one commits an offense on each day [of possession], and such items are forfeited.
Since they lack the status of being "auxiliary," only the five items—the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and so forth—are excluded.

Regarding the first of these two [sections], the explanation of the text necessarily excludes those who keep extra robes; even the "one hundred and one" items include long robes and alms bowls, yet such prescribed objects are not included in this category.
As for the phrase "not present," it refers to robes that ought to be purified but fail to arrive due to circumstances, even though the previous person had permitted the robes.
The same principle applies to alms bowls that have not yet appeared.
Among these three cases, such examples include purchasing them for future use, intending to take them along, or storing them elsewhere.

This extends even to grains, rice, money, treasures, and so forth; since possessing these as provisions for the path is permitted by the Dharma, there is no prohibition against keeping them for oneself.

This causes others to give away items of a similar nature that would otherwise increase their faults; it does not allow for comparison with worldly people, but rather instructs them to know what is pure so as to generate wholesome states and eliminate greed.

Among these four points, the first clarifies the permission to keep [possessions]; the latter two demonstrate the opening of what is pure, the increase of similar faults, and why they should not be compared to worldly people, as those [faults] are appropriate for them.
Generating wholesome states refers to transforming others, while eliminating greed refers to oneself.
Regarding the second [section], "Requesting the Donor," within that, the *tattvaviśuddhi* (true purity) is rare and difficult to obtain;

since it does not involve the *paramparāviśuddhi* (successive purity), it belongs to oneself, as the respective ritual formulas (*adhikāra*) are applied to both. Therefore, this practice is frequently performed.
Regarding the second point, requesting from a donor: the first section concerns the fault of handling authentic items on behalf of the donor;
thus, one hopes for them to circulate extensively through successive transfers, yet even that is rare nowadays.

As for requesting from a donor, some do not establish this requirement, but rather point to it from afar, as in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, stating that one should seek [a donor] who maintains the precepts.

The phrase "Dowen (Much Learning) Qiu" refers to a formal request. Furthermore, that text states: "When one reaches the speech of a layperson, one knows that the Dharma of a bhikṣu does not permit the possession of money or treasures;

you shall serve as the donor. This is the explicit text. Those who carry out the practice must specifically designate [the recipient], for there must be a basis for the entrustment of one's intentions.
If there were both observance and violation, or survival and extinction, clearly discernible, it would allow for a general designation according to the clothing.
If the distinction between the defiled and the pure were not maintained, how could one propagate the Way?

In the subsequent section concerning the necessity of requesting [the preceptor], the initial part describes what is improper; it then points distantly to the actual practice, as illustrated by the following citation from the treatise which clarifies that both the monastic and the lay must request [ordination].
Although there is no explicit text regarding the request, the two characters "seek" (求) and "speak" (語) [imply this requirement].

This is precisely the meaning [of the rule]. If, when practicing this, one fails to encourage others to rely on it and instead merely points vaguely to a "pure master" (śuddhasthāna) at the last moment—since such masters are numerous and vary according to the specific garment, and because one does not know whether they are alive or dead—the distinction between what is defiled and what is pure cannot be maintained. If one cannot clarify this for oneself, how can one transform others?
If the propagation of the Way is conducted in such a manner, the Dharma will certainly not flourish.

Some say that when the presiding master of the *zhēnshí jìng* (true purity) passes away, one must change the person; yet since this involves successive substitutions rather than a direct face-to-face encounter, why labor over it?

Now, the explanation is that these two types of offerings differ from others in their ownership, but not in their essence; therefore, they are both uniformly requested early, ten days prior. The details are as extensive as in the *Chao*.

Next, regarding the section on "Modification," the first part sets forth the interpretations of others; the following portion refutes them as being incorrect, stating that it is improper to forcibly divide what belongs to the owner of the object.
In the actual application of the ritual, the two conditions of separation and combination follow the procedures prescribed in the treatise.

Regarding the three procedures for the face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*), the middle section explains that each individual case is termed "separation from many robes" (*bahuvastu-viveka*), while the general case is termed "combination" (*saṃyoga*).

This section consists of three parts: first, it clarifies that when a donor fears incurring the offense of possessing an excess of robes (*atireka-vastra*), they relinquish the items to another person for the sake of "successive purification" (*paramparā-pariśuddhi*);

if one does not mention this succession, it implies the items are truly [theirs] to keep. Second, following the words of the recipient of the purification, it clarifies the preceding statement regarding the acceptance of the property. Third, it explains the intermediate statement concerning the acceptance of the property.

Passing it on from one to another without claiming exclusive ownership, one should further intend to give it to a *viśuddhika-dātṛ* (a pure owner). Since the person is not granted permission unilaterally, the Vinaya requires that one seek the consent of the original owner.
One asks the original owner, "To whom do you give this? Once the three parties have settled upon a pure owner, it is necessary to provide a remote instruction.

Furthermore, one must record the original circumstances to clarify that [the object] was previously accepted; then, recording the previous command, one intends to entrust it to the pure owner, saying, "I am returning this to you; you should act as the pure owner. This is virtuous.
Regarding the phrase "wearing and using for the sake of protection," the additions and subtractions are made according to the occasion.
In the first section of the Dharma, there are three parts: first, the direct handover by the owner to the recipient; second, the formal interrogation of the owner by the recipient;

and third, the formal transfer to a designated steward (*viśuddha-dhāraka*) from a distance, involving the wearing, using, adding, or subtracting—alternatively, discarding or retaining—as appropriate.
There is no fixed rule; perhaps the bowl or the medicine may be changed accordingly.

This process of successive transfer is as follows: first, the original owner hands it over to a pure person—this is the first transfer of purity. Then, that pure person further entrusts it to another person from afar—this is the second transfer of purity.
Finally, the pure person, unaware of the circumstances, returns it to the original owner to serve as the object of the pure master’s ownership—this is the third.
"Turning" (*parivartana*) means purification; it refers to the intention to purify attachment entirely.
In the first part of the subsequent section, the text explains "turning from one thing and receiving another," which involves three persons and thus constitutes three turnings.
This concludes the demonstration of the meaning of the instruction.
Since the mind is difficult to exhaust when one intends to abandon the pure dharma for another person, it is permitted to effect a transfer to extend the time limit;

however, this must ultimately be finalized through formal declaration (*pratideśanā*). This is unlike the case of receiving robes, which is not for the purpose of transferring attachment, but rather for adding sacred qualities so that they may be worn on the body.
Therefore, mental reception (*cittotpāda*) and formal declaration are identical in this regard.

Next, within the first section of the "Mental Recollection" (cittānusmṛti), the initial part describes the provisional opening of the pure dharma (*śuddha-dharma*) without descending [into formal ritual].

Next, it distinguishes between receiving robes for permanent purification (*nitya-śuddhi*) and receiving them for transfer and wearing; this involves focusing the mind on one thing—discarding one and taking up another—which is utterly distinct [from ordinary practice]. "Wearing" here refers to attachment and clinging.
Regarding the phrase "giving at will among the five assemblies," this does not mean that one must record the names of the donors for each individual garment;
rather, since the pure owner through whom the gift is transmitted is not present face-to-face, it applies generally to all five assemblies.
As for the addition of the ritual formula, it is fixed such that one person must specifically designate the property as belonging to that [particular assembly] and maintain it as such.

In the first section of the initial passage concerning the successive stages, the text first negates improper views, fearing that one might think the assignment of robes is merely a matter of ad hoc recording at the time;

it then clarifies the correct procedure: because the request was not made face-to-face, the practice applies to all five assemblies, yet the ritual action (*karmavācanā*) is fixed upon a single person.
The text is divided into three parts: first, because one would exceed the limit by giving to that person from afar, it says "on the eleventh day";

next, because one returns to adding [the gift] without transgressing the regular allowance, it says "only ten days"; finally, fearing that one might commit an offense based on the teaching regarding the following day, it further states that giving to that person is permissible as before, since one would otherwise exceed the limit.

Next, regarding the three sections of the textual analysis: the initial and final acts are given away to others, while the intermediate act is taken back; these are performed in rotation rather than simultaneously.
The mention of the eleventh day indicates that [the gift] belongs to another.

Regarding the practice of discarding the old and receiving the new, changing them once every ten days, this is yet another distinct method. One robe is a "long robe" (*atireka-cīvara*), while the other is a "robe held in possession" (*parihāra-cīvara*).
They are received in rotation for purification; one must not exceed the limit. For one who maintains possession, there is no fear of committing the offense of keeping a long robe;
however, as for the robe being purified, it will otherwise exceed the limit. Therefore, the rule specifies that the exchange must take place within ten days.
Regarding the second point concerning mutual exchange, there is another distinction that differs from what preceded.

This refers to the case where one who has not performed the *śuddhikaraṇa* (purification rite) may, in order to avoid the fault of possessing an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), receive the two robes by rotation without needing to perform the purification rite; however, if one who possesses an extra robe adds the reception of the purification rite, it may be applied according to the previous rule.
These two types of purity are also called "open permissions" (*kṣānti*) when, within the boundary (*sīmā*), there are no people present;

even if there are those who are ignorant or obstructed, or those who do not seek [the requisites] with regularity, it is difficult to obtain them. One may only rely on the aforementioned ten-day period to add to their use. However, if one suddenly travels elsewhere and returns during the night, one has not yet obtained this permission.

Regarding the three types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) performed within the assembly, when two persons face each other and there is no third person present, the prohibition against ignorance is waived; that is, it is not considered a formal offense (*āpatti*) for lack of knowledge.

However, if there is a fellow resident whose formal act has not yet been concluded, one must wait for them according to the principle that the rite is incomplete; thus, this is not a case where the restriction is waived.
In the *Suvarṇa-śāli-viśuddhi-dharma*,
"pure gold" refers to the seven precious substances and the five grains;

it cites the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* to explain that what is designated as "purified" (*viśuddha*) refers exclusively to gifts offered according to the Dharma from outside [the monastic community], and not to items obtained through seeking or other means.

Although it is said that impure items do not constitute [a valid gift] because they were acquired through early transgressions, this is not so: gold, money, and precious objects are permitted as the price for robes when sent by laypeople according to the Vinaya;
grains such as rice and other cereals are permitted when offered to a bhikṣu on the road according to the Vinaya;

and mottled beans and rice are permitted to be accepted as a gift when managed and stored by a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure steward). Thus, these various types of goods, though accumulated in abundance, serve as a means of sustenance at the appropriate time.

The opening of the section on "Listening to Explanations" is as follows: In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, it is permitted to give pure offerings to those of sincere faith.

In the first sub-section of the commentary, there is first a distinction regarding the pursuit of what is not the Dharma; this refers to wrong livelihood and impurity, such as engaging in trade and commerce, all of which constitute prior transgressions and thus do not enter into the category of purity.
Below, the text demonstrates what is in accordance with the Dharma by citing two passages from the *Kaiwen* (Opening Text), both of which are without exception [permissible].

The *Jidao yi jia* (Price of Robes for Deliverance) states that money, treasures, and currency notes—whether according to the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras—all must be given to others and not kept by oneself;
this clarifies that one should protect the Dharma in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* so as to preserve the Sangha-treasure and ensure that the Buddha-dharma remains in the world.

As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the fourfold criteria for seeking a trustworthy person are likewise [applied here]; it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to personally handle money, because doing so would corrupt his mental conduct.
The rest is as clarified in the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*, which cites the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The reason why the five assemblies (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs) may not act as donors of money or precious objects is that, according to the prohibitions of the precepts, such transactions should not be carried out.

Second, regarding the distinction between the primary subject and the middle [category]: because the two precepts concerning the possession and handling of wealth are established as common regulations for all five groups of practitioners, the commentary states that "wealth other than money and precious objects" refers specifically to clothing and property.

As for the statement that "money and precious objects, once purified through the act of giving (net-shi), can be easily exchanged for clothing and other items without requiring further purification," this is because at the initial acquisition of such wealth, it has already entered [the state of being purified].
Because it is pure, having now been exchanged for something that is not extraneous, it is inherently free from attachment; this is because it is inherently free from defilement.
Among the three types of pure wealth, exchanging clothes is pure by virtue of its original nature.
Furthermore, it is cited that if a *saṃghāṭī* robe’s donor dies within ten days, it has no owner;
this principle applies to both monastic and lay donors and must always be kept in mind.
Regarding the first section among the four, the commentary cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to clarify that secular rulers follow the same principles as those for monastic robes;
since the essential meaning of the two types of owners—real and nominal—is identical, it states, "This applies universally," and so forth.

Question: Regarding the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, it does not state that wealth obtained from purified jewels becomes purified. If the owner of the jewels dies, is the wealth and clothing purified? Answer:

Since the distinction between the status of the two owners—layperson or monastic—is easily changed, the principle for purifying wealth requires it to be passed through successive hands. However, because this is not "obtained from outside," it is permitted that the text does not mention it.
If the owner of the jewels has no one to whom they can be returned, one must still rely on purification; since there is no one to whom they can be entrusted, they remain as accumulated hoards.

[The text] is extensive. Next, regarding the question of how it is when the master who exchanges clothes with pure wealth dies, in the initial part of the response, it first clarifies that the previous [cases] are not mentioned as necessarily [applying here],
and below, it correctly resolves the doubt.
In the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, regarding "purity through combination," it refers to the three types of purity—staining, sewing, and washing—which together constitute purity;

if even one of these is missing, there is a *pātayantika* offense, and if two are missing, there is a *duṣkṛta*. This is as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: sewing that is not performed according to the Dharma must involve piercing [the cloth) to avoid the three faults.

Among the five [types of robes], it does not mention "pure" (śuddha) as one; "not stained" (anupalipta) refers to the second [type]. "Auspicious" (kalyāṇa) means that the cloth has not yet been purified by being sewn upon a pure garment.
Furthermore, among the five [types], there is the "intermediate purification" (antar-śuddhi): one dyes and sews it onto a garment of a proper color.

Because the source (the cloth) and the recipient (the garment) can merge into a single entity, it is called "harmonious" (saṃghāta). Below, this cites the text on sewing from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-vibhāṣā*.
Section Five: The Various Methods for the Uposatha (Poṣadha).
Regarding the title: it is called "various" (*zhū*) because it refers to the collective, individual, and distinct divisions of the *prātimokṣa* recitation.

Now, the Way relies on conditions for its cultivation, and practice is accumulated through causes; thus, one is able to purify and tranquilize body and mind, thereby severing the burdens of affliction.
With great compassion, he spreads transformation and extends his voice and teachings to move and benefit all beings, prioritizing wisdom and benefit.
First, he bestows the precepts and the Three Refuges as the foundation for the myriad practices; next, he provides them with clothing and medicine as the means of gathering and aiding them;

finally, he establishes the teachings and opens wide the path of propagation as the work of benefiting others according to their needs. When these three are complete, the intention to transcend the world is preserved.
Thus it is.

In the exposition of the meaning, the initial general account of the conditions for cultivation and realization refers to the causes such as robes and medicine, which constitute the reception of the precepts;

the subsequent conduct of body and mind in purity and tranquility constitutes the subduing of karma; and the severing of entanglements constitutes the destruction of delusions and the attainment of stillness.
This is a detailed exposition corresponding to the various chapters below. Since the teaching is proclaimed through sound, it is called "the teaching of sound.

Because ordinary and ignorant people are stubborn and deluded, they must be moved [toward awakening]. The root of the myriad practices is the essence of reception (*pratigraha*). The conditions for gathering and saving are the two types of provisions, internal and external.
The activities that benefit according to needs extend throughout the six chapters below. When these three are complete, it is like constructing a palace.
The first is like the foundation; the second is like the walls and battlements; the third is like the courtyard and buildings—these can be understood by comparison.
Within the main body of the text, this is the fourth section, which is further divided into two parts: first, the conditions (*pratyaya*), and second, the Dharma (*dharma*).
Regarding the explanation of the heading: according to the text, it constitutes five sections, but according to its meaning, it resides in four.

Within the preceding section on conditions, although many are confused by what they hear regarding the recitation of the precepts, I have briefly set forth this summary; the detailed citations are as clarified in the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü Shu Yichao*).
The commentary on the *Yuanbiaozhi* states that because its profound doctrinal intent was not fully elucidated, many were confused regarding its meaning.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* records that before the Buddha permitted the *poṣadha-karman* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* during the assembly, non-Buddhists mocked them, saying, "We still possess superior dharmas;
do the bhikṣus have none? It was for this reason that the Buddha first authorized the bhikṣus to recite the precepts and perform the *poṣadha*. This is recorded in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The King of Madhyadeśa desired that the bhikṣus assemble to hear the Dharma and that they interact with one another as do the various non-Buddhists;
the Buddha consequently permitted this.

To illustrate the first section of the *Madhyama-āgama*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* describes the assembly of the seat, wherein monks of all ranks—senior and junior—gather to perform the formal rites and engage in doctrinal discussion.
Regarding the term "opening through causes," this refers to opening [the practice] in response to derision; it establishes a rule that becomes a formal regulation (*prajñapti*).

In the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, specifically the *Poṣadha-khandhaka*, it is stated that because the King saw the gathering of non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) giving rise to wholesome states, he ordered them to emulate this.
However, because the Dharma teachings were first opened, there must necessarily be a gradual process. Among the ancient Buddhas' path and Dharma, what teaching is not present?
It is simply that the traces of the teaching were initially situated within other paths; therefore, they were collected together to form a unified transformation.

When non-Buddhists grasped the superficial aspects of these practices and followed them according to their outward forms, the Buddha subsequently established regulations to exhaust the fundamental principles, causing the mind to be purified and the physical form to respond to the work of the Way. Thus, it was done.

In the first section of the following division, it is narrated that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* was subject to external criticism; the *Caturvargika-vinaya* arose from the King’s instruction. One should know that the beginning of this teaching originated from the King’s command.
It should be understood that the exposition of the *Pravāraṇā* is the constant dharma of the ancient Buddhas. Because the teachings possess formal traces, they are called "traces of the teaching.

The compilers intended to collect those practices to establish the rules of our own Dharma; through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they sought to gather those of heterodox groups and cause them to take refuge in the True Dharma.
Ordinary people of little capacity do not understand this. Next, I shall clarify that while their intentions differ regarding secondary matters, they may temporarily appear to agree on the principle;
yet fundamentally, they ultimately aim for liberation. Though they seem similar, they are distinct, as vast as the distance between heaven and earth.

In the text, it quotes a treatise stating that "poṣadha" is the phonetic transcription from the Sanskrit original; this is translated according to its meaning as "abandoning evil and realizing wholesome dharmas.
This is generally the case.

Regarding the explanation of the name and meaning, the initial passage on abandoning evil and realizing the wholesome is fully cited in the commentary as "abandoning all evils and unwholesome [states]."
This refers to karma and afflictions; "attaining white dharmas" refers to untainted merit; and "the ultimate brahmacarya" refers to the fruit of no-more-learning.
Since the translations found in various texts do not exceed this meaning, it is said that the general principle is as follows.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is stated that even up to the male and female lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*) and those of the ninety-six kinds of renunciant practitioners all receive the *poṣadha* three times every half-month.
Thus, the text says: "The Buddha taught that purity is called *poṣadha*. This is just as the *vinaya* states:
"One who has committed an offense is not permitted to recite the precepts or hear the precepts," and further, regarding the dragon girl receiving the *poṣadha*, this refers to the eight [precepts].
The precepts (*śīla*) are the same as the fast (*upavāsa*); therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that "receiving the *poṣadha* protection" refers to the eightfold fast.
It further states that "food for the *poṣadha*" is simply the food for the pure fast. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) says that the *poṣadha* is also the eightfold fast.

The *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners) states: "The term *poṣadha* means 'pure dwelling' (*jìngzhù*) in the language of Qin; it is also called 'nurturing' (*chángyǎng*). This concludes the section on the fast according to the Wen [commentary].
Emperor Xuan compiled the *Jingzhuzi* (The Son Who Abides in Purity) in twenty fascicles, a great treatise on the ritual procedures for the *poṣadha*, including its vows, aspirations, and hymns.

It is intended for those who require extensive mental cultivation. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that severing transgressions and severing delusions so that body and speech are pure is the meaning of *poṣadha*;
sweeping the hall and arranging the seats is the practice of *poṣadha*. The same applies to the *pravāraṇā*.
In the first section of the following analysis, the *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe) and the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony) apply to both monastics and laypeople alike;

because they assemble every half-month on the third day to cultivate wholesome qualities, it is said that "the three receptions" and "the four divisions" must be free of transgressions before one is permitted to hear the exposition. These are nevertheless termed the "eight precepts," all of which carry the sense of purity.

In the *Abhidharmakośa*, the restraint of the precepts is divided into the protection of the three types of action (*trividha-karma-yoga*). Since *poṣadha* means "summoning food," it is known that the name applies broadly and does not refer exclusively [to monastics].

The exposition of the *Śīla-saṃvara* (Precepts for Pure Abiding) is as explained in the two aforementioned texts. "Pure Abiding" (*śuddha-vihāra*) takes the sense of distancing oneself from evil; "Nurturing" (*poṣadha*) takes the sense of generating goodness.

Xiao Ziliang of the Southern Qi dynasty was enfeoffed as Prince of Jingling and posthumously titled Wenxuan. His name, "Jingzhu zi" (Son of Pure Abiding), is derived precisely from the aforementioned scripture.
It is traditionally said to consist of twenty fascicles and primarily elucidates the *poṣadha* rites for laypeople; however, it has not yet been seen.
The discourse by Mother Wen on transgressions explains that the meaning of the lower fetters of karma all returns to purity;
the *prātimokṣa* (self-restraint) is likewise as explained above.

Therefore, in compiling these various texts, one must understand their fundamental intent; it is not merely a matter of hearing the teachings and failing to practice them, which would be of no benefit.
Of the three [sections], the first two lines conclude the preceding seven segments, showing that non-action is purity, which is precisely the original intent;
the latter two lines issue a formal admonition.

It is stated in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) that the reason the method of precept-observance establishes the True Dharma so that it remains indestructible is precisely because the Saṃgha is pure and free from faults.

Regarding transgressions, one should seek confession for any offenses committed; by universally abiding in pure conduct and maintaining the purity of the precepts, concentration and wisdom can be expected to converge.
It is precisely because this continuity remains unbroken that the characteristics [of the path] endure for a long time, and through this, they are widely propagated.

In the first section of the commentary on the "Abiding in the Maintenance [of the Dharma]," it is stated that the three trainings follow one another in their entry into the Way, all beginning with the precepts.
Thus we know that if the precepts are preserved, the Way proceeds; if the precepts are discarded, the Way perishes. This is indeed the natural order of things.

If, when the time for the teaching arrives, one lacks the intention to repent and purify oneself, or if the transgression is such that it cannot be repented of, or if one does not rely upon confession while others in the assembly hear the teaching and their minds reach a state of realization—yet one’s own afflictions, agitation, and distress increase because of unavoidable circumstances, or because one does not come out of principle, or out of shame for being excluded from the count—then hearing the teaching in such instances is insufficient for sustaining the Dharma;
or, if one hears nothing at all, a lifetime will pass in vain. Such are the examples.
Both are contrary to the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Within these two [categories], the first describes four types of non-compliance: (1) ignorance and failure to contemplate repentance; (2) grave offenses that cannot be repented of;

(3) failing to repent according to the Dharma—these are equally heard to be fundamentally contrary to the original regulations; and (4) not hearing [the teachings] at all, let alone seeking to repent.
To summarize as follows:

Nevertheless, even for those with defilements, if upon hearing [the teaching] they give rise to shame and remorse and constantly contemplate pure faith, it is appropriate to speak of their original nature;

however, if despite being stained by the dust of the world they fail to cultivate future practice, then speaking [of their nature] would be of no benefit. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* says: "One should examine oneself every half-month."
If one who has committed an offense performs repentance before those of like mind, is that not purification?
Among the three [sections], the first describes the offender’s deliberation over even a speck of dust; "immediate transgression" refers to the subsequent cause and effect.
Since it is said that [such confession] is called "clearing away faults," one knows it is of no benefit; therefore, the following passage cites an exhortation.

Regarding the textual analysis, there are three parts. First, from the perspective of the persons involved; second, regarding the aforementioned *saṃgha*, it is divided into two: the detailed and the abbreviated. Within the detailed section, there are again two parts:

from the beginning up to the point where the *bhikṣuṇī* appoints a person, this concerns the preliminary ritual for the recitation of the precepts; and from the instruction of the *bhikṣuṇīs* downward, this concerns the ritual for the seat during the recitation of the precepts.

Regarding the former (the preliminary ritual), it is divided according to the text into the sections for monks and nuns. Regarding the meaning of the *saṃgha*, there are four points: first, the time; second, the place; third, the number [of members]; fourth, the qualifications.
The different methods for gathering the assembly (1), the requisites for the *poṣadha* assembly (2), and various miscellaneous necessities (3) are explained in detail in the *Śāstra*;
when the time comes, they shall be cited and expounded. For now, we shall interpret them according to the text, dividing them into three sections.

Regarding the first section of the *Saṃgha-śīla-vyākhyāna* (Sūtra on the Monastic Precepts), concerning the four gates of timing—namely, the three days before and after the meal, and the day and night—the assembly is convened by striking the bell according to the boundaries, as set forth in the *Vyākhyāna*.
While this second gate is absent there, the third, the "Proper Ritual for the Recitation," is present;
however, it is merely indicated in general terms below.
Regarding the initial method for the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), it is to inform and command clearly. If one does not announce it in advance, there may be confusion;

furthermore, regarding the necessity of confession and purification, one must contemplate and recognize the doubts, and know that at the time of assembly, matters must be handled with due care for this reason.

In the first section of the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), there are two purposes: first, to cause [the monks] to reflect upon what they have transgressed;
and second, to cause them to know that the time, place, and ritual procedures must necessarily be present—hence it is said, "the matter exists."

Regarding the statement that "the three days are listed," this refers to the fact that while the black and white fortnights differ and their regional customs vary, all three are equally valid and orthodox;

they are established according to usage and may be followed as one wishes. If these three [specific dates] were not permitted, why would the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) also be performed on three days?
Furthermore, the *Vinaya-mūla-sūtra* itself states: "On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days"—this refers to the three days regardless of whether they are the black or white fortnight.

Regarding the *poṣadha*: the first two [methods] are for laypeople, consisting of preaching the Dharma and bestowing the refuges; the latter one is for those on the Path, consisting of purifying the mind and reciting the precepts.
As for the mention of the sixteenth day, this is an extension permitted due to difficulties and is not intended for regular use.

In the commentary on the text, first, the reason why [the observance] applies to all three [types of months] is clarified: because the "black moon" (the waning phase) ends with the shortest day and lacks a fifteenth day, regional differences exist as each country follows its own usage;
thus, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* increases the count by three and lists all three days, which is cited here as the authoritative basis.

Next, the erroneous views are refuted: there are those who insist that the half-month observance must necessarily fall on the fifteenth day, and this passage addresses them. Furthermore, the following section will definitively establish the correct position.

The *Vinaya-mūla* cites another text stating that the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*) are merely for illustrative purposes; the intent is to clarify that while the fourteenth day is the primary day, the sixteenth is not.
Furthermore, it explains that occasions such as kings or bandits provide exemptions, yet these too are not considered primary days. If this is so, may the two days before and after be used?
Answer: The fifteenth day is the constant, fixed day. However, if there are other circumstances, both the preceding and following days are permissible.
The reason one listens to the announcement of the *sthavira* is that the Buddha himself spoke of it when he was present to admonish the various classes of beings;

now, as this is the position being filled, it is not spoken of otherwise. The person currently making the announcement is mostly the *karmadāna*, for the *sthavira* does not personally undertake this task unless commissioned.
As for the person who recites the precepts (*poṣadha-vācaka*), they were originally the *sthavira*, but later the capacity for the role was opened to others; this too is a gradual development.
Of the two [sections], the first explains the intent of the teaching. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that a single elder shall take the place of the Buddha;

now, below, the matter of receiving the elder’s command and transmitting it to inform the Saṃgha is determined. Below, the analogy of the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is cited, by which the meaning may be understood.

Regarding the mention of a specific location in the text: because there are many halls within a single boundary (*sīmā*), it is necessary to designate a fixed place so as not to allow for confusion or disorder.

Among the three types [of monasteries], in the Indian Buddhist temples, a separate Precept Hall (*śīla-śālā*) was established; the text states that even if the hall is large and one regularly uses the same one, one must still formally announce it.
