Instructing those who are young and fully ordained in the etiquette regarding seniors and juniors, they must not act with levity or recklessness. Those who prepare pure water do so in anticipation of newcomers;

using *śalākā* grass as counting sticks (*cū*), they employ them for the purpose of conducting affairs and knowing whether the assembly is small or large when intending to attend the *poṣadha* gathering.
The rest is as indicated in the text.

In the first section of the "Correct Explanation" (Zhengshuo), there are three parts. First, regarding the upper part: since one must receive instruction from above and rely upon it below, it is said that there is a formal protocol for its arrangement.
Second, regarding the provision of pure water: this is intended for those who arrive first; that is, when guests come to wash their hands, it must be prepared beforehand.

According to the standards, this is not like the ordinary water-offering implements used within the monastic community. Third, regarding the *śalākā*: it is translated as "counting-stick," and thus it is employed according to the specific task at hand.

Regarding the reason why it is said that [the teaching] is not opened at all times: as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states, "The Dharma of the past Buddhas remains in the world for as long as the pure bhikṣus do not let the method of reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) fall into ruin. The same applies to the future and the present.

Therefore, in the subsequent section clarifying the main point, a bhikṣu asks the Buddha about the rise and fall, and the duration and brevity, of the Buddha-dharma throughout the three periods of time;

the Buddha answers him by using the observance of the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) as a criterion for verifying its survival or extinction. Nowadays, those who practice this dharma in the world [number] one hundred...
It is not the case that one or two individuals act in opposition to the Dharma; we know that the Buddha-Dharma will not remain in the world for long.

The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "Even if those of dull faculties and ignorance encounter difficulties such that they cannot go to another monastery to hear the precepts, the *Poṣadha* should be recited briefly, saying:
'Commit no evil,' and so forth."

Next, I shall cite evidence from the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* regarding the two conditions that permit abbreviation: first, those of dull faculties who are unable to recite; second, those who cannot proceed due to obstacles.
It is said that while the four lines are abbreviated, their meaning is profound. Although the Vinaya Piṭaka is extensive, it does not go beyond this.
How much more so for the Buddha-dharma as a whole—it is not only the Vinaya Piṭaka that is thus.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if four monks performing the *poṣadha* together are unable to benefit one another—that is, if they are unable to recite the entirety—they should recite four, three, two, or one section, down to a single verse or the introductory formula.
As for the remainder, they should chant what is commonly heard. If one does not recite even a single section while performing the *poṣadha*, it is a violation of the *vinaya*.
If the entire assembly is unable to benefit one another, the *sthavira* (elder) should go outside the boundary and perform the *poṣadha* through mental recitation (*cittena poṣadha*).
Within the boundary of the three persons, there are three recitations. If each person recites one chapter, it should be taught to one who is intelligent;

this is beneficial. When one forgets during recitation, others may orally transmit it, but one must not recite it repeatedly, recite it in reverse order, or recite it by combining sections. If something is forgotten, it may be supplemented.

The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] has three initial sections for opening the brief exposition: from the many to the few, they are opened in sequence; "raising the next" refers to opening the specific rules;
"if below, three" refers to opening the cases of forgetting, reciting over again, and repeating a chapter.

"Reciting in reverse" means receding backward from the end to the beginning; "reciting together" means two people chanting in unison; "obtaining what was forgotten" means reciting again that which was omitted.
Furthermore,
among the four divisions [of the Vinaya], when a person is sent to another monastery to recite them, they recite one entire section at a time; as the time for the next arrives,
they continue the recitation from where they left off.
The four divisions were each studied and successively joined together to form a single volume.
If this is so, why is it not held and read amidst such confusion? The answer is that both the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts) and the *Karmavācanā* (Formal Rituals) are both sacred teachings.

Just as worldly speech says "let [the text] be seen," one must hold the written text; what is transmitted today still follows the Buddha’s era, so how can one refuse to hold it when it is being recited?

Furthermore, even in this world, incantations and arts require recitation and retention to achieve their results; how much more so must one rely on the sacred regulations without seeking divergent interpretations?
If one constantly performs daily rites by merely reading the texts and following the procedures, other methods may still fail, but the fault is slight.
However, regarding the single matter of receiving the precepts, to fail oneself and thereby bring shame upon others is profound and utterly unacceptable.
In the response that clarifies doubts, the first part demonstrates the intent behind the establishment [of the rules]: originally, the *śīla* (precepts) were intended for general recitation;

because they are combined with *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), the admonitions of sovereigns and parents serve as sufficient examples to show that the meaning does not consist merely in reading texts or chanting mantras for empowerment. Next, the section on "time" refutes temporal errors and clarifies the application of *karmavācanā* and *śīla* recitation;
however, regarding other dharmas, one only incurs an offense against oneself, whereas the procedure for receiving the precepts causes others to be free from fault.
Regarding those for whom the precepts are too profound to be easily mastered, one should admonish them to reform their transgressions.
Within the category of those who have committed similar offenses, there is a distinction between those who recognize their guilt and those who harbor doubts.

How does one recognize a simultaneous offense? Although the world does not hold others accountable for transgressions they commonly practice, such as accepting money or precious gems, [one must nevertheless acknowledge the fault].

To receive bribes obtained through performing services for others, practicing the Way, prostrating before the Buddha, or reciting the sutras, and then to sit at ease with the assembly while knowing it is wrong and accept them—this constitutes one offense common to the Saṃgha.
Therefore, the Vinaya states that those who commit the *naiḥsargika* (relinquishment) offenses are precisely such persons.

Alternatively, depending on the specific individual and the particular offense committed, the names and categories may differ; yet when weighed against one another, their transgressions are equally impure. Although they are not... [the text continues].
Regarding those who have committed the same offense together, it should be explained that the principle is to confess and reveal the transgression in its entirety, whereby it is extinguished.

Second, the explanation of confession and revelation. Within the section on "recognizing the offense during confession," the first part consists of two sections: first, raising the question; and second, providing the general explanation.

Furthermore, this has two parts: first, concerning the collective community committing the same offense; and second, regarding the current assembly where, having passed noon, one accepts money or handles precious objects at an improper time.

One may know this by drawing parallels from scriptural citations; alternatively, the latter two cases concern individual offenses committed separately, both of which are subject to general confession (*sāmānya-deśanā*).

Regarding the conditions specified in the text, "the Sangha assembles for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*," this refers to a situation where time is pressing and there is no opportunity to go outside for confession.
As the Vinaya states: "If one has committed an offense together with others prior to the recitation, they should go to a nearby assembly of pure monks and designate a person [to represent them]."

In the past, one would go to confess and upon returning to the monastery, perform the confession in sequence; the meaning of opening [the practice] for "informing" (*kai-haku*) now is different from that.

In the first section of the commentary on the text, it is first clarified that this is only permitted when [death] is imminent; next, it distinguishes that at other times it is not allowed, as the entire assembly would incur an offense.
One person must be pure through confession to be fit to serve as the *pratideśanīya* (confessor).
Regarding those who have committed an offense and are not permitted to preach: the essence of the precepts is purity, intended to restrain one from transgression;
if one now sinks into it oneself, how can one rescue others?
Therefore, this is not permitted. Among the four subsequent prohibitions, the first refers to one whose conduct is deficient and thus unfit to instruct others.

Regarding those who have committed an offense and are not permitted to hear [the recitation]: when the introduction (*nidāna*) is being spoken, if one’s words and demeanor are entirely in accord with their transgression, that person should confess;

if they are pure, they should remain silent. Now, if you harbor your offenses within your mind while maintaining a composed and upright appearance, you are merely deceiving the worthy and the sages, which is a grave burden upon yourself and is utterly improper.
Second, since the substance [of the offense] is defiled, it is incompatible with pure teachings.
One may not perform repentance before an offender, for when sins accumulate, one must contemplate their removal; thus, citing scriptural evidence to counteract them is already insufficient.
Furthermore, it is also improper because if there is already a flaw, there is no way to dispel the accumulated burden.
Third, regarding the confession that does not distinguish between the impurity of the object and the impurity of the cleansing:
one who has committed an offense is not permitted to receive the absolution of another’s transgression. This is because the confession is termed "arising from above" (upper-arising);
since it cannot serve as the basis for generating the subsequent severance of defilement in another, it is prohibited by the regulations.

Fourth, one does not personally reflect upon one's faults; this is called "the confession for treating the illness of a non-ill person," which is known as the *uttarāpatti* (higher offense) in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Since these four meanings exist, one should perform the formal declaration (*jñapti*) according to the opening text and confess together, as this constitutes the purification rite (*viśuddhi-dharma*).

In the section on the conclusion and demonstration, it is asked: since there is no pure person present, when performing a *śukla-vinaya* (white confession), must the person who performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*) also be pure?

The answer is: since it is said that if the entire assembly has committed an offense, they must all confess together, there must necessarily be one pure person; therefore, it should naturally be performed face-to-face (*pratyekam-śiras*).
The Vinaya texts do not state that one must perform further repentance; it is clear that the original offense is extinguished along with it. How is this known?

Repentance for an offense is performed before another person so as to have them witness one’s flaws and burdens. Now, by making a formal announcement (*jñapti*), everything is made transparent without the slightest concealment.

Since neither party is pure, this serves as the condition for removal, like covering white offenses with grass. Disputes over offenses are likewise extinguished together, as both possess the characteristic of an offense and are thus exposed toward one another. Therefore, this was composed.

It is stated that all offenses of the *sthūlātyaya* category and below are entirely eliminated by this confession; however, as for the two higher categories of offenses, because they require specific procedures involving the Saṃgha or individuals, they are not discussed here.

Regarding the first of these three [sections], the initial portion establishes the judgment based on the preceding rules, while the subsequent part raises a question regarding the underlying intent. First, it describes the reason why one must confess before the assembly without concealment, so that the mind may be purified.

The removal of offenses follows this principle. Before making the formal announcement, one must necessarily inform the assembly, feeling shame and self-reproach, and disclose the offense to the Saṃgha.

This is as illustrated by the following examples; since the underlying meaning of the "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) method for settling disputes is largely the same, the following excludes redundancy: with the exception of the two preceding categories, all other offenses may be confessed.

Second, regarding offenses arising from doubt: this doubt arises from the action itself and must necessarily be removed by means of another person. For example, if one eats gruel at dawn thinking it is a formal meal, and then eats again at midday, there is doubt as to whether an offense has been committed;
in such a case, one must wait for a pure person (*śuci-pudgala*) before the status of the offense can be determined.

If the body is merely exposed and free of blemish, it should conform to the rules of purity; therefore, although the original offense remains unextinguished due to the mere exposure, it does not constitute a transgression because the matter was not yet fully understood.

The name "confession and severance" (*sāntana*) differs from the previous "informing the consciousness" (*jñapti-vijñāpana*); it involves reporting one's state of mind and the matter of the offense so that there is no doubt. This is similar to the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another), with this specific distinction.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If the entire Saṃgha commits the same offense together, they should perform a single *jñapti* toward the Saṃgha of the four directions and subsequently perform the confession according to the Dharma.
Thus, we know that [the offense] is not extinguished [by mere confession].

Regarding the first of the doubtful offenses (*saṃśaya-pāpattika*): it describes the characteristics of the transgression. When rice gruel that resembles a formal meal—meaning that which is thick and viscous—is first taken out of the cauldron, if the substance forms characters as it emerges, it constitutes a formal meal.
Because one has not yet asked a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) whether it is permissible, and the matter remains undecided, it is called "doubtful.

Although it is not lost even if left exposed, this differs from the previous case. The passage below cites scriptural evidence; "the four directions of the Saṃgha" refers to the point where the offense is incurred.
This is a disclosure.
Those who follow the teachings nowadays say, "I am not pure; it is improper for me to listen," yet this is a failure to understand that the practice of the teaching is not in vain.

The Vinaya is not for nothing; it is surely for the sake of future lives. One should only fear that the offense is too grave to be settled by a mere *jñapti* (simple announcement); even if grave, one must undergo training and repentance.
If one is still called "pure," how could one allow the body to die with all [impurities] collected?

In the first section of the following chapter, it is described that due to the initial false attachment and the shame of one’s own impurity, one consequently refuses to hear the precepts. Below this, the folly is rebuked and the gravity of the teaching is emphasized;

specifically, the four *ānantarya* offenses are grave and are termed "repentance through study" (*śikṣamāṇā*). For those who commit offenses without reflecting on them, the karma accumulates until death.

"To follow the consciousness and depart" means to collect [the transgression] in its entirety. Question: Now, these sinners believe they have not committed an offense, yet bystanders know for certain that they should be censured; if one wishes to raise this issue, it would contravene the teaching. According to the Vinaya text, one "must not coerce someone into repentance. How should one respond? Answer: There is a twofold significance here. First, regarding the belief that there is no offense: if the mind is pure, one hears the precepts. Second, regarding the bystanders' knowledge: if the mind is impure, one does not hear the precepts. Thus, whether one hears the precepts or not depends entirely on the state of one's own mind. Therefore, the Vinaya prohibits coercing others into repentance because one cannot force another to purify their mind. If one were to coerce them, it would be like trying to make a deaf person hear music by shouting at them—their ears remain closed and they do not perceive the sound. Consequently, the Vinaya stipulates that one must not compel others to repent. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the Vinaya also states that one must not obstruct others from repenting. This is because if one obstructs them, it is as if one were blocking a deaf person from hearing music; thus, the Vinaya prohibits obstructing others from repenting. This is the principle. Therefore, when a bystander knows of a transgression, they may inform the offender, but they must not coerce them into repentance. Among the four [purifications], sweeping, sprinkling water, and offering incense and flowers demonstrate that these are not merely routine tasks, but serve to stir the minds of sentient beings so that they revere the Dharma and honor the Path.

Regarding the question of who recites the *Poṣadha* for the Saṃgha: one person presides over the recitation while the rest remain silent and seated below; this applies down to the *Pratyekapratideśanīya* (confession in pairs), where each individual expresses their purity.

This is because the formal position within the Saṃgha possesses a powerful capacity for accomplishment. The announcement (*jñapti*) and recitation of the *Poṣadha* apply universally to all four directions; however, the specific [confessions] are distinct.
Since human strength is weak, one should simply manifest internal purity in accordance with the superior teaching; how can it be right to say that others sitting together remain silent?

Next, regarding the inquiry into the Dharma: to reveal the relative superiority and inferiority between the two methods of the Saṃgha and the individual (Pratimokṣa), the initial response clarifies that the communal method (Saṃghadharma) universally encompasses and subsumes the original [monastic] community;

thus, the individual method follows next. Furthermore, it clarifies that the face-to-face method (Prātimokṣa) constitutes the individual because it merely manifests internal purity, in accordance with the superior teaching.
This refers to the monastic rules (*saṃghadharma*).
Regarding the mental recitation (*cittavijñapti*), it may be understood according to the text.

As for the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* text, it is like that of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: if there are no visiting monks, one performs the mental recitation; if one obtains a pure monk, [the offense] is as follows.

Having set aside the mindfulness [of the specific faults], one should mentally reflect and verbally recite three times: "I perform the *poṣadha*. This is precisely the act of confessing before the Sangha of the four directions;
it is as detailed in the *Pañcaśata-praśna* (Five Hundred Questions). Even with only three people present, this should be followed as the proper procedure.

Regarding the first of the three ways of recollecting [the offense] before confession: citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is shown that when no guests have arrived and one is acting alone, one must first perform the recollection and disclosure, and only afterwards state the words of confession.
Below this, the *Pañcaśata-praśna* (Five Hundred Questions) provides a general rule for cases where one faces another person (*pratyekam-śiras*):
even if the quorum for a formal monastic confession (*saṃgha-karma*) is not met, one must still first perform the disclosure and only then engage in mutual confession.
The section on the confession of the characteristics of the *śīla* (precepts) states that because this is performed regularly, it constitutes the maintenance of the Dharma;
therein, one subdues the banner of pride, reveres the supreme teaching, and partially dispels afflictions.
In the first sentence of the subsequent section, there is an inquiry as to why the confession must precede the recitation of the *śīla*, which is then explained by the following passage.

The second line indicates the intent of expounding the precepts: by constantly performing the fortnightly ritual and frequently washing away transgressions, the categories of the precepts become pure;

once the precepts are purified, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) then become clear. This is the aspect of maintaining the Dharma. [The following] clarifies the intent of confession and disclosure: the "proud banner" refers to the egoism of self and others; the "sacred teaching" refers to the Dharma of the precepts.
By subduing the self and looking up to the Dharma, the Noble Path can be expected; therefore, one inclines the afflictions toward it for the time being.
Because there are two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is said that they are "divided.
