Furthermore, the essential point for subduing [the mind] is to attain non-self; only then is subduing achieved so that [defilements] do not arise. When a bhikṣu violates the precepts, if he repents according to the Vinaya:

for natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), which are primary karmic actions, one must reach the limit of correction; for prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), which concern non-sentient objects, they are extinguished according to the Dharma.

In the first section of the response, it first refers back to the preceding sūtras and śāstras, namely the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. According to the subsequent analysis of the meaning, this resolves the initial point:

clarifying that the activity of transformation is easily subverted and suppressed. This means that from the second stage upward—excluding those at the level of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)—once one has attained partial vision of non-self, [defilements] are suppressed and do not arise.
Prior to this, they still arise; only upon attaining the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) are they severed. Regarding the bhikṣus mentioned below... [text continues].

The definitive determination is that because the nature of a fundamental offense (prakṛti-sāvadya) is not extinguished through confession, it persists until the limit of its governance—that is, at the time of realization and cessation; however, because it is obstructed by lightness [of the offense], it is extinguished.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: "The resolution of delusion and the actual matter differ in both name and reality. What, then, is this?

In the subsequent section on investigation, it is said that because wisdom destroys delusion, "resolving delusion" is the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), while "matters" refers to ritual repentance (*shi-chan*).
This reality is the essence itself.

When ritual matters are extinguished through practice, they alternately suppress one another; subsequently, the superior aspect dispels the inferior. If there is an upper-grade evil karma, it is countered by a lower-grade repentance.

Because they are not its direct adversaries, the stronger side first draws it along; thus, evil is not extinguished unless one must necessarily arouse superior-grade wholesome karma to suppress the evil.
The same principle may be applied by analogy to the mutual opposition of the medium and inferior grades.

Regarding the extinction through the object (*vastu-nirodha*), because the object is extinguished by means of the object, it is said that there are offenses and confessions, each with its own superior, middling, and inferior grades;

these correspond and are extinguished one-to-one. This is like facing an adversary: the superior can extinguish the inferior, but the inferior cannot extinguish the superior, for since they do not face an adversary, even if one confesses, it is not extinguished.

In the principle of repentance (*yukti-paścattāpa*), the realization of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) takes precedence; this means that the lower understanding cuts off the higher afflictions (*kleśa*), while the higher understanding cuts off the lower afflictions.
How is this known? For instance, regarding various views (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which have been termed "heavy" since beginningless time—who can say what is right or wrong?

By investigating through non-conceptual attention (*amanasikāra*), one sees a single view forever as being like the metaphor of splitting a stone. One simply contemplates and discerns that the self (*ātman*) is ultimately non-existent, and from this, one gives rise to patience (*kṣānti*).

Thus, regarding the realization of non-arising, although it is well known by all that afflictions such as greed and hatred are deep-seated obscurations caused by conditions, they cannot be abandoned suddenly;
therefore, even up to the seventh stage of training, one remains entangled by them, requiring skillful means and superior wisdom to sever them, like the analogy of a lotus fiber.

In the "Ritual of Repentance through Principle" (*lǐchàn*), the first section provides a general demonstration: because the contemplation of emptiness (*kōng*) is the practice of principle, it is called "the practice of emptiness.

The lower "explanation" refers to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which destroys the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the upper "explanation" refers to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which destroys the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). Regarding the subsequent detailed explanation:

the lower [explanation] clarifies that the severing of the beginningless self-clinging and the extreme views of partiality and heterodoxy is termed the "upper delusions. This is illustrated by the analogy that one must necessarily split a stone [to reach its core].
There is no re-union. Furthermore, a sutra states: "If one sees a flash of lightning at night, one immediately attains the Path.
[This means that] one realizes the self was originally non-existent and was falsely conceived as existing; by understanding this falsity, one immediately realizes the emptiness of the self.

Abiding in this emptiness is called the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and is termed the "purity of the Dharma-eye. Next, to clarify the superior understanding that severs inferior greed and other delusions, it is contrasted with "seeing" (*darśana*).

The four stages of the three lower fruits are all termed "those in training" (śaikṣa); their superior wisdom—that is, their higher understanding—resembles [the state of] having severed [defilements], yet they have not actually severed them, as is known by the analogy of the lotus fiber.
Thus, these two [categories] differ in their mutual relationship.

The headings in these two sections differ slightly from the preceding ones; they employ the correlation of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*) to determine the depth of the subduing of afflictions.

First, regarding the difference in strength: karma that summons painful retribution is dominant within the causes of birth, while delusion that directly obstructs liberation is supreme within the causes of practice.

In the initial section of this commentary, it is explained that when the karma of ritual repentance (*sāmketikapratideśanā*) is the cause of birth, the causal force is strong while the habitual cause (*vāsanāhetu*) is weak;
whereas when rational contemplation (*yuktipratyavekṣaṇā*) breaks through delusions, the habitual cause is superior while the cause of birth is inferior.

Furthermore, because there are differences between the two types of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), both ritual repentance and karma possess two aspects that exclude one another; since these aspects have varying degrees of gravity, the methods for repenting delusions differ accordingly.
The wisdom that can treat these [afflictions] has emptiness as its essence and is unimpeded; that which is to be severed consists of frost and flames, which do not coexist.

Among these two, the repentance of karma exists simultaneously because one uses a phenomenon to subdue a phenomenon; thus, there are two aspects that exclude each other, which is the functioning of retribution.

The repentance of delusions is different, for it involves repenting what does not exist; "frost and flames" is a metaphor for the two entities of sin and repentance, which mutually overcome one another.
The essence [of these two] does not exist simultaneously, because the metaphor illustrates that when contemplation is perfected and delusion is destroyed, both are equally empty.

Third, the sequence differs; the methods for repenting karma are not fixed in their priority, as one enters the Dharma according to what is cited and gives rise to counteraction, thereby subduing and severing delusions.
Otherwise, one must first eliminate the self; thus the treatise states: "It is because of this self that one accumulates all various karmas."
Up until the fourth stage of abiding (*vihāra*), one subsequently abandons ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among these three [stages], the repentance for karma occurs as it arises; the subsequent citation of the abandonment of delusions (*kleśa*) must follow the sequential order.

As for the proponent of the treatise who points this out, it is the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* (Tattvasiddhi), which holds that the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the three realms constitute one stage of abiding, while the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the three realms constitute three stages of abiding, with ignorance being the final stage.

To abide in one [state] is called the five abodes; the afflictions have the "self" (*ātman*) as their root. Regarding the sequence of abandonment and realization: first, one abandons the self; next, views;
then, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and finally, ignorance (*avidyā*).

Fourth, as for the application of wisdom to eliminate delusions through categorization and differentiation: just as when one corner of a room is awakened, the remaining corners naturally turn back [toward it], so too does repentance proceed accordingly.
Each [precept] is individually distinguished and excluded, like sawing wood or felling a tree. If one prevents future transgressions, the principle is the same as severing the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Just as the karma of the first category is coarse and easy to abandon without requiring a superior mind, so it is with the fifth category;
these are similar to greed and delusion, and unless one specifically guards against them, how can one avoid them?

Among the four types [of offenses], those involving delusion are offenses to be eliminated by category (*jātisamudghāta*); they require separate confession for the transgression itself, whereas the prevention of future faults differs from this. Regarding the prevention of future non-transgressions, they are the same:
preventing a grave fault with a light mind is the same as eliminating by category, and preventing a light fault with a heavy mind is likewise the same. Both are elimination by category.
Third, regarding the correspondence between the small and great [vehicles] based on conditions: within the Mahāyāna, there are further distinctions between phenomena and principle.
First, concerning reliance on principle: one must recognize that the fundamental mind is the principle of the Mahāyāna; its essence is pure, and its wondrous function is empty and pervasive.
Because of deluded conceptualization, one knows that defilement is the mind and its mental factors; when speech does not arise, external objects are naturally dispelled. Why is this?
Originally failing to understand the mind, one falsely grasps at objective realms; following these realms, one gives rise to karma, and from karma, one undergoes false retribution.

Now, realizing that the essence of this fundamental delusion is empty and unreal, one feels deep shame for past karma—falsely constructed and created by oneself, like a silkworm spinning its own cocoon, entangled not by another but by itself.

Giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse, one vows to sever the habitual tendencies of delusion; as one maintains such mindfulness moment after moment, the immeasurable stains of transgression naturally vanish and become still—this is explained according to the text.

Third, regarding the Mahāyāna Liturgy of Repentance through Principle (*li-chān*), the first part demonstrates that the essence of principle is pure and thus free from defilement, and because it is empty and pervasive.

Because of unimpeded deluded thoughts, there are defilements; these "defilements" contain two aspects: namely, "affliction" (*kleśa*) and "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*). Below, the text clarifies the practice of repentance.
First, it describes how the arising of delusion leads to the formation of the three paths. Next, it explains the seeking of repentance, which has four parts:
first, awakening; second, self-reproach; third, making a vow; and fourth, contemplation. Because one knows that non-deluded objective conditions are nothing but mind, the following points this out.
As seen in the original commentary following the text:

second, ritual repentance (*vastu-pāpadeśanā*) refers to practices commonly performed in the world, such as relying on halls or stupas, or engaging in various activities like copying scriptures, reciting the names of Buddhas, and chanting sutras—all of which arise from external conditions.
One directs the mind based on these, calculating merit and establishing a schedule according to what is undertaken.
To indulge in affection according to one’s desires and to harbor resentment against that which opposes them—this impure mind is not yet sufficient to eliminate transgressions.

First, one must subdue the self-centeredness of "person and ego" (*pudgala-ātman*) and the greed for competition. Biting back with sorrow and reproaching oneself, one should bend the body and withdraw from the scene, yielding the honor to others.

Since even suppressing such behavior through external matters cannot subdue it when the delusions of the self are robust and one fails to contemplate the subtle, how much less can it be subdued by a mere special confession?
This is employed as the practice.

Regarding the ritual of repentance, the first section of the "Explanation of Intent" first indicates the place of reliance for the construction [of the altar], which is the sutra repository; below this, it clarifies the Buddha upon whom one relies.

Next, it clarifies the teachings of the sutras regarding the Buddhas' names, which refers to the practice of upholding their names through recitation. Below that, it clarifies the application of the mind, beginning with the general overview.
The section following "showing the names" provides a detailed explanation in two parts. First, it clarifies the faults; second, it reveals the correct mind, which is skilled at subduing evil.

Thus it is said that "matters are suppressed. To know only ritual recitation without simultaneously practicing subjugation is called "special repentance" (*te-chàn*); "special" (*te*) here means "solely" or "exclusively."
Therefore, the Great Sage has established this excellent rule to rectify us who are coarse and heavy of nature:

one must recite fifteen thousand times on the day of the Buddha Sun and one hundred thousand times on the day of Amitābha Buddha. In this manner, the number of recitations for all activities, including ritual services, shall be fixed;
one should calculate the merit and exert oneself in self-discipline.
The subsequent section states: "Regarding the phrase 'to treat us,' it is intended to cause those of later learning to know their own capacity and give rise to a sense of shame.

The mention of fifteen thousand [recitations] and so forth briefly cites the holding of the name to demonstrate meritorious practice; by setting time limits and counting recitations, one binds the mind to the task."
If one does not reach this point, it is merely indolence; how can such a person be said to fear sin? Such a person is truly a denizen of hell.
Thus one must lash the heart and thus establish one's resolve. Although this is called a coarse practice, it is rare in the world.
Even if some do engage in it, they mostly pursue fame and profit, using flattery and deception to exalt themselves; these are but soft thieves and rākṣasī-wives.
Among these three, because they contrast with the preceding contemplation of principle, they are called "coarse karma. At that time, such things were rare; now they can be known [abundantly].
As for the "soft thief," one does not realize their encroachment and theft; as for the "ghost wife," one ultimately meets with being devoured.
To consider these as good while unaware that they result in evil—the difficulty of cultivation and practice can thus be understood.
When one wishes to practice, five conditions must be fulfilled.

To clarify this explicitly: while the characteristics of the activity within the central focus are subtle and hidden, they can be verified by relying on external conditions; since the practice will not succeed if these are lacking, it is said that they "must be fulfilled."
First, one should request the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to serve as witnesses, thinking:

"Because my mind is weak and relies upon external conditions, although the Buddhas and others are always before my eyes, I do not see them due to the defilements of my sins—just as a blind person does not see.

Since this is so even when the Buddha moves his mind to respond to circumstances, how much more so now that he stands directly before me with pure eyes? To commit such grave offenses in his presence is deeply shameful. Thus, all practitioners [should reflect].
If even a slight evil thought arises, one should constantly contemplate the Buddha; then, out of shame, it will cease.

First, regarding the initial object of focus, the first part shows the intent of the request and the method of practice. The *Sūtra* says: "The Buddhas of the ten directions are always present in the world, yet because my turbid and evil eyes are obscured, I do not see them.
This concludes the movement [of the mind]. Below, there is the admonition to maintain solemnity; below that, the instruction on visualization.
Whenever an evil thought arises, recollecting the Buddha immediately eliminates it; this is because the object of focus is supreme.
Second, reciting sutras and dharanis serves as a wondrous medicine. While the sutras can treat whatever ailment arises, if one does not maintain a sincere heart, the mind will wander and scatter;
therefore, one must restrain the mind so that it remains focused upon the words being spoken.
Regarding the two [types of verbal restraint], because they follow the sūtras and their antidotes are neither superior nor inferior, one binds the mind to the mouth by means of names and phrases.
Third, one confesses one's own transgressions, as described in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as being "evil," "unwholesome," and so forth.
Regarding the third point, nirvāṇa, the tenth fascicle of that sutra states:
"To disclose all evils—to disclose all evils committed from the very limits of saṃsāra, reaching unto the place of no-arrival," and so forth.
Fourth, regarding the vow: from this day forward, blessings shall begin and transgressions shall end until the attainment of Buddhahood;

this is the essential core of the fundamental practice of repentance. Therefore, even though one performs repentance and subsequently leaves the ritual arena, if one again pursues former evils, it is because the original resolve was not firm.
Is it not evident that various habitual tendencies will once more surround and entangle one?
Among the four [sections], the first indicates the essential tenet; next, it warns against falling back because the foundation was not firm, resulting in relapse.

The fifth clarifies the evidence according to the teaching: whether in dreams or in waking states, one should perceive objective realms as they truly are, rather than regarding them as transformations of a deluded mind.
"Or am I being deluded by a demon? If this were a demon, my own conduct would not have transcended the realm of demons;
how then could a demon come here? Is it not rather the false manifestation of my own karma that causes my mind to become attached and gives rise to further delusions?
If I know that the mind and its objects do not truly perish, then is this merely a false projection of my own mind? Thus he reflected.
If the root is already remote, how can it be the fundamental? How could delusion be stilled? To know that delusion is not true is itself non-true;

this non-truth merely transmits further delusion. By thus reversing one's cognition, one discerns the cause of delusion; furthermore, by discerning this, one realizes that even this realization arises from delusion. Otherwise, one will rejoice in following delusion instead of returning [to the source].
One must practice this diligently and early on; there is no room for self-deception. Among those who understand this in the secular world, such people are rare even at the age of fifty.
If one does not even know these forty-nine [types of] non-[realities], how much less can one who studies the Path while harboring attachments do so?

Among the five sections, the first clarifies the objective conditions (*ālambana-viṣaya*): it means that signs of good and evil appear during dreams and waking states; this is not the second section, which clarifies investigation.

First, one suspects a transformation of the mind; next, one suspects the manifestation of a *māra*. If it is as described in the third section, one blames the manifestation of a *māra* resulting from karma.
Dwelling at the summit of the heavens of the desire realm, if one cultivates mundane dhyāna or untainted karma, it is only when about to transcend that state that one will encounter Māra.

If one knows that the four lower realms are the mind’s own delusions, then by thus tracing back the delusions from their manifestations down to their root, one realizes they are all not the fundamental reality.

By successively pushing back the delusions, one finds they are not the original source; knowing the delusions dispels the knowledge [of them], and understanding the delusions dispels the understanding [of them]. Thus, consciousness arises from delusion.

One must eliminate consciousness; if one eliminates that which eliminates, there is no end to it, and thus there is nowhere to abide. Otherwise, one would merely rejoice and form a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The following passage cites a worldly analogy for the Way: Zhuangzi says, "Qu Yuan, at age fifty, realized the errors of his forty-nine years;
Confucius, at age sixty, realized the errors of his fifty-nine years. Furthermore, the *Lunyu* says, "Add ten years to me..."

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "At fifty, one studies the *Yi* (Change) so as to be free from great transgressions. From this, we know that prior to this age, one had not yet attained realization of the Mandate of Heaven (*tianming*), and thus every action resulted in error.

Question: When practicing the rites of repentance (*chan*), must one perform ritual prostrations and recitations? Answer: The distinction between the ignorant and the wise is twofold, yet in terms of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), there is no duality.

Those of superior wisdom penetrate the principle and thus encounter no obstruction in their practice. Those of middling and lower capacities are obscured by emptiness; therefore, the gradual approach is maintained for them.
The "Inducing" [practice] should be summarized in four propositions to encompass all capacities of sentient beings: 1. One who has attained the principle but lost the practice:

their mind is fixed in meditative contemplation, yet externally they lack adornment; like having eyes but no feet, they cannot advance. 2. One who pursues phenomena while being deluded regarding the principle:

they calculate merit and divide their lessons, failing to understand dependent origination; like having feet but no eyes, they do not know where to go. 3. One for whom both phenomena and principle are... [dual]...
When fortune, insight, and practice support one another, the myriad practices are perfected and one will surely reach the other shore.

If one is ignorant of both principle and phenomena, being like a blind person without feet—deluded, lazy, and arrogant—one will never have a time of emergence. Thus we know that if principle and phenomena are established separately, one cannot avoid partiality and deviation;
if emptiness and existence are treated as such, it is not true cultivation. Therefore it is said: "In the ground of ultimate reality, not even a single thing is accepted."

Within the gateway of the Buddha’s work amidst the mundane dust, not a single dharma is abandoned; this is what the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have cultivated through kalpas of training, and what the patriarchs of China and India practiced as lifelong asceticism.
This principle is profound and subtle—how could it ever be fully expressed? I shall briefly indicate its general direction and roughly distinguish the essential from the superficial.
Second, regarding confession within the Vinaya of the Hīnayāna, there are also five conditions: first, the agent; second, the object; third, the mind;
fourth, the correspondence; and fifth, the completion.

First, concerning the agent: one is the person who has committed an offense among the five assemblies (pañca-saṃgha), and two is the preparation of the ritual to face the recipient for the additional [confession].
The manner of performing prostrations toward the superior is as explained previously.
Within the second section, the specific explanation of the Hīnayāna, there are initially two [aspects] regarding the ability to repent;
when four [aspects] are added below, they constitute the five protocols beginning with baring the right shoulder, excluding the act of prostrating at the feet.
There are seven points regarding the second [category], the objects of opposition: first, those who belong to the same community and share the same precepts and views;

second, those who possess pure precepts as described in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding the *araṇya* (forest-dweller), namely those who have committed the same offense and are permitted to confess it—this refers to cases involving life-threatening danger; the remainder is as explained in the subsequent text; third, making a formal request for instruction; fourth, speaking according to the teachings;

fifth, that which is subject to confession, namely the four minor categories of offenses; sixth, the proclamation of the names and types [of offenses]; and seventh, that they do not exist [in the case of the grave offenses].
Regarding the doubt concerning the overlapping of the seven categories of offenses and the distinction between being part of a separate assembly:

among the two types of persons addressed, the "five-part" assembly is mentioned; it says that if there is a life-threatening circumstance, the Buddha permits both those who have committed the same offense and those who have not to receive confession together, whereas if there is no such cause, they may not.
This should be understood as a standard for selecting the four [of the] five pure [factors].
Regarding those offenses that may be confessed: although the *pārājika* (defeat) is permitted to be confessed, it ultimately never returns to its original state.

Thus, there are three aspects to the mind of confession: first, inner shame and remorse, which is the most fundamental remedy; second, the establishment of a vow to sever [the offense] forever, which is itself the act of confession;
and third, disclosing the offense to others to feel shame for it and avoid further transgression.
Third, regarding confession within the mind: when one possesses a sense of shame (*hrī*) and reveals one's transgressions, there is no offense that is not liberated.
Fourth, "the correspondence of mind and object" means that the words and meanings of both parties are mutually understood.
Fifth, the accomplishment of the matter has three aspects: namely, the completeness of the ritual, the reprimand, and the making of a vow; through these, a sense of self-reproach arises.
"Disgust and renunciation" refers to this; "threefold acceptance without opposition" means responding with "so be it.
The five matters constitute three components, which together form a single whole: first, the performance of the ritual act without error; second, the solemn vow;
and third, the prior admonition and exhortation.
Regarding the four points on the characteristics of extinction as elucidated by the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
some say that those who perform Mahāyāna repentance attain the extinction of karma because: first, their principle is profound and their medicine is wondrous;
second, their awakening and remorse give rise to superior remedial practices; and third, they cultivate their karma through many bodies rather than attaining realization in a single form.

Regarding the four types of "understanding by others," the first refers to the superiority of the Dharma, the second to the superiority of practice, and the third to the superiority of retribution. Although these three forms of superiority exist, they do not distinguish between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).

The present explanation states that although the Sūtra speaks of cessation, it does so in an incomplete sense; it is merely a remote and general description in view of the subsequent contemplation of principle. However...

Because it belongs to the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi, it is comprised within the karma of segmented birth (*bhavāṅga-vedanīya-karma*) which serves to project rebirth. According to the Hīnayāna, within the stage of Superior Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one attains a semblance of outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*);
at that point, karma leading to the evil destinies or female rebirth can no longer be experienced. Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"One who has attained the worldly right view, though they may still come and go through births and deaths for even hundreds or thousands of lifetimes, will ultimately never fall into the evil destinies. This refers to the fact that, regarding specific retributions (*pratyeka-vipāka*), such karma is no longer experienced.

Because learning has not yet eliminated [delusions], there is the suffering of having the brain pierced and the pain of the body being shattered; as for the burning of the body in hell and the hunger that cuts into one's frame, what more need be said?

Now, in the first section of the current explanation, which correctly elucidates the middle part, the first point resolves the scriptural text as cited in the commentary from the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra*.

Alternatively, regarding the textual passages in various sutras that speak of "extinguishing" [defilements], these merely refer to the suppression [of afflictions] through principle-contemplation (*li-guan*). As for the capacity to extinguish them, there are two further points below:

first, it clarifies that even the three stages of worthiness (*san-xian*) prior to the ten stages (*daocheng*) of the Mahayana still possess birth-and-death with fixed duration (*fen-duan shengsi*); thus, one knows that [afflictions] are not extinguished [at those levels].

Second, it indicates that only upon reaching the stage of patience (*ren-wei*) in the Hinayana is one finally exempt from the evil realms; thus, one knows that prior to this, karma is likewise not extinguished.
The *Abhidharmasamaya-nirdeśa-śāstra* states that what is seen in the world is the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Furthermore, once one has transcended the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*), it is known that those above the level of the "Inner Ordinary Person" (*antarapudgala*) are about to border upon the stage of the Noble Ones (*ārya*). Because their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is superior, they are able to extinguish karma;

the evil destinies constitute the collective retribution, while other sufferings are the individual retributions. Thus, the four subsequent lines all concern the conditions for those who have attained the fruit to repay their debts, as explained initially in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
First, the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka was gravely ill; when the other bhikṣus questioned him, he said of himself, "My illness does not improve;
it is just as if a strong man were to bind my head and twist both my hands tightly—the pain in my head is exactly like that.
Second, like Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana went on almsround and was beaten by a brahmin until his flesh and bones were completely mangled. Third, like [the story of] the three... [text fragmentary].
From the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra*: The Arhat Liüè was practicing meditation in the mountains when he was falsely accused of stealing an ox.
He remained in prison for twelve years, confessing that in a past life he had falsely accused another of stealing an ox.

Because of this, he subsequently fell into the three evil realms and suffered immeasurable pain; as the remaining retribution was not yet exhausted, he received this karmic fruit. Fourth, according to the *Śata-ākāra-nidāna-sūtra*, Lì...
The nun Guṇavartman, after seven days of past hunger, became an Arhat; yet for another seven days she was unable to obtain alms-food and died from swallowing sand, as detailed in the *Zizhi*.
Reflecting on this, one realizes that both good and evil karma must not be committed. As an ancient said: "Be careful not to do even good."

This contains a profound purport: just as performing worldly good leads to rebirth at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) within the Sahā world-system of the triple realm, where the truth of suffering increases further—like a glowing gold ball that cannot be touched.

In the initial summary of the admonition, it first demonstrates the dreadfulness of the principle of karma: first, its power to project subsequent habitual tendencies; second, its non-perishing throughout successive kalpas.
Third, regarding how the drawing forth of rebirth and the experiencing of retribution do not depend on human agency: the following citation from the ancient texts provides proof.

It states that committing evil leads to falling into the three evil destinies, while performing good leads to falling into the three good paths; in neither case does one escape saṃsāra. Although good deeds constitute merit, they can obstruct the Path to the Sages even more effectively than committing evil.
When those born later hear this, let them be careful not to misunderstand it, as the intent will be clarified below.
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is none other than the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, where the lifespan is eighty thousand great kalpas; this constitutes the "difficult ground.
The burning of a golden ball serves as a metaphor for how ordinary merit can conversely become a source of harm.

Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of repenting for grave offenses within the Vinaya, although they do not constitute a fixed numerical count, there is a principle to be gathered: one should practice learning throughout the duration of one's life.
Because it obstructs the hells, the rest will be explained in the text.

In the next section, regarding the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) ritual of repentance, "not immediately [counted]" means that they have entered [the path]. "Those who may be gathered" refers to whether they come or not as they please.
Those who practice for the duration of their lives do not return to original purity; this is what is meant by the Small Vehicle.
This is not a text for repenting grave offenses.

The preceding summary of the meaning requires a mind of broad integration; otherwise, if one simply bows one’s head before the Buddha morning and evening while the mind is largely in a state of non-recording (amūrchita), it will only increase the habit of arrogance.
It would be better not to do it at all. When the time comes, contemplate: what is there? What exists?

In the initial exhortation within the summary, it clarifies that one must not let the mind sink; from the subsequent section on revealing faults and calamities down to the reprimand of the ignorant and dark, it urges those who observe to engage in self-reflection.
As for the question "What kind of thing is being made?", it means that one will inevitably fall into the evil realms.

Now, one must first clarify the preceding conditions and subsequently the Dharma through repentance. Since most people recite this together without understanding it, I shall cite the text to demonstrate it.
Second, regarding the division of the text for demonstration:
among those who recite it without knowing it, there are two types—one who understands both principle and phenomena, and another who does not.

The consciousness transforms and establishes three [categories]: non-cognition, extinction, and subduing. If one does not understand these three gates of teaching, then there will be confusion. First, regarding the listing of the ignorant and the wise:

for those whose deep hearts do not delight in committing sins, how could they ever encounter [the opportunity to transgress]? However, even if one commits [a fault], one should constantly contemplate and immediately repent.
In the final age, it is fortunate that it is said one does not see [others] committing offenses; this is because, having failed to study from the beginning, one falsely claims that there are none.

This is because they speak of being without offense due to ignorance; or when speaking of seeing an offense yet failing to perform a proper confession, although they know the characteristics of the transgression,
they merely recite the words of the text without understanding whether the specific facts of the offense are present or absent,

or they indiscriminately exaggerate the fault by claiming it is "everything," or they fail to understand the distinctions between granting or withholding instruction due to delusion regarding the object, or they recklessly sit in various distinct positions without counting [the proper sequence].
Therefore, although one may add recitation, it is termed "unlawful" (*adharma*) in general because it is not destroyed by conditions.

Regarding the first section on conditions, the *Vinaya* provides a general indication as noted in the commentary: among the two types of people—foolish and wise—there are two within each, thus making four people in total.
One who lacks deep resolve (*gambhīra-citta*) is precisely what the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* fully states: "the practitioner’s deep resolve."

Not delighting in committing offenses is called "purely maintaining the precepts. This is the initial explanation of the specific analysis. First, regarding "not seeing an offense," this refers to intentional transgression;
"non-existence" here means ignorance. Next, the subsequent explanation of "improper repentance" has four parts. First, the one who recites the text is deluded regarding the Dharma.
"Matter" refers to the objective circumstance, and "offense" refers to the *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* categories. Second, "confusing praise" refers to being deluded.

Since those below the three levels of worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*) have not yet lost their *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) existence, they continue to draw forth rebirth and experience retribution, revolving without end; how much more so for those at the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and below!

In the Mahāyāna, that which takes emptiness and consciousness as fundamental: "emptiness" means realizing that all phenomena arise through causes and conditions, and that arising is itself non-arising;

however, in the case of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class alone, once the confession has been performed, one must still undergo disciplinary treatment, which differs from the others.
Second, regarding the mental transgression of concealment, there is no offense in this instance; it is merely that one conceals internal flaws while outwardly appearing pure and innocent.

Because [the offender] has transgressed the ranks of the Sangha and treated these laws with contempt, he must undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) for each day [of concealment] as a supplementary practice.
Remaining humbled in the lowest seat, with body and mind subdued, it is as stated in the text: "one receives the *pārivāsika* according to the number of days.
This is called *pravāsanīya* (separate dwelling), so named because one dwells separately from the community, provided with a lower room and inferior bedding.

Of the two [sections], the first describes the faults of the underlying intention; therefore, the following explains the administration of punishment according to concealment and time. "According to the days" means that the length of the months and years corresponds to the appropriate punishment for the period of concealment.
This refers to the citation of scriptural evidence below, which provides the etymological explanation of the translated term; this constitutes the characteristics of the administration of punishment.

Third, regarding those whose offenses stem from mental transgressions (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*): as these crimes rank next only to the ultimate penalty, it is only fitting that they be treated with singular gravity.

Therefore, because one has committed such a grave offense through negligence, the mind cannot tolerate it; fearing that this habituation might persist into the future, the rule of six nights of rigorous penance within the Saṃgha is established.

This is intended to provide exhortation and to ensure that one reaches the utmost limit of shame, serving as a perpetual warning. As stated in the text: "Once the *parivāsa* has been completed, the *mānāpya* is then granted."

The term *tva* (埵) is translated here as "joy of mind" (*cittapramoda*). Because of the previous concealment of one's offenses, the diligent practice of confession—like washing away the sun and moon—is not without weariness and exhaustion.
However, since there is the prospect of purification after six nights, one takes personal joy and does not shrink from the hardship.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of the Saṃgha’s joy, seeing that while the offense is easy to commit, the confession is difficult; yet, if the transgression remains concealed in the heart, the fault follows the action and becomes as grave as an act of opposition.

Regarding the precepts, one conceives this [resolve] and generates diligence; furthermore, because the roots of transgression are about to be uprooted through the six-night communal celebration (*saṃgha-vaśīrta*), one likewise shares in the joy.

Among the three sections, the first describes the faults and the prohibition; the middle clarifies the remedy as shown below. There are two ways of explaining the reversal of the names, the first of which concerns...
Because one rejoices when a transgression is about to be expiated, it is also listed next; furthermore, it is listed next because the Saṃgha rejoices in accord with compassion.

"Transgressions following the matter" refers to emotional faults, while "matters" refers to the disciplinary methods. "In accord with the precepts" refers to the assembly of monks, who, being diligent in bringing forth [wholesome states], take pity on their toil.
Regarding the four *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: they constitute a fundamental and direct obstruction that causes the body and mind to stagnate;
because they must be extricated by the community of monks acting together at once, the text states that "twenty monks [are required] for the removal of the offense."
Among the four [sections], the first summarizes the faults; the following clarifies the remedy. Below, the scriptural evidence is cited:

"Twenty monks" refers to doubling the ten-monk quorum for the sake of added gravity. Some say it refers to thirty people for the repentance of heavy offenses. This is mentioned in the *Chūjiao jing* (Sutra on the Initial Teaching), which is a spurious scripture and insufficient for reliance.

As for the procedures regarding requesting the Dharma, bestowing it, performing *kṣānti*, taking it away, losing it, and staying overnight—these matters are extremely numerous and have been excerpted and listed in the supplementary fascicles.
At present, we only know of the existence of the *chán* (repentance) ritual; thus, we rely on the formal rules, as the occasions for such events gradually became rare and the texts were lost.
Should one necessarily perform these rites, they are fully detailed within the *Cāo* (Excerpts).

Briefly pointing to the first section of the middle [part], there are four dharmas to be presented at the outset: first, the preliminary petition; second, the *karmavācanā* and the performance of the rite;

third, the forfeiture of thirty-five matters; and fourth, the eight conditions for losing the overnight stay. "Now" below indicates the brief presentation, while "necessarily" below points to the detailed exposition.
The method for repenting the third category of offenses is titled "As in the Vinaya Commentary" (*Jieshu*). For now, I shall explain the conditions for these offenses;

as for those that arise independently (*doutou*) or from other sources, each is divided into three stages, as fully detailed in the text where their names and characteristics are clearly set forth. As for the actual methods of repentance, they are rare and thus I shall treat them briefly.
Among the three types of *sthūlātyaya*, the first is designated by name; this is translated as "great obstacle to the path of goodness," and is also translated as "coarse evil" or "coarse offense.
Now, regarding the commentary on the subsequent text: first, the three grades of independent offenses are listed, which are the actual resultant offenses (*phala-āpatti*);

next, the three grades of derivative offenses are listed, which are the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the two categories [of *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*]; finally, citing the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, those whose confession is identical to that of a *pāyattika* are categorized accordingly.

The three positions—*dàn-lán*, *jù-zuì-chóng-qīng*, and *sān-chàn-bù-hù-tí*—are merely three methods applied according to the circumstances, depending on the gravity of the offense, the number of people present, and the time.

The preceding text has already set forth these three methods of repentance to clarify their non-extensive nature and the passages concerning their entrustment; their characteristics are easily understood.
Xiao. Next, regarding the four sections of the main text within the general conclusion: first, it clarifies the vastness of the Dharma; next, it indicates following a teacher;

"the rest" refers to those who are not masters of the Vinaya school, necessarily [requiring them to] encourage reliance on the Dharma below; and finally, it reveals the intent of the abridgment, as previously shown.
The *Fazhi zhuihou zhi chao* (Excerpts on the Final Instructions) does not elaborate extensively; it is a matter of entrustment.

Regarding the method for repenting the fourth category of offenses (*caturtha-varga*), thirty items are fully listed as in the text. As for the requirement that repentance must be performed before the Sangha:

because these offenses arise from matters involving wealth, they give rise to transgressions of greed and arrogance; the state thus established is contrary to the Way. Therefore, if one wishes to wash away these offenses through repentance, this regulation establishes that they cannot be removed in private.

When one feels shame in the presence of the Saṃgha as the object of comparison, one is able to sever future transgressions. Regarding the latter ninety [offenses], the transgression arises according to the specific act;

since they do not involve the greed of hoarding, they do not require the testimony of the Saṃgha for their cessation. Because there is this distinct characteristic, they are divided into two categories.
Regarding the first thirty [rules], they are categorized into three based on the object, which corresponds to individuals.

Within the section concerning the Sangha, they are further divided into four positions: first, the relinquishing of material goods; second, the relinquishing of the intention; third, the relinquishing of the offense; and fourth, the returning of the robe.

In the preceding section on the relinquishment of material goods (*cīvara*), the causal divisions are twofold: first, the ritual for relinquishing material goods and the method of confession within the Sangha;
second, the purpose for which the relinquishment and confession are performed.

Regarding the former text: since one who has committed an offense regarding a garment subject to relinquishment is unable to give it away, the principle requires that the transgression be purified through relinquishment.
Feeling shame for one's transgressions, a mendicant should simply restrain their fundamental mind; why then rely on material wealth?

Therefore, it is not permitted to give with impure wealth, as one will inevitably receive defiled fruits in the future. Furthermore, if a mendicant wishes to follow the Vinaya in relinquishing the three robes and dharma-garments, they cannot tolerate anything that is non-pure or stained;
thus, such things are not permitted. However, the one hundred and one *pārikkhāra* (requisites) are also appropriate to accept and maintain.

Furthermore, one must use pure wealth; if it is impure, it is contrary to the rules for receiving. If one repeatedly wears such [impure] items, one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), which requires confession because it constitutes a transgression of separation.
Thus, the rule for forfeiture was established to penalize those who persist in wearing them. If the substance is already defiled wealth, how can it be fit for pure dharma?
This is the teaching for the ignorant. In all cases, one must first forfeit the item; only after that may one obtain another as before, according to the fivefold uses previously mentioned.

Regarding the four *pāyattika* rules concerning the forfeiture of wealth according to the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*), within the five regulations, the first section clarifies that for one who receives impure fruit from another, because it is due to impurity, one must perform the formal act of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) as prescribed by the Vinaya; only after it has been forfeited may it be given to others.

Next, the three types of robes (*tricīvara*) are prepared, and subsequently the "one hundred and one" items are prepared; all of these require receiving [the items] with pure wealth (*pariśuddha-vitta*).
The first four [sections] below explain the application of attachment, meaning that by breaking away from it, one abandons the offenses resulting from false conceptualizations.
The fifth section below explains the pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) mentioned above; this is the individual explanation, while the two sections below provide the summary.

This *niḥsargika* [offense] below clarifies the relinquishment (*pratyāpanna*) toward the object; the Sanskrit original is thus, and the Chinese translation says "complete relinquishment" regarding the three objects.
In the preceding section, "not separately from the assembly," there was no distinction.

Next, regarding the objects [of the offense], in the first sub-section of the Sanskrit *niḥsargika*—which here is translated as "complete relinquishment"—it means that the three factors of wealth, mind, and offense are all to be relinquished;
thus, the three objects correspond to the three stages of persons.

Question: Since it was previously stated that [the confession] must be made before the Saṃgha, what is meant by saying it may also be made before an individual? Why is it called "intense remorse" (yinkui)? Answer: The original rule concerns the Saṃgha;

although it is permitted for an individual, the boundary still belongs to the Saṃgha and the legal procedure cannot be performed separately. It is only when the rule is not established that one commits an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
Because it is extremely difficult to find a Saṃgha and there is no way to seek purification, one may proceed according to whichever of the three types of boundaries is available in the vicinity.

Is it not excellent that we permit a separate assembly to look toward the Saṃgha, generate a sense of gravity, establish [the rite] according to the individuals, and perform the relinquishment (*pratyosāraṇa*) to meet the immediate needs of the times?
In the question, it is because the domain of the Saṃgha is superior while the domain of the separate assembly is weak;

in the answer, first it clarifies that although the original rule (*dharmasthiti*) was established for the end and later opened for the beginning, even when facing a single person, it is nonetheless the Saṃgha; next, it clarifies the intent of the opening: that since the offense (*āpatti*) is light and easy to manage, [it is permitted].

Regarding the offenses that must necessarily be confessed before the Saṃgha, because it is difficult for such a gathering to be accomplished, one may instead assemble the monks within a specific boundary (*sīmā*);
this is not to be disparaged, as it praises the wisdom of knowing the appropriate occasion.

As for the statement that "the offenses apply to both the Saṃgha and individuals," the Vinaya says: "Who has committed a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*? Whether it be the Saṃgha, or a group of many people, or [an individual]."
Even for a single person, it is as if they were among the present Sangha; to jointly store wealth and receive money or jewels with the intent of seeking profit from profit is in every case impure.
Third, regarding the offenses of the Sangha and individuals: first, three persons are listed below; next, the offenses of the Sangha are shown, beginning with the joint storage of much wealth. Thus:
Taking money or treasures for oneself constitutes the same offense as receiving them; seeking profit from profit constitutes the same offense as trading.

Regarding the division of boundaries into two areas: there are both places where the Dharma exists and places where it does not; one must know the limits of both, each having its own designated assembly.
First, it clarifies that the two realms (dhātu) are distinct in terms of the rules for determining the Saṃgha, yet they are common to both realms in terms of the location.
Second, it clarifies that the purpose for which one must have five persons when performing the confession and relinquishment (*pratideśanā-utsarga*) is as follows:

when the presiding master (*karmavācaka*) performs the formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha, this is not a matter of his own calculation but requires another; since he requires the Saṃgha outside of himself, the number five encompasses the aforementioned meaning of the Saṃgha.

Second, clarifying the purpose for which [the ritual] is performed. Regarding the first section within the "Community" (saṃgha), the confession and relinquishment of the five persons is found in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*;
as this was seen in the preceding general meaning, it is referred back to the above.
Some say that according to the Vinaya regulations, the relinquishment of property must take place within the Saṃgha before all members have assembled; therefore, this is the meaning of "the Saṃgha.

However, the confession of offenses may be performed before a separate group, as it is the same as the ninety [offenses] involving a separate assembly. Since both involve the threefold proclamation of a *pāyattika* offense, how could there be any discrepancy between them?

In the first section of this chapter, the initial teacher establishes his thesis: first, he clarifies that the relinquishing of material wealth must be performed before the Saṃgha as opposed to an individual;

"assembling" means that even two or three people must assemble from throughout the entire boundary (*sīmā*) to perform the confession. Next, he clarifies that the repentance for the offense is performed before an individual, because its essential nature is the same as that of the [offenses] of the ninety [pārājika and saṃghāvaśeṣa] categories.

Some say that since offenses are based on matters of wealth, the abandonment [of the object] and the confession [of the offense] correspond and are consistent; how could it be that abandoning [the object] before the Sangha while confessing the offense individually would contradict the text?
According to the second master, both the abandonment of wealth and the confession of the offense must ultimately involve the Sangha from beginning to end.

That person explained that, according to the original regulations, the *Sengzheng* (Monastic Rectifier) must clarify the matter of the property. Once it has been relinquished and confessed within the assembly, the offense is separately removed;

thus, there must be prior evidence [of the relinquishment], and it is not appropriate to accept it arbitrarily. Because the intention is harmonious and the taking is permitted, there is a *jñapti* (single announcement).
If the use of the property is exhausted and one correctly repents the original *pāyattika* (offense of falling), it is treated like the ninety [rules]; one may then reconvene the assembly.

Among the three levels of rescues, the first clarifies that when a monk fundamentally relinquishes property, the confession must be announced to the Sangha; however, if the property is exhausted, there is no need to repent before the Sangha for the offense.

A previous commentator explained: "The holy regulations place the former [relinquishment] at the beginning because it constitutes a grave condition; since the matter of property gives rise to an offense, how could the offense be minor?"

Therefore, the principle of expiation by the Saṃgha is not distinct from other forms of removal; for instance, in the texts concerning the begging of cotton robes or the storing and trading of gems, although the offense is relinquished by the Saṃgha, the removal of the penalty is likewise performed by the Saṃgha.

Regarding the first section of the fourfold "repeated breaking," the initial establishment of the principle refers to the preceding list, which selects the thirty offenses as occurring prior to the ninety.
This depends solely on the gravity of the offense; as in the following cases, such as destroying silk from silkworms, or trading in precious objects, one must relinquish them to a layperson.
These are not relinquished by the Sangha alone, yet they require confession before the Sangha.

If this is so, why are they not listed among the confessions? To answer the previous question regarding the abandonment [of offenses] before the Saṃgha: it is explained that this confession is before the Saṃgha, whereas the former was before those who are not the Saṃgha;
for brevity, the latter is not mentioned. Since it can be omitted, it need not be confessed. However, as the text is not explicit, one must consult other schools;
both the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* prescribe that these be performed within the Saṃgha.

Regarding the resolution of objections: among the initial thirty objections, twenty-seven concern the precepts; while these all clarify the methods for relinquishing and repenting [transgressions], the texts concerning [the monks] Mian, Bao, and others are all abbreviated.
Therefore, in the response, the reason why they are not mentioned is first stated, followed by a counter-interrogation based on principle, and finally, other schools are cited as evidence.
If that were so, when the Saṃgha is enjoined to accept a confession, could one then confess both the ninety [days] and the two [days] at once? The answer is:
their gravity and lightness differ because they belong to the same category of offenses (*pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
Next, since the objection states that they are grave and light, the ninety days should not be combined with the other for confession; the response in the text is clear.

Question: Since both cases involve confession through communal agreement (*sāmagrī*), why distinguish between light and heavy? Answer: This distinction is based on the gravity of the mental karma. If the conditions for relinquishing the offense are met but the mind does not abandon it, the relinquishment is not accomplished;
therefore, one must confess before the Saṃgha. Regarding the offenses themselves, their falling into rebirth and the suffering of retribution are no different;
this is just as when one confesses before an individual, the threefold recitation is no different.

Regarding the three difficulties concerning the confession of the same substance (*samatā-svabhāva*), it should not be said that they are distinct. In the initial response, it is clarified that because the mental karma (*citta-karma*) differs, they are divided into preceding and succeeding stages;

subsequently, it is clarified that because the prohibitive teachings (*vinaya-śāsana*) are identical, they are collectively confessed. "In contrast to the distinct" refers to the *pratimokṣa* (confession before another).
Regarding the relinquishing of material goods, there are two parts.

First, to distinguish what must and what need not be relinquished: although the material goods to be relinquished are many, they are conceptually arranged into three fixed categories: first, fixed surplus goods; second, fixed robes to be received;
and third, fixed remaining items to be relinquished.

Regarding the determination of what constitutes "excess" (atireka), there are five types of items that do not require the ritual of declaration of purity (āviṣkaraṇa). Even if one possesses them beyond the limit, no offense is incurred. What are these?
According to the subsequent section on determining the nature of excess property, if an item is not subject to the declaration of purity, there is no offense regarding excess.

First, regarding "retaining according to what is received": this refers to cases such as possessing the three robes and the alms bowl, or keeping the necessary items for storage. This specifically excludes two categories:

staying overnight separated from one's robes, and the six-year period of not folding the rain-cloak; these are all instances of "receiving" and thus do not require an explicit statement of relinquishment. All other cases should be treated by analogy.
The first section of the commentary lists the three robes and the alms bowl as the primary objects to be formally maintained; the containers for these are the secondary items that accompany them.
Below this, it distinguishes the five precepts, noting that none of them involve long robes or folding, except for the sitting mat (niṣīdana).

Second, because they follow the weight of the object: as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā*, items such as beds, mattresses, rugs, mats, pillows, stools, bolsters, woolen carpets, robes, curtains, windows, doors, and window-shades—belonging to the dwelling—are not subject to the ritual of "purification" (*śuddhi*) for formal acceptance.
According to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, when others give these to one as bedding, these eight types of impure wealth do not fall within the limit of what is purified.
Among the items listed in the Vinaya treatises, there are none that do not encourage indolence; they are merely aids to the path rather than essentials.

For instance, the *yingnang* (a bolster) is like a small cushion or a *qushu* (carpet) woven from animal hair; according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, such items are included among the eight impurities of bedding.

Third, the "accessories" (*anuvartaka*) consist of the one hundred and one items; although they are not formally possessed (*parigṛhīta*), it is not permitted to perform the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*) for them.
These refer to minor items such as various bowls, needles, incense burners, boots, shoes, sandals, and socks.
Among the three types of *kañcika*, the small iron bowl refers to a tiny iron alms-bowl; *jue* refers to straw sandals.

Fourth, regarding the specific offenses incurred according to the transgression—such as taking a nun’s robe—the offense is committed the moment it enters one's hand, as there is no requirement for a formal declaration (*kathina*).
Thus, the purification rite (*śuddhidharma*) excludes such objects because they are defective due to the circumstances of their acquisition.
Among the four [categories], those who have previously committed an offense do not enter the *dīrgha* (long) list.
Fifth, because there is a specific cause for the *pāriśuddhi* (declaration of purity), it is permitted as follows:

when one has debts, when goods have not yet been received from another’s deposit, when purchased wealth has not yet entered [the inventory], when entrusted to another’s master, when there is no limit to the conditions, and when silk, hemp, wool, or cotton do not reach the prescribed dimensions—such cases as these are permitted.
Although an object may have been held for many days, it does not fall outside the scope of what must be confessed;

if it was received and then entrusted to another, it may be reclaimed, but one must assemble the items themselves rather than merely giving instructions from afar. Therefore, the treatise states that *niḥsargika* means "complete relinquishment";

if even a fragment remains, it can still cause defilement. Regarding items already belonging to oneself, those set aside for sharing are excluded until they have been divided into two portions, as one would not know which part belongs to whom.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to speak [of these as distinct offenses].

Among the five [cases], as in the six subsequent clauses, all are instances where a restriction is relaxed by relying on another; this refers to cases where the owner is absent. In frontier regions, five matters are permitted:
once long robes have come into one's possession, they constitute an offense; prior to their entry [into possession], there is no offense. This applies to silk, hemp, wool, and cotton.
Because the robes have not yet been completed, one may go to a lower-ranking person to borrow them from another for the time being; they must be returned once the [robes] are finished.
Next, regarding the distribution of what has been obtained, it is not yet determined.
Aside from these, whether heavy or light, sixteen types of vessels, merchandise, food, woolen blankets, silk, cotton, robes, or alms bowls are not permitted.

Regarding miscellaneous items such as jars, ladles, paper, and pens, although they do not constitute an offense of "exceeding the limit," if they are acquired through improper means or purchased at an exorbitant price, they all fall under the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense of forfeiture) for buying and selling.
The next category consists of sixteen types of vessels: namely, large cauldrons, their lids, large basins, and their ladles, as well as small cauldrons and their lids.

Small basins and ladles, washing bottles with their lids and basins and ladles, water jars with their lids and basins and ladles—thus, for each of the two cauldrons and two jars, there are four items.
All miscellaneous items listed below are not included in the long list.

Regarding the robes one receives and maintains, they must be refined to eliminate external conditions; since the original material is impure and lacks the nature of being "received," it cannot be discarded.

As for entering into renunciation, one must know by what conditions it is lost: whether by boundary, by partition, by sentient beings, or by defilement. One must reflect deeply on how negligence and arrogance lead to violation, and thus necessitate relinquishment.

Among the three [categories], the first excludes those who have already relinquished [the property] and proceeds to the next; subsequently, one must investigate the four obstacles to losing the conditions [for ownership].
Regarding the three stages of the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), other [types of] longing are not listed.

If one's wealth is abundant and it is impossible to collect it all by traveling everywhere, one must relinquish it at each respective location and then perform the ritual of confession (*kṣamaṇa*) all at once. Once the ritual is completed, the property is recovered in due order.

In the initial summary of the conclusion, first the brief exposition is shown; next, the difficulty of gathering [the robes] is clarified: each person should abandon their portion and perform the confession together, returning the robes to their respective owners as they find them.

Second, clarifying whether [the act] is accomplished when one forgets [the recipient]: if the intention to relinquish is pure, but the robes have not yet been returned and the words have not been spoken, and one subsequently remembers the object...

If one becomes defiled by attachment while in the process of relinquishing [an extra robe], one must undergo the procedure for forfeiture and the offense of *aticāra* (excess). If the announcement has been completed, whether the owner is seen or not yet returned, both cases rely on the subsequent relinquishment;

there is no defilement regarding the prior state of purity because there was no longer any keeping [of the robe]. If one originally intended to keep it but relinquished it without actually parting with it, although there is no defilement through forgetfulness, because there is still the mental intention of storing it, the relinquishment is not accomplished as a true relinquishment; it remains subject to the original offense of excess.

Regarding the second section, "In Response to Forgetfulness," there are three initial divisions: first, it clarifies that the formation of defilement applies to the previous case of repeated relinquishment;

next, it clarifies that if one speaks [of the latter], defilement is not formed and only the subsequent view is relinquished; finally, it clarifies that although the mind of possession has not been severed, even if one relinquishes it, defilement is not formed.
Someone said: "I later forgot and gave it to someone intentionally; how could I be stained by this? The answer was: "Your mind is coarse.

To give rise to the thought 'this is mine' as soon as you see it constitutes a stain; furthermore, you only gave it to the person after [the initial lapse]. Moreover, since the Buddha’s precepts encompass both [types of offenses], how can you claim to be without intent?"
In the first part of this section, various divergent views are presented; in the following part, the text directly refutes them, stating: "The mind is coarse" means it lacks self-examination.

"The mental state is subtle" means that because one clings to a prior attachment and then abandons it without realizing it oneself, it is said not to be defiled. However, the Buddha ordered that [the object] be relinquished and only then given away to others.
This constitutes both a violation of the marks [of purity] and a contravention of the Buddha’s regulations, resulting in the offenses of *pārājika* and *duṣkṛta*; hence, it is called "both."
[This constitutes] an offense.

Question: Regarding the relinquishing of property, if one claims it exists when it does not, the relinquishment is established; regarding the boundary, if one claims it is separate when it is not, the response should be the same.

Forgetting the property and the non-assembling [of the assembly] do not constitute obstacles, whereas the distinction between sentient beings and non-sentient things constitutes an obstacle. Because it is established as a *saṃgha*, both "it exists" and "it does not exist" each have their respective [consequences].
Regarding the essential point:

among the three [questions], the first concerns the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) within the Vinaya. Within the ritual sphere (*karmabhūmi*), if there are sentient beings present, the ritual procedure cannot be accomplished; this is cited as a parallel case.

In the response, one can see that there is a distinction between sentient and non-sentient objects, as well as a difference between those that possess resistance (*sapratigha*) and those that do not (*apratigha*).

In this text, it is said that there are three kinds of wealth that monks abandon which serve as conditions for transgression: they are unrighteous greed, hoarding, and contempt for the precepts; these are the conditions.

Regarding the "mind of abandonment," since greed and pride are the root, they must be abandoned first; if one continues to possess [these] after having abandoned them, it cannot be called a pure mind.

Regarding the "abandonment of transgression," if one does not wash away and repent [them], the karma of suffering will persist for long kalpas; therefore, one must be vigilant and clear-sighted. Thus it is said.
This is what is meant by "weighing.
Next, in the sequential explanation, the third section states: because wealth gives rise to the mind, wealth is the condition for transgression;

because transgression is accomplished through the mind, the mind is the cause of transgression; and because transgression brings about retribution, transgression constitutes the karma of birth and death. Therefore, [it is said] below:
The general conclusion and entrustment instructing one to clearly understand "weighing" refers to one of the ten conditions, namely, weighing the offense committed.

Regarding the inclusion of the three items within the ritual for relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*), they are returned separately because their prolonged presence can cause defilement and necessitates a mind of long-term purity.

Regarding the separation from one's robes: although they are relinquished, they must be returned to their original location immediately; this is not due to greed for accumulation, but rather because of pride and indolence.

Furthermore, if one allows them to remain overnight, causing another to incur an offense, they may not be kept together with those that have been kept for a long period. If a nun takes back property belonging to the Saṃgha, it is a solitary transgression of this matter.

As for the measure of relinquishment, it is because the contents are distinct; thus, while the bags are connected, they are collectively described as separate segments to be relinquished individually. The rest is as previously stated.
When the textual characteristics [of the procedure] reach their full expression, they become even more manifest; thus, the citations from the *Chao* (Excerpts) can be fully employed to explain them.

Next, regarding the ritual for relinquishing [the robes], it first indicates that the three items should each be wrapped separately when returning the robe, as they must not be mixed with one another;

they may, however, be marked and kept in the same place. Furthermore, the commentary notes the five types of long robes, the ten types of robes, the robes offered on the first day of the month, the robes offered on the fifteenth day, and those offered during times of emergency.

Regarding "medicine and bowl," one now takes three types from among the five [types of] robes; the remainder is shown as an abbreviation, and it is entrusted to the lecturer to provide incidental citations as the occasion demands.

The middle section clarifies the "mind of relinquishment" (*prahāṇacitta*); because the transgression regarding extra robes is established in accordance with a mind of greed, the treatise reveals this as "relinquishment."
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*):
within the central section on the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), the treatise analyzes each phrase to demonstrate that the purification of the mind through confession is based upon equanimity;
because the author of the treatise is skillful in his methods, he refers to this as "expedient means."
Regarding the three phrases of the text:
in the first phrase, although one obtains the original property through the three characteristics being in accordance with the Dharma, there is no offense of defilement.
In the combined explanation, the text explains the first phrase, while in the subsequent answer, the second phrase is seen; that is, the three characteristics refer to the robe.
This refers to a mind of transgression. Question:
In the previous explanation, it was required that one stay overnight in order to purify the mind; why is it different here, where the text says "on the same day"? Answer:
If the mind is not pure, one commits an offense even after many days, as stated in the second clause of the treatise. Since the mind here is pure, the reception [of the precepts] is permitted.
This is the same principle as the case in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* regarding the conditions for taking property from a distant journey and so forth on the very day it is obtained.

Alternatively, it may be that the original wealth was already one's own property and had never entered [the possession of another]; thus, what is subsequently obtained is not defiled, and as for other wealth, since there was no expectation of its being sent [to oneself], it is likewise not defiled.
In the question, the point of the previous five long-term [retentions] is taken up because there is still a contradiction regarding whether one must stay overnight or may depart.

In the answer, the first part explains it in terms of the purity of intention, as illustrated by the following example: the "conditions for a distant journey" refers to the method of immediate entrustment while seated.

Alternatively, the second part explains it in terms of the two types of wealth—the original and the derivative. "Original wealth" has never yet entered one's own possession; "derivative wealth" is that which was not previously expected but has been accumulated.
Since the mind has already been severed and there is no longer any defilement, although one may receive the robe on that very day, there is no offense.
Regarding the third case, where one commits a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense), the transgression must first be confessed before the robe is returned;
for to return it while violating the instruction and because the mind has been severed, one incurs only a minor offense.
Regarding the third case, although the mind has been severed and there is no defilement, because the conduct is merely perverted and chaotic, a minor offense (dukkaṭa) is prescribed.

The passage below, citing various schools as well as our own tradition, establishes that items such as those that have been cut or destroyed belong to the aforementioned pure state; one must not still harbor attachment to them.

Therefore, they are relinquished for practical use, yet one commits a *dubbhāsita* (offense of wrong speech). The meaning of this relinquishment is clear from the text and need not be further explained.

Next, among the various sections, the notes list the distinctions in the methods for relinquishing [objects] belonging to the various schools; since there is nothing that does not involve the severance of mindfulness, it is said that this establishes the preceding pure mind.

As for the principle of "not returning" and "exhaustion," they logically establish the impairment of theft; however, because it is merely judged as a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) on the grounds that the object does not belong to oneself, the text establishes the intention of relinquishment.

Regarding the three types of relinquishing offenses (*āpatti-pratyāgama*), there are seven conditions: first, requesting confession; second, inviting a presiding master; third, making a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to the assembly; fourth, declaring the characteristics of the offense;

fifth, relinquishing the offense; sixth, administering a reprimand; and seventh, making a solemn vow. Within the *saṃgha*, all seven conditions are required. For a group of many monks (*gaṇa*), there are only six, excluding the request for confession.

When the wording is modified to a single formal announcement (*ekajñapti*), it becomes a "questioning the boundary" (*pṛcchā-sīmā*).
