In the case of a face-to-face confession (*pratyakṣa-vinaya*), there are five conditions: there is no request for confession and no questioning, while the remaining characteristics are as before.
The details regarding the textual explanations and the lack of full comprehension are also as set forth in the *Chao* (Excerpts).

Regarding the third section on the abandonment of offenses, the first subsection first provides a general enumeration of the Sangha, followed by a specific distinction of three positions, with the number of participants decreasing accordingly and the methods adjusted to the individuals involved;
these may be understood by consulting the text.

One who requests confession from the Saṃgha does not necessarily undergo further formal ritual procedures; rather, they proceed directly to the manifestation of relinquishment as detailed in the text.

This should be understood according to the Vinaya for the extinction of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). One should know that the meaning of this request is expressed through the phrasing of the text.

Regarding the first section of the "Request for Confession" (*kṣamāpanā*): first, it indicates that the formal ritual (*vidhi*) is already established by relying on the preceding ritual, so there is no need to perform it again;

below, it presents the actual wording of the request, which refers to the text on the "Requesting Dharma" (*yācanā-dharma*) within the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (specifically the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha* chapter) of the Vinaya.
If one commits an offense and the item is used up over time until it is exhausted, although there is no forfeiture of the material object, the original offense still remains;

furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one commits an offense involving a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe that is subsequently burned by fire, rotted, gnawed by insects, torn apart, or lost through theft, the offense is extinguished according to the Dharma without the need for forfeiture.
If the item is lost or stolen, this itself constitutes "forfeiture," though a remainder of the offense persists.
One should not discard even a fragment; rather, one should repent for the offense according to the Dharma. When the Sangha lends robes, they may all be accepted and worn;

there is no need to repent for keeping them overnight. Regarding the "remnants" mentioned above, there is no need to treat them as discarded because they are merely broken pieces that do not measure a full span.
It is often said that regarding robes chewed by oxen, gnawed by rats, or burned by fire, if they remain beyond the [prescribed] day, one commits the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

In the first section of the following analysis, there are two parts: first, the explicit explanation of the ten [offenses]; second, the citation and demonstration. First, the explanation of the loss through destruction; next, the explanation of the loss through confiscation.

Regarding borrowing from the Saṃgha for acceptance [of robes]: this merely avoids the faults of being deficient in clothing or staying overnight apart from one’s robes, as it does not constitute relinquishing what is not one's own property.

Although the upper and lower layers cover the remaining fragments, this contradicts the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*; therefore, this [explanation] generally reconciles that regulation, and the offense of relinquishment (niḥsargika-pāyattika) is but a minor transgression.
If one uses a robe received from the *Mahāsāṃghika* school, the offense of transgression involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) is confessed together with other offenses of equal gravity;

however, if someone recites [the rules] from a different tradition, the forfeiture is not established, because within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, those of the same category are confessed together while those of different categories are not. The text states:
"If there has been concealment, first administer a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for the concealment, and subsequently treat the root offense."

Among the three [sections], the first cites the texts of other schools regarding the offense of using a robe improperly, wherein the confession for a *duṣkṛta* (light offense) and a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) follows the same ritual procedure.

The second section rebukes false usage; based on the clarifications of our own school’s tenets, it establishes the sequence of precedence, clearly showing that the legal system of our own school is well-ordered.

Second, regarding the text for requesting the Confession Master (*kṣamāpaka*), the reason many individuals are listed is that among worldly people, there are many who speak of various levels of offenses, down to those who have committed different transgressions.
If one is not pure due to negligence, it is improper; likewise, if one is hindered by shared karmic conditions or has committed the same offense, it is also an obstacle.

Since the Sūtra states that one must be free from the three roots of unwholesomeness and fully detailed in their conduct, how could one be used as a witness to certify the cessation of subsequent offenses? One must recognize those who are pure so that they may be employed to initiate the rite.
Regarding the superior mind:

among the two sections, the first part initially refutes erroneous explanations; the text is extensive because the commentary cites the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* in full detail.
Thus, it is said that if the offenses differ, one is immediately fit for confession. The following section reveals the correct principle.

It is anticipated that one should not encounter difficult conditions and must instead face a pure environment with leisure; since the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* permits [the practice] due to difficult circumstances, it is known that when such conditions do not exist, it is not appropriate [to do so].
"Must recognize purity" means that "recognition" (*śes pa*) refers to being thoroughly familiar with [the rules].

Not only because of the external object, but even if one has committed an offense requiring *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and undergoes double the ten-day probation (*parivāsa*), if one harbors the intent to go there [to commit suicide] and dies prematurely while seeking to offer a confession,
they have not yet requested the formal recitation of the purification from the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).

The next section concerns the object before one; that is, the person against whom one faces [the offense]. For the removal of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (monastic offense) through confession, twenty monks are required, all of whom must be pure.

Below, it is cited that if one dies prematurely while in the midst of the process of offering the desire for confession, it is precisely because the object is superior and the mind is powerful that one becomes purified even before the act has been completed.

Based on this, the object of measure is the mental object (*citta-viṣaya*), which functions as the object of the mind. Because the mind is subtle while the object is inferior, one must exercise discernment;
one must not act recklessly. Thus the text says: "that which is reached by the foolish and the simple."

Among the three [categories], "object" refers to the mental object (*ālambana*), meaning that because the mind exists due to the object and the mind varies according to the object, one must distinguish the object in order to give rise to a superior mind.
The following passage, which provides a rebuttal, refers to the two types of delusion cited in the commentary.
Regarding the response to the inquiry in the *Sāvaṃsaka-śukla* (Threefold Pure Response), it says: "The *ekavācika-karman* for receiving confession" is the general response.

When combined with the *sthūlātyaya*, it says: "For receiving confession regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*"; this constitutes one complete section. If the "prolonged separation" (*dīrgha-viyoga*) is added, that is a specific enumeration.

Among the three [categories], two levels involve both the general and the specific: first, the general applies across different groups; second, the general applies throughout a single section, which is specific in relation to what precedes it yet remains general in relation to what follows.

Finally, that which is restricted to a single precept is clearly the specific; as in the cases of the confession for keeping extra robes (*ātyaya-dhāraṇa*), the forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*), and the *jñapti-caturtha* motion.
Fourth, one should explain the names, categories, and characteristics of the offenses, for those who commit them do so out of ignorance, falsely claiming that what exists is not present;

one must explain the two faults of concealment and the principle by which they arise in whoever possesses them. One should explain the characteristics of the offenses regarding future retribution, the habitual karma of breaking the precepts, and the pointlessness of receiving offerings and sustenance, citing these according to the capacity of the individual.

Furthermore, one should address the three grades of offenses based on the fundamental principles of concealing transgressions through silence during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, or concealing them privately at night.
As one turns over the offenses throughout the evening, the transgressions are numerous and divided into nine grades.

If all [factors] are present, one must first repent of the preparatory acts (*prayoga*), then of the subsequent regret, as well as the two types of concealment and the actual wearing [of the garment]. This is explained in detail in the *Shu-chao*. If, upon examination, none of the nine grades are present, simply repent of the fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*) itself;
do not recite the standard formulas, which only cause others to become weary and confused.
Among the four [sections], the first explains the actual offense; because there is ignorance and lack of recognition regarding the three preceding [offenses], two faults are further explained:
namely, concealment (*praticchādana*) and speaking falsely while remaining silent during the recitation of the precepts (*jñapti-karma*).

This is done to make known the characteristics of the offense so that one recognizes having committed it, to cause fear by describing the retribution and residual habits (*vāsanā*) that follow, and to induce shame by explaining how one receives offerings in vain. Following this, the subsequent section explains what arises from these.
For example, there are three offenses: the original offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (long-dropping), its subsequent wearing and using, and the silent, false concealment.

Furthermore, each of these three offenses has a *pāyattika* for each night it is concealed; as this process repeats night after night, within each instance there are three [factors], thus constituting nine grades.

First, one confesses the preparatory acts (*prayoga*), which consist of six grades of *pāyattika*: those for each night and those for the intervening nights. Second, one confesses the concealment of the original offense, which consists of the concealment itself.
First, if there is silence, falsehood, or if [the confession] is entirely absent or incomplete, all such instances must be rectified. As the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

"After performing the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and reaching consensus, one first asks, 'Do you see your offense? If they say, 'I see it,' one says, 'In the future, do not commit it again. After they respond, 'Very well,' one then accepts their repentance.

This procedure applies even when the ritual for relinquishing [an offense] is performed before one, two, three, or as many as three persons; in each case, the inquiry is made at the edge [of the assembly].

After the person has finished speaking, one asks the transgressor; this is no different from [the procedure] within the Saṃgha. One must not fail to cite scriptural evidence, for the underlying intent is to ensure that [the offense] is severed.

This is the meaning of "confession" (*pratikarman*). Regarding the second [section], the first cites a treatise: one question and one admonition, down to the case of facing the example, it is necessary to ask this question; do not let it fall below.
To clarify the meaning:
regarding the five types of abandoning offenses, those who rely on the literal phrasing of the text suffer both a loss of the name and the reality, as they merely recite the words.

Why is it that one speaks of "rarely" when concealing an offense and clinging to its use? It is called "concealing an offense" (*paticchādana*) because one fears others will know of the transgression; it refers to the category of evil.

Now, regarding those who commit a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), if they announce it to others and the offenses of the first two categories (*pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*) have not yet been disclosed, why would they fear formal censure?

How could there be concealment [of such]? Therefore, cases of concealing a *pāyattika* are rare in the world today. As for wearing [the robe] or using [it], whether one speaks or remains silent—these two cases require that the preceding confession be formally restated, as explained above.

Regarding the first of the five conditions for relinquishing offenses, the initial section provides a general indication of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* category, while the subsequent section cites and explains it. First, it clarifies the offense of concealment;

within this, the text raises a question to indicate the characteristics of concealing an offense. "Insufficient number" (*akalpa*) refers to that which does not count toward the required number [of witnesses].

Now, the following passage rebukes those who lack shame and do not fear public knowledge, noting that even regarding the two categories [of *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*], such behavior persists—how much more so, then, regarding the *pāyattika*? Next, the following section clarifies the two types of offenses.
There are many offenses.
Within the text on the formal relinquishment of the offense (*āpatti-pratyaya*), there are eight sections.
Within the legal formula (*dharma-pada*), there are eight phrases.
First, the Venerable One’s thought was that, fearing his own prior negligence, he wished to inform [the assembly] to collect their attention before speaking.
Second, from "I, so-and-so" onwards, he recites the name of the person concerned.
Third, by listing the various categories of offenses from the minor ones downward, the specific number of transgressions is determined.
Fourth, "now facing the open air" signifies being without concealment; it refers to the fundamental basis for confessing one's offenses, and this single phrase constitutes the essence of repentance.

Regarding the five types of repentance that lead to peace and happiness: because they result in the attainment of the fruits of dhyāna and bring harmony to both body and mind, they are called the second [category].
As for the fifth, because one attains the fruits of dhyāna, body and mind become peaceful and harmonious, which is precisely what is meant by "happiness."
Sixth, "I do not repent" and below clarifies that being bound by evil karma leads to bodies in the three miserable realms; since the body is already not at peace, how could the mind harbor joy?
Seventh, "I pray that the Virtuous One" and below requests for witness and certification.

Regarding "one who is fully endowed with the eight precepts," this refers to one who previously committed offenses like a stain; now, by repenting in accordance with the fundamental principles, they are called "pure.

Regarding "the pure *poṣadha*," it means that while one's own conduct is internally pure, one's external perceptions and reports are also clean. Having repented for original offenses, one should fulfill the monastic dharma;
thus, one attains harmony between the internal and the external. For this reason, the three recitations express the diligence of manifesting profound sincerity.

Among the eight [verses], the first half-verse concerns one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), while the second half-verse concerns the practice for others (*para-caryā*); these three expositions express diligence, and all dharmas are likewise so.
Verses six and seven may be understood according to the text.
Next, the sixth and seventh [procedures] for reprimanding and establishing a vow are briefly indicated, as they have already been divided previously.
Within the fourth section on returning robes, there are two parts.
First is the procedure for the same seat; the preceding conditions are listed, and the meaning of the three dharmas is as explained above.
Regarding the fourth [case], the circumstances for returning the robe and transferring it on the spot: first, there is a general indication of the three dharmas, which will be explained below.
As for the reference "as mentioned above," it refers to the section on relinquishing property.

According to the text: "If the Sangha is numerous, because individual transgressions are difficult to resolve and it is clearly very difficult to request the harmony of the Sangha, they shall assemble again."

To further increase the burden of complications is to slight others; since this does not constitute a formal confession (*pratideśanā*), it is permitted to perform it on the spot without much labor or disturbance.

In the first section of the next chapter, the specific transgressions are discussed: "individual offenses" refers to those committed by an individual, while "requests for assistance" refers to matters that must be resolved through the mediation of others.

Second, regarding the difficulty of assembling [the quorum]: there may be cases where, due to separate karmic conditions, it is difficult for the assembly to meet; yet, it is also permitted to perform the ritual on the spot.
When combined with the case of "merging with others," these form a single condition of "difficulty in assembly. This explains multiple meanings, which are now divided into two parts.
By taking the variables of "many/few" and "difficult/easy" as mutual opposites, they can be clearly illustrated through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Of the two [sections], the first correctly explains individual karma (*pṛthag-karman*): it refers to cases where others are already engaged in the work, so that even if few [people] are difficult to assemble, this differs from what preceded.
The following [passage] refutes erroneous interpretations; the phrase "let [them] act" [applies to] four cases: (1) many monks, difficult to assemble; (2) many monks, easy to assemble;
(3) few monks, difficult to assemble; (4) few monks, easy to assemble. From this, one knows that a large number of monks does not necessarily entail difficulty.
Regarding the third case, where there is a distant traveler with whom one has a connection: this is for one's own sake and not for another’s.

Since the mind that has abandoned [the object] is exhausted and cannot remain, there must be a prior connection that serves as a necessary provision for the occasion; therefore, it is permitted to entrust it indirectly to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in private.
Yet, even then, one fears the possibility of defilement following from it. If one must sever ties completely, the principle is as explained in the treatise.

Among the three [types of retreat], the latter two involve external conditions, whereas this [first type] involves self-conditioning; it is opened up for the purpose of allowing a knowledgeable person—that is, a fellow practitioner—to act as a substitute.

Having received [the precepts] in private, one returns them below. This demonstrates the intent of the treatise: provided that the mind is severed [from the precepts], even if one returns them directly, there is no fault in the principle.
In the subsequent direct entrustment, since there is no further entanglement or obstruction, there is no need for successive transmission.
Furthermore, regarding the absence of entanglement or obstruction in the next direct entrustment, it is because there is no prolonged defilement.
As for the text concerning the many people, it is still indicated by two fingers.

Regarding the note in the middle of the "Face-to-Face" (pratimukha) section concerning the giving up of property and returning robes, it says "two fingers" because this follows the same procedure as the rules for the assembly (saṃgha).

Within the "Face-to-Face" section, the detailed procedures are fully explained; the main text provides the general outline, while the fine notes serve as a commentary (śāstra). It is not that there is no definitive interpretation [to be found therein].
This concludes the general outline.

Regarding the "One Person Facing the Head" (yīrén duìshǒu) section, which is also called a *zhù* (commentary), it takes up the meaning of "sparse penetration" (*shū-tōng*) and its textual explanations are extremely brief;

one must further provide a structural analysis (*kē-shì*). There are four sections in total: first, the relinquishing of wealth; second, the invitation of the presiding master; third, the confession of concealed offenses, which has two parts.

The preceding confession concerns the offenses arising from successive transgressions, while the subsequent confession concerns fundamental minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*). Regarding the fourfold proper confession for offenses involving a downfall (*pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*), one must subsequently return the property;
this is explained in the annotations.

As for the latter category of downfalls, although the ritual procedure is as previously described, even though the matter involves property, it is not to be relinquished before another person; there is another expedient means.
The root text lists them all in full.

Among the ninety [offenses], there are also those incurred due to wealth; however, while the methods for manufacturing [prohibited items] are numerous, they generally do not involve the accumulation of goods, so their forfeiture is not required.

According to the commentary, there are three [factors]: first, the host who invited [the monk]; second, the confession of concealment; and third, the sequence from the arising [of the offense] to the root.
This section concerns the three fundamental methods for repenting of primary offenses.
Regarding the fifth and sixth categories (*āpatti-skandhas*), the ritual procedures for confession are presented in full; however, one may read them by selecting and abbreviating where appropriate.

By grasping the general outline and carefully investigating the underlying principles, one will not lose the essential framework, and thus a detailed commentary is unnecessary. Should one wish to further examine these matters in depth, the specific regulations can be found in the *Shishi Yaolan* (Essentials of the Vinaya).
This is the confession of the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍ-varga*).
Regarding the explanation of the latter two sections, I shall merely indicate their textual characteristics and entrust you to seek them out for yourself;

now, I must briefly explain the *deśanā* (confession), beginning with the initial conditions and followed by the legal conditions. Within these, I shall briefly cite two precepts: [1] the offense regarding receiving food from a family under training (*śaikṣa-kula*), and [2] the offense regarding the *āranyaka* (forest-dweller).
Receiving food from a woman: first, the invitation; second, the declaration of the name and characteristics; third, the confession of the fundamental offense. Furthermore, there are five parts:

first, the formal disclosure of the fault, which is the *tishani* (translated as "the dharma that may be censured"); second, the question posed by the other person; third, the response according to the question;

fourth, the censure; and fifth, the taking of an oath. Regarding the initial conditions (*nidāna*), there are four sections in the commentary, the first of which defines the characteristics of the offense.
If one intentionally commits two offenses, both must be confessed face-to-face; if one commits one offense unintentionally, it is merely a matter of mental repentance (*cetanā*).

The *Vinaya-mūla* (the root of the Vinaya) refutes the errors of the ancients in its lower sections; these are "illustrious words," that is, the very words of the Buddha. Among the remaining categories of confession, the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) is collectively treated as a *pārājika*-like offense requiring confession, while the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) is not differentiated between intentional and unintentional acts.
The latter applies only to specific instances and is not universally applicable; furthermore, there is no forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) for a *sthūlātyaya*.

When wealth is returned, the robes are fewer; when they fall away, the opposite occurs, and thus they are many. Generally, the three citations below serve as evidence to clarify the fundamental offense above;
the remaining sections below demonstrate the offenses arising therefrom. Within the formal repentance (*samyak-pratikramaṇa*), first is the repentance for intentional acts:

(1) requesting a presiding master (*pratideśaka*), (2) declaring the specific characteristics of the offense, (3) formally expiating the transgression, (4) the admonition, and (5) the vow—all of which are identical to the preceding and following procedures for repenting unintentional offenses. First, the complete [ritual].
Facing the sacred image in accordance with the ritual, one gives rise to shame; this is the root of repentance. Thirdly, through verbal expression, one formally repents of one's offenses.

From the beginning up to this point, the explanations of the text according to its characteristics have all constituted the main body of the teaching. By following these established rules and methods in practice, one may hope to be free from doubt and anxiety.
In this conclusion, the preceding eight chapters are summarized and the reader is exhorted to follow them.
Chapter Ten: Miscellaneous Methods for Sustaining the Dharma.
This chapter lists various dharmas that are manifold and lack a fixed order; hence they are termed "miscellaneous methods. If bhikṣus rely upon these in their practice, then...
Because the light of the Buddha-dharma is made manifest, it is called "upholding" (zhuchi).
This constitutes the third major section, the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) division.
In the heading of the main text, it is stated that the transformation of the Dharma is spread abroad for future generations like flowing water, never ceasing; hence it is called "flowing" (*liu*).
General Introduction.

Now, those who wish to illuminate and manifest the legacy of their descendants and ensure the auspicious fortune of the abbot must rely upon the model of conduct; only then can they bring glory far and wide.

Therefore, this final section extensively sets forth these writings, which are divided into two parts: first, an exhortation based on the analogy of mindfulness regarding the white appearance (the physical form).
Because one’s own practice of supernormal powers does not conflict with or harm those outside, the work of attaining the Way flourishes daily, and faith arises on a vast scale;
this is precisely what protects the Dharma so that it does not fall into ruin. Second, the Buddha said there are five kinds of upholders of the Vinaya:

because they establish their realization through practice, they possess thorough knowledge of the heterodox and the orthodox, and they clearly understand the precepts, transgressions, and the proper decorum of conduct; thus, when they speak, their words accord with the Vinaya, and nothing they say deviates from the Vinaya.

To realize that conditioned phenomena arise in accordance with their characteristics, and that what is non-noble is not to be emulated—this is the correct Dharma; through this, one may once again embrace the distant [truth].
This is the general purport.
In the exegesis of the text, the initial statement of intent illuminates and clarifies, much like opening a door; "descendants" refers specifically to later students. Who could find it excellent?
"Fortune" refers to the period from Śākyamuni’s transformation [of the world] until the increase of the human lifespan to sixty thousand years;

"conduct" refers to the legal codes; "downward division" refers to the textual organization; "contemplation of conditions" refers to the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*); "recitation" refers to the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for entering a village;

"mutual inclusion of two dharmas" refers to censure and admonition; "metaphors" refer to the two types of offenses; and "the two within the two" refers to those who maintain the Vinaya. One should know these.
Discerning what may or may not be done refers to the knowledge that understands the teachings and the timing for advancing or withdrawing;
initiating action and uttering speech refers to the decision-making process; and "embracing the distant" means renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Regarding the five points in the preceding text:

first, it clarifies that by taking the Dharma as the object of mindfulness and focusing on the body, one seeks to maintain constant composure, binding the mind with single-mindedness to eliminate the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Within the initial six recollections, during the first recollection, the focus is divided into two aspects: knowing that the *poṣadha* is the path, and entering the assembly.

Falling [into the category of] the laity constitutes the second thought regarding food; first, one does not accept an invitation. In all three cases, it is said: "I am always without [the need for] the next.
Regarding the subsequent acceptance of an invitation, one must add whether there is or is not [an initial request]. First, if there is no initial request, there are three cases as mentioned above.

If there is a subsequent request, there are also three: first, going to the meal; second, turning back; third, abandoning. Within the abandonment, there are again two: first, abandonment through formal address (*pratyekam-śiras*); second, abandonment through mental recollection (*manasikāra*).

1. One should maintain mindfulness of the three things to be relinquished, so as to remember the duration of the summer retreat; 2. mindfulness of the robes and bowl, so as to know how to receive and purify them; 3.

mindfulness of being apart from the assembly, so as to know what is permitted and what is prohibited; 4. mindfulness of health and frailty, so as to prevent indolence. These six kinds constitute the objects of mindfulness, which are themselves mental states.
When the mind does not depart from the body and remains bound within oneself, it is free from wandering and distraction; therefore, it is said that one should "always be thus."

Second, regarding the two *śuddhika* (purification) announcements: these are divided into two based on the temporal sequence of the meal—namely, the *pūrvāhṇa-śuddhika* (morning purification) and the *paścāhṇa-śuddhika* (afternoon purification). This distinction is intended so that one may rely upon another for guidance, rather than having a teacher from whom one has personally received the transmission.

Of these two, the former (*pūrvāhṇa-śuddhika*) refers to the period before the meal; the latter (*paścāhṇa-śuddhika*) applies generally to both the afternoon and the initial part of the day and night.

If one goes to accept an invitation during the midday meal without first informing [the host], it causes distress to the donor; therefore, for invitations after midday or at improper times, one must inform [the host] in their presence and not act on one's own authority.

Third, regarding the performance of the *kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa* (the ritual for leftover food): the burden of the physical form has the mouth and belly as its priority, and because of this, one incurs distress and deep calamity.
Because these cases are numerous, this list of conditions is set forth to illustrate what constitutes non-Dharma characteristics.
Among the three types of causes that lead to affliction, the arising of greedy attachment illustrates non-Dharma; this is intended to make known the transgressions.

The commentary previously clarified the two kinds of food, excluding what is improper and retaining only what is proper for those who have committed offenses. Next, two Vinayas are cited to establish the definitive rule.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense, it is sufficient that the conditions are met for it to constitute a violation of another's teacher’s rule—namely, because one has eaten to satiety.

Within the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), even if one eats only a small amount, it signifies that one has finished what was left over by another; only then is one permitted to eat again. Once one person has performed the ritual, it applies universally to others as well, for there is nothing that does not count as "leftover" (vighasa).

Fourth, regarding the mutual relationship between teacher and disciple: because their fundamental principles and intentions differ and their paths are inherently divergent, even an initial request may be set aside depending on subsequent conditions.

Among these four points, two concern the Dharma; the former is the teacher’s reprimand, and the latter is the disciple’s departure. Regarding "the path and the fundamental": "path" refers to the Noble Path, and "fundamental" refers to the original basis.

Regarding those who are pure and upright but deviate from their initial request, they do not accept the instruction; therefore, the introductory note first indicates the fault, and the passage beginning with "The Buddha said" sets forth the words of reprimand according to the Dharma.
There are five such stages, ranging from light to heavy, corresponding to the depth of the transgression.

The procedure for *niśraya* (dependence) is largely the same, except that the fourth stage—having been reprimanded and seeking repentance—requires one to be humble and reverent, performing the full ritual protocol and making a formal petition. This is explained in the textual notes.
This fully clarifies that if a disciple departs while presenting five points of petition—namely, that the teacher neither understands nor instructs them—it is not the duty of a teacher;

therefore, it is annotated that if admonitions and remonstrances are not heeded, and there is no instruction according to the Dharma, one may listen and depart. *Kalinga* is translated here as "Co-life" (Gongming).
Regarding the five admonitions concerning the two transgressions of "acting" and "ceasing": the causes from which faults arise do not exceed these two. Those who possess innate knowledge are rare;
thus, affairs depend on friends for accomplishment. The rules are established according to circumstances, and the characteristics of admonition bring about the Path.
Among the five [categories], the first concerns the offense incurred upon being admonished; this further divides into two parts.

First, when one is admonished in accordance with the Dharma yet treats the admonisher with contempt—refusing the admonition out of pride—this constitutes the ninety-first *śaikṣa* rule regarding "not accepting admonition.

Second, if one refuses a legitimate admonition and instead causes the admonisher to question their teacher about further study, this reveals that the prior admonition was not in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the commentary, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* mentions six types of persons.

Because they cannot be admonished, one causes them to examine themselves; because the six [other] persons can be admonished, one causes them to encourage one another. Next, the admonition to cease transgressions consists of ninety [rules].

Regarding the words of admonition for encouraging study and the precepts, there are seven phrases: first, encouragement to study; second, encouragement to assist; third, encouragement not to disparage; fourth, encouragement not to transgress;
fifth, if one is rebuked by the wise, encouragement to depart from faults; sixth, receiving merit.

This refers to the seven long nights of peace and happiness as an immediate retribution, which is the future fruit; for the other bhikṣus, there is further exhortation regarding the lower [offenses], each being the reverse of the above.
As for the subsequent opening of resistance, it is as described above, and is therefore abbreviated.

Later, in the section clarifying the interpretation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not that there is no understanding; rather, because my intention lies in recording and practicing [the teachings], I have spoken briefly.
If one does not act according to what is taught, what benefit is there in mere words? Thus, the *Śāstra* states:

"Even if it be a discourse on the Dharma, if it is spoken at an inappropriate time or is not accepted, both are termed frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). There is a reason for the Sage’s prohibition; why labor to reject it? If you insist on a comprehensive clarification, wait for..."
In these leisurely days, I am gradually growing old, and now twilight has overtaken me; therefore, I have omitted further words, for my speech would not accord with my intent.

Next, regarding the Buddhist teachings, I first briefly state my intention: since the essence of the teachings is to guide practice, and the time for such practice has already passed, what benefit would mere words provide?

Consequently, I cite the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* to prove that one must necessarily act according to what is appropriate. Following this, I clarify that there is no end to leisurely days, meaning that there remains more to be said.
Regarding the timing: according to the original text, there are five sections concerning our own school (*sva-nikāya*). First, the explanation of the five types of those who uphold the Vinaya;

second, the five virtues of one who upholds the Vinaya; third, the four kinds of settling disputes; fourth, the four kinds of methods for extinguishing [disputes]; and fifth, the five kinds of responses.

All of the above belong to our own school. Regarding other schools: first, the *Mahāsāṃghika* has five benefits; the *Dharmaguptaka* (Twenty Recitations) has the initial exhortation to study the precepts by the Buddha.
The ten kinds of factors leading to extinction are proclaimed; those are listed as two sets of five, which are now combined to make ten.

Regarding the first set of five: "There is a bhikṣu... and so forth—these four phrases constitute the first factor. Furthermore, "not understanding" is the second factor. "Unable to... and the following two phrases constitute the third factor.
The phrase "and so forth" is an abbreviation for the fourth [factor]: there is one who preaches the Dharma, yet... [does not do so].
To engage in quarrels and disputes according to improper teachings and take no pleasure in submissiveness is the fifth factor;

furthermore, not being submissive is the second of the five factors, the first phrase of which is the first factor. [The text] omits the second [phrase], stating "not following the dharma of patience but following the dharma of impatience.
Not showing respect is the third factor, and the subsequent [omissions] constitute the fourth factor, leading to...
The "lower" refers to the fifth dharma, which consists of five points of fear as explained in the text: (1) not cultivating the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom;
(2) associating closely with bhikṣuṇīs; (3) delighting in composing literary verses and the like, as cited in the text;
(4) abandoning the *araṇya* (forest hermitage) for the sake of food and clothing and entering villages; and (5) seeking and searching extensively for food and clothing.
The *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā* on the five kinds of abiding dharmas is translated as the *Śāstra*; the *Vinaya* has four meanings that surpass those of the other two Piṭakas.

It extensively explains the four parts (*caturvarga*), clarifying that the *śāstra-dharma-vinaya* of the bhikṣus must be examined in detail—scrutinizing the words and determining right and wrong by using the teachings of the Tripiṭaka as a seal.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, these are called the "four [categories]."
Regarding the seals on the inked manuscript: first, what was heard directly from the Buddha; second, what was heard from the Saṃgha; third, what was heard from two or three people;

and fourth, what was heard from a single person. There are four such sources of what was heard; if one examines them together, they are consistent with the rest, as can be seen by consulting the records in the *Yaoji*.

Formerly, in the spring of the ninth year of the Zhenguan era, while traveling through the region of Mi, I stayed at a monastic residence in Luanchao Village, Mianshang County, where I produced two fascicles of commentaries for the purpose of exposition;
these were merely provisional pointers for those who had not yet mastered the study.
In the spring of the twenty-second year, at Fengde Monastery on Mount Zhongnan, three or five virtuous elders requested that I produce a revised edition once again.

Having no other recourse, I have again briefly set down my thoughts; though my own mind is clouded and worn out, I have managed to grasp the general outline of its essentials and subtleties, yet there are still points I have not fully exhausted.
On the twenty-seventh day of the second month, I finished reading it; I await a time for further revision, but who knows when that will be?
As for the scope of the volumes, the former is light while the latter is heavy; as for the meaning, the former is weighty while the latter is light; as for the underlying principle, the former...
Later, as no further words were heard appended to it, the beginning and end were easy to discern; the original consisted of fifty sheets, whereas the present version has doubled that length.
I imagine that those who examine it will not find fault with its lack of concealment.

At the beginning of the preface, the initial draft of the former version is described, followed by an explanation of the subsequent re-compilation of the present version, concluding with these final words.

The lecture on the *Yinji* (Record of Causes) is based on the dates and compares the two versions according to the following three pairs. There are four points: First, the initial phrase clarifies the volume;

because the preceding two [sections] are brief, they are "light," while the subsequent four are extensive, they are "heavy. Second, the second phrase clarifies the meaning; because the original text here is concise, the meaning is "heavy," while the subsequent text is expansive, the meaning is "light.
Third, the third phrase reveals the principle (*li*). Fourth, the fourth phrase indicates the text (*wen*). The paper follows at the end.
